viewers -> [edge PoP Mumbai] --miss--> [origin shield] --miss--> [origin / packager]
viewers -> [edge PoP Delhi ] --hit--> (served locally)
takeaways: A CDN serves from caches near users; the origin is hit only on misses.
Version asset URLs and cache them for a long time; purge only by exception.
Use signed URLs or cookies for private content.
For big live events, the edge carries terabits while the origin sends each segment once per rendition.

interactive.title: How much must the edge absorb?
interactive.prompt: A live event pushes 2 Tbps (2,000 Gbps) to viewers. Your origin can send at most 100 Gbps. Find the edge hit ratio you need.
interactive.takeaway: You need at least 95%: at 90% the origin would have to push 200 Gbps. Live streams pre-warm edges and often add an origin shield tier so that misses from many edges collapse into one request.

title: Redis Deep Dive
objectives: Shared in-memory caches scale out across nodes using sharding and replication.

cards.title: Redis data structures and scaling
cards.body: Redis offers data structures (sorted sets, hashes), persistence, replication and cluster sharding. Memcached is simple, multithreaded key-value. Clients shard keys with consistent hashing.

cards.title: A write in Redis Cluster
cards.body: The client hashes the key to a slot, sends the write to that slot’s primary, and the primary replicates to its replica asynchronously.
steps: App
Hash key
Pick shard
Redis primary
Async replica

cards.title: Worked example: a live leaderboard for a quiz show
cards.body: Assume: 5 million players in one sorted set; About 100 bytes per entry including member ID and skiplist plus hash overhead (an estimate; check with MEMORY USAGE); 200,000 score updates per second at peak.
steps: Memory = 5,000,000 × 100 bytes = 500,000,000 bytes ≈ 500 MB, which fits easily on one node.
ZADD and ZRANK are O(log N); log2 of 5 million is about 22, so each operation is a few dozen steps.
200,000 updates per second is above what one node handles comfortably, so split players into shards (for example 4 sorted sets by player ID), giving 50,000 updates per second per shard.
Global top 10 = take the top 10 from each of the 4 shards (40 entries) and merge them.
cards.note: About 500 MB of memory and O(log N) updates: sorted sets make a 5-million-player leaderboard cheap. Shard by player and merge the per-shard top 10s for the global top 10.

cards.title: Trap: one node, no replica
cards.body: Using a single Redis node for critical data with no replica: one restart wipes the hot set and floods the DB.

flashcards.back: Redis: data structures, persistence, replication; Memcached: simple multithreaded KV.
ZADD / ZREVRANGE on a sorted set.

mechanism.title: What happens inside Redis when you run a command
steps: Redis keeps all data in RAM and executes commands one at a time on a single main thread, so each command is atomic without locks. Network I/O can use extra threads in newer versions, but command execution stays single-threaded.

Because commands are tiny in-memory operations, a single node typically serves on the order of 100,000+ simple operations per second with sub-millisecond latency, until one slow command (KEYS *, a huge SORT) blocks everyone behind it.

Data structures do the work on the server: strings and counters (INCR), hashes (objects), lists (queues), sets, sorted sets (leaderboards, rate-limit windows), streams (append-only logs), plus HyperLogLog and bitmaps.
Persistence is optional: RDB snapshots write the whole dataset periodically; the AOF appends every write and can fsync every second, losing at most about a second of writes on a crash.
Replication is asynchronous: a replica follows the primary’s stream of writes. If the primary fails, a replica is promoted, and writes not yet replicated can be lost.

Redis Cluster splits the key space into 16,384 hash slots spread across primaries. A key’s slot is CRC16(key) mod 16,384; hash tags like {user:42} keep related keys in one slot so multi-key commands still work.

useWhen: Caches, sessions, rate limiting counters, leaderboards (sorted sets), short-lived locks, lightweight queues and pub/sub.
Anywhere you need atomic operations on small shared state at high throughput: INCR, ZADD, SET with NX and expiry.
avoidWhen: As the only copy of data you cannot lose, given asynchronous replication and memory-bound capacity.
Datasets far larger than RAM, or workloads needing complex queries and joins.

india.title: Free-to-play fantasy and quiz contests during IPL
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Free-to-play fantasy and live quiz apps in India see huge, synchronised spikes: when a wicket falls in an IPL match, millions of contest scores change at the same moment and players immediately check their rank. A sorted set per contest gives O(log N) score updates and rank lookups, and the whole leaderboard for a large contest fits in a few hundred megabytes. The heavy part is the write burst, so updates are batched per ball, contests are spread across many Redis primaries by contest ID, and very large contests are sharded internally. Final results and rewards are computed from the durable database, not from Redis, because Redis replication is asynchronous. (Real-money contests have been banned since the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 received assent on 22 Aug 2025; Dream11 stopped paid contests that day.)

pitfalls.trap: Running KEYS * or a huge range query in production.
pitfalls.say: “I’d use SCAN with a cursor and keep operations bounded; one slow command blocks the single command thread.”

pitfalls.trap: Using Redis as the system of record for money or orders.
pitfalls.say: “Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes; the database is the source of truth.”

deep.diagram:
client -> CRC16(key) mod 16384 = slot 9842
slots 0-5460     -> primary A (+replica)
slots 5461-10922 -> primary B (+replica)   <- slot 9842
slots 10923-16383-> primary C (+replica)
takeaways: Redis executes commands on one thread in RAM: fast and atomic, but slow commands block everyone.
Pick the data structure for the job: sorted sets for rankings, hashes for objects, streams for logs.
Replication is asynchronous; persistence is optional. Don’t make Redis your only copy of critical data.
Redis Cluster shards keys over 16,384 slots; use hash tags to co-locate related keys.

title: SQL vs NoSQL
objectives: Relational for joins and transactions; NoSQL for flexible schema and massive horizontal scale.

cards.title: Choosing by access pattern
cards.body: SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL) gives schemas, joins and ACID. NoSQL families: key-value (DynamoDB), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j). Choose by access pattern.

cards.title: Deciding between SQL and NoSQL
cards.body: List the queries first; joins and multi-row transactions point to SQL, a few huge key-based access patterns point to NoSQL, and the estimates confirm it.
steps: List the access patterns
Joins or multi-row transactions? Lean SQL
A few huge key-based patterns? Consider NoSQL
Check the choice against the estimates

cards.title: Worked example: does one SQL primary fit?
cards.body: Assume: 10 million users, 20 orders each per year, 2 KB per order row with indexes; Peak 3,000 order writes per second during a sale.
steps: Storage per year = 200,000,000 × 2 KB = 400,000,000 KB, which is about 400 GB.
Five years of orders is about 2 TB: large, but within what one primary with replicas can hold on modern SSDs.
3,000 writes per second is within reach of one tuned primary with batching and good indexes; reads go to replicas and caches.
cards.note: A single relational primary plus read replicas fits this workload for years. Shard or move a specific table to NoSQL only when measured growth says one machine will not cope.

flashcards.back: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
Access patterns, consistency needs, scale.

mechanism.title: How to choose a database from access patterns, step by step
steps: Write down the entities and the five to ten queries the product must serve, with rough rates: “get order by id, 2,000/s”, “list a user’s orders newest first, 500/s”, “monthly revenue by city, once a day”.

Mark which operations must change several rows atomically (move money, reserve a seat and create a booking). These want ACID transactions across rows or tables, which relational databases give you by default.
Mark which queries need joins or ad hoc filters you cannot predict yet. SQL handles unknown future queries well because the schema is normalised and the planner can combine tables.

Estimate data size and write rate. A single well-tuned PostgreSQL or MySQL primary on modern hardware comfortably serves a few terabytes and thousands of writes per second; most products never outgrow that.

Only if one machine clearly cannot hold the data or absorb the writes, or the access pattern is a pure key lookup at huge scale, consider a NoSQL family: key-value for lookups by id, document for self-contained nested records, wide-column for very high write rates partitioned by key, graph for many-hop relationship queries.
Validate the choice against the hardest query, not the easiest one, and say what you give up (joins, multi-row transactions, flexible queries) if you pick NoSQL.

useWhen: Money, inventory, bookings and anything with multi-row invariants: use a relational database with transactions.
Huge write-heavy streams read by a known key (sensor readings, chat messages by conversation, activity feeds): a wide-column or key-value store partitioned by that key fits.
avoidWhen: Do not pick NoSQL “because it scales” when the data is a few hundred gigabytes and relational; you lose joins and transactions for capacity you do not need.
Do not force a relational schema onto highly variable records that are always read whole, such as product attribute bags that differ by category; a document model or a JSONB column is simpler.

rows: Horizontal write scaling needs sharding work
Single-key get/put at very high rates
Queries by anything except the key
Nested records read and written whole

numbers.title: Does one SQL primary fit?
assumptions: 10 million users, 20 orders each per year, 2 KB per order row with indexes
Peak 3,000 order writes per second during a sale
steps: Storage per year = 200,000,000 × 2 KB = 400,000,000 KB, which is about 400 GB.
Five years of orders is about 2 TB: large, but within what one primary with replicas can hold on modern SSDs.
3,000 writes per second is within reach of one tuned primary with batching and good indexes; reads go to replicas and caches.
numbers.result: A single relational primary plus read replicas fits this workload for years. Shard or move a specific table to NoSQL only when measured growth says one machine will not cope.

india.title: A kirana-ordering app’s catalogue and orders
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Imagine a quick-commerce app in Bengaluru. Orders, payments and stock reservations live in PostgreSQL, because confirming an order must atomically decrement stock in one dark store and create the order; a partial write would sell items that are not on the shelf. Product details, though, vary wildly by category: atta has weight and brand, a phone charger has wattage and connector type. Those attribute bags are stored as a JSON document per product, either in a document store or in a JSONB column, and served through a cache. The live delivery-partner location stream, many small writes per second keyed by rider id, goes to a key-value or wide-column store with a short retention. Three stores, each chosen by its access pattern, not by fashion.

pitfalls.trap: “I’ll use MongoDB because it scales better.”
pitfalls.say: “Orders need multi-row transactions and joins, and two terabytes fits one PostgreSQL primary with replicas, so I’d start relational and move only the location stream to a key-value store.”

pitfalls.trap: Naming a database before listing the queries.
pitfalls.say: “Let me list the access patterns and rates first, then pick a store per pattern.”

takeaways: Choose by access pattern, invariants and size, not by brand.
One relational primary with replicas covers far more scale than most designs need.
NoSQL trades joins and multi-row transactions for partitioned scale; say that trade out loud.
Mixed workloads often deserve two or three stores, each with a clear job.
deep.diagram:
access patterns --> need multi-row ACID or joins? --yes--> SQL (+ replicas, cache)
                         |
                         no --> lookup by key? -> key-value
                                nested record? -> document
                                huge writes by key? -> wide-column
                                many hops? -> graph

interactive.title: SQL or NoSQL for orders?
interactive.prompt: Choose a store for these constraints.

choices.label: A relational database such as PostgreSQL
choices.feedback: Right: relational data, multi-row transactions and joins, at a write rate one well-tuned primary can often handle.

choices.label: A key-value store, with joins done in the app
choices.feedback: You’d rebuild transactions and joins by hand for data that is naturally relational.

choices.label: A graph database
choices.feedback: Nothing here is a deep relationship traversal; graphs fit social or fraud networks.

interactive.reveal: Choose by access pattern. Orders, items, payments and refunds need atomic multi-row changes and ad-hoc reports. Measure before assuming 2,000 writes/s is too much for one primary; add replicas and partitioning when numbers demand it.
setup: Orders with line items, payments and refunds
Finance runs reports joining all four
About 2,000 writes per second at peak

title: Types of NoSQL
objectives: Model for your queries: denormalise, pick partition and sort keys, avoid scatter-gather.

cards.title: Query-first data modelling
cards.body: In DynamoDB/Cassandra, design tables per query. Partition key spreads data; clustering/sort key orders within a partition. Duplicate data instead of joining.

cards.title: Modelling a table around its queries
cards.body: Pick a partition key that spreads load, a sort key that orders rows for the query, and duplicate data so each read hits one partition.
steps: List queries
Choose partition key
Choose sort key
Denormalise
Single-partition reads

cards.title: Worked example: sizing a chat partition
cards.body: Assume: Average message row 300 bytes; A busy group sends 2,000 messages a day; Target partition under 100 MB.
steps: Bytes per day = 2,000 × 300 = 600,000 bytes, about 0.6 MB.
Days to reach 100 MB = 100 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 167 days.
A conversation-only partition key would cross the target in under six months for busy groups and keep growing.
Bucketing by month, (conversation_id, month), caps a busy partition at about 0.6 × 31 ≈ 18.6 MB.
cards.note: Partition by conversation and month: newest-first reads touch one or two buckets, and no partition grows without bound.

cards.title: Trap: modelling NoSQL like SQL
cards.body: Modelling NoSQL like SQL with normalised tables and app-side joins.

cards.title: The four families
cards.body: Key-value (DynamoDB, Redis): get by key, simplest and fastest. Document (MongoDB): JSON-like records with nested fields. Wide-column (Cassandra): a partition key plus sorted rows, built for huge write volume. Graph (Neo4j): nodes and edges for questions like friends-of-friends.

questions.prompt: In Cassandra, what does the clustering (sort) key control?

choices.label: The order of rows inside a partition
The replication factor
Which node stores the partition
Which secondary index the query uses

questions.explanation: The partition key places data; the clustering key orders it.

questions.prompt: Which query fits a graph database best?

choices.label: Append a million sensor readings a second
Fetch a product document with nested specs
Get a session by id
Friends of friends who live in Pune

questions.explanation: Multi-hop relationship queries are what graph stores are for.

questions.prompt: Order the NoSQL modelling steps.

items.label: List the queries
Choose the partition key
Choose the sort key
Denormalise
Serve each query from one partition

questions.explanation: Design tables per query.

questions.prompt: A Cassandra schema copies SQL: normalised tables joined in the app. Result?

choices.label: Several round trips per page and scatter-gather reads
Joins run on the server side instead
Stronger consistency
Less storage and faster reads

questions.explanation: Wide-column stores have no joins; duplicate data per query instead.

questions.prompt: Chat messages are read as “latest 50 in a conversation”. Partition key and sort key?

choices.label: Partition by sender_id, sort by receiver_id
Partition by message time, sort by conversation_id
Partition by conversation_id, sort by message time
Partition by day, sort by message id

questions.explanation: One partition per conversation, already in time order. Partitioning by day would make today’s partition hot.

questions.prompt: A busy chat group writes 0.6 MB per day into a partition keyed only by conversation_id. What is the standard fix?

choices.label: Add a time bucket to the key, e.g. (conversation_id, month)
Use country as the partition key instead
Add secondary indexes on the message table
Increase the replication factor to five

questions.explanation: Bucketing by month caps partition size (about 18.6 MB per month here) while newest-first reads still touch only one or two partitions.

flashcards.back: Design tables around queries.
Partition picks the node; sort orders rows in it.

mechanism.title: Query-first modelling in a partitioned NoSQL store
steps: List every query with its filter and sort, for example “messages in conversation C, newest first, 50 at a time”.
Choose the partition key from the equality filter of the main query (conversation_id). All rows with the same partition key live together on one node, so the query reads one partition.
Choose the sort (clustering) key from the ordering you need (message timestamp or a time-ordered id). Inside the partition rows are stored sorted, so “newest 50” is a contiguous range read.

For each extra query with a different filter, create another table or a secondary index keyed for that query, and write to both. Duplicating data is normal; joins at read time are not available or are expensive.

Check partition size and heat: a single partition should stay well below the store’s comfortable limit (tens to low hundreds of megabytes in Cassandra guidance) and should not take a large share of all traffic.
If one key is too big or too hot, add a bucket to the key, such as (conversation_id, month) or (item_id, shard 0–9), and read the buckets you need.

useWhen: The queries are known and stable, and each can be answered by one partition.
Write volume or data size is beyond a single machine and you can live without joins.
avoidWhen: Queries are ad hoc or change weekly (analytics, admin search): put that data in SQL, a warehouse or a search index instead.
You need invariants across many partitions, such as a uniqueness check across all users, without a separate coordination step.

rows: Even spread, one-partition reads per user
Queries across users need another table
Hot partitions; India alone could swamp one node
Writes fan out; copies can drift

numbers.title: Sizing a chat partition
assumptions: A busy group sends 2,000 messages a day
steps: Bytes per day = 2,000 × 300 = 600,000 bytes, about 0.6 MB.
Days to reach 100 MB = 100 ÷ 0.6 ≈ 167 days.
A conversation-only partition key would cross the target in under six months for busy groups and keep growing.
Bucketing by month, (conversation_id, month), caps a busy partition at about 0.6 × 31 ≈ 18.6 MB.
numbers.result: Partition by conversation and month: newest-first reads touch one or two buckets, and no partition grows without bound.

india.title: Modelling a payments-history screen
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Suppose a UPI app shows “your transactions, newest first” and also lets support staff look up a transaction by its reference number. A NoSQL design would keep two tables: transactions_by_user with partition key user_id plus month and sort key timestamp descending, and transactions_by_ref with partition key reference_number. Each payment writes both rows. A user scrolling history reads one or two partitions; a support lookup reads exactly one row. Monthly buckets matter because a heavy merchant account can receive thousands of payments a day, which would make a single user_id partition grow without limit. The ledger of record still lives in a transactional store; this table is the read model.

pitfalls.trap: Modelling normalised tables and joining them in application code.
pitfalls.say: “I design one table per query: messages_by_conversation keyed by (conversation_id, month) with a time-ordered sort key.”

pitfalls.trap: Picking a low-cardinality partition key like country or status.
pitfalls.say: “I’d use a high-cardinality key such as user_id and add a bucket if one key gets hot.”

takeaways: List queries first; the schema follows the queries.
Partition key spreads data and decides which node answers; sort key orders rows inside it.
Duplicate data per query instead of joining at read time.
Bucket keys that grow without limit or get hot.

partition key (conversation_id, month) -> one node
  sort key: message_ts DESC
  [m_500][m_499][m_498] ... read newest 50 = one contiguous slice

interactive.title: Keys for a chat table
interactive.prompt: In Cassandra, the main query is “the latest 50 messages in conversation X”. Which keys fit?

choices.label: Partition by conversation_id, cluster by message time descending
choices.feedback: Right: one partition per conversation, already in the order you read.

choices.label: Partition by message_id
choices.feedback: Every message lands in a different partition, so one conversation is scattered everywhere.

choices.label: Partition by date
choices.feedback: All of today’s messages crowd into one hot partition.

interactive.reveal: Model NoSQL tables around the query. Very busy group chats may also need a time bucket in the partition key so no single partition grows without bound.

title: Indexing: B-Tree & LSM
objectives: Indexes (B-trees, hash, inverted) speed reads at the cost of writes and storage.

cards.title: What an index buys and costs
cards.body: A B-tree index turns a full scan into a log-time lookup. Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule. Each index slows inserts and updates.

cards.title: From full scan to index lookup
cards.body: Without an index the database scans every row; a B-tree turns that into a few page reads, paid for with extra work on every write.
steps: Query by column
No index: full scan
Add B-tree
Log(n) lookup
Extra write cost

cards.title: Worked example: how few levels a B-tree needs
cards.body: Assume: Fan-out of 200 keys per page; 500 million rows.
steps: One level covers 200 keys; two levels cover 200 × 200 = 40,000.
Three levels cover 40,000 × 200 = 8,000,000.
Four levels cover 8,000,000 × 200 = 1,600,000,000, which is more than 500 million.
So any row is at most four page reads away, and with the root and second level cached, about two reads from disk.
cards.note: A B-tree over half a billion rows is only four levels deep, which is why an indexed lookup takes milliseconds while a full scan of 500 million rows takes minutes.

cards.title: Trap: indexing every column
cards.body: Indexing every column. Writes slow down and the planner may still ignore them.

cards.title: LSM-trees
cards.body: LSM-tree stores (Cassandra, RocksDB) buffer writes in memory and flush sorted files to disk, merging them later (compaction). Writes are sequential and fast; a read may check several files, helped by Bloom filters. B-trees update pages in place: steadier reads, slower heavy writes.

questions.prompt: An index on (city, created_at). Which query uses it best?

choices.label: WHERE city = 'Pune' AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
WHERE status = 'paid'
WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01'
WHERE created_at = '2026-01-01' OR city = 'Pune'

questions.explanation: Leftmost prefix: the query must constrain city first.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of five more indexes on a busy table?

choices.label: Reads get slower because the planner has more choices
The table can no longer be sharded across machines
Nothing once they are built; indexes only cost time at creation
Every insert and update must also update five more structures

questions.explanation: Indexes trade write cost and storage for faster reads.

questions.prompt: Which workload favours an LSM-tree store over a B-tree?

choices.label: Small tables that fit in memory
Very high write volume, such as event logging
Complex joins across many tables
Mostly point reads on data that rarely ever changes

questions.explanation: LSM-trees turn writes into sequential appends.

questions.prompt: Order the story of adding an index.

items.label: Query filters by a column
No index: full table scan
Add a B-tree index
Lookups become log-time
Writes pay to maintain the index

questions.explanation: Faster reads, slower writes.

questions.prompt: A B-tree with fan-out 100 indexes 100M rows. About how many levels deep is it?
questions.explanation: Design implication: four levels means a lookup touches about four pages, and the top levels usually stay cached in memory, so an indexed lookup in 100M rows costs about one disk read.

questions.prompt: With 200 keys per page, how many B-tree levels are needed to index 500 million rows?

choices.label: About 500

questions.explanation: Three levels cover 8 million keys; four cover 1.6 billion, which exceeds 500 million.

flashcards.back: Composite index usable only from its first column(s).
Slower writes, extra storage.

mechanism.title: What a B-tree lookup and an LSM write actually do
steps: B-tree read: start at the root page, compare the key with the separators, follow one child pointer per level, and land on the leaf page holding the key or a pointer to the row.
With pages holding a few hundred keys each, three or four levels cover hundreds of millions of rows, and the top levels stay in RAM, so a lookup costs about one or two disk reads.
B-tree write: find the leaf, update it in place, and split the page if it is full; every extra index on the table repeats this work for the same insert.
LSM write: append to a write-ahead log for durability, insert into an in-memory sorted table (memtable), and acknowledge. When the memtable fills, flush it as an immutable sorted file (SSTable).
LSM read: check the memtable, then SSTables newest first; Bloom filters skip files that cannot contain the key, but a miss may still touch several files.
LSM compaction runs in the background, merging SSTables and dropping overwritten or deleted values; it costs extra disk I/O (write amplification) and can cause latency spikes if it falls behind.

useWhen: B-tree: read-heavy OLTP with point lookups and range scans, which is the default in PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB.
LSM: write-heavy workloads such as event logs, metrics and messaging, as in Cassandra, RocksDB and ScyllaDB.
avoidWhen: Do not add an index for every column “just in case”; each one slows every insert and update and uses storage and memory.
Do not choose an LSM store for a read-mostly workload with many point reads of cold keys unless you have measured read amplification.

rows: One path from root to leaf
Memtable plus several SSTables, helped by Bloom filters

numbers.title: How few levels a B-tree needs
steps: One level covers 200 keys; two levels cover 200 × 200 = 40,000.
Three levels cover 40,000 × 200 = 8,000,000.
Four levels cover 8,000,000 × 200 = 1,600,000,000, which is more than 500 million.
So any row is at most four page reads away, and with the root and second level cached, about two reads from disk.
numbers.result: A B-tree over half a billion rows is only four levels deep, which is why an indexed lookup takes milliseconds while a full scan of 500 million rows takes minutes.

india.title: Searching orders by phone number
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A food-delivery support tool lets agents find orders by customer phone number and date. Without an index, PostgreSQL scans the whole orders table, perhaps hundreds of millions of rows, for each lookup. A composite index on (phone, created_at) lets the planner jump to that phone’s entries and read them already sorted by date. The leftmost-prefix rule matters: the same index helps “phone = X” and “phone = X and created_at > Y” but not “created_at > Y” alone. The cost is that every new order now writes one more index entry, so the team adds this index and drops two unused ones rather than piling on more.

pitfalls.trap: “Indexes make everything faster.”
pitfalls.say: “Indexes speed the reads they match and slow every write; I’d add a composite index on (user_id, created_at) for the feed query and nothing else until I see slow queries.”

pitfalls.trap: Expecting an index on (a, b) to help a query filtering only on b.
pitfalls.say: “Composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix, so a filter on b alone needs its own index or a different column order.”

takeaways: B-trees give a few-level lookup path and are the default for OLTP.
LSM-trees turn writes into sequential appends and pay later in compaction and read amplification.
Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule.
Every index is a tax on writes; index for the queries you actually run.
deep.diagram:
B-tree:  [root] -> [internal] -> [leaf: keys + row pointers]   (3-4 levels)
LSM:     write -> WAL + memtable -> flush -> SSTable L0 -> compaction -> L1, L2 ...

interactive.title: How deep does a B-tree grow?
interactive.prompt: Grow the table and watch the depth of a B-tree with fan-out 100.
interactive.takeaway: From a thousand rows to ten billion, depth only goes from 2 to 5 levels. An indexed lookup stays a handful of page reads, and the top levels usually sit in memory, while a full scan grows with every row.

title: Normalisation vs Denormalization
objectives: Explain what normalisation buys you
Recognise when to denormalise for reads
Name the cost of keeping copies in sync

cards.title: Normalise first
cards.body: Normalisation stores each fact once: a customer’s address lives in one row, orders point to it by ID. Updates touch one place, so data cannot disagree with itself.

cards.title: Denormalize for hot reads
cards.body: If the order page must show product name and seller name, a normalised schema joins three tables on every view. At 5,000 order-page views a second during a sale, copying those names into the order row makes each view a single-row read; the cost is that a seller rename must now update every one of their order rows.

cards.title: Read path, before and after
cards.body: The normalised page joins three tables on every view; the denormalised page reads one row, at the cost of keeping the copies in sync.
steps: Order page request
Normalised: join orders + products + sellers
Denormalized: read one order row
Render page

cards.title: Trap: denormalising up front
cards.body: Denormalizing everything up front. Start normalised, measure the hot query, then denormalise that path and decide how copies stay in sync (same transaction, events, or accepted staleness).

questions.prompt: An order history page joins orders, products and sellers on every view and is now the slowest query. Most reasonable first change?

choices.label: Copy product and seller names into those order rows
Move all the data to a document store instead
Drop the foreign keys so the joins run faster
Denormalise every table in the schema at once

questions.explanation: Fix the measured hot path and keep the rest normalised; the copies cost a little on rare renames. Moving everything to a document store, or denormalising the whole schema, is a rewrite for one query, and foreign keys are checked on writes; they do not slow down reads that join.

questions.prompt: What is the main cost of copying the seller name into 10M order rows?

choices.label: Reads then need more joins to fetch each order
The database loses ACID properties for orders
A seller rename must update many rows
Orders can no longer be indexed by seller or date

questions.explanation: With 10M copies, one seller rename updates every row that seller has, possibly millions, so it belongs in a background job. Reads need fewer joins, not more, and ACID guarantees and indexing are unaffected.

questions.prompt: A wallet app shows the user’s balance on 6 different screens. Which data should stay in one normalised place?

choices.label: The display name on a cached profile card
The balance used to approve payments
The merchant name on past transactions
The product name printed on old invoices

questions.explanation: The balance decides whether a payment goes through, so two copies that disagree mean approving money that is not there; keep one authoritative row, updated in a transaction, and have the screens read it. Merchant names on past transactions and product names on invoices are snapshots that should not change, and a cached display name can be a little stale.

questions.prompt: Order the recommended process.

items.label: Start normalised
Measure the hot query
Denormalise that path
Decide how copies stay in sync

questions.explanation: Denormalise late and on purpose.

questions.prompt: Show product names on order history: copy or join?
constraints: Order history is the hottest page
Old orders should show the name at purchase time

approaches.label: Copy the name into the order row
Join the live product table

rationaleOptions.label: Keeping the name as it was at purchase is actually wanted
The hottest page becomes a one-row read
Copied names can never go stale

rationaleConflicts.r3: They can. Here staleness is acceptable, even wanted, but you still decide how renames propagate.

questions.explanation: Copying suits read-heavy pages whose data rarely changes.

questions.prompt: Why is copying the delivery address onto each order a sensible denormalisation?

choices.label: The order must keep the address it went to
SQL does not allow joining orders and customers
It makes editing a saved address much faster
It removes the need for a customers table

questions.explanation: It is a snapshot of a historical fact: the parcel went to that address even if the profile changes later, so it never needs syncing. SQL joins those tables fine, editing a saved address is unaffected, and customers still need their own table.

flashcards.back: Update anomalies: the same fact stored in two places disagreeing.
Faster reads for extra writes and the work of keeping copies in sync.
After a measured hot read path, with a clear sync strategy.

mechanism.title: From normalised tables to a denormalised read model
steps: Normalise first: each fact lives in one place. Orders reference customers by customer_id; the customer’s name lives only in the customers table.
Reads assemble data with joins. This keeps writes simple and consistent: changing a name is one update.
Measure: if a hot read joins five tables thousands of times per second and is slow even with indexes, consider denormalising that one read path.
Denormalise by copying the fields the read needs onto the row it reads, or by building a separate read table, for example an order_summary row that includes the customer name and the restaurant name.

Decide how copies are kept in step: in the same transaction, by an event or change-data-capture consumer, or by accepting that historical copies are deliberately frozen (the address at the time of the order).
Document which copy is the source of truth, and add a repair job or check for drift.

useWhen: Normalise the transactional core: users, orders, payments, inventory.
Denormalise hot, read-mostly views such as feeds, order history lists, search documents and dashboards.
avoidWhen: Do not denormalise fields that change often and must be correct everywhere immediately, such as a price used for billing.
Do not denormalise before measuring; joins on indexed keys are cheap at moderate scale.

rows: Slow hot reads at very high scale
Copies drift if a sync fails
Correct by design for historical facts

numbers.title: What a copied field costs to update
assumptions: A restaurant name is copied onto order_summary rows
Updates run at 5,000 rows per second
steps: Rows to rewrite on a rename = 2,000,000.
Time = 2,000,000 ÷ 5,000 = 400 seconds, nearly seven minutes of background writes.
If the order summary should show the name at order time, it is a snapshot and needs no rewrite at all.
If it should show the current name, read it by restaurant_id from a cache instead of copying it.
numbers.result: Copy fields that are snapshots or rarely change; look up fields that change and must be current.

india.title: Delivery address on an order
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: When someone in Pune orders food, the app copies the delivery address, item names and prices onto the order. This is deliberate denormalisation: if the customer later edits their saved address or the restaurant changes a price, the old order must still show what was actually delivered and charged, which also matters for GST invoices. Meanwhile the customer profile itself stays normalised, so editing the saved address is a single update. The order-history screen reads one denormalised row per order instead of joining orders, items, restaurants and addresses for every scroll.

pitfalls.trap: “Denormalisation is always faster, so I’ll denormalise everything.”
pitfalls.say: “I’ll keep the core normalised and add a denormalised order-history read model fed by events, because that list is read hundreds of times per order written.”

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting how copies stay in sync.
pitfalls.say: “The read model is updated by a CDC consumer; if it lags, the source of truth is still the orders table.”

takeaways: Normalise for correct writes; denormalise specific hot reads.
Snapshots of historical facts are the safest denormalisation.
Every copied field needs a sync plan and a source of truth.
Measure before denormalising.
deep.diagram:
normalised:   orders(customer_id) --join--> customers(name)
denormalised: order_summary(customer_name_at_order, restaurant_name, total)

interactive.title: Copy the seller name?
interactive.prompt: Choose the data model for this read path.

choices.label: Copy the seller name into each order row, and update copies when a seller renames
choices.feedback: Right: the hot read becomes one row, and the rare rename pays the cost.

choices.label: Keep it normalised and join three tables on every page view
choices.feedback: Correct but costly on the hottest path; fine until measurements say otherwise.

choices.label: Denormalize every table up front
choices.feedback: Copies everywhere make every write harder to keep consistent, for paths that may never be hot.

interactive.reveal: Start normalised, then denormalise the measured hot path and decide how copies stay in sync (same transaction, or an async update with a short staleness window).
