questions.explanation: Sharding is last because it is hard to undo.

questions.prompt: When is sharding justified?

choices.label: When reads are slow and the tables still have no indexes
When writes outgrow one primary, after cheaper steps
When the team adopts microservices and wants one DB each
As soon as traffic passes about 100 queries per second

questions.explanation: Justify it with write volume or data size.

questions.prompt: Where should user-uploaded profile photos live?

choices.label: In Elasticsearch, next to the profile
Object storage, with the URL saved in the database
In BLOB columns in the users table
In Redis, used as the primary store

questions.explanation: Files go to object storage; metadata to the database.

questions.prompt: Stores for a food-delivery app: orders and payments, menu search, session carts.

approaches.label: One MongoDB for everything
PostgreSQL for everything, searching with LIKE
PostgreSQL for orders, a search engine for menus, Redis for carts

rationaleOptions.label: One database is always the simplest to scale
Full-text search needs a search engine
Orders need transactions

rationaleConflicts.r3: A single store forced to serve every pattern gets slow somewhere; match patterns but keep the count small.

questions.explanation: Match stores to patterns.

questions.prompt: Writes are 1,500/s today, doubling yearly, and a primary handles about 10,000/s. When does sharding become necessary?

choices.label: In about three years, at 10,000/s
Immediately, before writes grow
Not needed: one primary will keep up
Next month, when writes double

questions.explanation: 3,000 then 6,000 then 12,000 per second: the third year crosses the limit.

flashcards.back: After indexing, caching, replicas and vertical scaling are exhausted.
Read throughput, not write throughput.

mechanism.title: A scaling ladder for the data layer
steps: Start with one relational primary, good schema and indexes. Fix slow queries with EXPLAIN before anything else.
Add a cache (Redis) for hot reads and a CDN for static content.
Add read replicas for read-heavy traffic, with read-your-writes routing where needed.
Scale the primary vertically (more CPU, RAM, faster disks), and move heavy analytics off it to a warehouse.
Move specialised workloads to purpose-built stores: search to Elasticsearch, files to object storage, metrics to a time-series database, events to Kafka.
Only when one primary cannot take the writes or hold the data, shard the hottest tables by a key used in most queries, or move them to a distributed database.

useWhen: Use the ladder to justify each component in an interview: say which numbers made you climb a rung.
Use purpose-built stores when a workload has a distinct access pattern: full-text search, blobs, time series, graphs.
avoidWhen: Do not jump to sharding or a distributed database before replicas and caching; you take on lasting complexity for unproven needs.
Do not add a new datastore for each feature; every store needs backups, monitoring, on-call expertise and data sync.

rows: Sub-millisecond to single-digit ms by key
Compression and rollups for time series
Columnar scans over billions of rows

numbers.title: When does a single primary run out?
assumptions: Primary handles about 10,000 simple writes per second
Product grows writes 2× per year from 1,500 per second today
steps: Year 1: 1,500 × 2 = 3,000 per second.
Year 2: 3,000 × 2 = 6,000 per second.
Year 3: 6,000 × 2 = 12,000 per second, which exceeds about 10,000.
So there are roughly two to three years before writes force sharding, plenty of time to plan rather than shard on day one.
numbers.result: Project growth against measured capacity to decide when to shard, and say that timeline out loud in an interview.

india.title: Stores behind a food-delivery app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A food-delivery platform in India might use PostgreSQL for orders and payments, Redis for menus and sessions, Elasticsearch for “biryani near me” search with typo tolerance in English and Hinglish, object storage plus a CDN for dish photos, Kafka for order events, a time-series store for rider-location metrics and a warehouse for city-level analytics. Each was added because one access pattern outgrew the previous setup, not on day one. A new team building a similar app for one city would start with PostgreSQL, Redis and object storage, and add the rest as numbers demand.

pitfalls.trap: Listing many databases without reasons.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd start with PostgreSQL and Redis; search moves to Elasticsearch once LIKE queries over millions of menu items get slow, and I'd shard orders only when writes approach one primary's limit.'

pitfalls.trap: Sharding on day one.
pitfalls.say: “At 1,500 writes per second and doubling yearly, one primary lasts about two to three years; I’d design the shard key now but shard later.”

takeaways: Climb the scaling ladder one measured rung at a time.
Match each specialised store to a distinct access pattern.
Every extra store has an operational cost.
Project growth to decide when to shard.
deep.diagram:
1 primary -> + cache/CDN -> + read replicas -> + bigger box -> + specialised stores -> shard
(climb a rung only when a measured number forces it)

interactive.prompt: A PostgreSQL primary sits at 70% CPU, mostly from a few slow, unindexed read queries. Writes are fine. What do you do first?

choices.feedback: Right: the cheapest fix for the actual cause.

choices.label: Shard the database now

choices.label: Migrate to Cassandra

interactive.reveal: Climb the ladder in order: fix queries and indexes, add a cache, add read replicas, move to a bigger instance, and partition only when writes or data size demand it.

title: Message Queues
objectives: Queues decouple producers from consumers, absorb spikes and enable async work.

cards.title: Decoupling with a queue
cards.body: Producers enqueue; workers consume at their own pace. Queues buffer bursts, isolate failures and allow retries. Use them when the caller does not need the result immediately.

cards.title: A job through a queue
cards.body: The producer enqueues and returns; workers pull at their own pace and ack on success, so failures are retried instead of lost.
steps: Producer
Enqueue
Queue buffers
Worker consumes
Ack / retry

cards.title: Worked example: sizing workers for a burst
cards.body: Assume: Sale spike: 50,000 receipt jobs per minute for 10 minutes; Each job takes 200 ms; one worker does 5 jobs per second; Acceptable backlog: cleared within 20 minutes of the spike starting.
steps: Arrival rate = 50,000 ÷ 60 ≈ 833 jobs per second.
To finish within 20 minutes (1,200 seconds) needs 500,000 ÷ 1,200 ≈ 417 jobs per second.
Workers needed = 417 ÷ 5 ≈ 84; to keep pace with the peak instead would need 833 ÷ 5 ≈ 167.
cards.note: The queue lets about 84 workers handle a peak that would otherwise need about 167, at the cost of receipts arriving up to 20 minutes late.

cards.title: Trap: queues for synchronous work
cards.body: Putting synchronous user-facing work behind a queue and then polling for the result.

cards.title: Poison messages
cards.body: A malformed message that crashes the consumer will be redelivered forever and block the queue. After a few failed attempts, move it to a dead-letter queue and alert someone.

questions.prompt: Which task is best moved to a queue?

choices.label: Showing the cart total on checkout
Validating a coupon before showing the price
Checking the password at login
Sending the order-confirmation email

questions.explanation: The user does not need the email’s result to continue.

questions.prompt: A flash sale brings 10× normal orders for 5 minutes; the invoice service handles 1×. What does a queue give you?

choices.label: Orders are rejected until the spike ends
Invoices are generated 10× faster
Orders are accepted now and invoices catch up after the spike
Nothing: the queue forwards at the same rate

questions.explanation: Queues absorb bursts; consumers work at their own pace.

questions.prompt: One malformed message crashes the consumer every time and blocks the queue. Fix?

choices.label: Retry it with no delay between attempts
Add more consumers until one of them succeeds
After a few tries, park it in a dead-letter queue
Purge the queue and ask producers to resend

questions.explanation: Park poison messages so the rest can flow.

items.label: Producer creates a job
Job is enqueued
Queue buffers it
Worker consumes it
Worker acks (or it is retried)

questions.explanation: Unacked jobs come back.

questions.prompt: During a spike, 6,000 jobs/min arrive and workers finish 4,000/min. How large is the backlog after 15 minutes?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the backlog only drains once arrivals drop below 4,000/min. At 2,000/min below capacity, clearing 30,000 jobs takes another 15 minutes, so add workers or shed load.

questions.prompt: 500,000 jobs must be cleared within 1,200 seconds, and each worker does 5 jobs/s. About how many workers are needed?

choices.label: About 84
About 8
About 833
About 5,000

flashcards.back: Decoupling and load levelling.
Consumer confirms processing so message is removed.

mechanism.title: The life of a message in a work queue
steps: The producer (for example the order service) writes a message such as “send receipt for order 123” to the queue and returns to the user immediately.
The broker stores the message durably (on disk, often replicated) and makes it visible to consumers.
A worker receives the message; the broker hides it from other workers for a visibility timeout or marks it unacknowledged.
The worker does the job and acknowledges. Only then does the broker delete the message.
If the worker crashes or the timeout expires without an acknowledgement, the message becomes visible again and another worker retries it, so handlers must be idempotent.
After a set number of failed attempts (say 5), the message moves to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for inspection, so one poison message does not block or loop forever.

useWhen: Work the user does not need to wait for: emails, SMS, thumbnails, invoices, search indexing.
Absorbing bursts: the queue buffers a spike while workers drain it at a steady rate.
avoidWhen: The caller needs the result in the same request, such as a price quote or a balance check.
Strict global ordering of all messages is required; ordinary queues order only loosely, and ordered queues cap throughput.

rows: Ordered jobs per entity at moderate rates
When the caller needs the answer now

numbers.title: Sizing workers for a burst
assumptions: Sale spike: 50,000 receipt jobs per minute for 10 minutes
Each job takes 200 ms; one worker does 5 jobs per second
Acceptable backlog: cleared within 20 minutes of the spike starting
steps: Arrival rate = 50,000 ÷ 60 ≈ 833 jobs per second.
To finish within 20 minutes (1,200 seconds) needs 500,000 ÷ 1,200 ≈ 417 jobs per second.
Workers needed = 417 ÷ 5 ≈ 84; to keep pace with the peak instead would need 833 ÷ 5 ≈ 167.
numbers.result: The queue lets about 84 workers handle a peak that would otherwise need about 167, at the cost of receipts arriving up to 20 minutes late.

india.title: Order confirmation SMS during a sale
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: When a big festive sale starts at midnight, an e-commerce checkout may confirm orders far faster than its SMS provider accepts messages. Calling the SMS gateway inside checkout would make every order slow, and a provider outage would fail payments. Instead checkout commits the order, puts “send confirmation” on a queue, and returns. Workers send SMS at the provider’s permitted rate (also respecting DLT template rules for commercial SMS in India), retry on errors with backoff, and move messages with invalid numbers to a DLQ. Customers might get their SMS a minute late during the peak, which they will not notice; failed checkouts they would.

pitfalls.trap: “The queue guarantees each message is processed once.”
pitfalls.say: “Most queues are at-least-once, so the handler is idempotent, keyed by order_id.”

pitfalls.trap: No plan for poison messages.
pitfalls.say: “After five attempts with exponential backoff the message goes to a DLQ with an alert, and we can replay it after a fix.”

takeaways: Queues decouple the user-facing request from slow work.
They buffer spikes so you size workers for the average plus backlog, not the peak.
Delivery is at least once; make handlers idempotent.
Always configure retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue.
deep.diagram:
producer -> [ queue | m1 m2 m3 ... ] -> worker (ack) 
                        |  after 5 failures
                        v
                      [ DLQ ] -> alert, inspect, replay

interactive.title: How many workers for the spike?
interactive.prompt: During a sale, 6,000 jobs per minute arrive for 15 minutes. Each worker finishes 2,000 per minute. Find how many workers stop the backlog growing.
interactive.takeaway: Three workers keep up. With two, 30,000 jobs pile up in 15 minutes and drain only after the spike ends. That is fine for emails that can wait, not for work a user is waiting on.

title: Kafka
objectives: Pub/sub fans one event to many subscribers; Kafka is a partitioned, replayable log.

cards.title: Partitions, ordering and replay
cards.body: Kafka topics are split into partitions; order is guaranteed per partition. Consumer groups share partitions. Messages are retained so consumers can replay.

cards.title: An event through a Kafka topic
cards.body: The producer keys the event to a partition; the log retains it, and each consumer group reads it independently at its own offset.
steps: Producer
Topic partition (by key)
Retained log
Consumer group A
Consumer group B

cards.title: Worked example: choosing a partition count
cards.body: Assume: Peak 60,000 events per second; One consumer instance processes 2,500 events per second; Plan for 2× growth.
steps: Consumers needed today = 60,000 ÷ 2,500 = 24.
With 2× growth = 24 × 2 = 48 consumers.
Since one partition is read by at most one consumer in a group, the topic needs at least 48 partitions.
Choose a round number such as 64 to allow headroom; increasing partitions later changes which partition a key maps to.
cards.note: Partition count caps consumer parallelism, so size it for future peak throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, with headroom.

cards.title: Trap: expecting global ordering
cards.body: Expecting global ordering in Kafka. Ordering is per partition: key by order_id to keep one order’s events in sequence.

questions.prompt: How do you keep all events for one order in sequence?

choices.label: Add timestamps and sort in each consumer
Rely on Kafka’s ordering across partitions
Use order_id as the message key so they share a partition
Use one partition per consumer

questions.explanation: Ordering holds only within a partition.

questions.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group runs 8 consumers. What happens?

choices.label: The group refuses to start
Six consumers get one partition each; two sit idle
Each message goes to all 8
Kafka splits the partitions into 8

questions.explanation: A partition is read by one consumer per group.

questions.prompt: A bug corrupted a downstream table for the last two hours. How does Kafka help?

choices.label: It cannot: messages are deleted once consumed
Restart the producer to resend
Reset the consumer’s offset and replay the retained messages
Add partitions

questions.explanation: Retention makes the log replayable.

choices.label: The producer calls each service directly
One consumer group shared by both services
Billing forwards each event on to the analytics service
Two consumer groups, each reading the whole topic

questions.explanation: Groups are independent subscribers.

Key picks the partition
Event is appended to the retained log
Group A reads it
Group B reads it independently

questions.explanation: Each group tracks its own offset.

questions.prompt: A topic has 12 partitions and a consumer group runs 20 instances. What happens?

choices.label: 12 instances get partitions and 8 sit idle
All 20 share each partition equally
Kafka adds 8 more partitions to the topic
Ordering is lost for each key

questions.explanation: Each partition goes to at most one consumer in a group, so parallelism is capped at 12.

flashcards.back: Per partition only.

flashcards.front: Max parallel consumers in a group?
flashcards.back: Number of partitions.

mechanism.title: How Kafka stores and serves events
steps: A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an append-only log on disk; every record gets an increasing offset.
The producer picks a partition by hashing the record key (for example order_id), so all events for one key land in one partition, in order.

Each partition has a leader broker and followers. With acks=all, a write is acknowledged once all in-sync replicas have it; with min.insync.replicas = 2 and replication factor 3, one broker can fail without losing acknowledged data.
Consumers in a consumer group split the partitions: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, so parallelism is capped by the partition count.
Consumers commit their offset (position). After a crash they resume from the last committed offset, which can reprocess some records, so processing must be idempotent.
Records stay for the retention period (for example 7 days) regardless of whether they have been read, so a new consumer group or a fixed bug can replay history from an earlier offset.

useWhen: High-throughput event streams with several independent consumers: analytics, search indexing, notifications all reading the same order events.
When you need replay, per-key ordering, or to feed stream processors.
avoidWhen: Simple task queues with per-message acknowledgement and retries, where SQS or RabbitMQ is simpler.
Request-response calls, or global ordering across all keys (that needs one partition and gives up parallelism).

rows: Many groups read the same data
Up to the number of partitions

numbers.title: Choosing a partition count
assumptions: One consumer instance processes 2,500 events per second
steps: Consumers needed today = 60,000 ÷ 2,500 = 24.
With 2× growth = 24 × 2 = 48 consumers.
Since one partition is read by at most one consumer in a group, the topic needs at least 48 partitions.
Choose a round number such as 64 to allow headroom; increasing partitions later changes which partition a key maps to.
numbers.result: Partition count caps consumer parallelism, so size it for future peak throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, with headroom.

india.title: Order events in a quick-commerce app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Each order in a 10-minute grocery delivery app emits events: placed, packed, picked up, delivered. They go to an orders topic keyed by order_id, so one order’s events stay in sequence. The rider-assignment service, the customer notification service, the analytics pipeline and the fraud checker each read the topic through their own consumer group at their own pace. When the analytics team finds a bug in how they computed delivery times, they deploy the fix and replay the last seven days from the retained log instead of asking every other team to resend data.

pitfalls.trap: “Kafka guarantees global ordering.”
pitfalls.say: “Kafka orders within a partition; I key by order_id so each order’s events stay in order.”

pitfalls.trap: Adding consumers beyond the partition count to go faster.
pitfalls.say: “Extra consumers in a group sit idle once each partition has one; I’d size partitions for peak parallelism up front.”

takeaways: Partitions give per-key ordering and parallelism.
Consumer parallelism per group is capped by the partition count.
Retention enables replay and many independent consumer groups.
acks=all with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 2 survives one broker failure.
deep.diagram:
producer --key=order_id--> topic orders
  P0: [0][1][2][3]... -> consumer A (group: notify)
  P1: [0][1][2]...    -> consumer B (group: notify)
  same partitions also read by group: analytics (own offsets)

interactive.title: More consumers than partitions
interactive.prompt: A Kafka topic has 6 partitions. You start 10 consumers in one consumer group. How many do work?

choices.label: 6; the other 4 sit idle
choices.feedback: Right: each partition goes to one consumer in a group.

choices.label: All 10, sharing partitions
choices.feedback: Within one group a partition is never split between consumers.

choices.label: Only 1; the others are standby
choices.feedback: The group spreads partitions across consumers, up to one each.

interactive.reveal: Partitions cap a group’s parallelism. Pick a partition count for the peak consumer throughput you need, with room to grow; idle consumers are useful only as hot spares.

title: Pub/Sub & Fan-out
objectives: Explain publish/subscribe and when to use it
Compare fan-out on write vs fan-out on read
Handle celebrity accounts in a feed

cards.title: Pub/sub decouples producers
cards.body: A publisher emits an event once (OrderPlaced); any number of subscribers (email, analytics, inventory) consume it independently. Adding a consumer does not change the producer.

cards.title: Fan-out on write vs read
cards.body: Fan-out on write pushes a new post into every follower’s feed at post time: fast reads, expensive writes. Fan-out on read assembles the feed when it is opened: cheap writes, slower reads.

cards.title: Posting with a hybrid feed
cards.body: Normal posts are pushed into followers’ feeds when written; celebrity posts are skipped at write time and merged in when a feed is read.
steps: User posts
Event published to topic
Workers push into normal followers’ feeds
Celebrity posts skipped at write time
Feed read merges celebrity posts on demand

cards.title: Trap: fan-out on write for celebrities
cards.body: Fan-out on write for everyone. A cricketer with 50 million followers turns one post into 50 million writes. Hybrid feeds treat high-follower accounts differently.

questions.prompt: An account with 50M followers posts. Why is pure fan-out on write a problem?

choices.label: Followers of celebrities cannot read feeds
One post becomes 50M feed writes
Pub/sub cannot deliver to more than 1M subscribers
Normal users’ reads get slower

questions.explanation: Write cost grows with follower count.

questions.prompt: Order service publishes OrderPlaced. Analytics wants it too. What changes in the order service?

choices.label: Publish a second event type for analytics
Add a direct call to analytics after each order
Write orders into analytics’ database too
Nothing: analytics subscribes to the topic

questions.explanation: Publishers do not know their subscribers.

questions.prompt: Fan-out on read means:

choices.label: The feed is assembled when the user opens it
Followers poll the poster’s phone
Only celebrities’ posts are stored
Posts are pushed into followers’ feeds at post time

questions.explanation: Cheap writes, slower reads.

questions.prompt: Order a post in a hybrid feed.

items.label: User posts
Event published to a topic
Workers push it into normal followers’ feeds
Celebrity posts are skipped at write time
Feed reads merge celebrity posts on demand

questions.explanation: Two paths by follower count.

questions.prompt: Feed strategy when most users have 200 followers but a few have 50M.

approaches.label: Fan-out on read for everyone
Hybrid: write fan-out for normal users, read-time merge for celebrities
Fan-out on write for everyone

rationaleOptions.label: Fan-out on read for everyone keeps every feed fast
Normal posts are precomputed, so most reads are fast
Celebrity posts merged at read time avoid millions of writes

rationaleConflicts.r3: Each open would gather posts from hundreds of followees; slow for the common case.

questions.explanation: Treat the long tail and the giants differently.

questions.prompt: Fan-out workers write 200,000 entries/s. How long does pushing one post to 10 million followers take?

choices.label: 50 seconds
0.5 seconds
5 minutes
2 seconds

questions.explanation: 10,000,000 ÷ 200,000 = 50 seconds of the whole fleet’s capacity.

flashcards.back: Producers from consumers: new subscribers need no producer changes.

flashcards.front: Fan-out on write is good for?
flashcards.back: Fast feed reads for accounts with modest follower counts.
Skip write fan-out for them and merge their posts at read time.

mechanism.title: Fan-out on write, fan-out on read, and the hybrid
steps: Pub/sub basics: a publisher sends an event to a topic; every subscriber receives its own copy, unlike a queue where workers compete for one copy.
Fan-out on write (push): when a user posts, a worker writes the post id into the timeline cache of every follower. Reading a feed is then one fast lookup.
Fan-out on read (pull): store the post once; when a user opens their feed, fetch recent posts from everyone they follow and merge them. Writes are cheap, reads are expensive.
Celebrity problem: an account with 10 million followers makes push cost 10 million writes per post, and the feed of people following it is delayed while workers catch up.
Hybrid: push posts from ordinary accounts; for accounts above a threshold (say 100,000 followers), skip the push and merge their recent posts at read time.
Feeds keep only the latest few hundred ids per user in cache; older pages are rebuilt from storage.

useWhen: Push for most users, because feeds are read far more often than posts are written.
Pull or hybrid for accounts with very large followings, and for inactive users who rarely open the app.
avoidWhen: Pure push when follower counts are extremely skewed.
Pure pull when users follow thousands of accounts and expect feeds in tens of milliseconds.

rows: One query per followed account, then merge
Push for normal, none for celebrities
Cache read plus a few celebrity lookups
More logic, two paths to test

numbers.title: Cost of pushing a celebrity post
assumptions: Fan-out workers write 200,000 timeline entries per second in total
steps: Writes for one post = 10,000,000 timeline inserts.
Time to finish = 10,000,000 ÷ 200,000 = 50 seconds.
Three posts in a minute would keep the whole fan-out fleet busy for 150 seconds, delaying everyone else’s posts.
With hybrid, the celebrity post is written once and merged at read time by followers who open the app.
numbers.result: Pushing to 10 million followers takes the whole fan-out fleet 50 seconds per post; the hybrid model removes that cost.

india.title: A cricketer’s post during a match
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: When a star Indian cricketer with tens of millions of followers posts after a match, a pure push model would generate tens of millions of timeline writes in seconds, delaying posts from everyone else. Social apps handle such accounts differently: the post is stored once, and when a follower opens their feed, the app merges their pushed timeline with the latest posts from the few celebrity accounts they follow. Ordinary users, who have a few hundred followers, still get push delivery, so their friends see posts instantly. We describe the general technique; it is not a claim about any specific app’s internal thresholds.

pitfalls.trap: Choosing pure push without addressing celebrities.
pitfalls.say: “Push for accounts under about 100,000 followers; above that, pull at read time and merge.”

pitfalls.trap: Confusing pub/sub with a queue.
pitfalls.say: “In pub/sub each subscriber gets every event; in a queue, competing workers each get a share.”

takeaways: Pub/sub copies each event to every subscriber.
Push makes reads cheap, pull makes writes cheap.
Skewed follower counts call for a hybrid.
Quantify fan-out as followers divided by worker throughput.
deep.diagram:
post by normal user -> fan-out workers -> follower timelines (push)
post by celebrity   -> stored once
feed open -> read own timeline + fetch celebrity posts -> merge by time

interactive.title: A celebrity posts
interactive.prompt: An account with 50 million followers posts. With fan-out on write for everyone, how many feed writes does that one post cause?

choices.label: About 50 million
choices.feedback: Right: one insert into each follower’s precomputed feed.

choices.label: One
choices.feedback: That is fan-out on read: store once, merge when feeds are read.

choices.label: About 50,000
choices.feedback: Off by a factor of 1,000.

interactive.reveal: Hybrid feeds push posts from normal accounts at write time and merge celebrity posts at read time, so one post doesn’t cause millions of writes.

title: Delivery Semantics
objectives: Compare at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once
Explain where duplicates come from
Make retries safe with idempotency and backoff

cards.title: Three guarantees
cards.body: At-most-once: send and forget; a crash can lose a message but never duplicates it. At-least-once: retry until acknowledged; nothing is lost but duplicates happen. Exactly-once: each message affects the result once, which in practice means at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional processing.

cards.title: Where duplicates come from
cards.body: A consumer processes a message, then crashes before committing its offset. On restart it reads the message again. Producers also resend after a lost acknowledgement.

cards.title: An at-least-once consumer
cards.body: If the consumer crashes after processing but before committing its offset, the message comes back; an idempotent write makes the replay harmless.
steps: Read message
Process it (write to the database)
Commit the offset
Crash before commit: message redelivered
Idempotent write makes the replay harmless

cards.title: Retries with backoff
cards.body: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter. Immediate retries from thousands of clients turn a blip into a thundering herd; jitter spreads them out.

cards.title: Trap: promising exactly-once
cards.body: Promising exactly-once delivery over a network. Delivery can only be at-least-once; you get exactly-once effects by making processing idempotent.

questions.prompt: Which guarantee can lose a message but never duplicates it?

choices.label: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
At-least-once with retries

questions.explanation: No retries means no duplicates, and no recovery.

questions.prompt: A consumer handles 1,000 messages/s and commits offsets every 5 seconds. It crashes just before a commit. About how many messages are replayed?
questions.explanation: Design implication: up to 5,000 messages will be processed twice after the crash, so the consumer’s writes must be idempotent. Committing more often shrinks the replay but adds overhead.

questions.prompt: Why add jitter to retries?

choices.label: To get exactly-once delivery of each message
So clients do not all retry at the same moment after an outage
To keep the retried messages in their original order
To make each individual retry attempt complete much more quickly

questions.explanation: Synchronised retries hit a recovering service all at once.

questions.prompt: Order the guarantees from weakest to strongest.

items.label: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once effects

questions.explanation: Each step adds work: retries, then idempotency.

questions.prompt: Delivery for payment settlement events.
constraints: A duplicate settlement would pay twice

approaches.label: At-least-once with idempotent processing
approaches.description: Retry, and dedupe by settlement id

approaches.label: At-most-once

rationaleOptions.label: Idempotent processing makes duplicates harmless
No settlement may be lost
At-most-once avoids duplicates, so it is safest for money

rationaleConflicts.r3: It avoids duplicates by risking loss; a lost settlement is just as bad.

questions.explanation: Exactly-once effects come from at-least-once plus idempotency.

questions.prompt: A consumer processes a message, then crashes before acknowledging it. Under at-least-once delivery, what happens?

choices.label: The message is redelivered and processed again
The message is lost
The broker marks it processed on its own
The ordering of all the other messages is reversed

questions.explanation: Without the acknowledgement the broker redelivers, so the handler must be idempotent.

flashcards.front: Which guarantee can lose a message but never duplicates it?
flashcards.back: At-most-once. No retries means no duplicates, and no recovery.
So clients do not all retry at the same moment after an outage. Synchronised retries hit a recovering service all at once.

mechanism.title: Where duplicates and losses come from
steps: At-most-once: the consumer acknowledges (or commits the offset) before processing. If it crashes mid-way, the message is gone. Simple and lossy.
At-least-once: the consumer processes, then acknowledges. If it crashes after processing but before acknowledging, the message is redelivered and processed again.

Producers duplicate too: if an acknowledgement from the broker is lost, the producer retries and the broker may store the message twice (Kafka’s idempotent producer removes this particular duplicate).
Exactly-once effect is built from at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing: deduplicate by a message id, or make the write itself idempotent (upsert by key).
Kafka transactions give exactly-once within Kafka (read, process, write to another topic, commit offset atomically), but side effects outside Kafka such as sending an email still need idempotency.
Retries use exponential backoff with jitter (for example 1 s, 2 s, 4 s with random spread) so failing consumers do not hammer a recovering dependency in sync.

useWhen: At-least-once plus idempotency for nearly all business events: payments, orders, notifications.
At-most-once for telemetry or metrics where losing a sample is cheaper than handling duplicates.
avoidWhen: Do not promise “exactly-once delivery” across arbitrary systems; promise exactly-once effect through idempotency.
Do not retry immediately in a tight loop; it turns a brief outage into a sustained overload.

rows: Ack after processing, retry on failure
At least once plus dedup or idempotent writes

numbers.title: Backoff schedule and total wait
assumptions: Full jitter: each wait is random between 0 and the cap
steps: Caps are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds.
Worst-case total wait = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31 seconds.
With full jitter the expected wait is half of each cap, so about 31 ÷ 2 = 15.5 seconds in total.
If 10,000 consumers fail at once, jitter spreads their first retry over a second instead of all hitting at the same millisecond.
numbers.result: Five doubling retries span about 31 seconds at most; jitter spreads the herd so the dependency can recover.

india.title: Duplicate payment webhooks
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Payment gateways commonly deliver webhooks (for example 'payment captured') at least once and retry if your server does not return success quickly. If a merchant's server credits the order and then times out before replying, the gateway sends the same event again. A naive handler would mark the order paid twice or send two 'thank you' emails and ship twice. The fix is to record each gateway event id in a table with a unique constraint, inside the same transaction as the order update, and treat a duplicate insert as 'already done'. The gateway's retries then become harmless.

pitfalls.trap: “We use exactly-once delivery.”
pitfalls.say: “Delivery is at least once; I get an exactly-once effect by deduplicating on the event id in the same transaction as the update.”

pitfalls.trap: Retrying without backoff.
pitfalls.say: “Retries use exponential backoff with jitter and a cap, then go to a DLQ.”

pitfalls.trap: Assuming Kafka transactions make an email send exactly-once.
pitfalls.say: “Kafka transactions cover reads and writes inside Kafka; the email side effect still needs its own dedup record keyed by the event id.”

takeaways: At-most-once loses, at-least-once duplicates; pick deliberately.
Exactly-once is an effect built from idempotency, not a network property.
Producers and consumers both create duplicates.
Use exponential backoff with jitter and a DLQ.
deep.diagram:
process -> crash before ack -> redelivered -> process again
            (at least once)        dedup table: event_id UNIQUE -> second time = no-op

interactive.title: Crash before the commit
interactive.prompt: A consumer writes a message’s result to the database, then crashes before committing its offset. What happens on restart?

choices.label: The message is delivered again
choices.feedback: Right: the committed offset is still before it.

choices.label: The message is lost
choices.feedback: At-least-once delivery doesn’t lose it; it repeats it.

choices.label: The consumer skips ahead to the next message
choices.feedback: It resumes from the last committed offset.

interactive.reveal: At-least-once delivery means duplicates after crashes. Make processing idempotent (upserts, dedup keys) so a replay changes nothing.

title: Idempotency
objectives: Explain why retries cause duplicates
Design an idempotency key flow
Apply it to payments and message consumers

cards.title: Retries create duplicates
cards.body: Networks time out after the server already did the work. The client retries, and without protection a UPI payment is charged twice. At-least-once queues redeliver the same way.

cards.title: Idempotency keys
cards.body: The client sends a unique key (Idempotency-Key header). The server stores key → result. A retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of repeating the action.

cards.title: A retried payment
cards.body: The server stores the idempotency key with the result, so a retry after a lost response gets the stored answer instead of a second charge.
steps: Client sends POST /pay with key K
Server charges, stores K → success
Response lost, client times out
Client retries with key K
Server finds K, returns stored success

cards.title: Trap: check, then write
cards.body: Checking for the key and then writing in two separate steps. Two concurrent retries can both pass the check. Make the key insert and the action atomic, for example with a unique constraint.

cards.title: Naturally idempotent operations
cards.body: Setting a value (status = shipped) is idempotent: doing it twice leaves the same result. Adding or appending (balance += 100) is not. Turn the second kind into the first by recording a key or checking a version.

questions.prompt: A payment request timed out on the client, but the server had already charged the card. The client retries. What prevents a double charge?

choices.label: An idempotency key: the server returns the stored result
A longer client timeout
Retrying faster
Exactly-once delivery from the network

questions.explanation: The retry is recognised and answered from storage.

questions.prompt: Two identical retries arrive in the same millisecond. Which design is safe?

choices.label: Keep keys in each server’s memory
Accept both and reconcile at month end
Check whether the key exists, then charge, in two steps
Insert the key under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the charge

questions.explanation: Check-then-act races; an atomic insert does not.

questions.prompt: Order a retried payment with an idempotency key.

items.label: Client sends POST /pay with key K
Server charges and stores K → success
Response is lost; client times out
Client retries with K
Server finds K and returns the stored success

questions.explanation: The second request never charges.

questions.prompt: Which operation is naturally idempotent?

choices.label: Add ₹100 to the user’s wallet balance
Set the address to “12 MG Road”
Increment the post’s view count
Append a comment to the thread

questions.explanation: Setting a value twice leaves the same state.

questions.prompt: You keep idempotency keys for 24 hours. 2M payments a day, about 100 bytes per stored key and result. Storage needed, in MB?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 200 MB fits comfortably in memory or a small table, so keeping idempotency keys for a full day is cheap. Retention is a correctness choice, not a storage problem.

questions.prompt: Why must the idempotency key be inserted under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the work?

choices.label: So two concurrent retries cannot both run
To make the request faster by skipping a lookup
Because idempotency keys must be stored sorted
So the client can safely skip TLS on retries

questions.explanation: A separate check then insert races; the unique constraint makes the second attempt fail atomically.

flashcards.front: What does an idempotency key do?
flashcards.back: Lets the server return the stored result for a retried request instead of repeating it.
At-least-once delivery means the same message can arrive twice.

flashcards.front: How do you stop two concurrent retries both running?
flashcards.back: Make the key insert atomic, e.g. a unique constraint in the same transaction.

mechanism.title: How an idempotency key makes a retry safe
steps: The client generates a unique key (a UUID) for the operation, such as “pay ₹500 for order 123”, and sends it with the request in a header like Idempotency-Key.
The server, in one transaction, inserts the key into an idempotency table with status “in progress”. A unique constraint makes a second insert with the same key fail.
If the insert succeeds, the server performs the operation and stores the response (status code and body) against the key, then commits.
If the client times out and retries with the same key, the insert fails; the server returns the stored response instead of charging again.
If the first request is still in progress, the retry gets “conflict, try later” rather than running in parallel.
Keys expire after a window such as 24 hours; the server also checks that a retried key comes with the same request body, rejecting reuse of a key for a different operation.

useWhen: Any non-idempotent POST that moves money, creates orders or sends messages, especially from mobile clients on flaky networks.
Consumers of at-least-once queues and webhooks.
avoidWhen: Naturally idempotent operations such as PUT setting a value or DELETE by id do not need a separate key.
Do not check and then insert in two steps without a unique constraint; two concurrent retries can both pass the check.

rows: Unique key per operation, stored with response
Unique constraint on business id, e.g. (order_id, event_type)
SET or upsert rather than increment

numbers.title: Storage for idempotency keys
assumptions: Each row about 500 bytes with stored response
steps: Storage = 172,800,000 × 500 bytes = 86,400,000,000 bytes, about 86 GB.
That is acceptable in a database table partitioned by day, or in Redis with a 24-hour TTL if the response bodies are small.
numbers.result: Idempotency keys at 2,000 requests per second for a day need tens of gigabytes; expire them by time.

india.title: Retrying a payment on a 2G connection
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A user in a small town taps “Pay ₹799” in a shopping app on a weak connection. The request reaches the server and the charge succeeds, but the response is lost, so the app shows a spinner and then retries. Without an idempotency key, the retry could charge the user twice, and refunds take days. With the key generated when the user tapped Pay, the server sees the same key, finds the stored success response and returns it, and the app shows “Payment successful” once. This is the same pattern that payment APIs such as Stripe document publicly with their Idempotency-Key header.

pitfalls.trap: “I’ll check if the order exists, then create it.”
pitfalls.say: “Check-then-insert races; I insert the idempotency key under a unique constraint in the same transaction as the order.”

pitfalls.trap: Generating a new key on each retry.
pitfalls.say: “The key is created once per user action and reused for every retry of that action.”

takeaways: An idempotency key turns a retry into a lookup.
Insert the key under a unique constraint, atomically with the work.
Reuse the same key for every retry of one user action.
Prefer natural keys and upserts when the business id already exists.
deep.diagram:
client --(key K)--> server: INSERT key K (unique) -> do work -> save response
retry  --(key K)--> server: key exists -> return saved response (no second charge)

interactive.title: Check, then charge
interactive.prompt: A server handles retries like this: check whether key K was seen; if not, charge the card and then store K. Two retries arrive at the same moment. What can happen?

choices.label: Both pass the check and the card is charged twice
choices.feedback: Right: the check and the store are separate steps.

choices.label: The second request waits automatically
choices.feedback: Nothing makes them wait unless you add a lock or constraint.

choices.label: Nothing; idempotency keys prevent duplicates by definition
choices.feedback: Only if recording the key is atomic with claiming the work.

interactive.reveal: Insert the key first under a unique constraint (or take a lock), then do the work. The loser of the race gets the stored result instead of a second charge.

title: Rate Limiting Algorithms
objectives: Protect services by capping requests per key using token bucket, leaky bucket or sliding windows.

cards.title: Token bucket and sliding windows
cards.body: Token bucket: tokens refill at rate r up to capacity b; each request spends one, so bursts are allowed. Sliding window counters smooth boundary spikes. Store counters in Redis for a shared limit.

cards.title: Checking a request against its bucket
cards.body: Look up the caller’s bucket; if a token is available spend it and allow the request, otherwise answer 429 with Retry-After.
steps: Request arrives
Lookup key bucket
Token available?
Yes: allow & spend
No: 429 Too Many Requests

cards.title: Worked example: token bucket for an OTP endpoint
cards.body: Assume: Allow on average 1 OTP per 30 seconds per phone; Allow a burst of 3.
steps: Refill rate R = 1 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.033 tokens per second.
Bucket size B = 3, so a user can request 3 OTPs back to back.
After the burst, the next token arrives after 30 seconds; in 10 minutes at most 3 plus 600 ÷ 30 = 23 OTPs can be sent.
A fixed window of 3 per minute would instead allow 6 in two seconds across a minute boundary.
cards.note: A token bucket of size 3 refilling every 30 seconds caps a phone at 23 OTPs in 10 minutes while still allowing an honest quick retry.

cards.title: Trap: fixed-window bursts
cards.body: Fixed windows let 2× traffic through at window boundaries. Mention sliding windows or token buckets.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm naturally allows short bursts?

choices.label: Token bucket
Fixed window counter
Leaky bucket
Sliding window log

questions.explanation: Saved-up tokens can be spent at once.

questions.prompt: A token bucket refills 5 tokens/s with capacity 20 and starts full. Maximum requests in the first 4 seconds?
questions.formula: 4 s × 5 tokens/s + 20 already in the bucket
questions.workedAnswer: Refill over 4 s: 4 × 5 = 20 tokens. Add the 20 already in the bucket: 40 requests.
questions.explanation: Design implication: capacity sets the allowed burst (20 at once) and the refill rate sets the sustained limit (5/s). Pick both from the traffic you want to allow.

questions.prompt: What should a rate-limited API return?

choices.label: 403 Forbidden for the rest of the day
429 Too Many Requests, ideally with Retry-After
200 OK with an error message in the body
500 Internal Server Error, so the client retries

questions.explanation: Tell clients to slow down, and when to come back.

questions.prompt: A fixed-window limit of 100 per minute. A client sends 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00. What happened?

choices.label: The second 100 were rejected
The window slid to block them
200 passed within two seconds
Only 100 passed in total

questions.explanation: Window boundaries allow double bursts; sliding windows smooth this.

questions.prompt: The limit is 100/min per user, but each of 20 API servers counts in its own memory, so users get far more. Click the component to fix.
questions.explanation: Keep the counter in a shared store such as Redis.

questions.prompt: A token bucket has size 3 and refills one token every 30 seconds. At most how many requests pass in 10 minutes starting full?
questions.explanation: 3 from the full bucket plus 600 ÷ 30 = 20 refills gives 23.

flashcards.back: 429 Too Many Requests.
Redis with atomic INCR/Lua.

mechanism.title: How the main rate-limiting algorithms decide
steps: Fixed window: count requests per client in the current minute; reject once the count passes the limit. Simple, but a client can send a full burst at 12:00:59 and another at 12:01:00, doubling the rate briefly.
Sliding window log: keep timestamps of recent requests and count those within the last 60 seconds. Accurate, but stores one entry per request.
Sliding window counter: blend the previous and current window counts weighted by time. Close to accurate at fixed-window cost.
Token bucket: a bucket holds up to B tokens and refills at R tokens per second; each request takes one token or is rejected. It allows short bursts up to B while enforcing an average rate R.
Leaky bucket: requests enter a queue drained at a fixed rate, smoothing output; excess is dropped.
In a fleet, the counters must be shared, typically in Redis with an atomic Lua script or INCR plus expiry, or approximated locally per node with the limit divided by the number of nodes.

useWhen: Protecting APIs and login endpoints from abuse and accidental floods.
Fair sharing of capacity between tenants, and protecting expensive dependencies such as SMS or payment providers.
avoidWhen: Do not use rate limiting as the only overload defence; also use timeouts, load shedding and autoscaling.
Do not rate limit by IP alone where many users share one IP, such as mobile carrier NAT in India; prefer user or API key.

rows: Good; average and burst both controlled

numbers.title: Token bucket for an OTP endpoint
assumptions: Allow on average 1 OTP per 30 seconds per phone
steps: Refill rate R = 1 ÷ 30 ≈ 0.033 tokens per second.
Bucket size B = 3, so a user can request 3 OTPs back to back.
After the burst, the next token arrives after 30 seconds; in 10 minutes at most 3 plus 600 ÷ 30 = 23 OTPs can be sent.
A fixed window of 3 per minute would instead allow 6 in two seconds across a minute boundary.
numbers.result: A token bucket of size 3 refilling every 30 seconds caps a phone at 23 OTPs in 10 minutes while still allowing an honest quick retry.

india.title: OTP abuse on a fintech login
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: OTP SMS cost money per message, and attackers sometimes trigger thousands of OTPs to random numbers ('SMS pumping') or to harass one person. A fintech app limits OTP requests with a token bucket per phone number and a second, looser bucket per device and per IP range, all stored in Redis so every server sees the same counts. Many Indian mobile users share carrier IP addresses through NAT, so a strict IP-only limit would block innocent users on the same carrier; per-phone and per-device limits are fairer. Rejected requests get HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.

pitfalls.trap: Rate limiting only by IP.
pitfalls.say: “Carrier NAT puts many users behind one IP, so I’d limit by user or phone first and use IP only as a loose second layer.”

pitfalls.trap: Keeping counters in each server’s memory.
pitfalls.say: “With 20 servers behind a load balancer, local counters allow 20× the limit; I’d use Redis with an atomic script.”

takeaways: Fixed windows allow double bursts at the boundary.
Token bucket controls both average rate and burst size.
Share counters across servers with atomic operations.
Choose the key carefully: user, API key or phone beats IP alone.
