interactive.title: Size the burst
interactive.prompt: A partner API refills 5 tokens per second. Partners send batches of 20 requests at once. Find a bucket capacity that lets a batch through, and see how many requests pass in the first 4 seconds.
interactive.takeaway: Capacity sets the burst and the refill rate sets the sustained limit. With capacity 20, a full bucket allows 20 + 5 × 4 = 40 requests in the first 4 seconds, then 5 per second.

title: Distributed Unique IDs
objectives: Generate unique IDs at scale: UUIDs, DB sequences, Snowflake, or ticket servers.

cards.title: UUIDs vs Snowflake IDs
cards.body: UUIDv4 is random and needs no coordination but indexes poorly. Snowflake 64-bit IDs (timestamp + worker + sequence) are sortable. UUIDv7 adds time ordering.

cards.title: Building a Snowflake ID
cards.body: Concatenate milliseconds since an epoch, a worker ID and a per-millisecond sequence into 64 bits that sort by time.
steps: Timestamp bits
Worker ID bits
Sequence bits
Combine
Sortable 64-bit ID

cards.title: Worked example: capacity of the Snowflake layout
cards.body: Assume: 41 timestamp bits in milliseconds; 10 machine bits, 12 sequence bits.
steps: Timestamp range = 2 to the power 41 ms, about 2,199,023,255,552 ms.
Divided by about 31,557,600,000 ms per year, that is roughly 69.7 years from the chosen epoch.
Machines = 2 to the power 10, which is 1,024.
IDs per machine per millisecond = 2 to the power 12, which is 4,096, so about 4,096,000 per second per machine.
cards.note: The classic layout lasts about 69 years, supports 1,024 generators and about 4 million IDs per second each.

cards.title: Trap: public auto-increment IDs
cards.body: Using auto-increment IDs exposed publicly: leaks volume and enables enumeration.

questions.prompt: Which ID is 64-bit and sortable by time?

choices.label: Auto-increment per shard
Snowflake
A random 64-bit number
UUIDv4

questions.explanation: Timestamp bits come first.

questions.prompt: Snowflake has a 12-bit sequence per millisecond per worker. Roughly how many IDs per second can one worker make?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about 4 million IDs per second per worker is far beyond most systems’ needs, so the worker-ID bits, not the sequence, usually set the limit (how many generators you can run).

questions.prompt: Why do random UUIDv4 primary keys hurt B-tree inserts?

choices.label: Inserts land on random pages, causing splits and cache misses
They are too short to stay unique at scale
They are not unique enough across servers
They need a central coordinator for each insert

questions.explanation: Time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, Snowflake) insert at the end.

questions.prompt: Public order URLs look like /orders/1043, from an auto-increment id. Main risk?

choices.label: The ids cannot be sorted by creation time
The URLs get too long for some browsers
Auto-increment ids cannot be indexed well
Anyone can guess other ids and estimate your order volume

questions.explanation: Sequential ids leak volume and invite enumeration.

questions.prompt: IDs for orders created on 50 app servers.

approaches.label: UUIDv4
Database auto-increment
Snowflake-style IDs

rationaleOptions.label: Worker bits avoid coordination
The timestamp prefix sorts by creation time
UUIDv4 is time-sortable

rationaleConflicts.r3: v4 is random; UUIDv7 is the time-ordered variant.

questions.explanation: Snowflake gives both properties.

questions.prompt: In the classic Snowflake layout, how many IDs can one machine generate per millisecond?

choices.label: Unlimited

questions.explanation: 12 sequence bits give 2 to the power 12 = 4,096 IDs per millisecond per machine.

flashcards.back: Time-ordered UUID.
Leak volume, enable enumeration.

mechanism.title: How a Snowflake-style ID is built
steps: A 64-bit integer is split into fields: 1 unused sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch, 10 bits of machine id and 12 bits of sequence.
Each ID generator knows its machine id, assigned at deploy time through configuration or a coordination service, so no two generators share one.
To create an ID, read the current millisecond. If it equals the last millisecond, increment the sequence; if the sequence overflows past 4,095, wait for the next millisecond.
Assemble the bits: timestamp shifted left by 22, machine id shifted left by 12, plus the sequence.
Because the timestamp is in the high bits, IDs sort roughly by creation time across machines, which keeps B-tree inserts near the end of the index and makes “newest first” cheap.
If the clock moves backwards (for example after an NTP correction), the generator must wait or refuse, or it could reissue an ID.

useWhen: Distributed systems that need unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs without a central database round trip: tweets, orders, messages.
UUIDv4 when IDs must be unguessable and ordering does not matter; UUIDv7 when you want time-ordered 128-bit IDs from a standard.
avoidWhen: Auto-increment from a single database across many shards; it becomes a bottleneck and leaks business volume through guessable sequential numbers.
Random UUIDv4 as a primary key in a B-tree-heavy table with a high insert rate; random inserts scatter across index pages.

numbers.title: Capacity of the Snowflake layout
steps: Timestamp range = 2 to the power 41 ms, about 2,199,023,255,552 ms.
Divided by about 31,557,600,000 ms per year, that is roughly 69.7 years from the chosen epoch.
Machines = 2 to the power 10, which is 1,024.
IDs per machine per millisecond = 2 to the power 12, which is 4,096, so about 4,096,000 per second per machine.
numbers.result: The classic layout lasts about 69 years, supports 1,024 generators and about 4 million IDs per second each.

india.title: Order IDs for a food-delivery platform
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A delivery platform creating orders across dozens of services and data centres cannot afford a single auto-increment counter: every order would wait on one database, and sequential IDs would reveal daily order volume to competitors. A Snowflake-style scheme lets each order service instance mint IDs locally. Because IDs are roughly time-ordered, the orders table’s primary key index grows at the right edge, and support tools can sort by ID instead of by a separate timestamp. The customer still sees a short friendly reference, derived separately, rather than a 19-digit number.

pitfalls.trap: Using a single auto-increment counter for a global system.
pitfalls.say: “A Snowflake-style ID lets each node generate unique, time-ordered IDs without a central round trip.”

pitfalls.trap: Using random UUIDv4 as the clustered primary key at a high insert rate.
pitfalls.say: “Random keys scatter inserts across the whole B-tree and hurt cache locality; a time-ordered id such as UUIDv7 or Snowflake keeps inserts at the right edge.”

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring clock skew.
pitfalls.say: “If the clock moves backwards, the generator waits until it passes the last timestamp rather than risk duplicates.”

takeaways: Snowflake IDs pack time, machine and sequence into 64 bits.
Time in the high bits makes IDs sortable and index-friendly.
Machine ids must be unique; clock rollback must be handled.
UUIDv4 for unguessable ids, UUIDv7 or Snowflake for ordered ones.
deep.diagram:
| 0 | 41 bits: ms since epoch | 10 bits: machine | 12 bits: sequence |
  sign   ~69 years                1,024 nodes        4,096 per ms

interactive.title: Auto-increment IDs in URLs
interactive.prompt: Why avoid exposing database auto-increment IDs in public order URLs?

choices.label: They leak how many orders you get and let anyone try neighbouring IDs
choices.feedback: Right: sequential IDs are guessable and reveal volume.

choices.label: Auto-increment IDs run out at about 2 billion
choices.feedback: A 64-bit column lasts effectively forever.

choices.label: Two orders can get the same ID
choices.feedback: A single database sequence doesn’t produce duplicates.

interactive.reveal: Use non-guessable public IDs (UUIDv4, or a random token) and still enforce authorisation on every lookup. Snowflake or UUIDv7 IDs add time ordering for indexes.

title: 2PC & Saga
objectives: Explain two-phase commit and why it blocks
Design a saga with compensations
Choose choreography or orchestration

cards.title: Two-phase commit
cards.body: A coordinator asks every participant to prepare (lock and promise), then tells all to commit or all to abort. It gives atomicity across databases, but each commit costs at least two round trips plus a forced log write at every participant, participants hold locks while waiting, and if the coordinator dies after prepare they are stuck.

cards.title: Sagas
cards.body: A saga splits the work into local transactions, one per service. If a later step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating actions (refund, release the seat). No global locks, but the system is briefly inconsistent.

cards.title: A trip booking saga
cards.body: When the payment step fails, the saga runs compensating actions in reverse order to undo the hotel and flight reservations.
steps: Reserve flight
Reserve hotel
Charge payment: fails
Compensate: cancel hotel
Compensate: cancel flight

cards.title: Choreography vs orchestration
cards.body: Choreography: each service reacts to the others’ events; no central brain, but the flow is hard to see. Orchestration: a coordinator calls each step and runs compensations; easier to follow and change.

cards.title: Trap: 2PC by default
cards.body: Defaulting to 2PC across microservices. It ties every service’s availability together and holds locks across network calls. Prefer sagas unless you truly need atomic commit. Expect the follow-up “what does the user see while the saga is half done?”: show “payment pending”, not a confirmed booking.

questions.prompt: Checkout uses two-phase commit across the order, payment and inventory databases. During a sale the inventory database is slow for 30 seconds. What happens to checkout?

choices.label: Orders and payments commit; stock catches up later
Checkout skips inventory and uses a cached count
Only stock updates slow down, not payments
Every checkout waits, holding locks in all three

questions.explanation: Under 2PC nothing commits until every participant has voted, so one slow database stalls every checkout while the other two hold their locks, slowing other work on those rows too. Committing without inventory is what a saga would do, and 2PC has no cached fallback.

questions.prompt: Order two-phase commit.

items.label: Coordinator sends prepare
Participants lock and vote yes
Coordinator decides commit
Participants commit and release locks

questions.explanation: Locks are held from prepare to commit.

questions.prompt: A saga’s payment step fails after the flight and hotel were reserved. What happens?

choices.label: The user keeps the reservations
Compensations cancel the hotel, then the flight
The database rolls back all three of the bookings
The saga keeps retrying the payment

questions.explanation: Each completed step is undone by a new action, in reverse order: cancel the hotel, then the flight. There is no cross-service transaction to roll back, leaving the reservations holds rooms and seats the user did not pay for, and retrying a declined card forever never ends. Compensations must be idempotent, because they can be retried too.

questions.prompt: Which is orchestration?

choices.label: The services share one database transaction
A coordinator calls flight, hotel and payment, then compensates
The client calls each service itself
Each service reacts to the previous service’s event

questions.explanation: Orchestration means one coordinator owns the flow: it calls each step and decides when to compensate. Services reacting to each other’s events is choreography, a shared transaction is not a saga at all, and a client calling services itself leaves compensation to an app that may close halfway.

questions.prompt: Checkout spans order, payment and inventory services.

approaches.label: Two-phase commit
Saga with compensations

rationaleOptions.label: Sagas keep data consistent at every instant
Compensations undo partial work
Services stay available independently

rationaleConflicts.r3: Sagas are briefly inconsistent between steps; design for it.

questions.explanation: Sagas trade instant consistency for availability.

questions.prompt: Participants in 2PC have voted yes and the coordinator crashes. What happens?

choices.label: Participants hold their locks until they learn the outcome
They all commit by themselves after a timeout
They all abort immediately and release locks
A compensating transaction undoes their work

questions.explanation: After voting yes a participant cannot decide alone, so it blocks with locks held.

flashcards.back: Participants hold locks and can be stuck if the coordinator fails after prepare. Blocking is the price of atomic commit.

flashcards.front: A saga’s payment step fails after the flight and hotel were reserved. What happens?
flashcards.back: Compensating actions cancel the hotel and then the flight. Sagas undo with new actions, in reverse order.
A booking coordinator calls flight, hotel and payment in turn and runs compensations. A central coordinator owns the flow.

mechanism.title: Two-phase commit versus a saga, step by step
steps: 2PC phase 1 (prepare): a coordinator asks every participant to prepare; each writes the change durably, holds its locks and votes yes or no.
2PC phase 2 (commit): if all vote yes, the coordinator logs “commit” and tells everyone to commit; any no means abort for all.
Blocking: if the coordinator crashes after participants voted yes, they must keep their locks until it recovers, because they cannot know the outcome on their own.
Saga: split the business transaction into local transactions, each committed independently (create order, reserve stock, charge payment, assign rider).
If a later step fails, run compensating actions for completed steps in reverse (refund payment, release stock, cancel order). Compensations must be idempotent and must themselves eventually succeed.
Orchestration: a saga coordinator service drives the steps and tracks state. Choreography: each service reacts to events and emits the next. Orchestration is easier to follow and debug as steps grow.

useWhen: 2PC inside one trust boundary with few participants that support it, such as two databases in one system, when atomicity matters more than availability.
Sagas for long-running business flows across microservices or external parties, such as payment gateways, that cannot hold locks.
avoidWhen: 2PC across services you do not control or over unreliable networks; a stuck coordinator blocks everyone.
Sagas where intermediate states must never be visible; users may briefly see “stock reserved, payment pending”.

rows: Two round trips with locks held
Each step commits on its own

numbers.title: Lock time under 2PC
assumptions: 4 participants, each 20 ms away from the coordinator
steps: Phase 1 takes about one round trip of 40 ms plus 5 ms of local prepare work, about 45 ms.
Phase 2 needs another 40 ms round trip, so locks are held for roughly 85 ms or more per transaction.
A row hit by 50 transactions per second would need 50 × 0.085 = 4.25 seconds of lock time every second, so they queue up and throughput collapses.
A saga commits each local step in a few milliseconds and holds no cross-service locks.
numbers.result: Cross-service 2PC holds locks for round trips; hot rows cannot sustain it, which is why microservices use sagas.

india.title: Booking a flight and hotel package
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A travel booking site in India sells a Goa package: flight, hotel and cab. The airline and hotel systems belong to other companies, so no 2PC is possible. An orchestrated saga reserves the flight seat, then the hotel room, then charges the card through a payment gateway. If the hotel step fails because the room has just gone, the orchestrator cancels the flight hold and the user sees “hotel unavailable, nothing charged”. If payment fails after both holds, it releases both. Each step and compensation is retried idempotently, and the saga’s state is persisted so a crash of the orchestrator resumes where it left off.

pitfalls.trap: Proposing 2PC across microservices.
pitfalls.say: “2PC blocks if the coordinator fails and holds locks across the network; I’d use an orchestrated saga with compensations.”

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting that compensations can fail.
pitfalls.say: “Compensations are idempotent and retried until they succeed, with alerts if they stall.”

takeaways: 2PC gives atomicity but blocks and holds locks across round trips.
Sagas commit locally and undo with compensations.
Sagas lack isolation; design for visible intermediate states.
Orchestration is easier to debug than choreography for long flows.
deep.diagram:
saga: [create order] -> [reserve stock] -> [charge] -> [assign rider]
 fail at charge:        <- release stock <- cancel order (compensate in reverse)

interactive.title: Payment fails mid-saga
interactive.prompt: A trip-booking saga reserved a flight, then a hotel, then the payment fails. What happens?

choices.label: Compensating steps cancel the hotel, then the flight
choices.feedback: Right: a saga undoes completed steps in reverse order.

choices.label: Two-phase commit rolls everything back atomically
choices.feedback: A saga has no global atomic rollback; that is what 2PC would try to provide.

choices.label: Nothing; the user keeps both reservations
choices.feedback: Then the user holds unpaid bookings.

interactive.reveal: Sagas trade atomicity for availability: each step commits locally and has a compensating action. Design compensations to be idempotent, because they may be retried.

title: Outbox Pattern & CDC
objectives: Explain the dual-write problem
Implement a transactional outbox
Use change data capture to publish database changes

cards.title: The dual-write problem
cards.body: A service saves an order and then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka. If it crashes between the two, the order exists but nobody hears about it; if the publish succeeds and the database write fails, consumers act on an order that does not exist.

cards.title: Transactional outbox
cards.body: Write the order and an outbox row in the same database transaction. A relay reads unsent outbox rows, publishes them to the broker and marks them sent. Either both are saved or neither is.

cards.title: Outbox to broker
cards.body: Follow one order through: the relay may run a few seconds behind the commit, so consumers hear about the order slightly later, but never about an order that was rolled back.
steps: BEGIN
Insert the order and an outbox event
COMMIT
Relay reads unsent outbox rows
Relay publishes to Kafka and marks them sent

cards.title: Change data capture
cards.body: CDC tools such as Debezium tail the database’s write-ahead log and turn each committed change into an event. No polling and no app changes; it can publish the outbox table or any other table.

cards.title: Trap: relays deliver twice
cards.body: Forgetting the relay delivers at least once. It can crash after publishing but before marking the row sent, so consumers must handle duplicates idempotently.

questions.prompt: A service writes an order to its database, then publishes to Kafka, and crashes in between. Result?

choices.label: Both are lost
The database retries the publish on its own
Kafka rolls back the order
The order exists but no event was published

questions.explanation: Two separate writes are not atomic.

questions.prompt: How does the outbox pattern avoid the dual-write problem?

choices.label: It publishes to Kafka before writing to the database
The event is saved in the same transaction as the data, then relayed
It uses two-phase commit between the database and Kafka
It retries the publish from memory until it works

questions.explanation: One local transaction, then an at-least-once relay.

questions.prompt: Order the outbox flow.

items.label: BEGIN
Insert the order and an outbox event
COMMIT
Relay reads unsent rows
Relay publishes and marks them sent

questions.explanation: The relay runs after commit.

questions.prompt: How does CDC capture changes?

choices.label: By intercepting HTTP requests to the service
By asking each developer to publish events
By reading the database’s write-ahead log
By running SELECT * on each table each second

questions.explanation: The log already has every committed change.

questions.prompt: The relay publishes an event, then crashes before marking it sent. What happens next?

choices.label: The database rolls back the order
The event is lost
Kafka removes the duplicate itself
It republishes, so consumers must be idempotent

questions.explanation: At-least-once relays create duplicates.

questions.prompt: A service updates its database, then crashes before publishing the event to Kafka. What pattern prevents this inconsistency?

choices.label: Writing the event to an outbox table in the same transaction
Publishing first, then updating the database
Increasing Kafka retention
Using a bigger database server

questions.explanation: The outbox makes the event part of the same atomic commit; a relay publishes it afterwards.

flashcards.front: A service writes an order to its database, then publishes to Kafka, and crashes in between. Result?
flashcards.back: The order exists but no event was published. Two separate writes are not atomic.

flashcards.front: How does the outbox pattern avoid the dual-write problem?
flashcards.back: The event is saved in the same transaction as the data, then relayed. One local transaction, then an at-least-once relay.
By reading the database’s write-ahead log. The log already has every committed change.

flashcards.front: The relay publishes an event, then crashes before marking it sent. What happens next?
flashcards.back: It publishes the event again, so consumers must be idempotent. At-least-once relays create duplicates.

mechanism.title: How the outbox pattern publishes events reliably
steps: The dual-write problem: a service writes to its database and then publishes to Kafka. If it crashes between the two, the database and the event stream disagree.
Outbox: in the same local transaction that changes business rows, insert an event row into an outbox table. Either both commit or neither does.
A relay process reads new outbox rows (by polling or by tailing the database log) and publishes them to the broker.

After the broker acknowledges, the relay marks the row as sent or advances its position. If it crashes before that, it publishes the row again, so consumers see duplicates and must be idempotent, using the event id.

Change data capture (CDC) tools such as Debezium read the database’s replication log (PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL binlog) and emit each committed change as an event, without the application writing to the broker at all.
Old outbox rows are deleted or archived after a retention period.

useWhen: Any service that must update its database and notify others: order created, payment captured, profile changed.
CDC when you want to stream changes from an existing database (to search, caches or a warehouse) without changing application code.
avoidWhen: Do not publish to Kafka inside the database transaction and hope; the two systems do not share a transaction.
Do not expose raw CDC table changes as a public contract to many teams; table schemas change. Publish curated outbox events instead.

numbers.title: Polling cost of an outbox relay
steps: Polls per second = 1 ÷ 0.1 = 10.
Events per poll on average = 300 ÷ 10 = 30.
Average extra delay is half the poll interval, about 50 ms.
A CDC relay tailing the log usually delivers in tens of milliseconds without any polling queries.
numbers.result: A 100 ms poller adds about 50 ms average latency and batches about 30 events per poll; CDC removes polling load.

india.title: Payment captured and order confirmed
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: When a payment succeeds in an Indian e-commerce checkout, the order service must mark the order paid and tell the warehouse, notification and loyalty-points services. If it updated the database and then crashed before publishing, the warehouse would never pack the item despite the customer being charged. With an outbox, “order paid” and the event row commit together; a relay publishes the event within milliseconds and retries until Kafka confirms. If a duplicate slips through, the warehouse ignores a second “pack order 123” because it deduplicates on the event id.

pitfalls.trap: “I’ll write to the DB, then publish to Kafka.”
pitfalls.say: “That dual write can lose events on a crash; I’d write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it.”

pitfalls.trap: Claiming the outbox gives exactly-once.
pitfalls.say: “The relay can publish twice after a crash, so consumers dedupe on the event id.”

takeaways: Dual writes to a database and a broker are not atomic.
The outbox puts the event in the same transaction as the change.
Relays and CDC are at least once; consumers must dedupe.
Publish curated events, not raw table changes, as contracts.
deep.diagram:
BEGIN; UPDATE orders SET paid; INSERT outbox(event); COMMIT
 relay/CDC --> Kafka --> warehouse, notifications (dedupe by event_id)

interactive.title: Save, then publish
interactive.prompt: A service saves an order and then publishes OrderPlaced to Kafka, with no outbox. It crashes between the two. What is the state?

choices.label: The order exists, but no event was ever published
choices.feedback: Right: the two writes were not atomic.

choices.label: Both are rolled back
choices.feedback: The database committed before the crash.

choices.label: The event is published twice
choices.feedback: It was never published once.

interactive.reveal: The outbox pattern writes the order and the event row in one transaction; a relay publishes the row later. The relay delivers at least once, so consumers must handle duplicates.

title: Consensus & Raft
objectives: Explain what consensus provides
Walk through a Raft write and election
Size a cluster for a number of failures

cards.title: What consensus solves
cards.body: Several nodes must agree on one ordered log of commands even when some crash. Raft and Paxos do this; etcd, Consul and ZooKeeper use them to hold config, locks and leader information.

cards.title: Raft in brief
cards.body: One leader accepts writes, appends them to its log and replicates them to followers. An entry is committed once a majority has stored it. If followers stop hearing heartbeats, one starts an election for a new term and wins with a majority of votes.

cards.title: A Raft write
cards.body: A Raft write is committed once a majority of nodes has it in their log; only then does the leader apply it and answer the client.
steps: Client sends the write to the leader
Leader appends it to its log
Leader replicates to followers
A majority acknowledges
Leader commits and applies it

cards.title: Majorities and fault tolerance
cards.body: N nodes need a majority, floor(N/2) + 1, so they tolerate floor((N − 1)/2) failures: 3 nodes survive 1, 5 survive 2. Even sizes add cost without adding tolerance.

cards.title: Trap: two-node consensus
cards.body: Running consensus on 2 nodes, or putting a high-latency link in every write. Two nodes cannot lose one and keep a majority, and every commit waits for the slowest member of the majority.

questions.prompt: How many failures does a 5-node Raft cluster tolerate?
questions.explanation: A majority of 3 must stay up.

questions.prompt: Smallest cluster that tolerates 3 failures with majority quorums?
questions.explanation: Design implication: every extra tolerated failure costs two more nodes and a larger majority on each write, so most clusters run 3 or 5 nodes.

questions.prompt: Order a Raft write.

items.label: Client sends the write to the leader
Leader appends it to its log
Leader replicates to followers
A majority acknowledges
Leader commits and applies it

questions.explanation: Commit needs a majority, not everyone.

questions.prompt: Followers stop receiving heartbeats from the leader. What happens?

choices.label: The cluster waits, accepting no writes, until the old leader comes back
Each follower declares itself leader and accepts writes in parallel
A follower starts an election for a new term and needs a majority of votes
The follower with the lowest id takes over at once without any vote

questions.explanation: Terms and majority votes prevent two leaders.

questions.prompt: Why run 3 nodes rather than 4?

choices.label: Four nodes split each election vote two to two, so no leader is chosen
Four nodes cannot elect a leader because a majority needs an odd count
Four nodes still tolerate only one failure but need three acknowledgements per write
Four nodes tolerate two failures, so they are safer but cost more

questions.explanation: Majority of 4 is 3, so tolerance stays at 1.

questions.prompt: How many node failures can a five-node Raft cluster tolerate while still committing writes?
questions.explanation: A majority of 5 is 3, so 2 nodes can fail and 3 still form a majority.

flashcards.front: How many failures does a 5-node Raft cluster tolerate?
flashcards.back: 2. A majority of 3 must stay up.

flashcards.front: Followers stop receiving heartbeats from the leader. What happens?
flashcards.back: A follower starts an election for a new term and needs a majority of votes. Terms and majority votes prevent two leaders.
Four nodes still tolerate only one failure but need three acknowledgements per write. Majority of 4 is 3, so tolerance stays at 1.

mechanism.title: How Raft elects a leader and commits an entry
steps: Every node is a follower, a candidate or the leader, and time is divided into numbered terms.

Followers expect regular heartbeats from the leader. If none arrives within a randomised election timeout (for example 150–300 ms), a follower becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself and asks others for votes.

A node grants at most one vote per term, and only to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader; randomised timeouts make split votes rare.
Clients send commands to the leader, which appends each command to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers.

Once a majority of nodes (including the leader) have stored the entry, the leader marks it committed, applies it to its state machine and replies to the client. Followers apply it when they learn the commit index.
A leader from an old term that comes back sees a higher term in any reply and steps down, so there is at most one leader per term whose entries can commit.

useWhen: Small, critical, strongly consistent state: cluster membership, configuration, leader election, locks, metadata (etcd, ZooKeeper’s similar Zab protocol, Consul, Kafka KRaft).
Replicated databases that need linearizable writes, such as CockroachDB and TiKV, which run Raft per range.
avoidWhen: Bulk high-throughput data paths where every write paying a majority round trip is too expensive and eventual consistency is acceptable.
Clusters of two or four nodes: the even node adds cost without adding fault tolerance.

numbers.title: Commit latency of a three-region Raft group
assumptions: Leader in Mumbai; followers in Hyderabad (about 20 ms round trip) and Singapore (about 60 ms), illustrative
steps: The leader needs one follower’s acknowledgement for a majority of 2 out of 3.
The fastest follower is Hyderabad at about 20 ms, plus about 1 ms fsync on each side.
Commit latency is therefore roughly 22 ms, set by the second-fastest node (counting the leader), not the slowest.
If Hyderabad fails, commits wait for Singapore and latency rises to roughly 62 ms.
numbers.result: Raft commit latency is the round trip to the nearest majority; placing replicas decides both latency and which failures you survive.

india.title: Configuration store for a payments platform
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A payments company might keep feature flags, routing rules for bank partners and service leadership in an etcd or ZooKeeper cluster of five nodes spread across three availability zones. If one zone goes down, the remaining nodes still form a majority of three, so a new leader is elected within about a second and configuration stays writable. Because every write goes through the Raft log, two services can never see conflicting answers to “which node is the settlement leader”. The trade-off is that this store is slow for bulk data, so transaction records live elsewhere; only small, critical metadata goes through consensus.

pitfalls.trap: Deploying a four-node consensus cluster “for more safety”.
pitfalls.say: “Four nodes need three for a majority and still tolerate only one failure; I’d use three or five.”

pitfalls.trap: Using consensus for every piece of data.
pitfalls.say: “Consensus pays a majority round trip per write; I’d use it for metadata and leader election and keep bulk data elsewhere.”

takeaways: A majority of 2f + 1 nodes tolerates f failures.
Randomised election timeouts make split votes rare.
An entry commits once a majority stores it.
Terms ensure an old leader steps down when it returns.
deep.diagram:
client -> LEADER (term 7) --AppendEntries--> F1 ack
                         \--AppendEntries--> F2 (slow)
 majority (leader + F1) stored -> commit -> apply -> reply

interactive.title: How many nodes to survive f failures?
interactive.prompt: A majority-quorum cluster (Raft, etcd, ZooKeeper) must keep working when some nodes fail. Change how many failures it must survive.
interactive.takeaway: You need 2f + 1 nodes: 3 survive one failure, 5 survive two. A fourth node adds cost without extra tolerance, and every extra node is one more acknowledgement on the write path, so most clusters run 3 or 5.

title: Leader Election & Distributed Locks
objectives: Coordinate exclusive access across services with leases, fencing, and caution.

cards.title: Locks with leases
cards.body: Redis SET NX PX gives a simple lock with TTL; ZooKeeper/etcd give safer locks. Always bound locks with TTLs and design for lock loss.

cards.title: Taking and losing a lock safely
cards.body: SET NX PX takes the lock with a lease; the holder works and releases it, and if it crashes the lease expires so others can proceed.
steps: Request lock
SET key NX PX
Got it? do work
Release
TTL auto-expires on crash

cards.title: Worked example: lease and renewal timing
cards.body: Assume: Lease TTL 10 s, renewal every 3 s; Worst observed GC pause 2 s, network delay 1 s.
steps: Between renewals there are 3 s of normal work, plus up to 2 s of pause and 1 s of network delay before the renewal lands.
Worst-case gap is 3 plus 2 plus 1, so 6 s, which is under the 10 s TTL, leaving 4 s of slack.
Failover takes up to the TTL: if the holder dies, others wait about 10 s before taking over.
A longer pause, say 12 s, would exceed the TTL, so fencing tokens are still required for safety.
cards.note: Choose the TTL so normal renewals have slack, and accept that failover takes about one TTL; fencing covers the pauses timing cannot.

cards.title: Trap: locks without a TTL
cards.body: Holding a lock without a TTL: a crashed holder blocks everyone forever.

cards.title: Fencing tokens
cards.body: A lock holder can pause (GC, network) past its lease while another node takes the lock. Give each grant an increasing token and make storage reject writes with an older token, so a paused former holder cannot corrupt data.

cards.title: Leader election
cards.body: Leader election is a long-lived lock: one node wins a lease in etcd or ZooKeeper, renews it while healthy, and another takes over when it expires. Use it for singletons such as a scheduler.

questions.prompt: Why must a distributed lock have a TTL?

choices.label: To spread the lock load across Redis nodes
To make acquiring the lock faster under very heavy load
To let the same holder take the lock twice
So a crashed holder does not block everyone forever

questions.explanation: Leases expire on their own.

questions.prompt: Lease TTL is 10 s; the holder hits a 12 s GC pause. Without fencing, how many nodes may believe they hold the lock at once?
questions.formula: A pause longer than the lease lets a second node acquire the lock: 1 + 1
questions.workedAnswer: The pause outlasts the lease, so a second node acquires the lock while the first still thinks it owns it: 2.
questions.explanation: Design implication: two holders at once means the lock alone cannot protect the data. The storage layer must reject stale writers using fencing tokens.

questions.prompt: How does a fencing token stop a paused former lock holder?

choices.label: Redis replicates the lock to all nodes, so the old holder sees it is gone
The lock service kills the old holder’s process as soon as the lease ends
Storage rejects writes carrying a token older than the newest it has seen
The token stops the lease expiring while the holder is paused

questions.explanation: Safety is enforced where the data lives.

questions.prompt: Order safe lock usage.

items.label: Acquire the lock with a TTL
Receive a fencing token
Do the work, sending the token with each write
Release the lock (or let it expire)

questions.explanation: The token travels with the writes.

questions.prompt: Run a nightly billing job once across 50 workers.
constraints: Exactly one worker should run it

approaches.label: Leader election through an etcd lease, with fencing
Every worker runs it
Redis SET NX without a TTL

rationaleOptions.label: A lock without a TTL is safest because it never expires
Fencing stops a paused former leader from writing
Only the lease holder runs the job

rationaleConflicts.r3: A crashed holder would then block the job forever.

questions.explanation: Leases plus fencing handle both crashes and pauses.

questions.prompt: A paused lock holder wakes up after its lease expired and tries to write. What stops it from corrupting data?

choices.label: The storage rejects its lower fencing token
Its lease renews itself in the background
The network drops all its packets
Nothing; this cannot happen

questions.explanation: Each new grant gets a higher token, and the resource rejects writes with a token lower than the highest seen.

flashcards.back: SET key value NX PX ttl.
Update only if current value matches expected.

mechanism.title: Taking a distributed lock safely
steps: A client asks the lock service (etcd, ZooKeeper, or Redis with care) for lock “invoice-job” with a lease time to live, such as 10 seconds.
If granted, the service also returns a fencing token: a number that increases with every grant (in etcd the revision, in ZooKeeper the zxid or a sequence node).
The holder renews the lease periodically, for example every 3 seconds, while it works.
If the holder pauses (a long garbage-collection pause or a network blip) past the lease, the lease expires and another client gets the lock with a higher token.

Every write to the protected resource carries the token, and the resource rejects any token lower than the highest it has seen. The paused old holder, waking up with token 33 after token 34 was issued, is rejected.
Leader election is the same idea: the lock holder is the leader, and it must stop acting as leader once its lease expires.

useWhen: One active scheduler or cron runner across replicas, single-writer jobs, and leader election for a partition owner.
Coarse-grained coordination where a few seconds of failover are acceptable.
avoidWhen: Do not use a lock where a database constraint or conditional write would do; locks add a dependency and failure modes.
Do not rely on a lease alone for correctness when the protected resource cannot check fencing tokens; a paused holder can still write.

rows: Lost on failover; no fencing by default
Simple if the resource is that database

numbers.title: Lease and renewal timing
assumptions: Lease TTL 10 s, renewal every 3 s
Worst observed GC pause 2 s, network delay 1 s
steps: Between renewals there are 3 s of normal work, plus up to 2 s of pause and 1 s of network delay before the renewal lands.
Worst-case gap is 3 plus 2 plus 1, so 6 s, which is under the 10 s TTL, leaving 4 s of slack.
Failover takes up to the TTL: if the holder dies, others wait about 10 s before taking over.
A longer pause, say 12 s, would exceed the TTL, so fencing tokens are still required for safety.
numbers.result: Choose the TTL so normal renewals have slack, and accept that failover takes about one TTL; fencing covers the pauses timing cannot.

india.title: One settlement job at a time
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Consider a lending app that runs a nightly job to compute EMIs due and trigger NACH auto-debit instructions to banks. Running it twice would debit customers twice, which is unacceptable. The job runs on three pods for availability, but each must take a lease in etcd before starting, and every debit instruction carries the fencing token and a per-loan idempotency key. If the leader pod stalls during a long pause and a second pod takes over, the stalled pod’s later writes carry the lower token and are rejected by the instruction table. The lock decides who should work, while the token and idempotency keys guarantee that no one does harm.

pitfalls.trap: “I’ll use Redis SETNX as a lock for payments.”
pitfalls.say: “A single Redis lock can be lost on failover; for correctness I’d use etcd leases plus fencing tokens checked by the resource.”

pitfalls.trap: Assuming the lock holder knows when its lease expired.
pitfalls.say: “A paused process cannot tell its lease expired, so every write carries a fencing token that the storage checks.”

takeaways: Locks need leases so a dead holder does not block forever.
Leases alone are unsafe under pauses; use fencing tokens.
Use a consensus-backed store for correctness-critical locks.
Prefer constraints and conditional writes when they suffice.
deep.diagram:
A gets lock (token 33) ... long GC pause ...   lease expires
B gets lock (token 34) -> write(34) accepted
A wakes -> write(33) -> storage: 33 < 34 -> REJECTED

interactive.title: A pause longer than the lease
interactive.prompt: A lock’s lease is 10 seconds. The holder pauses for 12 seconds (a long GC pause), then writes. Another client took the lock at second 10. Without fencing tokens, what happens?

choices.label: Both clients write as the owner, and the storage accepts the stale write
choices.feedback: Right: nothing tells the storage that the first client’s lease ended.

choices.label: The paused client’s write is rejected automatically
choices.feedback: Only if the storage checks a fencing token.

choices.label: The lease extends itself during the pause
choices.feedback: Leases expire on the lock service’s clock regardless of the holder.

interactive.reveal: Hand out a fencing token that increases with each lock grant and have the storage reject writes with an older token. A lock alone cannot protect data from paused clients.

title: Lamport & Vector Clocks
objectives: Wall clocks drift; use logical clocks (Lamport, vector) or hybrid clocks for ordering.

cards.title: Ordering without trusted clocks
cards.body: NTP-synced clocks can skew by milliseconds. Lamport clocks give a causal total order; vector clocks detect concurrency. Snowflake-style IDs combine time + machine + sequence.

cards.title: Lamport timestamps across two nodes
cards.body: Each node increments its counter per event and sends it; a receiver takes max(own, received) + 1, so causes always sort before effects.
steps: Event on A
Increment counter
Send with timestamp
B takes max+1
Causal order preserved

cards.title: Worked example: Lamport timestamps step by step
cards.body: Assume: Process P starts at 0, Q starts at 0.
steps: P does a local event: P = 1. P sends message m with timestamp 2 (incremented to 2 on send).
Q does two local events: Q = 1, then Q = 2.
Q receives m (timestamp 2): Q = max(2, 2) plus 1 = 3.
So the receive event (3) is ordered after the send (2), as causality requires, even though Q’s clock started independently.
cards.note: Lamport clocks always order a receive after its send by taking the maximum and adding one.

cards.title: Trap: last-write-wins on skewed clocks
cards.body: Using server timestamps to decide “last write wins” across regions without accounting for skew.

questions.prompt: Which can tell that two updates were concurrent?

choices.label: NTP-synced wall clocks
Lamport clocks
Snowflake IDs
Vector clocks

questions.explanation: Lamport clocks give an order but cannot detect concurrency.

questions.prompt: Node B has counter 7 and receives a message stamped 12. B’s new counter?
Two regions use server time for last-write-wins and region B’s clock runs 50 ms fast. Risk?

choices.label: Reads get slower
Writes from B are rejected as late
B’s older writes can beat newer ones
Nothing: NTP keeps clocks exact

questions.explanation: Skew decides the winner, not real order.

questions.prompt: Order a Lamport clock exchange.

items.label: Event happens on A
A increments its counter
A sends a message with its counter
B sets its counter to max(own, received) + 1
Causal order is preserved

questions.explanation: Receivers jump ahead of what they have seen.

questions.prompt: What does a Lamport clock guarantee?

choices.label: Timestamps match wall-clock time
Concurrent events get equal timestamps
If A’s timestamp is smaller, A happened before B
If A happened before B, A’s timestamp is smaller

questions.explanation: The implication only goes one way.

questions.prompt: Version vectors {P:2, Q:1} and {P:1, Q:2} belong to two updates of the same key. What are they?

choices.label: Concurrent: neither happened before the other
The first update happened before the second
The second happened before the first
Identical updates

questions.explanation: Neither vector is less than or equal to the other in every entry, so the updates are concurrent.

flashcards.back: Timestamp + machine ID + sequence.
Wrong ordering for last-write-wins.

mechanism.title: How logical clocks order events without trusting wall clocks
steps: Physical clocks drift and are corrected by NTP, so two servers may disagree by milliseconds or more; “later timestamp” does not reliably mean “happened later”.
Lamport clock: each process keeps a counter. Increment it before each event; attach it to messages; on receive, set the counter to the maximum of local and received, plus 1.
This guarantees that if A happened before B, then L(A) < L(B). The reverse is not true: L(A) < L(B) does not prove A caused B.
Vector clock: each process keeps a vector with one counter per process. It increments its own entry on each event and, on receive, takes the element-wise maximum and then increments its own entry.
Compare vectors: if every entry of V(A) is less than or equal to V(B) and at least one is smaller, A happened before B. If neither dominates, the events are concurrent: a true conflict.
Stores like the original Dynamo used version vectors to detect concurrent updates and keep both versions as siblings for the application to merge.

useWhen: Lamport clocks when you need a total order consistent with causality, for example ordering operations in a log, with ties broken by process id.
Vector clocks when you must detect concurrent writes to the same data, such as multi-leader or offline-first sync.
avoidWhen: Do not use wall-clock timestamps alone for last-writer-wins on important data; clock skew silently drops writes.
Do not use vector clocks with thousands of writers per key without pruning; the vector grows with each writer.

numbers.title: Working a Lamport example
assumptions: Process P starts at 0, Q starts at 0
steps: P does a local event: P = 1. P sends message m with timestamp 2 (incremented to 2 on send).
Q does two local events: Q = 1, then Q = 2.
Q receives m (timestamp 2): Q = max(2, 2) plus 1 = 3.
So the receive event (3) is ordered after the send (2), as causality requires, even though Q’s clock started independently.
numbers.result: Lamport clocks always order a receive after its send by taking the maximum and adding one.

india.title: Offline edits to a shared shopping list
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A family in Chennai shares a grocery list in an app. Amma edits “milk ×2” to “milk ×3” on her phone in a basement with no signal, while Appa, online, changes it to “milk ×1”. When Amma’s phone reconnects, wall-clock timestamps would let whichever phone’s clock happens to be ahead silently win. With version vectors, the server sees that neither edit includes the other, so the edits are concurrent, and the app shows both values or applies a merge rule (keep the larger quantity). Detecting that a conflict exists is the clock’s job; resolving it is a product decision.

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll order events by server timestamp.”
pitfalls.say: “Server clocks skew; for causality I’d use Lamport or hybrid logical clocks, and version vectors to detect concurrent writes.”

pitfalls.trap: Claiming Lamport clocks detect concurrency.
pitfalls.say: “Lamport ordering is consistent with causality but cannot tell concurrent events apart; vector clocks can.”

takeaways: Wall clocks drift, so timestamps do not prove order.
Lamport: if A happened before B then L(A) < L(B), not the reverse.
Vector clocks detect concurrent updates.
Detecting a conflict is separate from resolving it.
deep.diagram:
P: [1] --send m(2)--> 
Q: [1] [2] --recv m--> max(2,2)+1 = [3]
vectors: {P:1,Q:0} vs {P:0,Q:1} -> neither dominates -> concurrent

interactive.title: Lamport receive rule
interactive.prompt: Node A, with counter 5, sends a message to node B, whose counter is 3. What is B’s counter after receiving it?

choices.feedback: Right: max(3, 5) + 1.
That ignores A’s timestamp; causes must sort before effects.
Counters take the maximum, they don’t add.

interactive.reveal: On receive, a Lamport clock jumps to max(local, received) + 1, so a message’s send always sorts before its receipt. Vector clocks go further and can tell when two events were concurrent.

title: Gossip & Failure Detection
objectives: Explain how gossip spreads cluster state
Compare fixed timeouts with phi-accrual detection
Avoid false failure declarations

cards.title: Gossip
cards.body: Every second each node picks a few random peers and swaps what it knows: membership, heartbeats, versions. News reaches the whole cluster in about log N rounds with no central server, which is why Cassandra and Consul use it.

cards.title: Failure detection
cards.body: Nodes send heartbeats. A fixed timeout declares a node dead after one missed beat and flaps during GC pauses. Phi-accrual detectors output a suspicion level from recent arrival times, so slow-but-alive nodes are not evicted.

cards.title: One gossip round
cards.body: Each round, nodes swap state with a few random peers and keep the newer entries, so news reaches the whole cluster in a few rounds.
steps: Node picks random peers
They exchange state with version numbers
Each keeps the newer entries
Repeat every second
Cluster converges

cards.title: Suspect before dead
cards.body: SWIM-style detectors ask other nodes to ping a silent node before marking it suspect, then dead. Indirect checks avoid blaming a node for one bad network path.

cards.title: Trap: dead after one missed beat
cards.body: Declaring a node dead on one missed heartbeat. A GC pause triggers a rebalance, the node comes back, and data moves twice.

questions.prompt: Gossip reaches N nodes in roughly how many rounds?

choices.label: O(N²)
O(log N)
O(N)
Just one

questions.explanation: Each round roughly doubles who knows.

questions.prompt: Each node tells one random peer per round, so the number who know roughly doubles. About how many rounds to reach 1,000 nodes?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: gossip spreads in about log₂(N) rounds, so going from 1,000 to 1,000,000 nodes only doubles the rounds, from about 10 to about 20.

questions.prompt: What does a phi-accrual detector output?

choices.label: The leader’s term number
The node’s CPU usage
A suspicion level based on recent heartbeat timing
Dead or alive, decided after a single missed heartbeat

questions.explanation: A level lets you pick a threshold per use.

questions.prompt: Node A cannot reach node C. Before marking C dead, a SWIM-style detector:

choices.label: Waits for C to win the next leader election
Asks other nodes to ping C indirectly
Removes C at once
Restarts C

questions.explanation: One bad path should not condemn a node.

questions.prompt: Order one gossip round.

items.label: Node picks random peers
They exchange state with versions
Each keeps the newer entries
Repeat next second

questions.explanation: Versions decide what is newer.

questions.prompt: Why does SWIM ask other nodes to ping a node that missed a direct ping?

choices.label: So one bad network path does not mark it dead
To elect that node as the new leader
To copy its data to the other nodes
To raise the replication factor for all of its data

questions.explanation: Indirect probes distinguish a dead node from a single failed link, reducing false positives.

flashcards.front: Gossip reaches N nodes in roughly how many rounds?
flashcards.back: O(log N). Each round roughly doubles who knows.

flashcards.front: What does a phi-accrual detector output?
flashcards.back: A suspicion level based on recent heartbeat timing. A level lets you pick a threshold per use.

flashcards.front: Node A cannot reach node C. Before marking C dead, a SWIM-style detector:
flashcards.back: Asks other nodes to ping C indirectly. One bad path should not condemn a node.

mechanism.title: How gossip spreads state and detects failures
steps: Every second (one gossip round), each node picks a few random peers and exchanges what it knows: membership, heartbeat counters, versions of metadata.
Each node merges what it hears, keeping the newer version of each entry. Information spreads like an epidemic: the number of informed nodes roughly multiplies each round.
Failure detection: each node increments its own heartbeat counter; if a node’s counter stops increasing in what others hear, it becomes suspect.
A phi-accrual detector (used by Cassandra and Akka) outputs a suspicion level from the observed distribution of heartbeat arrival times, instead of a fixed timeout, adapting to slow networks.
SWIM-style indirect probing: if node A’s direct ping to B fails, A asks a few other nodes to ping B. Only if they also fail is B marked suspect, which avoids false alarms from one bad link.
Suspect nodes get a grace period to refute (by gossiping a higher incarnation number) before being declared dead.

useWhen: Large clusters (hundreds to thousands of nodes) that need membership and failure information without a central coordinator: Cassandra, Consul’s Serf, many service meshes.
Spreading eventually consistent metadata such as schema versions and load figures.
avoidWhen: Strongly consistent decisions such as electing exactly one leader; use consensus for those.
Tiny clusters where a simple central health check is easier to reason about.

rows: Server is a single point of failure
About log n rounds to spread
A few messages per node per round

numbers.title: How fast gossip reaches everyone
assumptions: Each informed node tells 2 random peers per 1-second round (fan-out 2)
steps: Informed nodes roughly triple each round at first: 1, then 3, then 9, then 27.
3 to the power 6 is 729 and 3 to the power 7 is 2,187, so about 7 rounds cover 1,000 nodes in the ideal case.
Random duplicates slow the tail, so in practice allow roughly 10 rounds, about 10 seconds.
Each node sends only 2 messages per round regardless of cluster size, about 2,000 messages per second cluster-wide.
numbers.result: Gossip spreads to 1,000 nodes in roughly log-base-3 of 1,000, about 7 rounds ideal and about 10 in practice, at a constant cost per node.

india.title: A storage cluster across zones
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Imagine a Cassandra cluster of 300 nodes for a messaging app, spread across three zones in an Indian cloud region. A brief network hiccup in one zone delays some heartbeats. A fixed 2-second timeout would mark healthy nodes dead and trigger needless data movement, while the phi-accrual detector notices that heartbeat delays were already variable and raises suspicion gradually. Membership changes spread to all 300 nodes through gossip within a few seconds, without any central server that could itself fail.

pitfalls.trap: “A central server will ping every node.”
pitfalls.say: “At hundreds of nodes I’d use gossip with SWIM-style indirect probes so there is no central failure point and fewer false positives.”

pitfalls.trap: Using gossip for leader election.
pitfalls.say: “Gossip is eventually consistent; leader election needs consensus such as Raft.”

takeaways: Gossip spreads information in about log n rounds.
Load per node stays constant as the cluster grows.
Phi-accrual adapts suspicion to observed network behaviour.
Indirect probes reduce false failure detections.
deep.diagram:
round 1: A -> B, C
round 2: A, B, C -> 6 more
round 3: ... ~3x per round -> all 1,000 nodes in ~7-10 rounds

interactive.title: How fast does gossip spread?
interactive.prompt: Each round, everyone who knows the news tells one random peer, so the number who know roughly doubles. Grow the cluster.
interactive.takeaway: Rounds grow with log₂ N: about 10 rounds for 1,000 nodes, 20 for a million. Real protocols need a few extra rounds because random peers overlap, but growth stays logarithmic, which is why gossip scales.

title: Bloom Filters/HyperLogLog/Count-Min
objectives: Choose the right probabilistic structure for a question
State the error each one makes
Size memory savings at scale

cards.title: Answers that are almost right
cards.body: At billions of items exact answers get expensive. Probabilistic structures trade a small, known error for tiny memory: kilobytes instead of gigabytes.

cards.title: Which one when
cards.body: Bloom filter: “have I seen this?” (false positives possible, no false negatives). HyperLogLog: “how many distinct?” (about 1% error in ~12 KB). Count-Min Sketch: “how often?” (may overcount, never undercounts).

cards.title: Crawler deduplication
cards.body: The crawler asks the Bloom filter first: “definitely new” URLs are fetched, “probably seen” ones are skipped (rarely, a new URL is skipped by mistake).
steps: New URL found
Check Bloom filter
Probably seen: skip
Definitely new: fetch and add to filter

cards.title: Trap: false positives that hurt
cards.body: Using a Bloom filter where a false positive is harmful, such as deciding a username is taken. A false positive there blocks a real user; confirm against the database.

questions.prompt: Count daily unique visitors across 500M events with little memory. Which structure?

choices.label: Count-Min sketch
HyperLogLog
A hash set of all visitor ids
Bloom filter

questions.explanation: HLL estimates distinct counts in kilobytes.

questions.prompt: A Bloom filter says a URL is not present. What do you know?

choices.label: It is probably not in the set
The filter is full
It is definitely not in the set
It might be there; check the database

questions.explanation: Bloom filters have false positives, never false negatives.

questions.prompt: Track how often each search term appears per minute in tiny memory. Which?

choices.label: Bloom filter
Count-Min sketch
HyperLogLog

flashcards.front: Which error can a Bloom filter make?
flashcards.back: False positives (says seen when not). Never false negatives.
The number of distinct items, with about 1% error in kilobytes.
Approximate frequencies; it may overcount but never undercounts.

mechanism.title: How the three probabilistic structures work
steps: Bloom filter: a bit array of m bits and k hash functions. To add an item, set the k bits its hashes point to. To query, check those k bits: if any is 0, the item is definitely absent; if all are 1, it is probably present.
False positives happen when other items happened to set all k bits. False negatives never happen, unless items are deleted, which a plain Bloom filter does not support.

HyperLogLog: hash each item, use the first few bits to pick one of many registers, and record the longest run of leading zeros seen in the rest. Rare long runs imply many distinct items; averaging across registers gives a count estimate.
Redis HyperLogLog uses about 12 KB per counter and has a standard error of about 0.81%, whether it counts thousands or billions of distinct items.

Count-Min Sketch: a small table of d rows by w counters. Each item increments one counter per row; its estimated count is the minimum of its d counters. Estimates may be too high (collisions), never too low.
All three trade a small, bounded error for huge memory savings, and all merge easily across servers.

useWhen: Bloom: skip disk lookups for keys that are not there (LSM SSTables), avoid cache penetration, check “username probably taken” before hitting the database.
HyperLogLog for unique visitors; Count-Min for heavy hitters such as top search terms or abusive IPs.
avoidWhen: Any case where a false positive causes harm without a fallback check, such as blocking a payment.
Exact billing counts; use exact counters or logs for anything charged money.

numbers.title: Sizing a Bloom filter
steps: Optimal bits per item is about 1.44 × log2(1 ÷ 0.01), and log2(100) ≈ 6.64, so about 9.6 bits per item.
Optimal number of hash functions is about 9.6 × 0.693 ≈ 6.6, so use 7.
numbers.result: A 1% Bloom filter over 100 million keys fits in about 120 MB with 7 hash functions, far smaller than storing the keys.

india.title: Daily unique viewers of a streaming show
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: An OTT app wants “unique viewers today” for each of thousands of shows across India. Exact sets of user ids would need gigabytes per popular show. A HyperLogLog per show per day takes about 12 KB in Redis, and the app can merge per-region counters to get national totals with under 1% error, which is fine for a dashboard. For billing advertisers by impressions, though, the company would use exact event logs processed in a warehouse, because an error of even 0.8% on a large invoice is real money.

pitfalls.trap: Saying a Bloom filter can return false negatives.
pitfalls.say: “A Bloom filter can say probably present when absent, but never absent when present.”

pitfalls.trap: Using approximate counts for billing.
pitfalls.say: “HyperLogLog is fine for dashboards; billing uses exact logs.”

takeaways: Bloom filters: no false negatives, tunable false positives.
About 9.6 bits per item gives a 1% false-positive rate.
HyperLogLog counts distinct items in about 12 KB with under 1% error.
Count-Min overestimates frequencies; never use sketches for billing.

Bloom (m bits, k=3): add 'ravi' -> set bits 3, 9, 14
query 'anu' -> bits 3, 7, 14 -> bit 7 is 0 -> definitely absent
query 'om'  -> bits 3, 9, 14 all 1 -> probably present (check DB)

interactive.title: A job for a Bloom filter
interactive.prompt: Which job suits a Bloom filter on its own?

choices.label: A crawler skipping URLs it has probably already fetched
choices.feedback: Right: an occasional skipped new URL is harmless.

choices.label: Telling a user at sign-up that their username is taken, with no second check
choices.feedback: A false positive would block a real, available username.

choices.label: Counting unique visitors exactly

interactive.reveal: Bloom filters never give false negatives but sometimes give false positives. Use them where a false positive is cheap, or confirm a positive against the real store.

title: Monolith vs Microservices
objectives: Start with a modular monolith; split services along team and domain boundaries when needed.

cards.title: What microservices cost
cards.body: Microservices give independent deploys and scaling but add network calls, distributed data and ops cost. A modular monolith keeps boundaries without the overhead.

cards.title: When to extract a service
cards.body: Start with a modular monolith; extract a module into a service only when team or scaling pressure justifies it, and give it its own data.
steps: Monolith
Modular boundaries
Team/scale pressure
Extract service
Own its data

cards.title: Worked example: what a network hop costs a request
cards.body: Assume: A page needs 6 sequential calls between components; In-process call about 0.01 ms; network call about 2 ms at p50 and 20 ms at p99.
steps: Monolith: 6 calls × 0.01 ms = 0.06 ms of call overhead.
Microservices at p50: 6 calls × 2 ms = 12 ms.
At p99, if each call independently has a 1% chance of 20 ms, the chance that at least one of 6 is slow is 1 minus 0.99 to the power 6, about 5.9%.
So roughly 1 request in 17 hits at least one slow hop, which is why tail latency grows with call depth.
cards.note: Every service boundary on the request path adds milliseconds and multiplies tail-latency risk; keep call chains shallow or parallel.

cards.title: Trap: 15 services for 3 people
cards.body: Splitting a 3-person team’s app into 15 services.

choices.label: Microservices are the modern default for any new application
A team needs to deploy and scale that part independently
A team wants to try a new language for that part
The codebase has passed 10,000 lines of code

questions.explanation: Split along team and scaling needs.

questions.prompt: Which is a real cost of microservices?

choices.label: Network calls, distributed data and more to operate
Less independent scaling of each part

Slower local function calls inside each single service

questions.explanation: Calls become network hops; data spreads out.

questions.prompt: A three-person startup wants clear boundaries without ops overhead. What fits?

choices.label: A serverless function per endpoint

questions.explanation: A modular monolith enforces module boundaries in code while keeping one deployable, so a team gets structure without network calls or distributed data.

Payments can scale separately

rationaleConflicts.r3: The service needs its own data, and function calls become network calls.

questions.explanation: Extract where team and scaling pressure are real.

questions.prompt: A request crosses 6 network hops, each with a 1% chance of being slow. About what share of requests hit at least one slow hop?

choices.label: About 6%
About 60%

questions.explanation: 1 minus 0.99 to the power 6 is about 5.9%, so tail latency grows with call depth.

flashcards.back: One deployable with strict internal module boundaries.
Each service owns its data.

mechanism.title: Growing from a modular monolith to services
steps: Start with one deployable application split into modules with clear boundaries: orders, payments, catalogue, users. Each module owns its tables, and other modules call it only through its public interface.
Enforce boundaries with code rules (no reaching into another module’s tables or internals), so a later split is mechanical rather than archaeological.
Watch for real pressure: a module that needs a very different scale (search), a different release cadence, a team that is blocked by everyone else’s deploys, or a different technology.
Extract that one module: give it its own database, replace in-process calls with an API or events, and run both paths behind a flag until the new service is proven (the strangler fig pattern).
Pay the new costs knowingly: network calls that fail, distributed tracing, versioned APIs, data duplication, sagas instead of transactions, and on-call for one more system.
Repeat only when another module shows the same pressure; many companies stop at a handful of services.

useWhen: Microservices when several teams need to deploy independently, or parts of the system have very different scaling or reliability needs.
A modular monolith for small teams, new products and domains that are still changing shape.
avoidWhen: Do not start a five-person startup with twenty microservices; you pay distributed-systems costs before having product-market fit.
Do not split along technical layers (a 'database service', a 'validation service'); split along business capabilities.

numbers.title: What a network hop costs a request
assumptions: A page needs 6 sequential calls between components
In-process call about 0.01 ms; network call about 2 ms at p50 and 20 ms at p99
steps: Monolith: 6 calls × 0.01 ms = 0.06 ms of call overhead.
Microservices at p50: 6 calls × 2 ms = 12 ms.
At p99, if each call independently has a 1% chance of 20 ms, the chance that at least one of 6 is slow is 1 minus 0.99 to the power 6, about 5.9%.
So roughly 1 request in 17 hits at least one slow hop, which is why tail latency grows with call depth.
numbers.result: Every service boundary on the request path adds milliseconds and multiplies tail-latency risk; keep call chains shallow or parallel.

india.title: A fintech start-up’s first three years
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A Bengaluru lending start-up launches with a modular monolith: onboarding, KYC, loan ledger, collections and notifications as modules in one codebase and one PostgreSQL database. In year two, KYC calls slow external verification APIs and needs to scale separately, and the notifications module is being changed weekly by a growth team, so both are extracted into services connected by events. The loan ledger stays inside the monolith because it needs multi-table ACID transactions and changes carefully. Three years in, they run five services, not fifty, each extracted for a reason they can state.

pitfalls.trap: “Microservices are the modern way, so I’d start with them.”
pitfalls.say: “With one team I’d build a modular monolith with strict module boundaries and extract a service only when scaling or team independence demands it.”

pitfalls.trap: Splitting the database last.
pitfalls.say: “A service that shares tables with others is not independent; extraction includes giving it its own data.”

takeaways: Start with a modular monolith and clear boundaries.
Extract services for scaling, team independence or technology needs.
Every service boundary costs latency, failure handling and operations.
Split by business capability, and give each service its own data.

interactive.reveal: Microservices pay off when teams and scaling needs diverge. Start modular, then extract a service when a boundary is proven and the team or load justifies it.

title: API Gateway
objectives: A single entry point that handles auth, rate limiting, routing, and request aggregation.

cards.title: What belongs in a gateway
cards.body: The gateway terminates client traffic, verifies tokens, applies quotas, routes to services and can aggregate responses. It keeps cross-cutting concerns out of each service.

cards.title: A mobile call through the gateway
cards.body: The gateway authenticates the token, applies rate limits and routes the call to the right service, keeping these concerns out of each service.
steps: Mobile client
API gateway
Auth + rate limit
Route
Microservice

cards.title: Worked example: latency of an aggregation endpoint
cards.body: Assume: Home screen needs profile (30 ms), offers (50 ms) and orders (80 ms); Gateway overhead 3 ms.
steps: Sequential calls: 30 + 50 + 80 = 160 ms, plus 3 ms overhead, so 163 ms.
Parallel calls: the slowest dominates, so 80 ms plus 3 ms = 83 ms.
If offers is optional, a 60 ms timeout with a fallback (empty carousel) caps its effect on the page.
Then the page waits for the slower of profile (30 ms) and orders (80 ms), still 83 ms; to go faster, orders itself must get quicker or be loaded after first paint.
cards.note: Parallel fan-out in a BFF roughly halves this screen’s latency from 163 ms to 83 ms; timeouts keep optional parts from dragging it out.

cards.title: Trap: business logic in the gateway
cards.body: Putting business logic in the gateway. It becomes a bottleneck and a deployment choke point.

questions.prompt: Which belongs in an API gateway?

choices.label: Choosing which products to recommend
Calculating order discounts

Writing orders to the database

questions.explanation: Cross-cutting concerns, not business logic.

choices.label: Force the app to call each service
Replace the four services
Call them and return one response
Store all four services’ data

choices.label: Each service must then share one database
The gateway can no longer route requests
Tokens stop being verified at the gateway
Each change needs a gateway deploy: a bottleneck

questions.explanation: Keep the gateway thin.

questions.explanation: Move discount logic into a service and keep the gateway thin.

choices.label: About 83 ms
About 163 ms
About 30 ms
About 240 ms

flashcards.back: Putting business logic in it.
Backend-for-frontend: a gateway tailored to one client type.

mechanism.title: What an API gateway does to each request
steps: Terminates TLS for the public domain and normalises the request (headers, request id).
Authenticates the caller: validates the JWT or session, or the API key, and attaches identity claims for downstream services.
Applies cross-cutting policy: rate limits per user or key, request size limits, IP allow or deny lists, and CORS.
Routes by path, host or version to the right internal service, often through service discovery, with timeouts and retries.
Optionally aggregates: a backend-for-frontend (BFF) endpoint calls several services in parallel and returns one response shaped for the mobile app.
Records metrics, logs and the trace id, so every downstream call can be correlated.

useWhen: One public entry point for many internal services, with consistent authentication, rate limiting and observability.
A BFF per client type when mobile and web need differently shaped responses.
avoidWhen: Do not put business logic (pricing rules, order validation) in the gateway; it becomes a shared monolith every team must change, and every release of it risks every API.
Do not chain many sequential downstream calls in an aggregation endpoint; parallelise or move the composition into a service.

numbers.title: Latency of an aggregation endpoint
assumptions: Home screen needs profile (30 ms), offers (50 ms) and orders (80 ms)
steps: Sequential calls: 30 + 50 + 80 = 160 ms, plus 3 ms overhead, so 163 ms.
Parallel calls: the slowest dominates, so 80 ms plus 3 ms = 83 ms.
If offers is optional, a 60 ms timeout with a fallback (empty carousel) caps its effect on the page.
Then the page waits for the slower of profile (30 ms) and orders (80 ms), still 83 ms; to go faster, orders itself must get quicker or be loaded after first paint.
numbers.result: Parallel fan-out in a BFF roughly halves this screen’s latency from 163 ms to 83 ms; timeouts keep optional parts from dragging it out.

india.title: Mobile home screen of a super-app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: An Indian super-app’s home screen shows wallet balance, recharge shortcuts, offers, recent transactions and movie tickets. Making the phone call five services over a patchy 4G connection would cost five round trips at maybe 100 ms each. Instead, a mobile BFF behind the gateway accepts one request, calls the services in parallel inside the data centre where each hop is a few milliseconds, applies timeouts and fallbacks (offers can be skipped), and returns one compact JSON payload. The gateway in front handles authentication and rate limits once for all of them.

pitfalls.trap: Putting discount calculation in the gateway.
pitfalls.say: “The gateway handles authentication, rate limits and routing; pricing lives in the pricing service so its team owns it.”

pitfalls.trap: Making the gateway a single point of failure.
pitfalls.say: “The gateway runs as several stateless instances behind a load balancer across zones, and its config is versioned and rolled out like code.”

pitfalls.trap: Treating the gateway as authorisation for everything.
pitfalls.say: “The gateway checks the token and scopes; each service still checks that this user may access this resource.”

takeaways: The gateway centralises TLS, auth, rate limiting, routing and tracing.
Keep business logic in services, not the gateway.
BFF endpoints aggregate in parallel with timeouts and fallbacks.
Services still enforce fine-grained authorisation.

choices.label: In the CDN
choices.feedback: CDNs cache and deliver; they shouldn’t compute prices.

interactive.reveal: Keep gateways thin: authenticate, apply quotas, route, maybe aggregate. Rules that change with the business go in services that own them and can be tested and deployed on their own.

title: Service Discovery
objectives: Explain why services need discovery
Compare client-side and server-side discovery
Keep registries accurate with heartbeats

cards.title: Why instance addresses keep changing
cards.body: Instances come and go with autoscaling and deploys, so their addresses change. Callers need a live list of healthy instances for each service.

cards.title: Registries and heartbeats
cards.body: Instances register with a registry (Consul, etcd, Eureka) on start and send heartbeats; dead ones expire. In Kubernetes, a Service and its DNS name do this for you.

cards.title: Client-side vs server-side
cards.body: Client-side discovery: the caller asks the registry and picks an instance itself. Server-side: the caller hits a load balancer or DNS name, which picks for it. Server-side keeps clients simple.

cards.title: A call with discovery
cards.body: Instances register and heartbeat; callers ask the registry for healthy instances, and entries that stop heartbeating expire.
steps: Instance starts and registers
It sends heartbeats
Caller looks up “payments”
Registry returns healthy instances
Caller calls one; dead instances expire from the list

cards.title: Trap: hard-coded IPs
cards.body: Hard-coding IPs in config, or caching lookups with no refresh. Deploys then send traffic to instances that no longer exist.

questions.prompt: Why do microservices need service discovery?

choices.label: To encrypt all traffic between the services
Instances come and go, changing addresses
To store each service’s data in one place
To version the APIs that services expose

questions.explanation: Callers need current, healthy addresses.

questions.prompt: An instance crashes without deregistering. How does the registry notice?

choices.label: Callers edit the registry by hand
The crashed instance sends a final message
It does not notice

A load balancer picks a healthy instance
The caller reads IPs from a config file
The caller queries Consul and picks an instance itself

flashcards.back: Instance addresses change with autoscaling and deploys. Callers need current, healthy addresses.
