steps: Analysis at index time: the analyser lowercases text, splits it into tokens, removes stop words if configured, and stems or normalises words ('running' to 'run'). Custom analysers can add synonyms or n-grams for typos and partial matches.
Each term maps to a postings list: the document ids containing it, with positions and frequencies.

Query time: the query string is analysed the same way, the postings lists for its terms are fetched and intersected or merged, and documents are scored, typically with BM25 using term frequency, inverse document frequency and field length.
Elasticsearch splits an index into shards across nodes; each query fans out to the shards and the coordinating node merges the top results.
New documents become searchable after a refresh (by default every second), so search is near real-time, not instant.
The primary database stays the source of truth; changes flow to the index through events or CDC, and the index can be rebuilt from scratch.

useWhen: Full-text search, typo tolerance, relevance ranking, facets and filters over millions of documents.
Log search and analytics (the ELK stack) over large volumes of semi-structured text.
avoidWhen: Do not use Elasticsearch as the primary store for orders or payments; it is not transactional and can lose recent writes in some failures.
Do not use LIKE '%term%' over a large table for search; it cannot use a normal B-tree index and scans every row.

numbers.title: Why a LIKE scan is slow
assumptions: 10,000,000 product rows, 200 bytes of searchable text each
Disk or memory scan at 1 GB per second
steps: Text to scan = 10,000,000 × 200 bytes = 2,000,000,000 bytes, about 2 GB.
At 1 GB per second that is about 2 seconds per query, with all CPU cores busy.
An inverted index looks up the postings for “paneer” directly, typically in milliseconds.
At 100 searches per second, LIKE would need about 200 seconds of scanning every second: roughly 200 cores busy just scanning, which is impractical, so you need an index.
numbers.result: Substring scans grow with table size; an inverted index grows with the number of matching documents.

india.title: Searching a grocery catalogue
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A quick-commerce app in India must find “paneer” when users type “panner”, “paneer 200g” or “पनीर”. Its search index uses an analyser with lowercasing, a synonym list (atta, wheat flour), n-grams or fuzzy matching for spelling mistakes, and a transliteration step for Hindi queries. Product data lives in PostgreSQL; a CDC pipeline updates the Elasticsearch index within a second or two of a price or stock change. Results are filtered by the user’s dark store and ranked by text match combined with popularity. If the index ever drifts, it is rebuilt from PostgreSQL overnight.

pitfalls.trap: Treating the search index as the source of truth.
pitfalls.say: “PostgreSQL owns the data; the index is a derived copy updated by CDC and rebuilt if needed.”

pitfalls.trap: Using LIKE for search at scale.
pitfalls.say: 'LIKE with a leading wildcard scans every row; I'd use an inverted index with an analyser for typos and synonyms.'

takeaways: An inverted index maps terms to the documents containing them.
The same analyser must run at index and query time.
Search is near real-time (refresh about every second).
Keep the database as source of truth; sync the index by CDC or events.
deep.diagram:
doc 7: 'Fresh Paneer 200g' -> analyse -> [fresh, paneer, 200g]
index: paneer -> [3, 7, 19]   fresh -> [7, 11]
query 'panner' -> fuzzy -> paneer -> [3, 7, 19] -> score (BM25) -> top 10

interactive.title: Why LIKE is slow
interactive.prompt: Product search runs WHERE name LIKE '%phone%' on 10 million rows. Why is it slow?

choices.label: A leading wildcard can’t use a B-tree index, so every row is scanned
choices.feedback: Right: the index is sorted by prefix, and there is no fixed prefix.

choices.label: LIKE is case-sensitive
choices.feedback: That changes results, not speed.

choices.label: The table has too many columns
choices.feedback: Columns affect row size, not the need to scan every row.

interactive.reveal: An inverted index maps each term to the documents containing it, so a search reads a few posting lists. Keep the database as the source of truth and sync the search index with CDC.

title: MapReduce & Spark
objectives: Explain map, shuffle and reduce
Say why Spark beats MapReduce for multi-step jobs
Spot and fix skew in a shuffle

cards.title: MapReduce
cards.body: Map: each worker reads a chunk and emits key-value pairs, such as (word, 1). Shuffle: pairs with the same key go to the same reducer. Reduce: combine the values per key. Moving computation to the data beats moving data.

cards.title: Counting words
cards.body: Map emits (word, 1) pairs, the shuffle groups pairs by word across machines, and reduce sums each group.
steps: Split input into chunks
Map: emit (word, 1)
Shuffle: group by word
Reduce: sum per word
Write the results

cards.title: Spark
cards.body: Spark keeps intermediate data in memory across steps instead of writing to disk after every MapReduce stage, so multi-step jobs and iterative ML run much faster. Lost partitions are recomputed from lineage.

cards.title: Shuffles are expensive
cards.body: The shuffle moves data across the network. A skewed key, such as one celebrity’s id, sends most data to one reducer, which runs for hours while the rest finish. Salt hot keys or pre-aggregate.

cards.title: Batch or stream?
cards.body: Batch jobs process a bounded dataset, such as yesterday’s orders, with high throughput and minutes-to-hours latency. Use streaming when decisions must happen in seconds.

questions.prompt: In a MapReduce word count, what happens in the shuffle?

choices.label: Each input line is split into separate words
The input files are compressed for transfer between nodes
Pairs with the same word are sent to the same reducer
The counts for each word are added together

questions.explanation: Grouping by key happens between map and reduce.

questions.prompt: Why is Spark faster than classic MapReduce for multi-step jobs?

choices.label: It runs the job on a single large machine
It keeps intermediate data in memory between steps
It skips recomputing anything, even after a failure
It skips the shuffle step between map and reduce

questions.explanation: Disk round trips between stages dominate MapReduce.

questions.prompt: Order a word-count job.

items.label: Split input into chunks
Map: emit (word, 1)
Shuffle: group by word
Reduce: sum per word
Write results

questions.explanation: Map, shuffle, reduce.

questions.prompt: A nightly job groups views by creator. One creator has 40% of all views, and one reducer runs for hours. Click the bottleneck.
questions.explanation: Salt the hot key or pre-aggregate on the map side.

questions.prompt: Which fits a nightly batch job?

choices.label: Blocking a fraudulent card swipe
Recomputing yesterday’s seller payouts
Live match score updates
Surge pricing recalculated every 30 seconds

questions.explanation: Bounded data, hours of acceptable latency.

questions.prompt: One reducer receives 20% of all records while 99 others share the rest. What dominates job time?

choices.label: The overloaded reducer, so the job slows dramatically
Nothing; Spark rebalances the keys
The map phase
The network between client and driver

questions.explanation: A job ends when its slowest task ends; a hot key creates a straggler. Salting the key spreads it.

flashcards.front: In a MapReduce word count, what happens in the shuffle?
flashcards.back: Pairs with the same word are sent to the same reducer. Grouping by key happens between map and reduce.

flashcards.front: Why is Spark faster than classic MapReduce for multi-step jobs?
flashcards.back: It keeps intermediate data in memory instead of writing to disk between steps. Disk round trips between stages dominate MapReduce.

flashcards.front: Which fits a nightly batch job?
flashcards.back: Recomputing yesterday’s seller payouts. Bounded data, hours of acceptable latency.

mechanism.title: How a MapReduce or Spark job runs
steps: Input is split into chunks (often one per storage block), and one map task per chunk runs on a node near the data.
Map: each task reads records and emits key-value pairs, for example (city, order_value) for every order.
Shuffle: pairs are partitioned by key (hash of city), written to local disk and pulled over the network so that all values for one key reach the same reducer. This is usually the most expensive step.
Reduce: each reducer aggregates the values for its keys, for example summing order values per city, and writes output files.

Spark generalises this into a graph (DAG) of stages, keeps intermediate data in memory where it fits, and recomputes lost partitions from lineage instead of writing every step to disk, which makes multi-step and iterative jobs much faster.

Skew: if one key has far more records (one huge city), its reducer runs long after the others finish. Fixes include salting the key into several sub-keys and combining afterwards, or broadcasting a small table instead of shuffling the big one.

useWhen: Large batch transformations and aggregations over data far bigger than one machine: daily reports, feature generation, backfills.
Spark for multi-step pipelines, iterative machine learning and SQL over a data lake.
avoidWhen: Interactive queries on small data; a single database or DuckDB is faster and simpler.
Real-time needs measured in seconds; use stream processing instead.

numbers.title: Effect of skew on job time
assumptions: 100 reducers; total work 10,000 reducer-seconds spread evenly would be 100 seconds each
One key (Mumbai) holds 20% of all records
steps: Even spread: each reducer does 10,000 ÷ 100 = 100 seconds of work.
The Mumbai reducer gets 20% of all work: 10,000 × 0.2 = 2,000 seconds.
The job finishes when the slowest reducer does, so about 2,000 seconds instead of 100, a 20× slowdown.
Salting Mumbai into 20 sub-keys gives each about 100 seconds, then a tiny second step adds the 20 partial sums.
numbers.result: One hot key can make a job 20 times slower; salting spreads it across reducers.

india.title: Daily settlement reports
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A payments aggregator in India computes daily settlement files for lakhs of merchants: total captured, refunds, fees and GST per merchant. A Spark job reads the day’s transaction files from the data lake, maps each transaction to (merchant_id, amounts), shuffles by merchant and sums. A handful of very large merchants produce a large share of transactions, so the job salts their ids to spread the work, then combines the partial sums. The output feeds settlement and reconciliation, and because it is batch, a rerun after a bug fix simply recomputes the day from immutable input.

pitfalls.trap: Using Spark for a query over 2 GB.
pitfalls.say: “Two gigabytes fits on one machine; PostgreSQL or DuckDB answers faster without cluster overhead.”

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring skew.
pitfalls.say: “Merchant volume is skewed, so I’d salt the biggest merchant keys or broadcast the small dimension table to avoid one slow reducer.”

takeaways: Map emits key-value pairs; shuffle groups by key; reduce aggregates.
The shuffle is usually the most expensive step.
Spark keeps intermediates in memory and recovers via lineage.
Skewed keys dominate job time; salt them.
deep.diagram:
input splits -> map (merchant, amt) -> shuffle by key -> reduce (sum per merchant) -> output
 hot key 'M1' -> salt: M1#0..M1#19 -> partial sums -> combine

interactive.title: Which step moves the most data?
interactive.prompt: In a MapReduce word count over terabytes, which step usually sends the most data across the network?

choices.label: The shuffle
choices.feedback: Right: every (word, count) pair travels to the reducer that owns its word.

choices.label: The map
choices.feedback: Maps usually run where the data already sits.

choices.label: Writing the final result
choices.feedback: Reduced output is far smaller than the shuffled pairs.

interactive.reveal: Shuffles dominate cost, so combine early: a combiner sums counts on each mapper before the shuffle. Spark has the same rule for wide transformations.

title: Stream Processing
objectives: Contrast stream and batch processing
Explain windows and event time vs processing time
Handle late and duplicate events

cards.title: Results while data flows
cards.body: Batch jobs answer questions about yesterday. Stream processors (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming) update answers continuously, such as fraud scores within seconds of a UPI transaction.

cards.title: Windows over an unbounded stream
cards.body: Streams are unbounded, so you aggregate over windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping) or session (gaps of inactivity). Use event time, when it happened, not processing time, when it arrived.

cards.title: Counting clicks per minute
cards.body: Clicks are grouped by ad into one-minute event-time windows, and the watermark decides when a window is complete enough to emit.
steps: Clicks land in Kafka
Processor groups by ad and 1-minute event-time window
Watermark decides when a window closes
Results written to a store for dashboards

cards.title: Trap: in-order, exactly-once events
cards.body: Assuming events arrive in order and exactly once. Mobile clients send late events and brokers redeliver, so use watermarks for lateness and idempotent or transactional sinks for duplicates.

questions.prompt: Phones go offline and upload clicks 10 minutes late. Which time should per-minute counts use?

choices.label: Processing time, because it is simpler
The broker’s append time
The time the server received the upload
Event time, with a late-data watermark

questions.explanation: Count clicks when they happened.

questions.prompt: Which fits stream processing rather than a nightly batch?

choices.label: Monthly GST reports
Recomputing yesterday’s payouts
Flagging a suspicious UPI transaction within seconds
Training a model on last year’s data

questions.explanation: Seconds matter only for the first.

questions.prompt: The broker redelivers messages after a consumer restart. What keeps counts correct?

choices.label: Idempotent or transactional writes to the sink
Ignore them: counts are only approximate anyway
Use larger windows
Switch to processing time

questions.explanation: Redelivery is normal; the sink must absorb it.

questions.prompt: Order a clicks-per-minute pipeline.

items.label: Clicks land in Kafka
Processor groups by ad and 1-minute event-time window
Watermark decides when a window closes
Results written to a store for dashboards

questions.explanation: The watermark trades lateness for latency.

questions.prompt: Count clicks per ad in non-overlapping 1-minute buckets. Which window?

choices.label: Sliding
A single global window
Session
Tumbling

questions.explanation: Tumbling windows are fixed-size and do not overlap, so each event lands in exactly one window; sliding windows overlap and session windows close after a gap.

questions.prompt: Why do stream processors window by event time rather than processing time for mobile events?

choices.label: Events can arrive late, and should count in the window when they actually happened
Processing time is not available on stream servers
Event-time windows use less memory than processing time
It removes the need for checkpoints and state backups

questions.explanation: Delayed events would otherwise fall into the wrong window; watermarks decide when a window is complete.

flashcards.back: When the event happened vs when the system saw it.
Fixed-size, non-overlapping time buckets.
How long to wait for late events before closing a window.

mechanism.title: How a stream processor computes a windowed count
steps: Events (clicks, payments, rider pings) arrive continuously from a log such as Kafka, partitioned by key.
The processor (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming) reads each partition and keeps state per key, for example counts per merchant, in a local store that is checkpointed regularly.
Windows group events in time: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping 1-minute buckets), sliding or hopping (5-minute windows every minute) and session windows (closed after a gap of inactivity).
Event time is when the event happened; processing time is when it is processed. Mobile events can arrive minutes late, so correct results use event time.

Watermarks estimate how far event time has progressed ('no more events older than 12:04:30 expected'). When the watermark passes the end of a window, the window is emitted; later stragglers go to a side output or update the result.
On failure, the job restarts from the last checkpoint and replays input from the matching offsets; with transactional sinks or idempotent writes, results are exactly-once in effect.

useWhen: Fraud detection, live dashboards, alerting, surge pricing and anything that must react within seconds.
Continuous ETL that keeps search indexes, caches or warehouses fresh.
avoidWhen: Jobs where hourly or daily results are fine; batch is simpler and cheaper.
Complex joins over months of history; precompute those in batch and join the stream to the result.

numbers.title: State size for per-user 5-minute windows
assumptions: Sliding window of 5 minutes, advancing every minute, so each event belongs to 5 windows
State per user per window about 100 bytes
steps: Windows open per user at any time = 5.
State = 2,000,000 × 5 = 10,000,000 window entries.
Memory = 10,000,000 × 100 bytes = 1,000,000,000 bytes, about 1 GB, spread across the job’s parallel tasks.
A 60-minute sliding window advancing every minute would need 12 times as much, about 12 GB.
numbers.result: Window length divided by slide sets how many windows each key keeps; size state before choosing windows.

india.title: Card-fraud checks on UPI and cards
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A payments processor wants to flag a card used in Delhi and then in Chennai within ten minutes, or more than five failed attempts in a minute. A stream job keyed by card or VPA keeps recent locations and failure counts in state, using event time from the terminal or app so that delayed events from patchy networks still land in the right window. The watermark allows, say, 30 seconds of lateness; events arriving later are routed to a side output for review rather than silently dropped. Decisions flow back within a second or two, quickly enough to step up authentication on the next attempt.

pitfalls.trap: Treating late events as impossible.
pitfalls.say: “I’d set an allowed lateness, route anything later to a side output, and monitor how many events arrive late so the watermark can be tuned.”

pitfalls.trap: Windowing by processing time for mobile events.
pitfalls.say: “Mobile events arrive late, so I’d window by event time with watermarks and a lateness allowance.”

pitfalls.trap: Assuming the stream never replays.
pitfalls.say: “After a failure the job replays from the checkpoint, so sinks are idempotent or transactional.”

takeaways: Streams give second-level latency with always-on state.
Use event time and watermarks for correct windows.
Window size divided by slide multiplies state.
Checkpoints plus replay need idempotent or transactional sinks.
deep.diagram:
Kafka (keyed) -> operator (state per key, checkpoints) -> window [12:00-12:01) closes when watermark > 12:01 -> sink
 late event 12:00:40 arriving at 12:03 -> side output / update

interactive.title: A late click
interactive.prompt: Clicks are counted per minute by event time, with a 30-second watermark delay. A click from 12:00:50 arrives at 12:02:10 because the phone was offline. What happens?

choices.label: It is late: dropped, or sent to a correction path if you allow lateness
choices.feedback: Right: its window closed at about 12:01:30.

choices.label: It is counted in the 12:02 window
choices.feedback: Event-time windows place it by when it happened, not when it arrived.

choices.label: The whole stream restarts
choices.feedback: Late events are handled per window, not by restarting.

interactive.reveal: Watermarks trade completeness for latency. Pick an allowed lateness from real data, and send very late events to a correction job if exact counts matter (billing).

title: Warehouse/Lake/OLAP
objectives: OLTP serves transactions; OLAP column stores serve aggregates over huge datasets.

cards.title: Row stores vs column stores
cards.body: Row stores suit point reads/writes. Column stores (ClickHouse, BigQuery) compress columns and scan aggregates fast. Time-series DBs handle append-heavy metrics with downsampling.

cards.title: From OLTP writes to dashboards
cards.body: CDC or ETL copies changes from the transactional database into a columnar warehouse, where aggregations feed dashboards.
steps: App writes OLTP
CDC / ETL
Warehouse (columnar)
Aggregations
Dashboards

cards.title: Worked example: why columnar scans are cheaper
cards.body: Assume: 1,000,000,000 order rows, 40 columns of 8 bytes each; Query sums one column grouped by one other column.
steps: Row store reads every column: 1,000,000,000 × 320 bytes = 320,000,000,000 bytes, about 320 GB.
Column store reads 2 columns: 1,000,000,000 × 16 bytes = 16,000,000,000 bytes, about 16 GB.
With typical 5× compression on columnar data, that is about 3.2 GB.
So the same query reads roughly 100 times less data.
cards.note: Reading only the needed columns, compressed, is why warehouses scan billions of rows in seconds.

cards.title: Trap: analytics on the OLTP primary
cards.body: Running heavy analytical queries on the production OLTP database.

questions.prompt: Best store for “average delivery time per city per hour over two years”?

choices.label: The search cluster, with an aggregation query
The production PostgreSQL primary, with a new index added
Redis, with one sorted set per city
A columnar warehouse such as BigQuery or ClickHouse

questions.explanation: Large aggregates belong in OLAP.

questions.prompt: Why are column stores fast for “average price by city”?

choices.label: They read only the needed columns, which compress well
They index each column with a B-tree
They keep all rows in memory
They avoid aggregation

questions.explanation: A query touching 3 of 50 columns reads only those 3, and similar values stored together compress far better, so the scan reads a fraction of the bytes.

questions.prompt: Analysts run heavy reports on the production OLTP database. Risk?

choices.label: Long scans slow down checkout queries
Reports will be inaccurate
The database switches itself to read-only
Writes get lost

questions.explanation: Separate analytics from the transaction path.

questions.prompt: Order the path from app to dashboard.

items.label: App writes to OLTP
CDC or ETL copies changes
Warehouse stores them in columns
Aggregations run
Dashboards read them

questions.explanation: Analytics reads a copy.

questions.prompt: Which is an OLTP query?

choices.label: Top 100 products last quarter
Revenue by month over the last three years
Average delivery time per city
Insert one order and decrement its stock

questions.explanation: Small, transactional, row-level.

questions.prompt: A query sums one column of a 40-column table with a billion rows. Why is a columnar store much faster?

choices.label: It reads only the needed columns, compressed
It keeps all of the table in CPU registers
It skips about half the rows at random
It builds B-tree indexes on each column first

questions.explanation: Column stores read the touched columns only: here about 16 GB raw instead of 320 GB.

flashcards.back: Transactions vs analytics.
Reads only needed columns; high compression.

mechanism.title: From production database to dashboard
steps: OLTP databases serve the app: many small reads and writes by key, row-oriented storage, strict transactions.
Extract: copy changes out of OLTP, by nightly dumps or, better, CDC streaming.
Land raw data cheaply in a data lake (files such as Parquet on object storage).

Transform: clean, deduplicate, join and model into fact tables (orders, payments) and dimension tables (customers, cities, products). With ELT the transformation runs inside the warehouse using SQL tools such as dbt.

Load into a columnar warehouse or OLAP engine (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, ClickHouse). Columnar storage reads only the columns a query touches and compresses them well, so scans of billions of rows are fast.
Dashboards and analysts query the warehouse, never the production primary.
Partition big fact tables by date and cluster them by common filters such as city, so a query for one week reads only that week’s files instead of the whole history.

useWhen: Warehouse or OLAP for aggregates over large history: revenue by city and month, cohort retention, funnels.
A lakehouse (open table formats such as Iceberg or Delta on object storage) when many engines must read the same data cheaply.
avoidWhen: Do not run heavy analytical queries on the OLTP primary; full scans evict hot pages and slow the app.
Do not use a warehouse to serve per-user app requests at thousands per second; it is built for scans, not point lookups.

rows: Small, by key, many per second

numbers.title: Why columnar scans are cheaper
assumptions: 1,000,000,000 order rows, 40 columns of 8 bytes each
Query sums one column grouped by one other column
steps: Row store reads every column: 1,000,000,000 × 320 bytes = 320,000,000,000 bytes, about 320 GB.
Column store reads 2 columns: 1,000,000,000 × 16 bytes = 16,000,000,000 bytes, about 16 GB.
With typical 5× compression on columnar data, that is about 3.2 GB.
So the same query reads roughly 100 times less data.
numbers.result: Reading only the needed columns, compressed, is why warehouses scan billions of rows in seconds.

india.title: City-wise sales for a festive season
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: An Indian retail chain wants Diwali-week revenue by city, category and payment method, compared with last year. Running that on the order database during the sale would scan years of orders and slow checkouts. Instead, CDC streams orders into a lake every few minutes, dbt models build an orders fact table with city and product dimensions, and the warehouse answers the query over hundreds of millions of rows in seconds. The finance team accepts data that is 15 minutes old, and the checkout database never sees an analytical query.

pitfalls.trap: Assuming the warehouse is real time.
pitfalls.say: “CDC into the warehouse gives minutes of delay; for a live operations screen I’d use a stream processor or an OLAP engine like ClickHouse fed from Kafka.”

pitfalls.trap: Running reports on the production primary.
pitfalls.say: “I’d stream changes via CDC into a warehouse; dashboards query that, so the OLTP database only serves the app.”

pitfalls.trap: Serving app traffic from the warehouse.
pitfalls.say: “The warehouse is for scans; precomputed results needed by the app are exported to a cache or key-value store.”

takeaways: OLTP serves the app; OLAP serves analysis.
Columnar storage reads only needed columns and compresses well.
Use CDC and ELT to feed the warehouse without loading production.
Model analytics as facts and dimensions.
deep.diagram:
OLTP (Postgres) --CDC--> lake (Parquet) --transform (dbt)--> warehouse (facts + dims) --> dashboards
          app traffic stays here           analytics traffic stays here

interactive.title: Why the column store wins
interactive.prompt: “Average order value by city” runs over 1 billion rows in a 40-column table. Why is a column store much faster?

choices.label: It reads only the two columns it needs, compressed, instead of all 40
choices.feedback: Right: much less data comes off disk.

choices.label: Column stores always have more memory
choices.feedback: Hardware isn’t the difference; the layout is.

choices.label: It caches the query result
choices.feedback: The first run is fast too.

interactive.reveal: Row stores suit point reads and writes (OLTP). Column stores suit scans and aggregates (OLAP). Copy data from one to the other with CDC or ETL.

title: Geospatial Indexing
objectives: Explain geohash and quadtree indexing
Answer “nearby” queries without scanning every row
Handle cell boundaries and dense cities

cards.title: Nearby without a full scan
cards.body: Computing distance to every restaurant in India per request is too slow. Geospatial indexes bucket locations into cells so a query only checks nearby cells.

cards.title: Geohash and quadtrees
cards.body: Geohash encodes lat/long into a string; a shared prefix means nearby. Quadtrees split space into four until each cell holds few points, so dense Mumbai gets small cells and rural areas get big ones.

cards.title: Finding restaurants within 2 km
cards.body: Look up the user’s cell and its eight neighbours, fetch candidates from those cells, then compute exact distances and sort.
steps: Get user’s geohash cell
Add the 8 neighbouring cells
Fetch candidates from those cells
Compute exact distance and sort

cards.title: Trap: searching one cell
cards.body: Searching only the user’s own cell. A restaurant 50 m away can sit across a cell boundary, so always include neighbouring cells.

questions.prompt: A user stands at the edge of a geohash cell. Why also search the neighbouring cells?

choices.label: Geohash requires 9 cells
A restaurant 50 m away can sit just across the boundary
Neighbouring cells are already cached
To balance load across shards

questions.explanation: Cells are arbitrary lines on the map.

questions.prompt: Why might a quadtree beat fixed-size grid cells for India?

choices.label: Quadtrees need no memory beyond the points themselves
Fixed grids cannot store latitude, only longitude
Quadtrees give exact road distances between places
Cells split where points are dense (small in Mumbai)

questions.explanation: Adaptive cells keep candidate counts even.

questions.prompt: Order a “nearby within 2 km” query.

items.label: Get the user’s geohash cell
Add the 8 neighbouring cells
Fetch candidates from those cells
Compute exact distance and sort

questions.explanation: Coarse filter, then exact check.

questions.prompt: Two geohashes share a long prefix. What does that tell you?

choices.label: They are in the same country only
They are close together
One is north of the other
Nothing: prefixes are random

questions.explanation: A shared prefix means a shared cell.

questions.prompt: Index for “restaurants near me” across India.

approaches.label: Fixed grid of large cells
Quadtree (or geohash) index
Scan every restaurant

rationaleOptions.label: Each query touches only a few cells
Dense cities get finer cells
Scanning every restaurant is fine on fast CPUs

rationaleConflicts.r3: Computing distance to every restaurant per request is far too slow at this scale.

questions.explanation: Index space so queries stay local.

questions.prompt: Why does a nearby search read the user’s geohash cell plus its 8 neighbours?

choices.label: Close points can sit just across a cell boundary with a different prefix
To make the geohash index smaller in memory
Because geohashes only work in groups of nine cells
To avoid computing any distances to the points

questions.explanation: Cell edges split nearby points; the neighbours cover that, then exact distance filters the candidates.

flashcards.front: What does a shared geohash prefix mean?
flashcards.back: The points are close (with edge cases at cell boundaries).

flashcards.front: Why do quadtrees suit uneven density?
flashcards.back: They split dense areas into smaller cells.
Nearby points can fall just across a cell boundary.

mechanism.title: Finding nearby drivers with geohashes
steps: A geohash encodes latitude and longitude into a string by repeatedly halving the world, interleaving longitude and latitude bits, and writing them in base 32. Each extra character narrows the cell.
Points in the same cell share a prefix, so a prefix lookup in a sorted index or a hash map finds them quickly.
Precision examples (approximate): 5 characters is about 4.9 km by 4.9 km; 6 characters about 1.2 km by 0.6 km; 7 characters about 153 m by 153 m.
To search “within 2 km”, choose a precision whose cells are about the radius, look up the user’s cell and its 8 neighbours, because a nearby driver may sit just across a cell edge.
Filter candidates by exact distance (haversine) and rank by distance or estimated arrival time.
Alternatives: quadtrees split dense areas into smaller cells adaptively; Google’s S2 and Uber’s H3 use hierarchical cells (H3 uses hexagons, which have uniform neighbour distances).

useWhen: Nearby search for drivers, restaurants, stores, and geofencing such as “is this rider inside the delivery zone”.
Geohash or H3 keys in Redis, Elasticsearch or a key-value store; PostGIS for rich polygon queries.
avoidWhen: Do not scan all drivers and compute distances one by one; it grows linearly with fleet size.
Do not search only the user’s own cell; nearby points across the edge are missed.

rows: Simple prefix search in any store

numbers.title: Why the 9-cell lookup is cheap
assumptions: 50,000 active drivers in a city of about 1,500 square km
Search with 6-character geohash cells of about 1.2 km × 0.6 km (0.72 square km)
steps: Driver density = 50,000 ÷ 1,500 ≈ 33 drivers per square km on average.
Nine cells cover 9 × 0.72 = 6.48 square km.
Expected candidates = 33 × 6.48 ≈ 214 drivers, instead of 50,000.
Computing 214 exact distances takes microseconds; dense areas may need finer cells or a cap on candidates.
numbers.result: The 9-cell geohash lookup cuts the candidates from 50,000 to about 200 before exact distance checks.

india.title: Auto-rickshaw matching in Bengaluru
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A ride-hailing app receives location pings from auto drivers every few seconds. Each ping updates the driver’s cell key (a geohash or H3 index) in an in-memory store. When a rider in Koramangala requests a ride, the dispatcher reads the rider’s cell and its neighbours, filters by vehicle type and availability, and ranks by estimated arrival time using road distance rather than straight-line distance, since a flyover or one-way street can make a near driver slow to arrive. In dense areas at peak time, the dispatcher uses finer cells to keep candidate lists short.

pitfalls.trap: Searching only the rider’s cell.
pitfalls.say: “I’d search the cell plus its 8 neighbours, then filter by exact distance, because the nearest driver may be across a cell boundary.”

pitfalls.trap: Ranking by straight-line distance.
pitfalls.say: “I’d shortlist by distance, then rank by estimated arrival time from a routing service.”

takeaways: Geohashes turn 2D proximity into string prefixes.
Pick a precision near the search radius and include the 8 neighbours.
Filter candidates by exact distance, rank by ETA.
Quadtrees and H3 adapt better to density and geometry.
deep.diagram:
+----+----+----+
| NW | N  | NE |
+----+----+----+
| W  | ME | E  |   query = my cell + 8 neighbours -> filter by exact distance
+----+----+----+
| SW | S  | SE |
+----+----+----+

interactive.title: Searching one cell
interactive.prompt: A user stands 50 m from the edge of their geohash cell. You search only that cell for restaurants within 1 km. What is the risk?

choices.label: Nearby restaurants just across the cell boundary are missed
choices.feedback: Right: closeness doesn’t respect cell borders.

choices.label: Duplicate results
choices.feedback: Searching one cell can’t produce duplicates from other cells.

choices.label: It’s too slow
choices.feedback: One cell is the fastest option; the problem is wrong results.

interactive.reveal: Search the user’s cell plus its eight neighbours, at a precision where cells are at least as large as the search radius, then filter by exact distance and sort.

title: Time-Series DBs
objectives: Recognise time-series workloads
Explain downsampling and retention
Avoid high-cardinality labels

cards.title: Append-heavy, time-ordered
cards.body: Metrics, sensor readings and prices arrive as timestamped points, mostly appended and read as ranges (last hour, last week). Time-series databases compress and index for exactly that.

cards.title: Retention and rollups
cards.body: Raw 10-second points for 7 days, 1-minute averages for 90 days, hourly for years. Downsampling keeps dashboards fast and storage bounded.

cards.title: A metric’s life
cards.body: A sample is appended to the current block, compacted later, rolled up into coarser averages and finally deleted when retention ends.
steps: Agent emits cpu{host=web-12}
Ingest appends to the current time block
Compaction compresses old blocks
Rollup job writes 1-minute averages
Raw data expires after retention

cards.title: Trap: high-cardinality labels
cards.body: Putting user IDs or request IDs in labels. Every unique label combination is a new series, so cardinality explodes and memory with it.

questions.prompt: Metrics memory jumped 50× after a deploy that added a user_id label. Why?

choices.label: Compaction was turned off by the same deploy
user_id values are stored as long strings per sample
Each user id makes a new series, so series explode
The database cannot index numeric label values

questions.explanation: Every label combination is a series.

questions.prompt: Dashboards over a year of 10-second data are slow and storage keeps growing. What helps most?

choices.label: Downsample older data and set retention
Move metrics into a relational database
Keep raw data on faster disks
Add more labels

questions.explanation: Rollups keep old data cheap to query.

questions.prompt: Which workload is most time-series shaped?

choices.label: A product catalogue
Orders with joins to customers
User profiles edited occasionally
CPU use sampled on 5,000 servers

questions.explanation: Timestamped, append-heavy, read as ranges.

questions.prompt: Order a metric’s life.

items.label: Agent emits cpu{host=web-12}
Ingest appends it to the current block
Compaction compresses old blocks
Rollup job writes 1-minute averages
Raw data expires

questions.explanation: Raw data is short-lived; rollups last.

questions.prompt: 5,000 hosts each report 50 metrics every 10 s. How many points per second are ingested?
questions.workedAnswer: 5,000 × 50 = 250,000 series; one point per 10 s gives 25,000 points/s.
questions.explanation: Design implication: 25,000 points/s is easy to ingest; the real limit is the 250,000 series. Each new label value multiplies the series count, so cardinality is what to cap.

questions.prompt: Labels have 20, 25, 5 and 10 possible values. How many series can the metric create?
questions.explanation: Series multiply across labels: 20 × 25 = 500, 500 × 5 = 2,500 and 2,500 × 10 = 25,000.

flashcards.back: Replacing old raw points with coarser aggregates like 1-minute averages.
Unbounded label values such as user or request IDs.
A range scan over a time window for a series.

mechanism.title: How a time-series database stores and ages data
steps: Each series is identified by a metric name plus labels, such as http_requests_total{service='checkout', status='500'}. Each sample is a timestamp and a value.
Incoming samples are appended to the current time block in memory and to a write-ahead log, then compressed into immutable blocks (for example 2 hours in Prometheus).
Compression exploits regularity: timestamps are delta-of-delta encoded and values XOR-encoded (the Gorilla technique), which brings typical samples down to roughly 1–2 bytes.
Queries select series by labels and aggregate over time ranges: rate over 5 minutes, p99 over an hour.
Retention and rollups: keep raw 15-second samples for, say, 15 days, 5-minute rollups for 90 days and 1-hour rollups for years, deleting whole old blocks cheaply.
Cardinality, the number of unique label combinations, drives memory and index size; a label such as user_id or order_id can explode it into millions of series.

useWhen: Metrics, IoT sensor readings, prices and other append-mostly, time-stamped numeric data queried by time range.
Prometheus for monitoring; TimescaleDB, InfluxDB or ClickHouse for longer-term or richer time-series analytics.
avoidWhen: Do not store per-event business records (orders, payments) as metrics; they belong in a database or logs.
Do not use unbounded labels such as user id, request id or full URL.

rows: Bounded disk, long history at low resolution

numbers.title: Cardinality and storage
assumptions: Metric with labels service (20), endpoint (25), status (5), instance (10)
Scrape every 15 s, about 1.5 bytes per compressed sample
steps: Samples per series per day = 86,400 ÷ 15 = 5,760.
Samples per day = 25,000 × 5,760 = 144,000,000, so about 216 MB per day compressed.
Adding a user_id label with 1,000,000 values would multiply series by up to a million, which no monitoring setup can hold.
numbers.result: Labels multiply series counts; a few bounded labels are cheap, one unbounded label is fatal.

india.title: Monitoring a payments switch on festival days
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: During peak days such as Diwali, UPI volumes are publicly reported to hit records. A bank’s payment team watches success rate, latency and error codes per partner bank and per API in Prometheus and Grafana, with labels kept to bounded sets such as partner bank, API and response code. Raw 15-second data shows exactly when a partner bank started timing out; hourly rollups kept for two years let the team compare this Diwali with the last two. Investigating one customer’s failed payment uses logs and traces keyed by transaction id, not a metric label.

pitfalls.trap: Alerting on raw per-instance metrics with no aggregation.
pitfalls.say: “I alert on aggregated SLO signals such as checkout error rate across instances, and use per-instance series only to drill down.”

pitfalls.trap: Adding user_id as a metric label to debug one customer.
pitfalls.say: “Per-user detail goes in logs and traces; metric labels stay bounded, such as service, endpoint and status.”

pitfalls.trap: Keeping raw samples forever.
pitfalls.say: “Raw data for 15 days, then 5-minute and hourly rollups, so storage stays bounded.”

takeaways: Time-series stores append, compress and query by time range.
Cardinality, not sample count, is the usual scaling limit.
Retention plus rollups keep long history affordable.
Per-entity detail belongs in logs and traces, not labels.
deep.diagram:
series = name + labels  -> [t1,v1][t2,v2]... (delta-of-delta + XOR, ~1.5 bytes/sample)
raw 15 s (15 d) -> 5 min rollup (90 d) -> 1 h rollup (2 y)

interactive.title: A user_id label
interactive.prompt: You add a user_id label (5 million users) to a request-latency metric. What happens?

choices.label: The number of series explodes, and memory and ingestion suffer
choices.feedback: Right: each label value combination is a separate series.

choices.label: Queries become more precise at no extra cost
choices.feedback: Precision comes at the cost of millions of new series.

choices.label: Nothing changes
choices.feedback: Every new value creates a new series to store and index.

interactive.reveal: Keep labels to bounded sets (service, endpoint, status). Put per-user detail in logs or traces, which are built for high cardinality.

title: Blue-Green/Canary/Feature Flags
objectives: Compare blue-green and canary releases
Use feature flags and kill switches safely
Keep schema changes rollback-safe

cards.title: Blue-green
cards.body: Run two full environments. Deploy to the idle one (green), test it, then switch the router from blue to green. Rollback is switching back. It needs double capacity during the switch, and database changes must work for both.

cards.title: Canary
cards.body: Send a small share of traffic (1%, then 5%, 25%) to the new version and watch error rates and latency. Roll back automatically if they get worse. It catches problems only real traffic shows.

cards.title: Feature flags
cards.body: Ship code dark and turn features on per user, region or percentage at runtime. Kill switches turn a broken feature off without a deploy. Remove flags once rolled out, or they pile up as untested paths.

cards.title: A canary rollout
cards.body: A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version, compares its errors and latency with the old one, and widens or rolls back.
steps: Deploy v2 next to v1
Route 1% of traffic to v2
Compare errors and latency
Increase to 25%, then 100%
Roll back if metrics worsen

cards.title: Trap: irreversible schema changes
cards.body: Shipping a schema change the old version cannot read, then rolling back. Make changes backward compatible: add the new column, switch code, remove the old column later.

questions.prompt: What does a canary release do?

choices.label: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate
Tests only in staging
Switches all traffic at once, then rolls back if many users complain
Deploys to all servers at 2 AM

questions.explanation: Real traffic, limited blast radius.

questions.prompt: In blue-green, how do you roll back?

choices.label: Redeploy the old build to each server
Wait for the next release
Restore the database from last night’s backup
Point the router back to the old environment

questions.explanation: The old environment is still running.

questions.prompt: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?

choices.label: Flip its kill-switch flag off
Hotfix and redeploy
Add servers
Roll back the release everywhere

questions.explanation: Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

questions.prompt: Order a canary rollout.

items.label: Deploy v2 next to v1
Route 1% to v2
Compare errors and latency
Increase to 25%, then 100%

questions.explanation: Grow only while metrics hold.

questions.prompt: Order a rollback-safe column rename.

items.label: Add the new column
Write to both columns
Switch reads to the new column
Remove the old column

questions.explanation: Every step works with the previous code version.

questions.prompt: Why use expand-and-contract for a column rename during a canary?

choices.label: Old and new code run together and both must work
Because SQL databases cannot rename a column in place
To make the canary roll out faster to all users
So that feature flags are not needed for this change

questions.explanation: During a gradual rollout both versions are live, so schema changes must stay compatible with both.

flashcards.front: What does a canary release do?
flashcards.back: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate. Real traffic, limited blast radius.

flashcards.front: In blue-green, how do you roll back?
flashcards.back: Point the router back to the old environment. The old environment is still running.

flashcards.front: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?
flashcards.back: Turn it off with its kill-switch flag. Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

mechanism.title: How a canary release with flags rolls out
steps: Blue-green: run the new version (green) alongside the old (blue) on full capacity, test it, then switch all traffic at the load balancer. Rollback is switching back.
Canary: send a small share of real traffic (say 1%) to the new version, compare its error rate and latency with the old, and step up through 5%, 25%, 50% and 100% if healthy.
Automated analysis checks the canary against guardrail metrics and rolls back on a breach without waiting for a human.
Feature flags separate deploy from release: code ships dark, and the feature is turned on per user, per city or per percentage, and off instantly if it misbehaves.
Database changes use expand and contract: add the new column or table first (compatible with old code), deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and only later drop the old column.
Clean up flags after rollout; stale flags become hidden complexity.

useWhen: Canary for risky changes to high-traffic services where real traffic reveals problems tests miss.
Feature flags for gradual product launches, A/B tests and kill switches for risky features.
avoidWhen: Blue-green for stateful systems where both versions cannot safely share the database schema.
Long-lived flags for permanent configuration; they are for rollouts, not settings.

numbers.title: How many users a canary exposes
assumptions: A bug fails 20% of requests on the new version
steps: Canary traffic = 1,000,000 × 0.01 = 10,000 requests per hour, so about 5,000 in 30 minutes.
Failed requests = 5,000 × 0.2 = 1,000.
A big-bang deploy with the same bug for the same 30 minutes would fail 500,000 × 0.2 = 100,000 requests.
With automated rollback after 5 minutes instead of 30, failures drop to about 167.
numbers.result: A 1% canary with fast automated rollback limits a bad release to hundreds of failures instead of a hundred thousand.

india.title: Launching a new checkout in one city
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A food-delivery app redesigns its checkout. The code ships to all servers behind a flag that is off. The team turns it on for employees, then for 1% of users in Jaipur, watching payment success rate and order completion against the old flow. Payment success drops slightly for one bank’s netbanking users, so they turn the flag off for that segment within minutes, fix it, and resume. Over two weeks the flag goes to 100% across cities, and the old code and the flag are deleted. No deploy was ever rolled back; only flags moved.

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll deploy on Friday night when traffic is low and fix bugs Monday.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d canary at 1% with automated rollback on error and latency guardrails, during working hours when the team can respond.”

pitfalls.trap: Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it.
pitfalls.say: “I’d expand and contract: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, and drop the old column in a later release.”

takeaways: Separate deploy from release with feature flags.
Canaries limit blast radius; automate rollback on guardrails.
Blue-green gives instant switch-back but needs double capacity.
Use expand and contract for schema changes.
deep.diagram:
deploy v2 dark --> flag on: staff --> 1% --> 5% --> 25% --> 100% --> delete flag
          metrics guardrails breached at any step --> flag off / shift traffic back

interactive.title: Canary results are in
interactive.prompt: A canary takes 1% of traffic. Its error rate is 0.5%; the old version’s is 0.1%. What next?

choices.label: Roll back and investigate
choices.feedback: Right: five times the error rate is a regression.

choices.label: Go to 100%: only 1% of users were affected
choices.feedback: The canary exists to stop this before 100% of users see it.

choices.label: Leave it at 1% for a week
choices.feedback: Users on the canary keep hitting errors while you wait.

interactive.reveal: Define success metrics before the rollout and automate the comparison. Roll back fast, keep schema changes backward compatible so a rollback is always possible.

title: Containers & Kubernetes
objectives: Explain what a container packages
Describe what Kubernetes schedules and heals
Use readiness vs liveness probes correctly

cards.title: Containers package the process
cards.body: A container image bundles your app and its dependencies, so it runs the same on a laptop and in production. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in seconds rather than minutes like a VM.

cards.title: Kubernetes runs the fleet
cards.body: You declare the desired state (5 replicas of checkout, 512 MB each). Kubernetes schedules pods onto nodes, restarts crashed ones and replaces pods when a node dies.

cards.title: A rolling deploy
cards.body: Kubernetes starts a new pod, waits for its readiness probe, sends it traffic and only then removes an old pod.
steps: New image pushed
Deployment creates a new pod
Readiness probe passes
Service starts sending traffic
One old pod is removed, repeat

cards.title: Trap: database checks in liveness
cards.body: Using the liveness probe to check the database. If the DB blips, every pod fails liveness and gets restarted at once. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: The database blips and every pod restarts in a loop. What is misconfigured?

choices.label: The image is too large
The readiness probe checks the database
The rolling update is too fast
The liveness probe checks the database

questions.explanation: Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: A node running three checkout pods dies. What does Kubernetes do?

choices.label: Reschedules them on healthy nodes
Restarts the node
Waits for the node to come back
Moves traffic to another cluster

questions.explanation: Controllers restore the declared state.

questions.prompt: Order one step of a rolling deploy.

items.label: New image pushed
Deployment creates a new pod
Readiness probe passes
Service sends it traffic
One old pod is removed

questions.explanation: Old pods leave only after new ones are ready.

questions.prompt: Why does a container start in seconds while a VM takes minutes?

choices.label: Containers skip the network stack
Containers only run on bare-metal servers
It shares the host kernel instead of booting its own OS
Containers have no filesystem to mount

questions.explanation: No guest OS boot.

questions.prompt: You declared 5 replicas of checkout and one crashes. What happens?

choices.label: The Deployment is deleted and must then be reapplied by hand
Nothing happens until you run kubectl apply again
The other 4 pods restart to rebalance the traffic
Kubernetes sees 4 running instead of 5 and starts a new pod

questions.explanation: Reconciliation loops close the gap.

questions.prompt: A pod is still loading its cache and should not get traffic yet. Which probe handles this?

choices.label: Readiness probe
Liveness probe
No probe; Kubernetes can tell by itself
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

questions.explanation: Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; liveness decides whether to restart it.

flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel and start in seconds.
Failing it removes the pod from traffic without restarting it.
Failing it restarts the container.

mechanism.title: How Kubernetes keeps an app running
steps: A container image packages the app and its dependencies; it runs as an isolated process using Linux namespaces and cgroups, sharing the host kernel.
You declare desired state in a Deployment: image version, 6 replicas, CPU and memory requests and limits, probes.

The scheduler places pods on nodes with enough free requested resources; controllers continuously compare actual state with desired state and fix differences, for example restarting a crashed pod or replacing pods from a failed node.
Probes: the liveness probe restarts a stuck container; the readiness probe controls whether the pod receives traffic; the startup probe gives slow starters time before liveness kicks in.
Rolling update: change the image tag; Kubernetes creates new pods and removes old ones gradually, bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable, sending traffic only to ready pods.
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts the replica count from metrics such as CPU utilisation against the requested CPU.

useWhen: Many services needing consistent deploys, autoscaling, self-healing and service discovery.
Teams with the skills (or a managed offering such as EKS, GKE or AKS) to operate it.
avoidWhen: A single small app where a managed platform (a PaaS or serverless) is simpler and cheaper.
Do not use the liveness probe to check downstream dependencies; a database blip would restart every pod at once.

numbers.title: Sizing replicas and a rolling update
assumptions: Peak 3,000 requests per second; one pod handles 250 at target CPU
Rolling update with maxSurge 25% and maxUnavailable 0
steps: Pods needed at peak = 3,000 ÷ 250 = 12.
Add N+2 headroom for a node failure and deploys: 14 replicas.
maxSurge 25% of 14 is 3.5, rounded up to 4 extra pods during the rollout; maxUnavailable 0 keeps all 14 serving.
So the cluster needs room for 14 plus 4 = 18 pods’ worth of requested resources during deploys.
numbers.result: Size replicas from peak load per pod plus headroom, and reserve surge capacity so rolling updates never reduce serving pods.

india.title: Exam-results day for an ed-tech app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: When board exam results are published, an ed-tech app’s result-lookup service can see traffic jump many times over within minutes. On Kubernetes, the team pre-scales the Deployment the night before, sets a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with a higher ceiling, and makes sure the cluster autoscaler can add nodes. Readiness probes keep new pods out of rotation until they have loaded the cache of school codes. When one node fails under load, the controller reschedules its pods elsewhere within a minute, and students only see slightly slower responses.

pitfalls.trap: Liveness probes that check the database.
pitfalls.say: “Liveness checks only that the process can respond; dependency health goes in readiness or metrics, so a database blip does not restart every pod.”

pitfalls.trap: Setting CPU limits far below what a JVM or Node process needs at peak.
pitfalls.say: “I set requests from measured usage and leave headroom on limits, because CPU throttling shows up as latency spikes that are hard to diagnose.”

pitfalls.trap: No resource requests.
pitfalls.say: “Pods get CPU and memory requests so the scheduler can place them and the autoscaler has a baseline.”

takeaways: Containers package apps; Kubernetes reconciles desired state.
Readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts, startup protects slow boots.
Rolling updates are bounded by maxSurge and maxUnavailable.
Size replicas from per-pod throughput plus headroom.
deep.diagram:
Deployment (replicas: 14, image: v2) -> ReplicaSet -> pods
controller loop: desired 14 vs actual 13 -> create 1
rolling: +4 new (ready?) -> remove old -> repeat

interactive.title: Liveness checks the database
interactive.prompt: Every pod’s liveness probe checks the database. The database blips for 20 seconds. What happens?

choices.label: Every pod fails liveness and is restarted at once
choices.feedback: Right: the restarts turn a blip into an outage.

choices.label: Pods are marked not ready and stop receiving traffic
choices.feedback: That’s what a readiness probe does; liveness restarts the container.

choices.label: Nothing
choices.feedback: Repeated failed liveness checks restart the pod.

interactive.reveal: Liveness should answer “is this process stuck?” Dependency checks belong in readiness, which takes a pod out of rotation without killing it.

title: Offset vs Cursor Pagination
objectives: Explain why deep offsets are slow
Implement cursor pagination with a stable key
Pick offset or cursor for a given screen

cards.title: Offset pagination
cards.body: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000 is simple and lets users jump to page 500, but the database still walks past 10,000 rows, and inserts shift pages so items repeat or vanish.

cards.title: Cursor pagination
cards.body: Return an opaque cursor (the last item’s sort key) and fetch WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor LIMIT 20. Each page is an index seek, and new inserts do not shift what comes next. There is no jumping to page 500.

cards.title: Paging a feed with cursors
cards.body: Each page returns a cursor that encodes the last item seen, and the next query seeks past it using the index instead of counting rows.
steps: Client asks for the first 20
Server returns items and next_cursor
Client sends next_cursor
Server seeks past it using the index
Repeat until there is no cursor

cards.title: A stable sort key
cards.body: Cursors need a unique, ordered key. created_at alone can tie: at lunch peak a food-delivery feed may get 40 orders in the same second, and a cursor on the timestamp alone skips or repeats the ones on the boundary. Use (created_at, id), with an index on that pair.

cards.title: Trap: OFFSET for infinite feeds
cards.body: Using OFFSET for an infinite feed. Deep pages get slower and new posts push items onto the next page, so users see duplicates.

questions.prompt: Why is OFFSET 100000 slow?

choices.label: It reads and discards 100,000 rows first
The response holds 100,000 rows
It locks the table while paging through
OFFSET stops the index being used

questions.explanation: The database still reads and throws away 100,000 rows before returning 20, so each deeper page costs more. The response is still 20 rows, OFFSET takes no table lock, and an index can still supply the order; it just cannot skip ahead by a count.

questions.prompt: A feed uses offset paging. New posts arrive while a user scrolls. What do they see?

choices.label: The new posts appended at the bottom of the feed
Repeats, as earlier items shift down a page
No change, since each page is fixed
An error once the offsets go stale

questions.explanation: With newest-first offsets, each new post pushes everything down one place, so the last items of page 1 reappear at the top of page 2. New posts are not appended at the bottom, pages are not fixed, and offsets do not raise errors; they just point at different rows.

questions.prompt: A feed pages with WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor, newest first, 20 at a time. Which index makes each page a single seek?

choices.label: Two indexes: one on created_at, one on id
One composite index on (created_at, id)
One index on id alone
No index; the cursor already skips rows

questions.explanation: A composite index on (created_at, id) lets the database seek straight to the cursor and read the next 20 entries in order. Two separate indexes cannot give that order in one seek, an index on id alone ignores the time order, and without an index every page scans and sorts the table.

questions.prompt: Order cursor paging.

items.label: Client asks for the first 20
Server returns items and next_cursor
Client sends next_cursor
Server seeks past it
Repeat until no cursor

questions.explanation: Each page starts from the last one seen.

questions.prompt: Pagination for an admin table of 5,000 rows where staff jump to arbitrary pages.

approaches.label: Offset pagination
Cursor pagination

rationaleOptions.label: Cursors let staff jump straight to page 37
Offset supports jumping to any page
At 5,000 rows the skipped rows cost little

rationaleConflicts.r3: Cursors only move forward from a known position.

questions.explanation: Small, stable tables with page jumps suit offsets.

questions.prompt: Why is (created_at, id) used as the cursor instead of created_at alone?

choices.label: Rows share timestamps; the id breaks ties so none repeat
Ids are shorter than timestamps, so cursors are smaller
Because OFFSET pagination requires both columns in the key
To make the cursor human-readable in the page URL

questions.explanation: The sort key must be unique; adding the id makes the order total.

flashcards.back: The database still reads and discards 100,000 rows. Offsets are skipped, not jumped over.

flashcards.front: A feed uses offset paging. New posts arrive while a user scrolls. What do they see?
flashcards.back: Duplicates, as earlier items shift onto the next page. Inserts move everything down.
(created_at, id). Unique and ordered.

mechanism.title: How offset and cursor pagination execute
steps: Offset: SELECT … ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000. The database must walk and discard 10,000 rows before returning 20, so later pages get slower.
Offset is also unstable: if new rows are inserted while the user scrolls, items shift between pages, causing duplicates or gaps.

Cursor (keyset): return the sort key of the last item as an opaque cursor. The next query asks for rows strictly after it: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20.
With an index on (created_at, id), the database seeks directly to the cursor position and reads 20 entries, so every page costs about the same.
The sort key must be unique and stable; add the id as a tie-breaker because many rows can share a timestamp.
Encode the cursor (for example base64 of the values) so clients treat it as opaque and you can change its format later.

useWhen: Cursor pagination for infinite scroll, feeds, chat history, API list endpoints and large tables.
Offset pagination for small admin tables where users jump to page 7 and data rarely changes.
avoidWhen: Do not use deep offsets on large tables; page 5,000 scans 100,000 rows to show 20.
Do not build a cursor on a non-unique column alone; ties cause skipped or repeated rows.

rows: Unique sort key and matching index

numbers.title: Rows touched by deep pages
steps: Offset skips (5,000 − 1) × 20 = 99,980 rows, then reads 20, so about 100,000 rows touched.
Cursor seeks once in the index (a few page reads for a B-tree) and reads 20 rows.
At 200 such requests per second, offset touches about 200 × 100,000 = 20,000,000 rows per second; the cursor touches about 4,000.
That gap is the difference between a struggling database and an idle one.
numbers.result: Offset cost grows linearly with page depth; cursor cost stays at one index seek plus the page.

india.title: Scrolling a long transaction history
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A user of a UPI app scrolls back through two years of payments, perhaps thousands of entries. With offset pagination, each “load more” asks the database to skip more and more rows, and if a new payment arrives mid-scroll, one entry shifts and appears twice. With a cursor of (transaction_time, transaction_id), each request seeks directly to where the last page ended using the index and returns the next 20, and a new payment at the top does not disturb older pages. The app sends the opaque cursor string it received; it never computes page numbers.

pitfalls.trap: Exposing raw database ids and timestamps as the cursor format.
pitfalls.say: “The cursor is an opaque, encoded string, so clients cannot tamper with its meaning and I can change the sort key later without breaking them.”

pitfalls.trap: Using OFFSET for an infinite feed.
pitfalls.say: “I’d use keyset pagination on (created_at, id) with a matching index, so every page costs one seek.”

pitfalls.trap: Cursor on timestamp only.
pitfalls.say: “Timestamps collide, so the cursor includes the id as a tie-breaker.”

takeaways: Offset cost grows with page depth; cursor cost is constant.
Cursors are stable when rows are inserted.
Use a unique sort key with a tie-breaker and a matching index.
Offset is fine for small admin tables with page jumps.
deep.diagram:
offset: [skip skip skip ... 99,980 rows][read 20]
cursor: index seek -> (ts, id) < cursor -> [read 20]

interactive.title: OFFSET on a live feed
interactive.prompt: An infinite feed pages with OFFSET 10000 LIMIT 20 while new posts keep arriving. What goes wrong?

choices.label: Deep pages slow down, and new posts shift items so users see duplicates
choices.feedback: Right: OFFSET still walks the skipped rows, and positions move.

choices.label: Cursors expire
choices.feedback: There is no cursor in offset pagination.

choices.label: Nothing, as long as there’s an index
choices.feedback: The index still walks past every skipped row.

interactive.reveal: Cursor pagination seeks past the last item seen (WHERE created_at < ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20) using the index, so pages stay fast and stable.

title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
objectives: Contrast optimistic and pessimistic locking
Pick one based on contention
Implement version checks

cards.title: Two ways to stop lost updates
cards.body: Pessimistic locking takes a lock before reading (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic locking reads freely and checks a version at write time; if someone changed it, retry.

cards.title: Pick by contention
cards.body: Low contention (editing your own profile): optimistic, no waiting. High contention on one row (the last Tatkal seat): pessimistic or atomic updates, because optimistic retries would mostly fail.

cards.title: Optimistic update
cards.body: The update only succeeds if the version is unchanged; zero rows updated means another writer won, so re-read and retry.
steps: Read row with version 7
Compute new value
UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = 7
0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry

cards.title: Trap: locks around external calls
cards.body: Holding a pessimistic lock while calling an external payment API. The lock lives for seconds and everything else queues behind it. Keep lock scopes short.

questions.prompt: Thousands race for the last 10 seats on one train at 10:00. Which approach suits the seat row?

choices.label: No locking, reconcile later
Pessimistic locking, or an atomic conditional update
Optimistic locking with retries
Read committed with no extra checks

questions.explanation: Under heavy contention, optimistic retries mostly fail.

questions.prompt: An optimistic UPDATE … WHERE version = 7 changes 0 rows. What happened?

choices.label: The transaction deadlocked with another concurrent one
The database deleted the row by mistake
The version column overflowed its type
Someone else updated it first; re-read and retry

questions.explanation: The version moved on.

questions.prompt: Users edit their own address now and then. Which approach fits?

choices.label: Optimistic locking
A distributed lock in Redis
Serializable isolation for each query
A pessimistic lock held for the edit form’s lifetime

questions.explanation: Low contention: no waiting needed.

questions.prompt: Order an optimistic update.

items.label: Read the row with version 7
Compute the new value
UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND version = 7
If 0 rows changed, re-read and retry

questions.explanation: Check at write time.

questions.prompt: Checkout locks the order row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, then calls a payment API that takes 3 s. Other requests pile up. Click the cause.
questions.explanation: Do not hold locks across external calls; keep lock scopes short.

questions.prompt: An optimistic update succeeds only 20% of the time because of contention. How many attempts does it take on average?
questions.explanation: Expected attempts are 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5, which is why hot rows suit pessimistic or atomic updates.

flashcards.front: How does optimistic locking detect conflicts?
flashcards.back: A version check in the UPDATE; 0 rows updated means retry.
High contention on the same rows.

flashcards.front: What should never happen inside a lock?
flashcards.back: Slow external calls like payment APIs.

mechanism.title: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking in practice
steps: Pessimistic: read the row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside a transaction. Other writers (and other FOR UPDATE readers) wait until you commit, so your read-modify-write is safe.
Optimistic: read the row and its version number without locking. When writing, run UPDATE … SET …, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?.
If the update affects 1 row, you won. If it affects 0 rows, someone else changed it first: re-read, reapply the change, and retry or report a conflict.
Under low contention, optimistic locking avoids holding locks while users think or while the app does other work.
Under high contention, optimistic locking wastes work on retries, while pessimistic locks queue writers in order.
Keep lock scope small either way: lock one row, not a table; hold locks for milliseconds, never across a user’s think time or an external API call.

useWhen: Optimistic for edits that rarely collide: profile updates, document metadata, admin forms (and HTTP ETag with If-Match).
Pessimistic (or a single conditional update) for hot rows such as inventory counts or seat holds during a flash sale.
avoidWhen: Optimistic retries on a hot counter where most attempts conflict; throughput collapses.
Pessimistic locks held across user interaction, such as while a checkout form is open.

numbers.title: Retries under contention
assumptions: Each attempt succeeds with probability p (no one else wrote in between)
Case A: p = 0.95; case B: p = 0.2
steps: Expected attempts = 1 ÷ p.
Case A: 1 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 1.05 attempts, so retries are almost free.
Case B: 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 attempts on average, each doing the read and computation again.
At case B contention, a pessimistic lock or one atomic conditional UPDATE is cheaper.
numbers.result: Optimistic locking costs 1 ÷ p attempts; it shines when conflicts are rare and hurts on hot rows.

india.title: Editing a restaurant menu versus selling the last biryani
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Two managers of a restaurant on a delivery platform edit the same menu item from different laptops. Conflicts are rare, so the item carries a version number; if the second save finds the version changed, the app shows 'this item was updated by someone else, review changes'. Meanwhile, during dinner rush, the 'portions left' counter for a popular biryani is updated by many orders at once. Here the platform avoids read-modify-write entirely with UPDATE items SET left = left − 1 WHERE id = ? AND left > 0, which the database serialises on that row and which never oversells.

pitfalls.trap: Forgetting deadlocks with pessimistic locks.
pitfalls.say: “Every transaction locks rows in the same order, such as by ascending id, and has a lock timeout, so two transactions cannot wait on each other forever.”

pitfalls.trap: Using optimistic locking for a flash-sale counter.
pitfalls.say: “At high contention most optimistic attempts fail; I’d use an atomic conditional decrement or a short row lock.”

pitfalls.trap: Holding a lock while waiting for the payment gateway.
pitfalls.say: “I reserve stock with a short transaction, call the gateway outside it, then confirm or release.”

takeaways: Optimistic checks a version at write time; pessimistic blocks others.
Expected optimistic attempts are 1 ÷ p.
Use atomic conditional updates for hot counters.
Never hold locks across user think time or external calls.
deep.diagram:
optimistic: read (v=7) -> compute -> UPDATE ... WHERE version=7 -> 1 row: ok | 0 rows: retry
pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (others wait) -> compute -> UPDATE -> COMMIT (release)

interactive.title: Locking for wiki edits
interactive.prompt: Choose a concurrency control for these constraints.

choices.label: Optimistic: a version column, and reject the save if it changed
choices.feedback: Right: rare conflicts make retries cheap, and nobody holds a lock.

choices.label: Pessimistic: lock the page while someone edits for ten minutes
choices.feedback: Everyone else waits, and abandoned edits hold locks.

choices.label: No control: last write wins
choices.feedback: One person’s edit silently disappears.

interactive.reveal: Optimistic locking suits low contention; pessimistic suits high contention on short operations. Never hold a lock across user think time or external calls.
setup: Wiki pages, edited occasionally
Two people rarely edit the same page at once
An edit can take minutes

title: OT vs CRDT
objectives: Explain why collaborative editing needs conflict resolution
Contrast OT and CRDTs
Know which needs a central server

cards.title: Concurrent edits collide
cards.body: Two people type into the same Google Doc paragraph at once. If each simply applies the other’s edit at the original position, their copies diverge.

cards.title: OT vs CRDT
cards.body: Operational Transformation rewrites incoming operations against concurrent ones, usually through a central server that orders them. CRDTs design data types whose merges always converge, so peers can sync in any order, even offline.

cards.title: Two users insert at once
cards.body: The server shifts A’s insert position to account for B’s delete, so both users end up with the same document.
steps: A inserts “X” at position 5
B deletes position 2
Server transforms A’s insert to position 4
Both copies converge

cards.title: Trap: last-write-wins on documents
cards.body: Using last-write-wins on whole documents. One user’s entire edit disappears. Merge at the operation or character level.

questions.prompt: Users edit notes offline on flights and merge later without a central server. Which fits better?

choices.label: A pessimistic lock per note
Operational transformation
CRDTs
Last-write-wins on each note

questions.explanation: CRDT merges converge in any order.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong with last-write-wins on a whole document?

choices.label: The server rejects both edits
Both edits merge cleanly
One person’s entire edit disappears
The document gets duplicated into two copies

questions.explanation: Merge at the operation level instead.

questions.prompt: Why does classic OT usually have a central server?

choices.label: It stores users’ passwords for the document
OT cannot run inside web browsers
OT needs special hardware to run its transforms
It orders ops so all clients transform alike

questions.explanation: A single order keeps transforms consistent.

questions.prompt: Order two concurrent edits under OT.

items.label: A inserts “X” at position 5
B deletes position 2
Server transforms A’s insert to position 4
Both copies converge

questions.explanation: Positions are adjusted for concurrent ops.

questions.prompt: Collaboration engine for an always-online editor with a central server.
constraints: A central server is always available
A proven, mature approach is wanted

approaches.label: Last-write-wins per document
Operational transformation through the server

rationaleOptions.label: The central server can order every operation
Last-write-wins is simple and safe for documents
Transforming concurrent operations keeps copies in sync

rationaleConflicts.r3: It silently drops one user’s edits.

questions.explanation: With a central server, OT is a natural fit.

questions.prompt: Alice inserts one character at position 0 while Bob deletes position 3. Under OT, how is Bob’s delete applied after Alice’s insert?

choices.label: Transformed to position 4
Applied at position 3 unchanged
Discarded
Applied at position 0

questions.explanation: Alice’s insert shifts later characters right by one, so the delete is transformed to position 4.

flashcards.front: What does OT usually rely on?
flashcards.back: A central server that orders and transforms operations.
Replicas converge regardless of merge order, so offline sync works.
It silently discards concurrent edits.

mechanism.title: How OT and CRDTs merge concurrent edits
steps: Problem: two users edit the same document at once. Alice inserts “X” at position 0 while Bob deletes the character at position 3. Applying each other’s operations naively shifts positions and corrupts the text.

Operational transformation (OT): operations go through a central server that orders them. When Bob’s delete arrives after Alice’s insert, the server transforms it (position 3 becomes 4) so it still deletes the intended character.
OT needs carefully proven transformation functions for every pair of operation types and is easiest with a central server, which is the approach Google Docs is publicly known to use.

CRDTs (conflict-free replicated data types) give every character a unique, ordered id (for example based on site id and counter), so inserts and deletes refer to ids, not positions, and replicas can apply operations in any order and still converge.
CRDTs work peer-to-peer and offline, at the cost of metadata per character and tombstones for deletions, which need compaction.
Last-writer-wins on the whole document is not collaborative editing: one user’s changes silently disappear.
