useWhen: OT for server-centred real-time editors where a central service orders all operations.
CRDTs for offline-first and peer-to-peer apps, and for structured data such as counters, sets and maps (libraries such as Yjs and Automerge).
avoidWhen: Do not use last-writer-wins for documents edited concurrently.
Do not implement OT transformation functions from scratch unless you must; they are notoriously easy to get wrong.

numbers.title: Metadata cost of a text CRDT
assumptions: About 16 bytes of id and ordering metadata per character (illustrative)
Another 20,000 deleted characters kept as tombstones
steps: Live characters: 50,000 × 16 bytes = 800,000 bytes, about 0.8 MB of metadata.
Tombstones: 20,000 × 16 bytes = 320,000 bytes.
Total metadata is about 1.12 MB for 50 KB of text, more than 20 times the text itself.
Libraries reduce this with run-length encoding of consecutive inserts and periodic garbage collection.
numbers.result: CRDT convergence is paid for in metadata, so production libraries compress runs and collect tombstones.

india.title: Co-editing a project report
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Three engineering students in Pune edit a project report together: two online in a browser editor, one on a train with patchy network. In a server-centred editor using OT, each keystroke travels to the server, which orders and transforms it, so the offline student cannot edit meaningfully until reconnected. In a CRDT-based editor, the offline student keeps typing, and when the train reaches a station with signal, their changes merge with the others’ without conflicts or lost paragraphs. Whole-file last-writer-wins, the behaviour of naive file sync, would keep only the last person’s save.

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring tombstone growth in a CRDT.
pitfalls.say: “Deleted elements stay as tombstones, so I’d rely on a library that compacts them and snapshot documents periodically.”

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll lock the document while someone edits.”
pitfalls.say: “Real-time editors merge concurrent edits; I’d use OT with a central server or a CRDT library such as Yjs if offline editing matters.”

pitfalls.trap: Proposing last-writer-wins for documents.
pitfalls.say: “LWW drops a user’s edits silently; text needs OT or a sequence CRDT.”

takeaways: Positions shift under concurrent edits; merging needs OT or CRDTs.
OT transforms operations through a central server.
CRDTs use unique ids so replicas converge in any order, even offline.
Last-writer-wins on documents loses work.

text 'abcd'
Alice: insert X at 0 -> 'Xabcd'      Bob: delete pos 3 ('d') -> 'abc'
OT: Bob's delete transformed to pos 4 -> 'Xabc'   CRDT: delete id(d) -> 'Xabc'

choices.label: CRDTs
choices.feedback: Right: replicas merge in any order without a central server.

choices.label: Operational transformation (OT)
choices.feedback: OT typically relies on a central server to order operations.

choices.label: Last-write-wins on the whole document

interactive.reveal: CRDTs are designed to converge whatever order updates arrive in, which suits offline and peer-to-peer sync. OT is the classic choice behind server-centred editors.

title: Interview Playbook
objectives: Run a 45-minute interview in six stages
Ask clarifying questions before designing
Close with risks and next steps

cards.title: 45-minute map
cards.body: Six stages: requirements (0–5 min), estimation (5–10), API (10–15), high-level design (15–25), deep dive (25–40), wrap-up (40–45). The same plan runs in Interview mode.

cards.title: Drive the whiteboard
cards.body: Draw the hot path left to right: client, edge, services, data stores. Mark each arrow sync or async and label each store with its key and access pattern. Keep a corner for the numbers (peak QPS, storage, latency budget) and point at them when you pick a component. Narrate one failure per box as you draw it, such as “if this cache is cold, reads fall back to the database”, rather than saving failures for the end.

cards.title: What to cover in each stage
cards.body: Requirements: core flows, scale, exclusions. Estimation: peak QPS, storage, the number that drives the design. API: key endpoints and safe retries. High-level design: the hot path end to end. Deep dive: the riskiest part and its failure modes. Wrap-up: trade-offs, bottlenecks, next steps. These are the same six stages as Lesson 1 and Interview mode.

cards.title: Signals interviewers want
cards.body: Interviewers score how you reason, not the final picture. Scope: ask before drawing and say what is out of scope. Numbers: one or two estimates that change a decision, such as whether one primary can take the write rate. Trade-offs: name what each choice costs, for example “async replication: faster commits, a few seconds of possible loss”. Failures: timeouts, retries with idempotency keys, behaviour when a dependency is down. Operations: the metrics and alerts you would add. “I would measure X before deciding” beats a confident guess.

cards.title: Closing script
cards.body: Keep the last 3–5 minutes for a short close: restate the design in two sentences; name the top two bottlenecks and what changes at 10× load; list the three signals you would alert on (for example error rate, p99 latency, queue lag); mention one simplification you made on purpose; and say what you would build or load-test first. A crisp close shows judgement and hands the interviewer easy follow-ups.

flashcards.back: Requirements 5, estimation 5, API 5, high-level design 10, deep dive 15, wrap-up 5 minutes.

title: URL Shortener
objectives: Scope URL Shortener: create short link from long URL, redirect short link to original
Size it: 100M redirects/day, about 5,800/s at peak
Defend the design: generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 characters ≈ 3.5 trillion IDs)

cards.title: What URL Shortener must do
cards.body: URL Shortener: A short-link service for SMS links sent by Indian banks and shopping apps, where a 160-character SMS cannot fit a long tracking URL. In scope: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry.

cards.title: URL Shortener: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Redirect p99 < 50 ms. 100:1 read/write. Links never collide. Out of scope: Link-in-bio pages and QR design; Full marketing analytics dashboards.

cards.title: One reference path for URL Shortener
cards.body: Generate IDs with a counter/Snowflake encoded in base62 (7 characters ≈ 3.5 trillion IDs). → Store id → URL in a key-value store; cache hot links in Redis; 301/302 redirect. → Async click analytics via a queue; CDN/edge caching for viral links.

cards.title: Where URL Shortener breaks first
cards.body: Id generation: Hashing the long URL and truncating causes collisions that need retries; a counter or Snowflake id encoded in base62 never collides. 301 versus 302: 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics and makes link edits sticky; 302 keeps every click visible.

cards.title: Closing URL Shortener in one minute
cards.body: Summarise in four points: the peak you designed for (about 5,800 redirects per second under the brief’s assumptions), the main path (load balancer, stateless services, cache, NoSQL store, CDN), the riskiest part (id generation) and the one mitigation you would build first.

questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, durability and availability: Redirect p99 < 50 ms; 100:1 read/write; Links never collide. The others are features (functional) or out of scope.

questions.prompt: URL Shortener: assume 50M daily users each doing about 2 redirects a day, with traffic peaking at 5× the daily average. Estimate peak redirects per second.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the peak is 5× the average of about 1,200/s, so capacity sized for the average would run short at the busy hour. What it means for the design: the problem is read latency and caching, not storage.

questions.prompt: The create-link call (POST /v1/links) times out on a phone and the app retries. How do you avoid making two short links?

choices.label: Send an Idempotency-Key; retries get the stored result
Rely on TCP retransmission to drop the duplicate request
Generate the short code on the client from the current time
Raise the client timeout so the app need not retry

questions.explanation: The first request may have succeeded before the timeout. An idempotency key lets the server recognise the retry and return the same short link; TCP cannot tell two HTTP requests apart.

questions.prompt: A link goes viral and redirects jump 10× with no cache in front of the store. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: KV store partition for that code

questions.explanation: Every redirect for one code hits the same key, so one partition of the store takes the whole spike. Stateless redirect servers scale out; caching the hot code in Redis or at the edge absorbs it.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism guarantees two new links never get the same short code?

choices.label: Let each server count from one on its own
Pick a random code and hope collisions stay rare
Pre-allocated counter ranges per server, encoded in base62
Hash the long URL and keep just the first seven characters

questions.explanation: Counter ranges handed out by a coordinator are unique by construction. Truncated hashes and random codes collide and need a check-and-retry; independent counters repeat.

questions.prompt: Marketing wants every click counted, while ops wants the fewest redirect requests. Which redirect fits marketing?

choices.label: 302, so each visit passes through the service first
301, so browsers cache the redirect and later clicks skip you
Client-side JavaScript redirect after the page fully loads
200 with the long URL in the body for the client to follow

questions.explanation: A 301 is cached by browsers, so repeat clicks never reach the service and are not counted. A 302 keeps every click visible at the cost of more traffic.

flashcards.back: Create short link from long URL; Redirect short link to original; Optional custom alias & expiry

flashcards.back: 50M × 2 = 100M redirects/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,200/s on average; × 5 peak ≈ 5,800/s.

steps: Create: POST /v1/links with the long URL (and Idempotency-Key). The service takes an id from a Snowflake-style generator or a pre-allocated counter range and encodes it in base62.

Expired or abusive links are blocked by a flag checked at redirect time; a malware-scanning worker checks new long URLs.

deepDives.title: Id generation
deepDives.body: Hashing the long URL and truncating causes collisions that need retries; a counter or Snowflake id encoded in base62 never collides. Counters can be handed out in ranges of, say, 10,000 per server so no request waits on a central database.

deepDives.title: 301 versus 302
deepDives.body: 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load but hides repeat clicks from analytics and makes link edits sticky; 302 keeps every click visible. Banks sending OTP-adjacent links usually prefer 302 plus edge caching with a short TTL.

rubric: States read-heavy ratio (100:1) and puts a cache or CDN in front of the store.
Uses a collision-free id scheme and explains code length from 62 to the power 7.
Makes analytics asynchronous so redirects stay under 50 ms.
Covers expiry, abuse scanning and idempotent link creation.

title: Pastebin
objectives: Scope Pastebin: create a paste, read a paste by ID
Size it: 15M reads/day, about 520/s at peak
Defend the design: metadata in SQL, content in object storage

cards.title: What Pastebin must do
cards.body: Pastebin: Share code snippets and logs between developers, with expiry, like Pastebin or a GitHub gist. In scope: Create a paste; Read a paste by ID; Expire pastes.

cards.title: Pastebin: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Reads p99 < 100 ms. Durable storage. Read-heavy. Out of scope: Real-time collaborative editing; Code execution of pastes.

cards.title: One reference path for Pastebin
cards.body: Metadata in SQL, content in object storage. → Cache popular pastes; CDN for raw views. → TTL cleanup worker deletes expired pastes.

cards.title: Where Pastebin breaks first
cards.body: Content in the database or object storage?: Small pastes could live in SQL, but object storage keeps the database small, makes backups fast and lets a CDN serve public pastes directly; metadata stays in SQL for queries by owner and expiry. Unguessable ids: Sequential ids let anyone scrape private pastes; random ids from a large space (62 to the power 8 ≈ 218 trillion) make guessing impractical.

cards.title: Closing Pastebin in one minute
cards.body: Summarise in four points: the peak you designed for (about 521 reads per second under the brief’s assumptions), the main path (load balancer, stateless services, cache, SQL database, object storage, CDN), the riskiest part (content in the database or object storage?) and the one mitigation you would build first.

choices.label: Syntax-aware code execution

Paste version diffing

questions.explanation: Sanity check: the peak is 3× the average of about 170/s, so capacity sized for the average would run short at the busy hour. What it means for the design: a modest system where object storage plus a cache is plenty.

questions.prompt: Creating a paste (POST /v1/pastes) times out and the client retries. How do you avoid two copies?

choices.label: Raise the timeout so the client need not retry
Deduplicate by comparing paste text across all users
An Idempotency-Key; retries get the first paste’s id
Make paste creation a GET so a repeat is harmless

questions.explanation: Only the client knows the two requests are the same attempt; an idempotency key carries that. Two users may legitimately paste the same text, so content matching is wrong.

questions.prompt: A popular paste is opened 10× more than usual and bodies are read straight from the object store on every view. What saturates first?

diagramNodes.label: Object storage reads for that key

questions.explanation: Every view fetches the same body. Putting the CDN in front of /raw/{id} serves it from the edge so the store and service barely notice.

questions.prompt: Why keep paste bodies in object storage rather than in the SQL row?

choices.label: SQL cannot store text longer than one kilobyte
Object storage gives transactions across many pastes
It removes the need for a paste id altogether
Bodies are big and cold; SQL keeps the metadata lean

questions.explanation: Most pastes are read rarely and can be megabytes. Object storage is cheap, durable and CDN-friendly; SQL keeps only the small, indexed metadata.

questions.prompt: Expired pastes must disappear. Which approach balances correctness and cost?

choices.label: Delete each paste with its own timer thread on a server
Only a nightly sweeper, with reads trusting whatever exists
Check expiry on read, and let a sweeper or lifecycle rule delete later
Never delete them, and just hide the expired pastes in the user interface

questions.explanation: Checking on read gives exact expiry for users; the sweeper or an object-store lifecycle rule reclaims space in bulk later.

Nothing; silently drop the connection to save work

The client counts its own requests and reports them

title: Unique ID Generator
objectives: Scope Unique ID Generator: generate unique 64-bit IDs on demand, IDs roughly sortable by time
Size it: 1B IDs/day, about 35,000/s at peak
Defend the design: each generator node has a unique worker ID (Snowflake: timestamp + worker + sequence)

cards.title: What Unique ID Generator must do
cards.body: Unique ID Generator: Generate unique, roughly time-sortable 64-bit ids for orders, messages and payments across data centres. In scope: Generate unique 64-bit IDs on demand; IDs roughly sortable by time; Work across many data centres.

cards.title: Unique ID Generator: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Under 1 ms per ID. No duplicates, ever. No single point of failure. Out of scope: Human-readable vanity IDs; Cryptographic secrecy of IDs.

cards.title: One reference path for Unique ID Generator
cards.body: Each generator node has a unique worker ID (Snowflake: timestamp + worker + sequence). → Clock moving backwards is detected and the node waits or refuses. → No central counter on the hot path.

cards.title: Where Unique ID Generator breaks first
cards.body: Clock skew: NTP corrections can move clocks backwards; issuing ids then could repeat a timestamp with a reused sequence. Alternatives: UUIDv4 needs no coordination but is 128 bits and random, which hurts B-tree locality; UUIDv7 is time-ordered and standard; database ranges (ticket servers) are simple but depend on a central database.

questions.prompt: A service calls nextId() and the call fails halfway. What makes retrying safe?

choices.label: Reuse the previous id if the call looked like it failed
Store every issued id in a database before returning it
Ask the clock service for permission before each retry
Nothing extra: a fresh id is unique, so an unused one is just skipped

questions.explanation: Snowflake ids are cheap and unique; losing one leaves a gap, which is harmless. Reusing ids would risk collisions.

questions.prompt: Id demand rises 10× and ids come from one central id service. What saturates first?
questions.explanation: A central service is a hot spot and a single point of failure. Embedding the generator as a library with leased worker ids removes the network hop entirely.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism keeps ids unique across 1,024 workers without coordination per id?

choices.label: A global counter incremented in SQL for each id
A unique worker id in each 64-bit id, plus timestamp and sequence
Random 64-bit numbers with no structure at all
The hostname hashed into the lower bits each time

questions.explanation: Timestamp, worker id and a per-millisecond sequence make each id unique by construction; the worker id is leased once at startup.

questions.prompt: A server’s clock jumps backwards by 2 seconds. What should the generator do?

choices.label: Refuse to issue ids until the clock passes the last timestamp
Reset the sequence to zero and carry on regardless
Keep issuing ids with the earlier timestamp as normal, unchanged
Switch to random ids until somebody notices and restarts it

questions.explanation: Issuing with an older timestamp can repeat ids already handed out. Waiting (or failing fast) preserves uniqueness.

steps: Each generator process gets a unique worker id at start-up, leased from ZooKeeper or etcd, or assigned by deployment config.
To generate: read the clock in milliseconds; if it equals the last timestamp, increment the sequence, otherwise reset it to 0; if the sequence overflows, wait for the next millisecond.
Compose the id from the timestamp shifted left 22 bits, the worker id shifted left 12, and the sequence.
Services usually embed the generator as a library, so there is no network call; a small id service is an alternative for languages without the library.
If the clock goes backwards, refuse or wait until it passes the last timestamp, and alert.

steps: Partition keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes; each key lives on the next N = 3 distinct nodes on the ring.

cards.title: What WhatsApp must do
cards.body: WhatsApp: One-to-one and group messaging used across India, with receipts and offline delivery. In scope: Send 1:1 messages; Group chats; Delivery/read receipts.

cards.title: WhatsApp: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Low latency. Messages never lost. Offline delivery. Out of scope: Voice and video calls; Payments in chat.

cards.title: One reference path for WhatsApp
cards.body: WebSocket gateways hold connections; a registry maps user → gateway. → Messages persisted in Cassandra-style store partitioned by conversation. → Offline users get push notifications; receipts flow back as events.

cards.title: Where WhatsApp breaks first
cards.body: Ordering and duplicates: Per-conversation sequence numbers give order; client-generated message ids let the server and receivers drop retried duplicates. End-to-end encryption: With end-to-end encryption, as WhatsApp publicly describes using the Signal protocol, the server stores only ciphertext, so search and moderation must happen on devices.

bossDeep.pitch: Netflix-style streaming: browse a catalogue, stream at adaptive quality and resume where you left off.

functional: Stream a title at adaptive quality
nonFunctional: Smooth playback on poor mobile networks

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 20 video segment requests each per day
This quiz scenario is deliberately small; real viewing generates hundreds of segment requests per hour watched
steps: Daily video segment requests = 50,000,000 × 20 = 1,000,000,000.
Peak ≈ 11,600 × 4 ≈ 46,000 video segment requests per second (the quiz target is about 46,000).
Segment egress at about 46,000 requests per second × 1 MB is about 46,000 MB per second, about 368 Gbit per second.
Such bandwidth must come from CDN caches inside or near ISPs; Netflix publicly describes its own Open Connect appliances placed in ISP networks.
Resume points are tiny writes, for example one every 30 seconds per active viewer, stored in a key-value store.
capacity.result: About 46,000 segment requests per second already means hundreds of Gbit per second: delivery is a CDN problem, the control plane is ordinary services.

steps: The catalogue and personalised rows are served by stateless services and caches from the control-plane region.
Pressing play fetches a manifest listing renditions and segment URLs on the nearest CDN or ISP cache.
The player downloads segments, measuring throughput and switching bitrate to keep the buffer healthy.
The player reports progress periodically; a key-value store keeps (user, title) → position for resume on any device.
Control-plane services run in more than one region with failover; content is pre-positioned at edges overnight.

app -> catalogue/personalisation (control plane, multi-region)
play -> manifest -> segments from ISP/edge cache (adaptive)
progress -> KV store (user, title) -> resume

title: Uber/Ola
objectives: Scope Uber/Ola: request a ride, match nearby driver
Size it: 80M ride requests/day, about 3,700/s at peak
Defend the design: drivers stream locations via WebSocket into a geo index (geohash in Redis)

cards.title: What Uber/Ola must do
cards.body: Uber/Ola: Match riders with nearby drivers in Indian cities and track trips live. In scope: Request a ride; Match nearby driver; Live location tracking.

cards.title: Uber/Ola: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Match < 5 s. Location updates every 4 s. No double assignment. Out of scope: Fare surge pricing model details; Driver onboarding and KYC.

cards.title: One reference path for Uber/Ola
cards.body: Drivers stream locations via WebSocket into a geo index (geohash in Redis). → Matching service queries nearby drivers and locks one with CAS. → Trips in SQL; surge via stream processing.

cards.title: Where Uber/Ola breaks first
cards.body: No double assignment: A conditional update on the ride row, or a compare-and-set on the driver’s status, guarantees one winner even if two acceptances arrive together. Hot zones: Airports and stations at peak overload a few cells; finer cells and per-zone dispatch partitions keep queries fast.

assumptions: 20 million daily users, about 4 ride requests each per day
500,000 online drivers sending a location every 4 seconds
steps: Daily ride requests = 20,000,000 × 4 = 80,000,000.
Average = 80,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 926 per second.
Peak ≈ 926 × 4 ≈ 3,700 ride requests per second (the quiz target is about 3,700).
Location writes = 500,000 ÷ 4 = 125,000 per second, larger than ride requests.
Each update is about 100 bytes, so about 12.5 MB per second of location ingest.
Only the latest position matters for matching, so it lives in memory; history goes to a stream for analytics.
capacity.result: Ride requests peak around 3,700 per second, but location updates reach about 125,000 per second: the geo index is the hot path.

steps: Drivers stream locations over a persistent connection to location gateways, which update an in-memory geo index (geohash or H3 cell → drivers) partitioned by city.
A ride request goes to the dispatch service, which reads nearby cells, filters available drivers and ranks by estimated arrival time.
Dispatch offers the ride to one driver at a time (or a few in sequence) with a short timeout.
Acceptance uses a conditional write on the ride (status = requested → assigned) so two drivers cannot both get it.
During the trip, driver locations are forwarded to the rider’s app; trip events go to Kafka for billing and analytics.

driver app -> location gateway -> geo index (city shard, cells) 
rider -> dispatch -> nearby cells -> rank by ETA -> offer -> accept (conditional write)
trip events -> Kafka -> billing, analytics

rubric: Identifies location updates as the dominant write load.

title: Zomato/Swiggy
objectives: Scope Zomato/Swiggy: browse & search restaurants, place order & pay
Size it: 30M orders/day, about 2,100/s at peak
Defend the design: order service with saga: payment → restaurant accept → rider assign

cards.title: What Zomato/Swiggy must do
cards.body: Zomato/Swiggy: Browse restaurants, order and pay, and track the delivery rider live. In scope: Browse & search restaurants; Place order & pay; Track rider live.

cards.title: Zomato/Swiggy: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Peak at lunch/dinner. Order state consistent. ETA accuracy. Out of scope: Restaurant POS integration; Grocery delivery.

cards.title: One reference path for Zomato/Swiggy
cards.body: Order service with saga: payment → restaurant accept → rider assign. → Search on Elasticsearch with geo filters. → Rider location via WebSocket; notifications via queue.

cards.title: Where Zomato/Swiggy breaks first
cards.body: Order state consistency: An explicit state machine (placed → paid → accepted → picked → delivered) in SQL, changed only by valid transitions, prevents impossible states. Lunch and dinner peaks: Peaks are predictable, so autoscaling is scheduled ahead, and non-critical work such as review prompts is queued.

steps: The client splits files into chunks and hashes each one (SHA-256).
It asks the metadata service which chunk hashes are missing, then uploads only those via presigned URLs to object storage (resumable).
Once chunks are stored, the client commits a new file version: the list of chunk hashes, in a transactional metadata database.
The metadata service publishes a change event; other devices, connected by long-polling or WebSocket, fetch the changed file list and download only missing chunks.
Sharing writes permission entries (user or link, role) checked on every access; conflicting edits from two devices create a “conflicted copy”.

commit version (SQL) -> change event -> other devices sync -> download missing chunks

cards.title: Where Payment System UPI-style breaks first
cards.body: Exactly-once debit: The unique transaction reference is enforced at the PSP and checked by the banks, so a retried request can never trigger a second debit. bossDeep.pitch: A UPI-style payment app (PSP) on top of NPCI: pay to a VPA, collect requests and history.

assumptions: 150 million daily users, about 3 transactions each per day
Each transaction writes about 5 ledger and state rows of 500 bytes
Peak days such as festivals add more; UPI volumes are publicly reported by NPCI monthly
steps: Peak ≈ 5,210 × 5 ≈ 26,000 transactions per second (the quiz target is about 26,000).
Daily transactions = 450,000,000; storage ≈ 450,000,000 × 2,500 bytes = 1,125,000,000,000 bytes, about 1.1 TB per day.

Peak of about 26,000 transactions per second, each writing several indexed rows with synchronous durability, is likely beyond a comfortable margin for one primary, so plan to partition the transaction store (for example by payer id) and confirm with a load test.
Every transaction involves calls to NPCI and banks, so most latency is external; the app must handle timeouts and pending states.
capacity.result: About 26,000 transactions per second with external dependencies: idempotency, a clear state machine and reconciliation matter more than raw speed.

steps: The app creates a transaction with a unique transaction reference (idempotency key) and status INITIATED in a SQL ledger sharded by user.
The PSP sends the request to NPCI, which routes the debit to the payer’s bank and the credit to the payee’s bank.
Responses move the state machine (INITIATED → PENDING → SUCCESS or FAILED); retries reuse the same reference, so no double debit.
Timeouts leave the transaction PENDING; a status-check job queries NPCI and a reconciliation job compares daily settlement files.
History is served from a read model; every state change is written to an append-only audit log.
architecture.diagram:
app -> PSP txn svc (unique txn ref, SQL ledger) -> NPCI -> payer bank (debit) / payee bank (credit)
responses -> state machine | timeouts -> status check | daily recon files

deepDives.title: Exactly-once debit
deepDives.body: The unique transaction reference is enforced at the PSP and checked by the banks, so a retried request can never trigger a second debit.

deepDives.title: Pending states
deepDives.body: Network timeouts are common; showing “pending, we will update you” and resolving via status checks is safer than guessing success or failure.

rubric: Uses a unique transaction reference end to end.
Models an explicit state machine including PENDING.
Reconciles with settlement files.
Keeps an append-only audit trail.

title: BookMyShow
objectives: Scope BookMyShow: view shows & seat map, hold seats for 10 min

cards.title: What BookMyShow must do
cards.body: BookMyShow: View shows and seat maps, hold seats for 10 minutes, then pay and confirm. In scope: View shows & seat map; Hold seats for 10 min; Pay and confirm.

cards.title: BookMyShow: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: No double booking. Spikes on blockbuster releases. Fair queueing. Out of scope: Food and beverage add-ons; Dynamic pricing.

cards.title: One reference path for BookMyShow
cards.body: Seat holds via conditional update or short Redis lock with TTL. → Payment saga releases hold on failure/timeout. → Virtual waiting room queue for blockbuster drops.

cards.title: Where BookMyShow breaks first
cards.body: Double booking: Because the hold only succeeds when the seat is FREE in the same statement, two users clicking the same seat cannot both succeed. boss.referenceNotes: Core flows: search trains and availability; book Tatkal berths; pay, then allocate and issue the PNR. Must hold: survive the cliff-shaped burst at 10:00 (AC) and 11:00 (non-AC); never oversell; refund or release the mandate when allocation fails. Key mechanisms: pre-scale before the window; Aadhaar-OTP-authenticated users only and an agent blackout for the first 30 minutes (Railway Board order of 10 Jun 2025); waiting-room tokens plus rate limits; availability from a short-TTL cache; payment first (or an Autopay mandate/lien), then an atomic conditional decrement per train, date, class and quota that generates the PNR; if no berth is left, the payment is refunded or the lien released. bossDeep.pitch: IRCTC Tatkal: survive the 10:00 AM rush, take payment, then allocate berths without overselling and issue PNRs.

functional: Pay, then allocate and issue PNR
nonFunctional: Refund or release the lien if allocation fails

assumptions: About 1,000,000 booking attempts in the first minute after Tatkal opens (illustrative)
Tatkal opens at 10:00 for AC classes and 11:00 for non-AC, as publicly documented by IRCTC
A popular train-class has a few hundred Tatkal berths
steps: Window = 60 seconds.
Peak = 1,000,000 ÷ 60 ≈ 16,700 booking attempts per second (the quiz target).
Spread over a whole day the same attempts would average about 12 per second, which is why daily averages mislead here.
Seats per popular train-class are a few hundred, so most attempts must fail fast and fairly.
Search and availability reads are cacheable; only the final allocation must hit the inventory of record.
capacity.result: About 16,700 booking attempts per second in a cliff-shaped opening minute, competing for a few hundred berths: admit users at a safe rate, take payment, then allocate atomically.

steps: Pre-scale web, search and booking tiers before 09:55, and serve static content from a CDN.

Only Aadhaar-authenticated users can book Tatkal online (from 1 July 2025), with Aadhaar OTP (from 15 July 2025, rolled out train by train); authorised agents are blocked for the first 30 minutes (10:00–10:30 AC, 11:00–11:30 non-AC). Source: Railway Board order of 10 Jun 2025, PIB 11 Jun 2025.
A waiting room issues queue tokens and admits users to the booking flow at a rate the payment and reservation systems can handle; availability is shown from a cache that may lag by seconds.
The user pays first (or authorises an iPay Autopay mandate, which is debited only when the PNR is generated). No berth is held while the user pays, so availability can change in the meantime.

After payment, the reservation system (PRS) allocates with a conditional decrement per (train, date, class, quota). Success generates the PNR; if no berth is left, the payment is refunded or the mandate released. Bots are limited with CAPTCHAs and per-account limits.
architecture.diagram:
users -> CDN -> waiting room (tokens, Aadhaar OTP) -> booking svc -> payment / Autopay lien -> PRS allocation (conditional decrement per train/class/quota) -> PNR
no berth -> refund / release lien | availability from cache

deepDives.title: Fairness
deepDives.body: A queue with tokens admits users in arrival order and rate, instead of rewarding whoever retries fastest. The 2025 rules add identity checks (Aadhaar OTP) and keep agents out of the first 30 minutes, so bulk and bot bookings cannot take the opening burst (PIB, 11 Jun 2025).

deepDives.title: Pay, then allocate
deepDives.body: IRCTC takes payment (or an Autopay lien) before the reservation system allocates a berth and generates the PNR. That avoids holding scarce berths for users who never pay, at the cost of refunds when allocation fails. A hold-then-pay design, as used for cinema seats, is the alternative trade-off.

deepDives.title: Graceful degradation
deepDives.body: Under overload, turn off non-essential features (detailed history, recommendations) and keep search and booking alive.

rubric: Quantifies the opening-minute burst.
Uses a waiting room, rate limiting and authenticated users.
Takes payment, then allocates atomically and issues the PNR.
Refunds or releases the lien when allocation fails, and blocks bots.

title: Leaderboard
objectives: Scope Leaderboard: update scores live, show rank and top-N
Size it: 400M score reads/day, about 37,000/s at peak
Defend the design: score events streamed; workers update Redis sorted sets per contest

cards.title: What Leaderboard must do
cards.body: Leaderboard: Live free-to-play fantasy-contest leaderboards during IPL matches: update scores, show rank and top N. In scope: Update scores live; Show rank and top-N; Millions per contest.

cards.title: Leaderboard: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Updates within seconds. Massive spikes at match time. Accurate final ranks. Out of scope: Reward fulfilment; Team creation UI.

cards.title: One reference path for Leaderboard
cards.body: Score events streamed; workers update Redis sorted sets per contest. → Sharded sorted sets for huge contests; top-N cached. → Final ranks computed in batch for rewards.

cards.title: Where Leaderboard breaks first
cards.body: Update fan-out: One wicket changes points for every team containing that bowler, possibly millions of teams; recomputing per team in batches every few seconds is cheaper than per ball per team in real time. Accurate final ranks: Live ranks can be approximate, but final standings use a deterministic batch computation with tie-break rules, audited before rewards are announced. Real-money contests are banned in India since the Online Gaming Act, 2025, so rewards are non-cash.

cards.title: Closing Leaderboard in one minute
cards.body: Summarise in four points: the peak you designed for (about 37,000 score reads per second under the brief’s assumptions), the main path (load balancer, stateless services, cache, NoSQL store, queue, workers, stream), the riskiest part (update fan-out) and the one mitigation you would build first.

steps: Peak ≈ 4,630 × 8 ≈ 37,000 score reads per second (the quiz target is about 37,000).
A Redis sorted set entry costs on the order of 100 bytes, so 10,000,000 entries ≈ 1,000,000,000 bytes, about 1 GB per contest, fine for one shard.
Rank lookups and top-N reads are O(log n) in a sorted set: log2 of 10,000,000 ≈ 23 steps.
Score reads at about 37,000 per second are mostly “my rank” and “top 100”, both cacheable for a few seconds.

steps: Ball-by-ball events from the scoring feed go to Kafka; a points service converts them into point changes per real-world player.
Workers compute each team’s new total (teams contain 11 players) and update Redis sorted sets per contest in batches with ZADD.
Top-N comes from ZREVRANGE and “my rank” from ZREVRANK, cached for a few seconds and pushed to clients.
Very large contests can be split into buckets by score range, or ranks approximated during play and computed exactly at the end.
Final ranks are recomputed from the authoritative scores in batch after the match before rewards are announced.

scoring feed -> Kafka -> points svc -> team totals -> Redis ZADD (per contest)
app -> rank svc -> ZREVRANK / ZREVRANGE (cached seconds)
match end -> batch recompute -> final ranks

title: Typeahead

cards.title: What Typeahead must do
cards.body: Typeahead: Search suggestions for an e-commerce app, including Hinglish and typos. In scope: Suggest top queries for prefix; Update with trending queries; Handle Hinglish/typos.

cards.title: Typeahead: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: p99 < 50 ms. Very read-heavy. Fresh within minutes. Out of scope: Full search results page; Personalised suggestions per user.

cards.title: One reference path for Typeahead
cards.body: Trie / prefix index of top-k completions cached in memory. → Query logs aggregated by stream/batch jobs to update rankings. → Client debouncing and CDN caching of popular prefixes.

cards.title: Where Typeahead breaks first
cards.body: Freshness versus cost: Rebuilding the full index every few minutes is cheap at 50 MB; a separate trending layer handles sudden spikes such as a new phone launch. Filtering: Offensive or out-of-stock suggestions are filtered at build time, with a block list that applies immediately.

bossDeep.pitch: Typeahead search suggestions for an e-commerce app, including Hinglish and typos.

assumptions: 50 million daily users, about 20 keystrokes each per day
Each prefix stores its top 10 completions, about 500 bytes
steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 keystrokes per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).
Suggestion cache = 100,000 × 500 bytes = 50,000,000 bytes, about 50 MB, small enough for every server’s memory.
Peak of about 35,000 keystroke requests per second is served from memory with p99 well under 50 ms.
Debouncing on the client (wait about 100 ms after typing) cuts requests noticeably.

steps: Search logs stream into an aggregation job that counts queries over a sliding window (for example the last 7 days with decay).
A builder produces a trie or prefix map where each prefix holds its top-k completions, then publishes a snapshot every few minutes.
Suggestion servers load the snapshot into memory and answer GET /suggest?q=pan in microseconds; a CDN can cache very short popular prefixes.
Normalisation handles case, spacing, transliteration (pani puri, panipuri, पानी पूरी) and common misspellings before lookup.
Trending queries are blended from a fast streaming counter so new terms appear within minutes.

steps: Peak ≈ 11,600 × 3 ≈ 35,000 click events per second (the quiz target is about 35,000).

steps: Click servers validate and log each click with a unique click id, then publish to Kafka keyed by ad_id.

Fraud filters (bots, repeated clicks) run in the stream and mark clicks as invalid before billing.

click servers (click id) -> Kafka (key ad_id) -> Flink: dedup, window per minute (event time) -> OLAP store
raw -> object storage -> daily batch recompute -> reconcile

title: Stock Exchange Matching

cards.title: What Stock Exchange Matching must do
cards.body: Stock Exchange Matching: Accept orders, match by price-time priority, publish trades. In scope: Place limit and market orders; Match buy and sell orders by price-time priority; Publish trades and order book updates.

cards.title: Stock Exchange Matching: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Matching latency in microseconds to low milliseconds. Deterministic, auditable ordering. No lost or duplicated orders. Out of scope: Portfolio analytics; KYC onboarding.

cards.title: One reference path for Stock Exchange Matching
cards.body: One single-threaded matching engine per symbol for deterministic order. → Every order sequenced and journaled before matching. → Hot standby replays the journal on failover.

cards.title: Where Stock Exchange Matching breaks first
cards.body: Determinism: A single thread per symbol and a sequenced input log mean replaying the log always reproduces the same trades, which is what makes audit and failover possible. Latency: Avoiding locks, network hops and garbage-collection pauses in the matching path keeps latency in microseconds; persistence is the replicated log, not a database write per order.

About 5,000 listed symbols, with trading concentrated in a few hundred
steps: Session = 6.25 × 3,600 = 22,500 seconds.

steps: Orders arrive through gateways that validate them and run risk checks (margin, limits).
A sequencer assigns a global sequence number and writes each order to a replicated log before matching.
A single-threaded matching engine per symbol keeps the order book in memory: buy and sell sides sorted by price, then time; incoming orders match against the best opposite prices.
Trades and book updates are published to market-data feeds and to clearing; every event is in the log.
Hot standby engines replay the same log; on failure, a standby with the same state takes over deterministically.

bossDeep.pitch: An online judge like LeetCode or Codeforces: submit code, run tests in a sandbox, show a verdict.

assumptions: 2 million daily users, about 10 submissions each per day
Each submission takes about 2 seconds of sandbox time
steps: Average = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second.
Peak ≈ 231 × 10 ≈ 2,300 submissions per second (the quiz target is about 2,300).
Peak of about 2,300 submissions per second × 2 seconds = 4,600 sandbox-seconds per second, so about 4,600 sandboxes busy at once.
If one worker machine runs 16 sandboxes, that is about 4,600 ÷ 16 ≈ 288 machines at contest peak.
Outside contests the fleet can scale down to a small fraction of that.
capacity.result: About 2,300 submissions per second at contest peak needs thousands of concurrent sandboxes: queue, isolate and autoscale.

steps: The API stores the submission and puts a job on a queue (separate queues per contest for fairness).
Workers pull jobs and run code in sandboxes (containers or microVMs such as gVisor or Firecracker) with no network, CPU and memory limits, time limits and a read-only filesystem.
Tests run against hidden inputs; outputs are compared and a verdict (accepted, wrong answer, time limit) is produced.
Verdicts are written back and pushed to the user; contest leaderboards update from verdict events.
Workers autoscale on queue depth before and during contests.
architecture.diagram:

title: Distributed Counter
objectives: Scope Distributed Counter: increment a counter (likes, views), read the current count
Size it: 2B increments/day, about 120,000/s at peak
Defend the design: hot counters sharded into N sub-counters summed on read

cards.title: What Distributed Counter must do
cards.body: Distributed Counter: A distributed counter for likes and views that handles very hot counters. In scope: Increment a counter (likes, views); Read the current count; Handle very hot counters.

cards.title: Distributed Counter: targets and exclusions
cards.body: Targets: Increments under 10 ms. Counts may lag by a few seconds. No lost increments. Out of scope: Per-user like history UI; Fraud detection.

cards.title: One reference path for Distributed Counter
cards.body: Hot counters sharded into N sub-counters summed on read. → Increments batched by workers before hitting storage. → Consumers idempotent per event ID.

cards.title: Where Distributed Counter breaks first
cards.body: No lost increments: Redis alone can lose recent writes on failover; the Kafka log or periodic durable snapshots allow counts to be rebuilt exactly. Lag versus cost: Summing 32 keys on every read is cheap with a short cache; allowing counts to lag a few seconds is what makes the design scale.

Peak overall is about 120,000 increments per second across all counters, easily spread over a cluster.
One viral counter at 50,000 per second sits uncomfortably close to a single key’s limit and its shard’s CPU.
Splitting it into 32 sub-counters gives about 50,000 ÷ 32 ≈ 1,560 increments per second each.
capacity.result: About 120,000 increments per second overall, with single hot counters near one key’s limit: shard hot counters and sum on read.

steps: Increments go to a counter service, which writes to Redis with INCR on the counter key, or on one of N sub-keys chosen at random for hot counters.
Reads sum the N sub-counters (cached for a second or two), so counts may lag slightly.
Increments are also written to a log (Kafka) so counts can be rebuilt and persisted to a durable store periodically.
Counters become hot automatically: when a key’s rate passes a threshold, the service starts spreading it over more sub-keys.
Duplicate increments (such as a double like) are prevented by storing the like itself with a unique (user, post) constraint; the counter counts accepted likes.
architecture.diagram:
like -> unique (user, post) insert -> counter svc -> INCR counter:post:7#r (r = 0..31)
read -> sum 32 sub-keys (cache 1 s) | log -> Kafka -> durable store

deepDives.title: No lost increments
deepDives.body: Redis alone can lose recent writes on failover; the Kafka log or periodic durable snapshots allow counts to be rebuilt exactly.

deepDives.title: Lag versus cost
deepDives.body: Summing 32 keys on every read is cheap with a short cache; allowing counts to lag a few seconds is what makes the design scale.

rubric: Shards hot counters into sub-counters.
Sums on read with a short cache.
Persists increments durably for rebuilding.
Deduplicates the underlying action, not the counter.

title: Clarifying Requirements
objectives: Separate functional from non-functional requirements
Ask the questions that change the design
State assumptions when answers are vague

cards.title: Functional first
cards.body: Ask what users do: the three or four core actions, such as post, follow and view the feed. Say out loud what is out of scope.

cards.title: Non-functional next
cards.body: Scale (users, QPS, data), latency targets, availability, consistency needs and the read/write ratio. These shape the architecture more than features do.

cards.title: Five clarifying minutes
cards.body: Five questions, in order, that scope almost any prompt; finish by stating your assumptions so the interviewer can correct them.
steps: Who are the users and what do they do?
Which features are core and which are later?
How many users and requests?
Latency, availability and consistency needs
State assumptions out loud

cards.title: India-scale anchors
cards.body: Useful anchors: about 900M internet users, UPI in the tens of billions of transactions a month, IPL streams with tens of millions of concurrent viewers. Use them to sanity-check numbers.

cards.title: Trap: too many questions, or none
cards.body: Asking twenty questions without stating assumptions, or asking none. Ask what changes the design, then say “I’ll assume X; tell me if that is off.”

questions.prompt: For “Design Instagram”, which is a functional requirement?

choices.label: 500M daily users
Feed p99 latency under 200 milliseconds
Users can post photos and follow others
99.95% availability

questions.explanation: Functional = what users can do.

questions.prompt: Which question uncovers a non-functional requirement?

choices.label: Do we support stories that expire after a day?
Can users tag friends in their photo posts?
How quickly must a new post appear in followers’ feeds?
Can users add filters to their photos before posting them?

questions.explanation: Freshness is a latency/consistency requirement.

questions.prompt: Order the clarifying minutes.

items.label: Who are the users and what do they do?
Which features are core?
How many users and requests?
Latency, availability and consistency needs
State assumptions

questions.explanation: Features, then scale, then qualities.

questions.prompt: The interviewer shrugs at “how many users?”. Best move?

choices.label: State an assumption, such as 100M daily users, and continue
Refuse to continue until you are given a number
Skip the estimation step entirely and move on
Design for unlimited scale just to be safe

questions.explanation: Assumptions keep you moving and can be corrected.

questions.prompt: UPI crossed 20B transactions in a month in August 2025 (publicly reported by NPCI). Roughly what is the average per second?
questions.formula: A month is about 2.6M seconds; 20B ÷ 2.6M ≈ 7,700 per second.
questions.workedAnswer: A month is about 2.6M seconds; 20B ÷ 2.6M ≈ 7,700 per second.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 7,700/s is only the average. Payments cluster around meals, evenings and salary days, so you would design for a peak several times higher and say the factor you assumed.

questions.prompt: 10 million DAU each make 2 requests a day with a 3× peak factor. What is the approximate peak request rate?

choices.label: About 700 per second
About 230 per second
About 20,000 per second
About 70 per second

questions.explanation: 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231 per second on average; × 3 ≈ 693 at peak.

flashcards.front: For “Design Instagram”, which is a functional requirement?
flashcards.back: Users can post photos and follow others. Functional = what users can do.

flashcards.front: Which question uncovers a non-functional requirement?
flashcards.back: How quickly must a new post appear in followers’ feeds?. Freshness is a latency/consistency requirement.

flashcards.front: The interviewer shrugs at “how many users?”. Best move?
flashcards.back: State an assumption, such as 100M daily users, and continue. Assumptions keep you moving and can be corrected.

mechanism.title: The first five minutes, step by step
steps: Restate the problem in one sentence to confirm scope: “A service where riders request autos and nearby drivers accept, in one country, mobile apps only.”
Functional requirements: list 3–5 core user actions and agree which are in scope (request ride, match driver, track trip, pay) and which are out (ratings, scheduled rides, chat).
Non-functional requirements: ask for scale (daily active users, peak factor), latency targets, availability, consistency needs per feature, durability, and regional or regulatory constraints.
Write explicit assumptions where the interviewer has no preference: “10 million DAU, peak 3× average, 99.9% availability, match within 5 seconds at p99.”
Turn assumptions into anchor numbers you will reuse: requests per second, storage per year, bandwidth. Do the arithmetic aloud and round sensibly.
Confirm priorities: “I’ll focus on matching and location updates, and treat payments as a black box unless you want me to go there.”

useWhen: Always, in the first few minutes, before drawing any boxes.
Again whenever the interviewer adds a twist ('now make it work offline'): restate the changed requirement before redesigning.
avoidWhen: Do not spend more than about 5 minutes of a 45-minute interview on requirements; move on with stated assumptions.
Do not ask questions you will not use; every number you gather should change a design decision.

rows: How many daily users? Peak factor?
How fast must a match feel?
Can two drivers accept one ride?
Conditional writes or locks on the ride

numbers.title: Turning assumptions into anchor numbers
assumptions: 10 million DAU; each user makes 2 ride requests per day
steps: Average per second = 20,000,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 231.
Peak per second = 231 × 3 = 693, call it about 700.
Driver location pings: 500,000 online drivers every 4 seconds gives 500,000 ÷ 4 = 125,000 writes per second, far larger than ride requests, so location ingestion is the scaling hot spot.
numbers.result: Anchor numbers show that location pings, not ride requests, dominate load, which tells you where to spend the deep dive.

india.title: Clarifying a “design an IRCTC-like booking system” prompt
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: If asked to design a train-booking system for India, strong candidates first separate normal booking from the Tatkal window, when demand spikes sharply at the opening minute. They ask whether the focus is search, seat inventory or payments, whether waitlist and RAC (reservation against cancellation) rules are in scope, and what consistency is required: a berth must never be sold twice, so seat allocation is strongly consistent while availability displays can be slightly stale. Stating “I’ll assume a burst of a few lakh booking attempts in the first minute, an illustrative estimate” lets them size queues and inventory locks instead of guessing later.

pitfalls.trap: Jumping straight to drawing a load balancer and a database.
pitfalls.say: “Before designing, let me confirm the core features and the scale, so I size the right parts.”

pitfalls.trap: Collecting numbers and never using them.
pitfalls.say: “At about 700 peak ride requests per second but 125,000 location writes per second, I’ll focus the design on location ingestion.”

takeaways: Clarify scope before drawing anything.
Ask only questions that change design decisions.
Write assumptions down and turn them into anchor numbers.
Use the numbers to choose where to deep-dive.
deep.diagram:
restate -> functional (in/out) -> non-functional (scale, latency, consistency, availability)
 -> assumptions -> anchor numbers -> agreed focus

interactive.title: The question that matters most
interactive.prompt: “Design a food-delivery app.” Which question changes the design most?

choices.label: Is live rider tracking in scope, and for how many concurrent orders?
choices.feedback: Right: it adds a high-rate location stream and real-time push.

choices.label: Which programming language should we use?
choices.feedback: It rarely changes the architecture.

choices.label: What colour is the logo?
choices.feedback: Irrelevant to the design.

interactive.reveal: Ask questions whose answers change components or scale, then state assumptions out loud ('I'll assume 1M concurrent orders at dinner peak') so the interviewer can correct them.

title: Deep Dives & Trade-off Language
objectives: Choose the part of the design worth a deep dive
Phrase trade-offs with requirement, cost and mitigation
Avoid absolute claims

cards.title: Choosing the deep dive
cards.body: Pick the part most likely to break at your numbers. For IRCTC Tatkal booking that is the 10:00 a.m. burst on a few thousand seats per train, not the login page. Or ask which part the interviewer wants. Spend 10–15 minutes deep on one area rather than shallow on five.

cards.title: Trade-off sentences
cards.body: Use: “A or B. I choose A because requirement X; the cost is Y; I’ll mitigate with Z.” For example: “Async replication, because checkout writes must finish in under 50 ms; the cost is losing a few seconds of writes on failover; payment records take a synchronous path.” It shows judgement instead of memorised answers.

cards.title: A deep dive
cards.body: A strong deep dive puts a number on the risk, shows how the design fails, compares two fixes and names the cost of the one you pick.
steps: Name the risk with a number
Show how the design fails
Propose two fixes
Pick one and name its cost
Say how you would monitor it

cards.title: Soften absolutes
cards.body: Avoid “always” and “never”. Say “for this read-heavy feed I’d cache with a short TTL”, not “caching is always right”. An interviewer can break an absolute with one counterexample (“even for a write-heavy ledger?”), and you spend the next five minutes retreating.

cards.title: Trap: an option with no downside
cards.body: Presenting one option as obviously correct with no downside. Interviewers push back until you name the cost; naming it first earns the point. Have the next answer ready too: “what breaks first if traffic grows 10×?”

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest trade-off statement?

choices.label: Async replication, since it is faster than sync and simpler to run
Async, for fast writes; failover may lose seconds, so payments go sync
Kafka, since most large companies already run it in production
Either works; I would go with whatever the team knows best

questions.explanation: It names the requirement (fast writes), the cost (seconds of writes lost on failover) and a mitigation (a synchronous path for payments). “Faster and simpler” names no cost, popularity is not a requirement, and “either works” skips the decision the interviewer asked you to make.

questions.prompt: Order the trade-off sentence.

items.label: State the options
Pick one
Tie it to a requirement
Name the cost
Say how you mitigate it

questions.explanation: The cost and mitigation are what interviewers listen for.

questions.prompt: Design IRCTC Tatkal booking: sales open at 10:00 a.m., a train has a few thousand seats, and requests in the first minute far exceed them. You have 15 minutes for one deep dive. Which?

choices.label: The login page and its OTP flow
The admin tool for adding new trains
Seat inventory under the opening burst
The PNR status page and its caching

questions.explanation: A burst on a small, contended seat inventory is where the design breaks: double-booked seats or a melted database. PNR status is read-heavy but easy to cache, the admin tool has a handful of users, and login matters but is a solved problem worth one sentence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is best in an interview?

choices.label: Caching is always the right answer for reads
Microservices always beat a monolith at scale
For this read-heavy feed, I’d cache with a short TTL
Never use SQL once traffic gets large

questions.explanation: It scopes the claim to this workload and names a choice with a limit (a short TTL). The others are absolutes an interviewer can break with one counterexample: a write-heavy ledger where a cache adds staleness, a small team for whom a monolith is simpler, or the many large systems that run on SQL.

questions.prompt: Order a deep dive.

items.label: Name the risk with a number
Show how the design fails
Propose two fixes
Pick one and name its cost
Say how you would monitor it

questions.explanation: Evidence, options, decision, follow-up.

questions.prompt: Which statement best follows the trade-off template?

choices.label: “A conditional update in PostgreSQL costs a hot row; at 700/s that is fine, so I choose it”
“PostgreSQL is the best database, so I always pick it for every system I design”
“Redis scales infinitely, so I put everything in Redis and skip the database”
“We should always use microservices, because they scale better than monoliths”

questions.explanation: It names the cost (a hot row), puts a number on the load, and then decides. The others are absolutes with no cost: no database is best for every system, Redis does not scale without limit and is a weak sole system of record, and microservices bring network and operational costs of their own.

flashcards.front: Which is the strongest trade-off statement?
flashcards.back: Async replication, because writes must be fast; we may lose seconds on failover, so payments use a sync path. Requirement, cost, mitigation.

flashcards.front: URL shortener at 100K redirects/s. Best deep-dive choice?
flashcards.back: The redirect read path and caching of hot links. Dive where the numbers bite.

flashcards.front: Which sentence is best in an interview?
flashcards.back: For this read-heavy feed, I’d cache with a short TTL. Scope claims to the problem.

mechanism.title: Running a deep dive
steps: Pick the component where the requirements are hardest: the hot path at peak, the strongest consistency need, or the biggest data volume. Say why you picked it.
State the problem precisely: “Two drivers can accept the same ride within milliseconds; we must allow exactly one.”
Offer two or three options, each in one sentence.
Compare with the trade-off template: “Option A gives X at the cost of Y; option B gives Y but costs Z. Given our requirement W, I choose A.”
Go one level deeper on the chosen option: data model, the exact query or write, failure cases, and the numbers it must handle.
Close the loop: name what would make you switch options later (for example, 'if accepts exceed 10,000 per second on one city partition, I'd split by zone').

useWhen: Whenever you choose a technology or pattern, and whenever the interviewer asks “why not X?”.
On the one or two components that carry the most risk; depth beats breadth.
avoidWhen: Do not deep-dive into something generic, like the load balancer algorithm, while the hard problem (matching, consistency) stays vague.
Do not use absolutes such as “always use Kafka” or “NoSQL is faster”; tie every claim to a requirement.

rows: “X fits because we need …; the cost is …”
“It scales to about N per second per node; we need M, so about M ÷ N nodes”
“Cache menus for 5 minutes, invalidate on edit; prices at checkout from the database”
“Strong for ride acceptance, eventual for driver locations shown on the map”

numbers.title: Comparing two options with numbers
assumptions: Ride accept rate at peak 700 per second across a city
Option A: conditional update on the ride row in PostgreSQL, about 2 ms each
Option B: a Redis lock per ride, about 0.5 ms each plus lock expiry handling
steps: Option A load: 700 writes per second, each touching one row, which one PostgreSQL primary handles comfortably.
Total busy time for option A = 700 × 2 ms = 1,400 ms of work per second, spread over many connections and cores.
Option B is faster per call but adds a second system whose failover can drop locks, plus a lease to manage.
Since option A meets the load with the source of truth, choose A and mention B only if accepts grow 10× or more.
numbers.result: Use numbers to show the simpler option is enough, and name the threshold at which you would switch.

india.title: Deep dive on Tatkal seat allocation
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: In a train-booking interview, the right deep dive is seat allocation during the Tatkal opening, not the search page. A good answer compares a queue in front of the inventory service (fair and smooth, but adds waiting time), conditional decrements per train-class-date row (simple and strongly consistent, but one hot row per popular train), and pre-splitting a train’s quota into several counters (more parallelism, slightly more complex rebalancing). The candidate then picks, for example, a queue plus conditional decrements, explains the failure cases (payment fails, hold expires and the seat returns), and states the illustrative load the design must take.

pitfalls.trap: “Cassandra is better than PostgreSQL.”
pitfalls.say: “For ride acceptance we need a conditional write on one row; PostgreSQL does that at 700 per second easily, so I’d keep it there.”

pitfalls.trap: Diving into a generic component.
pitfalls.say: “The hard part here is double acceptance, so I’ll go deep on that rather than load-balancer algorithms.”

takeaways: Deep-dive where the requirements are hardest.
Use “X gives A at the cost of B; given W, I choose X”.
Replace absolutes with numbers and requirements.
Say what would make you change your mind.
deep.diagram: pick hardest part -> state problem -> 2-3 options -> trade-off template -> deeper on choice -> 'switch if ...'

interactive.title: The sentence that earns the point
interactive.prompt: Which sentence earns the trade-off point?

choices.label: “Async replication keeps writes fast, but failover can lose about a second of data: fine for likes, not for payments.”
choices.feedback: Right: a choice, its cost, and when the cost is acceptable.

choices.label: “Async replication is always better.”
choices.feedback: An absolute with no cost named invites pushback.

choices.label: “We’ll use Kafka because it scales.”
choices.feedback: A tool name is not a trade-off; what does it cost, and why here?

interactive.reveal: Name the option, what it buys, what it costs, and why the cost is acceptable for this requirement. Interviewers push until you do; doing it first earns the point.

title: Common Mistakes
objectives: Recognise the most common design-interview mistakes
Keep designs proportional to the numbers
Recover when you get stuck

cards.title: Designing before scoping
cards.body: Drawing boxes before knowing scale or features. Ask three or four questions first: daily users, the read/write ratio, the latency target and what is out of scope. A chat app for 50 people and one for 50 million share a name, not a design.

cards.title: Over-engineering
cards.body: Kafka, microservices and sharding for 1,000 users. A single database on a modest server handles thousands of indexed queries a second, far more than 1,000 users generate. Start simple, add a component when a number forces you, and say which number would.

cards.title: Unused numbers
cards.body: Estimating, then never using the estimate. If you computed 50K read QPS, say what it means: one cache node can serve that, you would run a few for headroom and failover, and at a 90% hit rate the database sees about 5K QPS.

cards.title: Recovering from a stall
cards.body: When you stall, say so, go back to the requirements, pick the simple option and park the hard question for the deep dive.
steps: Notice you are stuck
Say what you are weighing
Go back to the requirements
Pick a simple option and move on
Note it for a later deep dive

cards.title: Silent thinking
cards.body: Long silences leave the interviewer guessing. Think aloud, check in (“should I go deeper here?”) and take hints. Interviewers often hint on purpose to see how you use help, so a hint picked up well works in your favour.

questions.prompt: At 1,000 daily users, which design is reasonable?

choices.label: Cassandra sharded across three regions
Kubernetes with a service mesh
Kafka and twelve microservices
One app server and a managed database

questions.explanation: 1,000 daily users is well under one request a second on average; one server and a managed database, with backups and a tested restore, carry that easily. Cross-region Cassandra, a service mesh and twelve microservices each add operational work that no number asks for.

questions.prompt: You estimated 50K read QPS. What should follow?

choices.label: Use it to size the cache and app servers
Move on; estimation is only a warm-up phase
Re-estimate it more precisely, with exact figures
Ask whether 50K is right, then stop there

questions.explanation: An estimate earns credit only when it changes the design: 50K reads a second means a cache in front of the database and several app servers. Treating it as a warm-up wastes it, more precision rarely changes a decision, and checking the number without using it stops halfway.

questions.prompt: You are stuck on the database choice. Best move?

choices.label: Stay silent until you are completely sure of the right answer
Think aloud about the options and check in with the interviewer
Switch to talking about the frontend to fill the time
Pick one quickly without explaining to them why you chose it

questions.explanation: Reasoning out loud lets the interviewer follow, correct or hint, and earns credit even when you are unsure. Silence hides your thinking, changing the subject looks like avoidance, and a quick unexplained pick gives them nothing to assess.

questions.prompt: Order a recovery from a stall.

items.label: Notice you are stuck
Say what you are weighing
Go back to the requirements
Pick a simple option
Note it for a deep dive

questions.explanation: Keep moving, flag it, return later.

questions.prompt: Which is a sign you skipped scoping?

choices.label: Early on, you asked about the read/write ratio
Early on, you asked what is out of scope
You stated your traffic assumptions aloud
Halfway in, you learn it gets 10 writes a day

questions.explanation: Learning the write rate halfway through means the first half was built on guesses, and probably sized for far more traffic. Asking about the read/write ratio and the scope, and stating your assumptions aloud, are what scoping looks like.

questions.prompt: A system handles about 1–12 events per second. A candidate proposes a three-broker Kafka cluster. What is the best feedback?

choices.label: Overkill: a table or managed queue is enough
Kafka is needed for any event-driven design
Use five brokers instead, to leave room to grow
Fine, because Kafka is popular and widely known

questions.explanation: At 1–12 events a second, a database table polled by a worker, or a managed queue, is plenty, while a three-broker cluster adds brokers to run, monitor and upgrade. Nothing ties events to Kafka, more brokers make it worse, and popularity is not a requirement. Have the follow-up ready: switch when the rate reaches thousands a second, or when many consumers need to replay history.

flashcards.front: At 1,000 daily users, which design is reasonable?
flashcards.back: One app server and one managed database, with backups. Proportional to the load.

flashcards.front: You estimated 50K read QPS. What should follow?
flashcards.back: Use it: say a cache is needed and roughly how many app servers. Numbers should drive decisions.

flashcards.front: You are stuck on the database choice. Best move?
flashcards.back: Think aloud about the options and check in with the interviewer. Reasoning out loud earns credit even when unsure.

flashcards.front: Which is a sign you skipped scoping?
flashcards.back: Halfway through, you learn the system only needs 10 writes a day. The design was built on guesses.

mechanism.title: How common mistakes unfold, and how to catch them
steps: No scope: the candidate starts drawing before agreeing on features and scale, then designs the wrong thing for 20 minutes.
Over-engineering: Kafka, microservices, multi-region active-active and a service mesh for a system with 50 requests per second.
Unused numbers: the estimate says 2 TB per year, then the design ignores it (or contradicts it by sharding across 100 nodes).
Silence: long stretches of thinking without speaking, so the interviewer cannot follow or help.
Ignoring hints: the interviewer asks “what if two users book the same seat?” and the candidate moves on.

Recovery: when you notice any of these, say so plainly ('I over-built this; at 50 requests per second one service and PostgreSQL are enough'), simplify and continue. Correcting yourself is a positive signal.

useWhen: Use this list as a self-check every ten minutes: scope agreed? numbers used? speaking aloud? following hints?
Use the recovery script whenever you realise you are off track.
avoidWhen: Do not hide a mistake and hope the interviewer misses it; they almost never do.
Do not overcorrect into designing nothing; keep a working end-to-end design on the board.

rows: Restate and agree core features first
Tie each component to a number
Narrate the options you are weighing
Treat a repeated question as the priority

numbers.title: Is Kafka justified here?
assumptions: Internal tool: 5,000 users, each creating 20 events per day
Kafka cluster minimum: 3 brokers, plus operations effort
steps: Events per day = 5,000 × 20 = 100,000.
Average per second = 100,000 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1.2.
Even at a 10× peak that is about 12 events per second, which a PostgreSQL table or a simple managed queue handles easily.
A three-broker Kafka cluster adds cost and on-call load for no benefit at this scale.
numbers.result: About 1 event per second does not need Kafka; matching tools to numbers is the cure for over-engineering.

india.title: Over-building a college fest ticketing app
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: A candidate asked to design ticketing for a college fest in Kolkata, about 20,000 tickets sold over two weeks, proposes Kubernetes, Kafka, Cassandra and multi-region failover. The interviewer asks for the numbers: 20,000 tickets over 14 days is about 1,430 a day, and even if a quarter sell in the first hour, that is about 5,000 in an hour, around 1.4 per second. The strong recovery is: “I over-built this. A single web app with PostgreSQL, a unique constraint on seat ids, a payment gateway webhook and a CDN for the poster is enough; I’d add a queue only if launch traffic proves bursty.”

pitfalls.trap: Defending an over-built design when challenged.
pitfalls.say: “You’re right, at about 1.4 tickets per second this is over-built; let me simplify to one service and PostgreSQL.”

pitfalls.trap: Ignoring a repeated question from the interviewer.
pitfalls.say: “You’ve asked about double booking twice, so let me address it now: a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_id) makes the second booking fail cleanly.”

pitfalls.trap: Long silent thinking.
pitfalls.say: “I’m weighing a queue against direct writes; the queue smooths bursts but adds latency. Given our numbers, direct writes are fine.”

takeaways: Agree scope before designing.
Match every component to a number.
Think aloud; silence hides good reasoning.
Recover openly; self-correction is a strength.
deep.diagram:
every ~10 min: scope agreed? -> numbers used? -> talking aloud? -> hints followed?
 off track -> name it -> simplify -> continue

interactive.title: Your design ignores your own number
interactive.prompt: Mid-design, you notice your architecture ignores the 10× spike you estimated earlier. What is the best move?

choices.label: Say so, and add what the number calls for, such as an admission queue or pre-scaling
choices.feedback: Right: using your numbers is exactly what is being graded.

choices.label: Keep going and hope the interviewer doesn’t notice
choices.feedback: Unused numbers are a classic mistake; noticing it yourself is a strength.

choices.label: Start over from scratch
choices.feedback: Adjust the design; a restart wastes the time you have.

interactive.reveal: Estimates exist to drive decisions. Tie each major component back to a number ('the 10× spike is why the queue is here').

title: Communication in the Interview
objectives: Narrate decisions with their reasons
Grow a design step by step from the numbers
Work with the interviewer’s hints

cards.title: Narrate the design
cards.body: Say what you are drawing and why: “Reads dominate, so I’m putting a cache here.” The interviewer grades reasoning they can hear.

cards.title: Evolve, don’t jump
cards.body: Start with the simplest design that works, then add a component each time a number forces you: one server, then a load balancer, cache, replicas, shards.

cards.title: Growing a design aloud
cards.body: Grow the design one bottleneck at a time and say which number forces each step, instead of drawing the final architecture first.
steps: One server
Add a load balancer and stateless apps
Add a cache and CDN
Add read replicas
Add shards and regions

cards.title: Work with the interviewer
cards.body: Check in at transitions (“requirements look settled; shall I estimate?”). Treat hints as help, and if you do not know a tool, describe the property you need.

cards.title: Trap: bluffing
cards.body: Arguing with a hint or bluffing about a technology. Say “I haven’t used X, but I need a store with property Y” instead.

questions.prompt: Which is good narration?

choices.label: This is how Netflix does it, so we will copy that design
Now I’ll add a box here, and then another box over here
Reads are 100× writes, so I’ll put a cache in front of the database
I’ll add Redis here because Redis is what everyone uses

questions.explanation: Decision plus reason.

questions.prompt: You do not know a database the interviewer mentions. Best move?

choices.label: Refuse to use it and insist on your own
Change the subject to a database you know
Say so, and describe the properties you need from it
Pretend you know it and keep talking

questions.explanation: Honesty plus reasoning beats bluffing.

questions.prompt: At 1K users, what should your first diagram be?

choices.label: The final multi-region design
Microservices with Kafka
A sharded cluster
One server and a database

questions.explanation: Start simple, then grow.

questions.prompt: Order the growth of a design.

items.label: One server
Load balancer and stateless apps

flashcards.back: Say so, and describe the properties you need from it. Honesty plus reasoning beats bluffing.
