questions.explanation: 443 is the default HTTPS port, so the scheme, host and port all match.

questions.prompt: Which request triggers a preflight?

choices.label: A GET with no custom headers
A HEAD request
A POST with a form-encoded body and a cookie
A POST with Content-Type: application/json

questions.explanation: application/json is not one of the three safelisted content types (form-encoded, multipart form data, plain text), so the browser asks first. A GET or HEAD without custom headers is simple, and so is a form-encoded POST with a cookie: cookies do not trigger a preflight, which is why CSRF defences are still needed.

questions.prompt: A server returns no CORS headers. What happens when a cross-origin page sends a simple POST to it?

choices.label: The server rejects it with a 403 Forbidden error
The browser blocks the request before it is sent
The response is readable, but cookies are stripped from it
It reaches the server; the page just cannot read the reply

questions.explanation: Simple requests are sent; CORS decides whether the script may read the response, which is why CSRF defences are still needed.

questions.prompt: An API must accept cookies from https://app.example only. Which response headers are correct?

choices.label: Allow-Origin: * only
Allow-Origin: https://app.example, Allow-Credentials: true
Allow-Origin: * and Allow-Credentials: true
Allow-Origin: https://app.example without Allow-Credentials

questions.explanation: Credentialed responses need an explicit origin and Allow-Credentials: true. The wildcard alone hides credentialed responses from scripts, the wildcard plus credentials is rejected by browsers, and an explicit origin without Allow-Credentials still hides the response.

questions.prompt: Order a preflighted cross-origin request.

items.label: Browser gives the response to the script
Browser sends the PUT
Script asks the browser to send PUT to another origin
Browser sends OPTIONS with the requested method and headers
Server answers with the allowed origins, methods and headers

questions.explanation: Permission first, then the real request. If the OPTIONS answer does not allow PUT or the requested headers, the PUT is not sent at all and the script only sees a network error.

questions.prompt: CORS policy for an API used by your two front ends, with cookie sessions.
constraints: Third-party sites must not read user data

approaches.label: Allow-Origin: * with credentials
Echo any Origin with credentials
Check Origin against an allowlist and echo it back, with credentials and Vary: Origin

rationaleOptions.label: Reflecting every Origin is safe because cookies are SameSite
Only listed origins can read credentialed responses
Vary: Origin stops caches from serving one origin’s headers to another

rationaleConflicts.r3: SameSite does not cover every case (same-site subdomains, older browsers), and reflecting all origins opens the data to any site.

questions.explanation: An allowlist plus Vary: Origin is the standard safe configuration for credentialed CORS.

flashcards.back: Scheme + host + port.
For non-simple requests: other methods, non-safelisted headers, or a content type such as JSON.
No; browsers reject it. Use an explicit origin.

mechanism.title: How the browser enforces origins and CORS
steps: The same-origin policy restricts how a document or script from one origin interacts with resources from another. Embedding is mostly allowed (images, scripts, stylesheets, iframes); reading cross-origin responses from script and reaching into another origin’s DOM are not.

CORS is a protocol in the Fetch standard that lets a server relax that rule for specific origins. The browser adds an Origin header to cross-origin requests and checks the response headers before handing the response to the script.

Simple requests (GET, HEAD or POST with safelisted headers and content types) are sent directly. If the response lacks a matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin, the browser blocks the script from reading it, but the server has already processed the request.

Other requests are preflighted with OPTIONS, carrying Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers. The server answers with what it allows; Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache that answer for a while.

Credentialed requests (cookies, HTTP authentication) need the script to opt in and the server to respond with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true and an explicit origin, never *. Responses that vary by Origin should send Vary: Origin so shared caches keep them apart.
CORS errors are deliberately vague in scripts for security; the browser console shows the real reason. Testing with a command-line client will not reproduce them, because only browsers enforce CORS.

useWhen: Use an explicit allowlist of origins when an API serves a few known front ends.
Serve the front end and API from the same origin (for example behind one reverse proxy) to avoid CORS entirely.
avoidWhen: Avoid reflecting any Origin back with credentials; it makes user data readable by every site.
Avoid treating CORS as access control; authenticate and authorise every request on the server.

rows: Safe if the list is tight
Any site can read user data

numbers.title: What preflights cost
assumptions: Round trip 120 ms between the user and the API (example)
A page makes 10 different non-simple API calls on load
steps: Each call needs an OPTIONS round trip before the real request: 10 × 120 ms = 1.2 s of extra round trips if made one after another.
With Access-Control-Max-Age: 600, the browser reuses the preflight result for 10 minutes for the same URL and method (browsers cap this value: Chromium at 2 hours, Firefox at 24 hours).
Serving the API from the same origin removes the preflights entirely.
Requests made in parallel overlap their preflights, but each still adds at least one round trip to its own latency.
numbers.result: Preflights can add one round trip per call; caching them with Max-Age or using one origin removes most of that cost.

india.title: The Fetch standard
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: CORS is specified in the WHATWG Fetch standard, which every major browser implements. It defines exactly which methods, headers and content types are “CORS-safelisted”, how preflight results are cached, and why the wildcard origin is refused for credentialed requests. When a browser’s behaviour seems surprising, the Fetch standard and MDN’s CORS guide are the places to check rather than blog posts.

pitfalls.trap: “CORS stops attackers calling my API.”
pitfalls.say: “CORS only stops other sites’ scripts from reading responses in a browser; I still authenticate requests and defend against CSRF.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just set Allow-Origin to * and Allow-Credentials to true.”
pitfalls.say: “Browsers reject that combination; I’d allow an explicit list of origins and add Vary: Origin.”

takeaways: Origin is scheme + host + port.
Simple requests are sent; CORS decides whether script can read the response.
Non-simple requests are preflighted with OPTIONS.
Credentials need an explicit origin, never *.

interactive.title: Does the browser send a preflight?
interactive.prompt: A page on https://app.example calls https://api.example with a GET and an Authorization header.

choices.label: Yes: Authorization is not a safelisted header
choices.feedback: Right: any non-safelisted request header makes the request non-simple.

choices.label: No: GET requests never need a preflight
choices.feedback: GET is a simple method, but the header makes the request non-simple.

choices.label: No: same-site subdomains share an origin
choices.feedback: Different hosts are different origins, even on one site.

interactive.reveal: A request is simple only if its method, headers and content type are all on the safelist. Adding Authorization means the browser sends OPTIONS first.

seeAlso.why: Security essentials across the whole system

title: XSS and CSRF Basics
objectives: Tell cross-site scripting from cross-site request forgery
Apply output encoding and a Content Security Policy
Stop forged requests with SameSite cookies and tokens

cards.title: Two attacks with similar names
cards.body: Cross-site scripting (XSS) gets the attacker’s script to run inside your page, with all the user’s access. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) makes the user’s browser send a request to your site from another site, carrying the user’s cookies, without running any script on your page.

cards.title: Misconception: input filtering stops XSS
cards.body: Stripping “<script>” from input misses event handler attributes, URLs with script schemes and many encodings. The reliable defence is encoding output for the exact place it is inserted (HTML text, attribute, URL, script) when rendering.

cards.title: How a stored XSS plays out
cards.body: The attack starts as data and becomes code only when a page renders it without encoding.
steps: Attacker posts a comment containing markup with an event handler
Server stores it unchanged
Another user opens the page; the comment is inserted as raw HTML
The handler runs in that user’s session and can act as them

cards.title: Defence in depth for XSS
cards.body: Encode output by context, prefer APIs that set text rather than HTML, sanitise only where rich HTML is truly needed, and add a Content Security Policy that blocks inline scripts and limits script sources, so a missed bug is harder to exploit.

cards.title: Trap: a CSRF token in a GET link
cards.body: State-changing actions sent as GET requests can be triggered by an image tag on another site, and tokens in URLs leak through logs and the Referer header. Make state changes use POST (or other non-GET methods) with a token in the body or a header.

cards.title: Failure story: a modified script on a payment page
cards.body: Publicly reported: in 2018 attackers altered JavaScript served on British Airways’ booking pages so that card details typed into the payment form were also sent to an attacker-controlled domain. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office reported that data of more than 400,000 customers and staff was affected and fined the airline £20 million in 2020. Defences: Subresource Integrity on third-party scripts, a CSP that limits where scripts may send data (connect-src), and monitoring for changed script files.

questions.prompt: Which attack needs the attacker’s code to run inside your page?

choices.label: Clickjacking
A brute-force login attempt
Cross-site request forgery
Cross-site scripting

questions.explanation: XSS runs script in your origin; CSRF only causes a request.

questions.prompt: A user’s display name is inserted into an HTML page. What is the main defence?

choices.label: Reject any display name longer than 20 characters
Strip the word “script” from the input before saving
Store the name in a cookie instead of the page
HTML-encode it on output so markup shows as text

questions.explanation: Context-aware output encoding is the core XSS defence.

questions.prompt: Which defence stops a hidden cross-site form from transferring money with the user’s cookie?

choices.label: Making the transfer endpoint respond with JSON
HTML-encoding each field shown in the transfer form
A per-session CSRF token checked on state changes
A Content Security Policy on the bank’s own pages

questions.explanation: The attacker’s page cannot read the token, so the forged request fails the check.

questions.prompt: What does a Content Security Policy add if an encoding bug slips through?

choices.label: It encrypts the page so scripts cannot read it
It replaces server-side validation
It stops other sites from sending requests to you
It can block inline and unlisted scripts

questions.explanation: CSP limits which scripts the page will execute, which reduces the impact of an injection that slips past encoding. It does not encrypt anything, cannot replace server-side validation, and cannot stop other sites from sending requests to your server; that is what CSRF defences are for.

questions.prompt: Order a classic CSRF attack.

items.label: The browser attaches the bank cookie
User logs in to the bank; a session cookie is stored
The page auto-submits a hidden form to the bank
User visits the attacker’s page
The bank acts on the request as the user

questions.explanation: SameSite cookies or a CSRF token break the chain at step four or five.

questions.prompt: A forum must let users post comments with bold, italics and links.
constraints: Comments are shown to other users

approaches.label: Insert the comment HTML as written
Strip the word “script” and insert the rest
Sanitise with an allowlist of tags and attributes, plus a strict CSP

rationaleOptions.label: A CSP limits damage if the sanitiser misses something
An allowlist keeps only known-safe tags and attributes
Blocking the word script stops all script execution

rationaleConflicts.r3: Event handler attributes and script URLs run code without any script tag.

questions.explanation: When rich HTML is needed, use a maintained allowlist sanitiser and back it with a CSP.

flashcards.back: Attacker-controlled script runs in your page.
Another site makes the user’s browser send a request to yours with their cookies.
Context-aware output encoding (plus CSP as a second layer).

sources.title: OWASP: Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

mechanism.title: How each attack works and where each defence acts
steps: Reflected XSS: input in a request (for example a search term) is echoed straight into the response page. Stored XSS: the input is saved and shown to other users later. DOM-based XSS: the page’s own script copies data from the URL or storage into the page as HTML.

In every XSS variant, data crosses into a code context. Output encoding keeps it data: in HTML text, < becomes <; in an attribute, quotes are encoded; in a URL, only safe schemes are allowed; inside script, data goes through a safe serialiser rather than string concatenation.

Sanitisation is a different tool: it parses untrusted HTML and keeps only allowed tags and attributes. Use a maintained library for it when users must submit rich text; do not write your own with regular expressions.

A Content Security Policy is a response header listing where scripts, styles and other resources may come from. A strict policy using nonces or hashes blocks inline event handlers and injected script tags, which turns many XSS bugs into failed attempts.

CSRF relies on the browser attaching cookies automatically. Defences make a forged request distinguishable: SameSite cookies stop them being attached cross-site; a synchroniser token (a random value the page includes and the server checks) cannot be read by the attacking site; checking the Origin header rejects requests from unexpected sites.
XSS defeats CSRF defences: script running in your page can read the token and send requests itself. Fix XSS first; CSRF protection assumes your own page is not compromised.

useWhen: Context-aware output encoding everywhere data is rendered, plus a strict CSP as a safety net.
SameSite cookies plus CSRF tokens (or Origin checks) on every state-changing request.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on input blacklists to stop XSS.
Avoid state changes on GET requests; links and images can trigger them from any site.

numbers.title: How small the attack surface needs to be
assumptions: A page renders 40 pieces of user data in different places (example)
1 in 40 output sites is mis-encoded by hand (illustrative)
steps: Expected encoding bugs per page: 40 × 1/40 = 1.
One missed encoding is enough for XSS, so relying on manual escaping at each insertion point does not scale.
Using rendering that encodes by default (templates or APIs that set text) moves the risk to the few places that deliberately insert HTML.
A strict CSP adds a second barrier for those few places.
numbers.result: With dozens of insertion points, auto-encoding by default plus CSP is far safer than escaping each one by hand.

india.title: The OWASP cheat sheets
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, maintained by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project, is the standard reference for these defences. Its XSS prevention sheet is organised by output context (HTML body, attribute, URL, script, CSS) because the right encoding depends on where data lands. Its CSRF sheet recommends synchroniser tokens or signed double-submit cookies, with SameSite cookies as defence in depth rather than the only control.

pitfalls.trap: “We sanitise input, so we are safe from XSS.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d encode on output for each context and add a CSP; input filtering misses event handlers and encodings.”

pitfalls.trap: “CORS protects us from CSRF.”
pitfalls.say: “CORS controls reading responses; a forged form POST is still sent. SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens address CSRF.”

takeaways: XSS runs attacker script in your page; CSRF forges requests with the user’s cookies.
Encode output for its context; use CSP as a second layer.
SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens stop forged requests.
XSS bypasses CSRF defences, so fix XSS first.

interactive.title: Which defence fits?
interactive.prompt: Your banking site has an endpoint that transfers money on POST. An attacker controls an unrelated website and can make visitors’ browsers submit forms. Pick the defence that targets this attack.

choices.label: A CSRF token checked on the transfer endpoint, plus SameSite cookies
choices.feedback: Right: this is CSRF; the attacker can make requests but cannot read your token.

choices.label: A Content Security Policy on the bank’s pages
choices.feedback: CSP limits scripts on your pages; the attack comes from another site’s form.

choices.label: HTML-encoding the transfer amount on the confirmation page
choices.feedback: Encoding stops XSS; this attack does not inject script.

interactive.reveal: Name the attack first. Forged cross-site requests are CSRF; the defences are SameSite cookies plus a token or Origin check on state-changing requests.

seeAlso.why: Security essentials at the system level
Authentication and authorisation basics
Injection in the browser: the same mistake in HTML instead of SQL
Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity in depth

title: Web Accessibility Fundamentals
objectives: Use semantic HTML so assistive tech understands the page
Make every action work by keyboard with visible focus
Check text alternatives, labels and colour contrast

cards.title: The accessibility tree
cards.body: Browsers build an accessibility tree from the DOM: each element’s role (button, link, heading), name (its label) and state (expanded, checked). Screen readers and voice control read that tree, so the right element gives the right role for free.

cards.title: Misconception: ARIA fixes everything
cards.body: The first rule of ARIA use in the W3C guidance is to prefer a native HTML element when one exists. A div with role="button" still needs focusability, Enter and Space handling and a visible focus style written by hand; a button element has all of that built in.

cards.title: Checking a page by keyboard
cards.body: Unplug the mouse and try the main tasks. Each step finds a common failure.
steps: Tab: every interactive control is reachable in a logical order
Focus: you can always see where you are
Enter or Space: buttons and links activate
Escape: dialogs close and focus returns to where it was

cards.title: Text alternatives, labels and contrast
cards.body: Informative images need alt text describing their purpose; decorative ones need empty alt so they are skipped. Every form field needs a programmatic label. WCAG level AA asks for 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

cards.title: Trap: hint text as the only label
cards.body: Hint text shown inside an empty field disappears as soon as someone types, is often low contrast, and is not reliably announced as a label. Keep a visible label element tied to the field and use in-field hint text only for an example value.

cards.title: Edge case: aria-label on a plain div or span
cards.body: ARIA 1.2 does not allow naming generic elements: aria-label on a div or span without a role is ignored by many screen readers. The label only works on elements with a role that supports a name, such as a button, link, image or region. Use the right native element first; add ARIA to fill gaps, not to decorate generic containers.

questions.prompt: You need a clickable control that submits a form. What should you use?

choices.label: A span styled to look like a button
A native button element
A div with role="button" and a click handler
A link with href="#"

questions.explanation: A button element is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, submits its form and is announced as a button with no extra code. A span or a div needs all of that rebuilt by hand, and a link with href="#" is announced as a link, jumps to the top of the page and does not activate on Space.

questions.prompt: A design uses light grey text measured at 3.2:1 against its white background. Where may it be used under WCAG level AA?

choices.label: Body text, because it is above 3:1
Large text only, such as 24 px headings
Nowhere, as level AA needs 7:1
Anywhere, as contrast is an AAA rule

questions.explanation: AA asks for 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (at least 24 px, or about 18.7 px bold), so 3.2:1 suits headings but not body copy. 7:1 is the stricter AAA level for normal text, and contrast is already part of AA.

questions.prompt: A decorative divider image adds nothing to the meaning. What alt text should it have?

choices.label: alt="decorative divider image"
An empty alt attribute (alt="")
alt="image"
No alt attribute at all

questions.explanation: Empty alt tells assistive tech to skip it; a missing alt may cause the file name to be read.

questions.prompt: A modal dialog opens. What should happen to keyboard focus?

choices.label: Jump to the first link on the page, then into the dialog
Into the dialog, trapped while open, then back to the trigger
Move to the browser address bar until the dialog closes
Stay on the page behind the dialog so users can keep reading

questions.explanation: Moving focus into the dialog, keeping it there while it is open and returning it to the button that opened it keeps keyboard and screen-reader users where the action is. Leaving focus behind the dialog lets them tab through a page they cannot see, and jumping to the first link or the address bar loses their place.

questions.prompt: Order how a “Pay now” button reaches a screen-reader user.

items.label: The browser exposes the accessibility tree to the platform
The browser parses the HTML into the DOM
The user hears “Pay now, button”
The browser computes each element’s role, name and state
The screen reader reads the node that has focus

questions.explanation: Assistive technology never reads your markup directly; it reads the tree the browser derives from the DOM. That is why a div with a click handler is announced with no button role: nothing in the DOM told the browser it was one.

questions.prompt: A custom dropdown menu built from divs fails keyboard testing.

approaches.label: Use native elements (a button and a list of links or a select) and style them
Add role attributes to the divs and stop
Hide it from assistive tech

rationaleOptions.label: Role attributes add keyboard support automatically
Styling native elements is usually less work than rebuilding their behaviour
Native elements come with keyboard handling and roles

rationaleConflicts.r3: ARIA changes what is announced, not how the element behaves.

questions.explanation: ARIA describes; it does not add behaviour. Native elements are the cheapest accessible option.

flashcards.back: Prefer a native HTML element with the semantics you need.
4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text.

flashcards.front: Alt text for a decorative image?
flashcards.back: Empty: alt="".

sources.title: W3C: Using ARIA (rules of ARIA use)

mechanism.title: How assistive technology understands a page
steps: The browser exposes an accessibility tree alongside the DOM. Each node has a role, an accessible name and states. A button element is exposed as role button, named by its text; a heading as level 2 heading; a checkbox with its checked state.
Screen readers navigate by those roles: jump between headings, landmarks (header, nav, main), links or form fields. A page built from divs gives them nothing to jump to, even if it looks fine.
Accessible names come from content, a label element, alt text or ARIA attributes. Every interactive element and informative image needs one; a button that contains only an icon needs a text name.

Keyboard access depends on focusable elements. Native links, buttons and form fields are focusable and respond to Enter or Space. Custom widgets need tabindex, key handlers and focus management, which is why native elements are preferred.

WCAG (the W3C’s Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) groups success criteria into levels A, AA and AAA. Many laws and procurement policies reference level AA, which includes the 4.5:1 contrast rule, keyboard operability and visible focus.
Automated checkers catch missing alt text, labels and contrast problems, but not whether alt text is meaningful or a flow makes sense; manual keyboard and screen-reader testing is still needed.

useWhen: Semantic HTML first for headings, lists, buttons, links, forms and landmarks.
ARIA for widgets HTML has no element for, such as tabs, following the ARIA authoring practices.
avoidWhen: Avoid removing focus outlines without a visible replacement.
Avoid conveying information by colour alone, such as red fields with no text error.

rows: Role, tabindex, key handlers, focus style

numbers.title: Checking a colour pair for contrast
assumptions: WCAG relative luminance: white is 1.0; #767676 works out to about 0.181
steps: Contrast ratio = (lighter + 0.05) ÷ (darker + 0.05).
4.54 is at least 4.5, so this grey just passes AA for normal text.
A slightly lighter grey such as #777777 drops just below 4.5:1 and fails.
numbers.result: Mid greys on white sit right at the AA boundary, so check the ratio rather than judging by eye.

india.title: WCAG 2.2 and its adoption
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: WCAG 2.2 became a W3C Recommendation in October 2023, adding criteria such as a minimum target size for pointer inputs and making focused elements not entirely hidden by sticky headers. Many public-sector accessibility rules reference WCAG level AA, for example the European standard EN 301 549 that public bodies in the EU follow. Checking against AA is therefore a practical baseline for most products.

pitfalls.trap: “We added ARIA labels everywhere, so it is accessible.”
pitfalls.say: “ARIA only changes what is announced; I’d start with native elements, then test by keyboard and with a screen reader.”

pitfalls.trap: “Automated tools passed, so we are compliant.”
pitfalls.say: “Automated checks catch a minority of issues; keyboard and screen-reader testing find the rest.”

takeaways: Native HTML elements give roles, names and keyboard support for free.
Prefer native elements to ARIA; ARIA does not add behaviour.
Everything must work by keyboard with visible focus.
AA contrast: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text.

interactive.title: What does a screen reader announce?
interactive.prompt: An icon-only close button is written as a div with a click handler and an X icon, and nothing else.

choices.label: Nothing useful: it is not focusable, has no role and no name
choices.feedback: Right: a div is not a control, and the icon has no text name.

choices.label: “Close button”, from the X icon
choices.feedback: The icon gives no accessible name, and a div has no button role.

choices.label: “Button”, because it has a click handler
choices.feedback: Click handlers are not exposed as roles.

interactive.reveal: Use a button element with an accessible name, such as visually hidden text or aria-label="Close". It becomes focusable, is announced as “Close, button” and works with Enter and Space.

seeAlso.why: Focus management for dialogs, menus and live regions
Right-to-left layouts and locale-aware text for all users

title: Web Performance Metrics: LCP, INP, CLS
objectives: Define LCP, INP and CLS and their “good” thresholds
Tell field data from lab data
Name the usual fix for each metric

cards.title: Three questions, three metrics
cards.body: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) asks “did the main content load quickly?”. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) asks “does the page respond quickly to input?”. Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) asks “does content stay put?”.

cards.title: Misconception: a fast lab score means fast for users
cards.body: A lab test runs one device on one network. Field data comes from real visits on many devices and networks, and Core Web Vitals are judged at the 75th percentile of those visits. A page can score well in the lab and still fail in the field.

cards.title: The good thresholds, at the 75th percentile
cards.body: A page passes when at least 75% of visits meet each threshold.
steps: LCP: 2.5 s or less
INP: 200 ms or less
CLS: 0.1 or less
Poor starts above 4 s, 500 ms and 0.25 respectively

cards.title: What usually fixes each one
cards.body: LCP: fetch the main image or text sooner and remove render-blocking work. INP: shorten long tasks in event handlers and render less after input. CLS: reserve space for images, ads and embeds with width and height or aspect ratios, and avoid inserting content above what the user is reading.

cards.title: Trap: lazy-loading the hero image
cards.body: Marking the largest above-the-fold image as lazy delays its request until layout decides it is visible, which pushes LCP later. Lazy-load images below the fold and let the main image load eagerly, even with a high fetch priority.

cards.title: Edge case: what INP does not see
cards.body: INP counts clicks, taps and key presses. Scrolling and hovering are not interactions for INP, and a visit with no interactions has no INP value at all. A page can therefore feel janky while scrolling yet pass INP; check scroll smoothness separately in the Performance panel.

questions.prompt: Which metric measures how quickly the page responds to clicks and key presses?

choices.label: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
Time to First Byte (TTFB)

questions.explanation: INP replaced First Input Delay as the responsiveness Core Web Vital in March 2024.

questions.prompt: What is the “good” LCP threshold?

choices.label: 1 second
200 milliseconds
4 seconds
2.5 seconds

questions.explanation: 4 s is where “poor” begins; 200 ms is the INP threshold.

questions.prompt: At what percentile of page visits are Core Web Vitals assessed?

choices.label: The 75th percentile
The 95th percentile
The median (50th)
The single fastest visit

questions.explanation: The 75th percentile balances typical and slower experiences.

questions.prompt: Text jumps down when a banner ad loads above it. Which fix targets this?

choices.label: Lazy-load the article text below the banner
Compress the ad image to a smaller file
Load the ad script with the async attribute
Reserve the ad slot’s height in advance

questions.explanation: CLS comes from unreserved space; reserving it stops the shift.

questions.prompt: Order the three parts of one interaction’s latency, as INP measures it.

items.label: Presentation delay: style, layout and paint of the next frame
Input delay: the main thread finishes what it was doing
Processing: the event handlers run

questions.explanation: INP spans from the input to the next painted frame, so all three parts count.

questions.prompt: 1,000 page views have LCP values; 780 are at or below 2.5 s. Does the page pass LCP? Enter the percentage of visits within the threshold.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: passing needs at least 75% of visits within the threshold, so 78% passes, but only just; a slower network week could tip it under.

flashcards.front: Good thresholds for LCP, INP, CLS?

flashcards.back: 75th percentile of real visits.
Reserve space: width/height or aspect-ratio on media and slots.

mechanism.title: How each metric is measured
steps: LCP is the time from navigation start until the largest image or text block in the viewport is rendered. It is usually a hero image, a video poster or a headline. Delays come from slow server responses, render-blocking resources, late discovery of the image, or a large image download.

INP observes all clicks, taps and key presses during a visit and reports roughly the worst latency from input to the next frame being painted (ignoring a few outliers on pages with many interactions). Each interaction includes input delay (main thread busy), processing time (event handlers) and presentation delay (rendering the update).

CLS adds up unexpected layout shifts: each shift scores the fraction of the viewport that moved multiplied by how far it moved. Shifts within 500 ms of user input do not count. Shifts are grouped into windows and the worst window is reported.

Field data comes from real users, for example through the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) or your own monitoring with the web-vitals library. Lab data comes from controlled tests such as Lighthouse. Use lab data to debug and field data to judge.
Each metric is assessed at the 75th percentile of page loads, separately for mobile and desktop. A page passes the Core Web Vitals assessment when all three meet their “good” thresholds.
The metrics are related to work covered in earlier lessons: LCP depends on the critical rendering path and caching, INP on the event loop, and CLS on layout.

useWhen: Use field data to decide whether there is a problem and lab tools to find its cause.
Track the 75th percentile per page type, on mobile and desktop separately.
avoidWhen: Avoid optimising for a single lab score on a fast developer machine.
Avoid fixing LCP by hiding content until everything loads; it makes the experience worse.

rows: Slow server, render-blocking CSS, late or large hero image
Long tasks in event handlers, heavy re-rendering
Media without dimensions, late-inserted banners, web fonts swapping

numbers.title: Scoring one layout shift
assumptions: A banner pushes an article down after load (illustrative)
The shifted article covers 60% of the viewport height before and after the move combined (impact fraction 0.6)
It moves down by 25% of the viewport height (distance fraction 0.25)
steps: Layout shift score = impact fraction × distance fraction.
0.15 is above the 0.1 “good” threshold from this one shift.
Reserving the banner’s height in advance makes the shift score 0.
numbers.result: One late banner can fail CLS on its own; reserving space removes the shift entirely.

india.title: The move from FID to INP
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: In March 2024 Google replaced First Input Delay (FID) with Interaction to Next Paint (INP) as the responsiveness Core Web Vital, as announced on web.dev. FID measured only the delay before the first interaction’s handler started; INP covers all interactions and includes handler time and the time to paint the result. Many sites that passed FID failed INP at first, mostly because of long tasks in event handlers.

pitfalls.trap: “Our Lighthouse score is 95, so performance is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “Lighthouse is a lab test on one profile; I’d check field data at the 75th percentile on mobile.”

pitfalls.trap: “Lazy-load every image to improve LCP.”
pitfalls.say: “Lazy-loading the hero image delays LCP; I’d lazy-load below-the-fold images only.”

takeaways: LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, judged at the 75th percentile.
Field data judges; lab data debugs.
INP is about long tasks in handlers; CLS about reserving space.
Never lazy-load the LCP image.

interactive.title: Which metric does this hurt?
interactive.prompt: A product page’s “Add to cart” click handler recalculates prices for 2,000 variants on the main thread, taking 350 ms before the button shows its new state.

choices.label: INP
choices.feedback: Right: input to next paint takes at least 350 ms, above the 200 ms “good” threshold.

choices.label: LCP
choices.feedback: LCP is about when the main content first renders, not about clicks.

choices.label: CLS
choices.feedback: Nothing moves unexpectedly here.

interactive.reveal: Interactions that run long tasks on the main thread delay the next paint. Show the button’s pressed state first, then do the heavy work in chunks or a worker.

seeAlso.why: Field thresholds such as p75 LCP work like the percentile targets behind SLOs
Measuring these metrics from real users in the field

title: Loading Assets Efficiently
objectives: Use resource hints and fetch priority on purpose
Serve right-sized, compressed images and text
Lazy-load and split code without delaying what matters

cards.title: Send fewer, smaller bytes, sooner
cards.body: Asset loading comes down to three moves: discover critical files early, make every file as small as it can be, and delay anything the first view does not need. The stakes are easy to work out: on a 10 Mbit/s mobile link (illustrative), a 1 MB hero image needs about 0.8 s of transfer alone, while a right-sized 150 KB version needs about 0.12 s.

cards.title: Worked example: one hero image, three sizes
cards.body: Serving a phone the desktop image wastes most of its bytes.
steps: Assume: a hero shown 400 CSS px wide on a phone with a device pixel ratio of 2
The phone needs about 800 px wide; the desktop file is 2,400 px wide
Pixels scale with width squared: (2,400 ÷ 800)² = 9× more pixels than needed
With srcset offering 800, 1,600 and 2,400 px versions, the browser picks the 800 px file
cards.note: Result. Roughly a ninth of the pixels to decode, and usually a similar cut in bytes, for the same sharpness on that phone.

cards.title: Hints that change when things load
cards.body: Resource hints tell the browser about work it would otherwise discover late.
steps: preconnect: open the connection to a third-party origin early
preload: fetch a specific critical file now (a font, the hero image)
fetchpriority="high": raise one image above others
loading="lazy": wait until an image or iframe is near the viewport

cards.title: Compression and code splitting
cards.body: Text assets (HTML, CSS, scripts, JSON) compress well with gzip or Brotli. Splitting scripts by route means a visitor downloads the code for the page they opened, not the whole application.

cards.title: Trap: preloading everything
cards.body: Every preload competes for bandwidth with the files the browser already knows are critical. Preloading many files can delay the hero image or the main stylesheet. Preload one or two late-discovered critical files and measure.

cards.title: Edge case: the hero image found too late
cards.body: A hero image set as a CSS background, or inserted by script, is invisible to the preload scanner and is fetched only after CSS or JavaScript runs, which delays LCP. Use an img element in the HTML with fetchpriority="high", or a preload hint, and never mark it loading="lazy".

questions.prompt: A web font is referenced only inside a stylesheet, so it is discovered late. Which hint helps?

choices.label: preload the font file
preconnect to your own origin
fetchpriority="low" on the stylesheet
font-display: swap in the @font-face rule

questions.explanation: The font is found only after the stylesheet downloads and is parsed; preload starts it alongside the HTML. Preconnecting to your own origin does nothing because that connection is already open, a low priority on the stylesheet delays the font further, and font-display: swap changes how text appears while waiting, not when the font is fetched.

questions.prompt: A product image is shown 360 CSS px wide on a phone with a device pixel ratio of 3. Its srcset offers 480, 1,080 and 2,160 px files. Which does the browser normally fetch?

choices.label: The 480 px file, because it is smallest
The 1,080 px file, enough for 360 × 3
The 2,160 px file, because it is sharpest
All three, keeping the best one it gets

questions.explanation: The browser needs about 360 × 3 = 1,080 device pixels and picks the smallest candidate that covers it. 480 px looks blurry at three times density, 2,160 px decodes four times the pixels for no visible gain, and only one candidate is downloaded. Browsers may choose a smaller file on a slow connection or with data saving on.

questions.prompt: A sale page has a hero banner, 4 products above the fold and 60 product images further down. Which images should get loading="lazy"?

choices.label: All 65, to save the most bytes
Only the 60 below the fold
Only the hero, as it is the largest
None, because lazy-loading hurts LCP

questions.explanation: Lazy-loading the 60 below-the-fold images saves bytes for visitors who never scroll that far. Lazy-loading the hero or the first products delays what the user sees first, often the LCP element, and lazy images far down the page do not affect LCP, so skipping lazy-loading entirely just wastes bandwidth.

questions.prompt: Which asset gains least from gzip or Brotli on the server?

choices.label: A JavaScript bundle
An HTML page
A JPEG photo
A JSON API response

questions.explanation: JPEG, PNG and WebP are already compressed, so gzip saves almost nothing and costs CPU. Text formats such as script bundles, HTML and JSON usually shrink by more than half.

questions.prompt: Order these by how early they should load on a product page.

items.label: Reviews widget below the fold
Hero product image
Critical CSS and the HTML
Script for the add-to-cart button

questions.explanation: The HTML and critical CSS come first and below-the-fold extras last. The hero image and the add-to-cart script both serve the first view, so either order between them is accepted.

questions.prompt: A marketing page loads a 400 KB chat widget script on every visit.
constraints: Chat is used by 3% of visitors
Chat must still work when opened

approaches.label: Load it synchronously in the head
Preload it with high priority
Load the widget only when the visitor clicks the chat button

rationaleOptions.label: 97% of visitors never download the 400 KB
The first view’s critical resources no longer compete with it
Preloading makes the widget cheaper to download

rationaleConflicts.r3: Preload changes timing, not size, and steals bandwidth from critical files.

questions.explanation: Load rarely used features on interaction; keep the critical path for what every visitor needs.

flashcards.back: preconnect opens a connection to an origin; preload fetches a specific file.

flashcards.front: When not to lazy-load an image?
flashcards.back: When it is above the fold, especially the LCP image.
Text: HTML, CSS, scripts, JSON, SVG. Not JPEG/PNG/WebP.

mechanism.title: How the browser schedules and sizes downloads
steps: The browser assigns each request a priority: render-blocking CSS and fonts high, scripts by type and position, images low until layout shows they are in the viewport. Hints and attributes adjust these defaults.
preconnect performs DNS, TCP and TLS for an origin ahead of time, saving those round trips when the first request to it happens. Use it for a few critical third-party origins, such as an image CDN.

preload fetches a specific URL with a stated type immediately and keeps it ready. It suits files the HTML does not mention directly, such as fonts referenced from CSS or a background hero image. An unused preload wastes bandwidth and triggers a console warning.

Responsive images give the browser options: srcset lists candidate files and their widths, sizes says how wide the image will be in the layout, and the browser picks the best match for the screen. Modern formats such as WebP and AVIF are usually smaller than JPEG at similar quality; picture with source elements offers them with a fallback.
Native lazy loading (loading="lazy") defers offscreen images and iframes until they approach the viewport. Width and height attributes still matter so the layout reserves space and does not shift.
For scripts, split the bundle by route and load rarely used features on demand. Compress text responses with Brotli or gzip, and cache hashed files for a long time so repeat visits skip the download.

useWhen: Preload one or two late-discovered critical files such as the LCP image or a primary font.
Serve responsive images in a modern format with dimensions set.
avoidWhen: Avoid preloading large numbers of files; it dilutes priorities.
Avoid lazy-loading anything visible in the first viewport.

rows: Saves connection round trips to a third party
Starts a late-discovered critical file early
Steals bandwidth from other critical files
Delays LCP if applied to the hero

numbers.title: How much compression saves on a script
assumptions: Text like this often compresses to about a quarter to a third of its size with Brotli (an illustrative ratio; measure your own)
steps: Uncompressed: 900 KB × 8 = 7,200 kbit ÷ 5,000 kbit/s ≈ 1.4 s.
At a quarter of the size, 225 KB: 1,800 kbit ÷ 5,000 ≈ 0.36 s.
Compression does not cut parse and execution time; the browser still processes 900 KB of code.
Splitting so the first page needs only 300 KB of code cuts both transfer and execution time.
numbers.result: Compression cuts transfer time, but only shipping less code cuts execution time too.

india.title: Native lazy loading in browsers
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The loading attribute for images and iframes is part of the HTML standard and supported in all major browsers. web.dev’s guide explains that browsers start fetching lazy images some distance before they scroll into view, with the distance depending on connection speed, and warns specifically against lazy-loading images in the initial viewport because doing so delays LCP.

pitfalls.trap: “Preload all our fonts and images so they are ready.”
pitfalls.say: “Preloading everything competes with the critical files; I’d preload only the LCP image or primary font and measure.”

pitfalls.trap: “Gzip solves our big bundle.”
pitfalls.say: “Compression cuts bytes on the wire, not parse and execution time; I’d split the bundle by route.”

takeaways: Discover critical files early, shrink every file, delay the rest.
Responsive images send the right pixels for each screen.
Preload and preconnect sparingly; lazy-load below the fold only.
Compress text; split code so the first view needs less.

interactive.title: Size or round trips?
interactive.prompt: A page needs a script bundle after 4 round trips of 100 ms on a 5 Mbit/s mobile link. Slide the compressed bundle size and see which part of the wait dominates.
interactive.takeaway: Below about 0.25 MB the 400 ms of round trips dominate, so preconnect and fewer sequential requests help most. Above it the bytes dominate: 1 MB alone takes 1.6 s at 5 Mbit/s, so code splitting and compression matter more.

seeAlso.why: CDNs that serve and resize images at the edge
Loading web fonts without blocking or shifting text
Third-party scripts, often the biggest source of extra bytes

title: Forms and Validation
objectives: Split validation between browser and server correctly
Show errors people and assistive tech can find
Prevent duplicate submissions and lost input

cards.title: Two layers, two jobs
cards.body: Validation in the browser is for the user: fast feedback before a round trip. Validation on the server is for the system: it is the only check an attacker cannot skip, because requests can be sent without your page at all.

cards.title: Misconception: the browser already checked it
cards.body: Constraint attributes such as required, type="email", min and pattern can be removed in developer tools, and scripts or command-line clients can post anything. Treat every field as untrusted on the server, even if the form validated it.

cards.title: One submission, done well
cards.body: A form that behaves well on slow networks follows the same few steps.
steps: Validate in the browser on submit; focus the first invalid field
Disable the submit button and show progress
Server validates again and saves, using an idempotency key
Success: redirect to a result page (Post/Redirect/Get)
Failure: show field errors next to the fields and keep the input

cards.title: Errors people can find
cards.body: Put each error message in text next to its field, associate it with the field so screen readers announce it, and summarise errors at the top for long forms. Never rely on a red border alone.

cards.title: Trap: refresh resubmits the order
cards.body: If a successful POST returns a page directly, pressing refresh asks to send the POST again. Redirecting to a GET page after success (Post/Redirect/Get) makes refresh safe; an idempotency key on the server catches the remaining double clicks and retries.

cards.title: Edge case: what maxlength counts
cards.body: The HTML maxlength attribute counts UTF-16 code units, so many emoji count as 2, while a server may count bytes (UTF-8: up to 4 per character) or user-visible characters. A 20-character limit can then pass in the browser and fail on the server. Define the limit in one unit, enforce it on the server, and show the same rule in the form.

questions.prompt: A rail-booking form allows at most 6 passengers, using a max attribute and a script check. A tester posts 9 passengers with a command-line client. Which check stops the booking?

choices.label: The passenger limit enforced by the booking server
The max attribute on the passenger-count field
The script that validates the form before submit
The browser’s built-in constraint validation

questions.explanation: The command-line client never loads the page, so the max attribute, the form script and the browser’s constraint validation never run. Only the server sees every request; browser checks exist for fast feedback, not for enforcement.

questions.prompt: After a successful POST, what stops a page refresh from submitting again?

choices.label: Returning the result page directly from the POST
Redirect to a GET page (Post/Redirect/Get)
Adding a required attribute to each field
Setting the form to autocomplete="off"

questions.explanation: With Post/Redirect/Get the page being refreshed is a GET, so refresh just reloads the result. Returning the result straight from the POST is what causes the resubmit prompt, and required attributes or autocomplete only affect how the form is filled in.

questions.prompt: On a 12-field checkout form, the PIN code fails validation after a screen-reader user submits with Enter. Which feedback works for them?

choices.label: A toast message that fades out after two seconds
A red border drawn around the PIN code field
Focus moves to the field, with error text linked to it
A short shake animation on the submit button

questions.explanation: Moving focus to the first invalid field, with the message linked to it (for example through aria-describedby), means the error is announced where the user now is. A fading toast may vanish before it is read, a red border carries no text and fails people who cannot see colour, and a shake says nothing about which field is wrong.

questions.prompt: A user double-clicks “Pay” on a slow connection. Which server-side measure prevents a double charge?

choices.label: A pattern attribute on the amount field in the form
Returning 200 OK for both of the requests
Validating the card number twice before charging
An idempotency key the server checks

questions.explanation: The server stores the key with the first result, so the second request with the same key returns that result instead of charging again. A pattern attribute is a browser check the request skips, returning 200 twice still charges twice, and validating the card twice just validates two charges.

questions.prompt: Order a robust form submission.

items.label: Validate in the browser
Validate again on the server
Redirect to the result page
Disable the button and show progress
Save with an idempotency key

questions.explanation: Feedback first, the authoritative check on the server, then a safe redirect.

questions.prompt: Sign-up form: username must be unique and 3–20 characters.
constraints: Two people may pick the same name at once

approaches.label: Only check on the server, no browser checks
Only check uniqueness in the browser by calling an API while typing
Length check in the browser, plus a unique constraint enforced on the server

rationaleOptions.label: Only a server-side unique constraint closes the race between two sign-ups
The browser gives instant feedback on length
A browser availability check guarantees uniqueness

rationaleConflicts.r3: Two users can both see “available” and submit; only the server constraint decides.

questions.explanation: Browser checks improve experience; the server enforces the rule, including races.

flashcards.front: Why validate on the server if the browser does?
flashcards.back: Requests can bypass the browser; the server is the only enforceable check.
After a successful POST, redirect to a GET page so refresh does not resubmit.
Next to its field, linked programmatically, not colour alone.

mechanism.title: How a form submission travels and where each check belongs
steps: HTML has built-in constraint validation: required, type (email, url, number), min, max, minlength, maxlength and pattern. On submit the browser blocks invalid forms and shows a message, and scripts can read each field’s validity state to show custom messages instead.

Choose input types for the job: type="email" and type="tel" bring suitable on-screen keyboards on phones, autocomplete attributes let browsers fill known values, and inputmode tunes the keyboard without changing validation.

On the server, validate every field for type, length, range and format, then apply business rules (the username is free, the coupon is valid). Use allowlists where possible. Return errors per field in a structured form so the page can show them next to the right input.

Uniqueness and similar invariants belong in the database as constraints. A browser check that a username is “available” is a hint; two people can submit the same name at the same moment, and only the constraint settles it.

A submit can be sent twice by double clicks, retries on a flaky network or refresh. Disable the button while sending, follow Post/Redirect/Get after success, and accept an idempotency key so the server can return the first result for a repeated request.

Errors must be perceivable by everyone: text next to the field, linked with an attribute such as aria-describedby, focus moved to the first invalid field, and the user’s input kept so they can fix rather than retype it.

useWhen: Browser constraints for quick feedback on format and required fields.
Server validation and database constraints for every rule that must hold.
avoidWhen: Avoid clearing the whole form when one field fails.
Avoid relying on in-field hint text or colour alone to explain errors.

rows: Feedback in the browser; enforcement on the server
Retries and double clicks come from the client

numbers.title: How often double submissions happen
assumptions: A checkout gets 20,000 orders a day (illustrative)
0.5% of payments see a retry or double click while the first request is in flight (illustrative)
steps: Expected repeat submissions: 20,000 × 0.005 = 100 per day.
Without idempotency, each could become a duplicate charge or order.
Disabling the button stops most double clicks but not network retries.
An idempotency key makes all 100 return the original result.
numbers.result: Even a small retry rate means dozens of duplicates a day at modest volume; the server must make repeats harmless.

india.title: Payment APIs and idempotency keys
india.label: Public documentation
india.body: Several public payment APIs document an Idempotency-Key request header: the client generates a unique key per intended operation and resends the same key on retries, and the server returns the stored result of the first request instead of performing the action again. The IETF has a draft standard for this header. A form submission can use the same idea by generating the key when the form is rendered.

pitfalls.trap: “The form validates emails, so the server can trust the field.”
pitfalls.say: “Anything in the browser can be bypassed; the server validates every field again.”

pitfalls.trap: “We disable the button, so duplicates cannot happen.”
pitfalls.say: “Disabling helps with double clicks; retries and refreshes still need Post/Redirect/Get and an idempotency key.”

takeaways: Browser validation is for users; server validation is for the system.
Uniqueness belongs in a database constraint.
Post/Redirect/Get plus idempotency keys make repeats harmless.
Show errors as text next to fields and keep the input.

interactive.title: What happens when the user refreshes?
interactive.prompt: A payment form POSTs to /pay, and the server responds with the receipt page directly (status 200). The user presses refresh on the receipt.

choices.label: The browser offers to send the POST again, which could pay twice
choices.feedback: Right: refreshing a page that came from a POST repeats the POST.

choices.label: The receipt reloads safely with a GET
choices.feedback: That is what happens after a redirect to a GET page, not here.

choices.label: Nothing: browsers never resend forms
choices.feedback: Browsers ask to resend form data on refresh after a POST.

interactive.reveal: Post/Redirect/Get: respond to a successful POST with a redirect (303 See Other) to a receipt URL. Refresh then repeats a harmless GET. Keep an idempotency key on the server for retries.

seeAlso.why: Idempotency keys across services
Locale formats, plural rules and dates in messages
How the server decodes, normalises and length-checks the text a form submits

title: Client State and Data Fetching
objectives: Tell server state from UI state
Avoid stale and out-of-order responses
Choose optimistic or confirmed updates

cards.title: Two kinds of state
cards.body: UI state belongs to the page: which tab is open, the half-typed delivery note. Server state is a copy of data owned elsewhere: the cart, whether the restaurant is still taking orders. Leave a food-ordering page open for 20 minutes and the restaurant may have closed, but your selected tab is still right. Server state goes stale, so it needs fetching, caching and refresh rules; UI state does not.

cards.title: Misconception: the last request sent wins
cards.body: Responses can arrive in a different order from requests. If a search for “ca” is slow and “cat” is fast, showing whichever arrives last can display results for “ca” under the “cat” box.

cards.title: Searching as you type, safely
cards.body: A search box needs to ignore answers to questions the user is no longer asking.
steps: Wait briefly after typing stops (debounce)
Send the request and remember its query
When a newer query starts, cancel or mark older requests stale
Render a response only if it matches the latest query

cards.title: Optimistic updates
cards.body: An optimistic update changes the screen before the server confirms, then rolls back if the request fails. It suits likes, toggles and reordering, where failure is rare and easy to undo; it does not suit payments or anything whose result the user must be able to trust.

cards.title: Trap: copying server data into many places
cards.body: Storing the same user record in several components means an update to one copy leaves the others stale. Keep one cache entry per resource and let views read from it.

cards.title: Edge case: two components ask for the same data at once
cards.body: When a header and a sidebar both request the current user as the page loads, a naive cache misses twice and sends two identical requests. Data-fetching layers keep a map of in-flight requests by key and give the second caller the same pending result, which removes duplicate requests and keeps both components consistent.

questions.prompt: A food-ordering page has sat open for 20 minutes. Which value is most likely wrong now unless the page refetches it?

choices.label: Which menu tab the user selected
Whether the restaurant still accepts orders
The half-typed note for the rider
Whether the filter drawer is open

questions.explanation: The restaurant’s status is owned by the server and can change while the page sits idle, so it is server state and needs a refresh rule, such as refetching when the tab regains focus. The selected tab, the draft note and the drawer are UI state: the page itself is their source of truth, so they cannot go stale.

questions.prompt: Search for “ca” returns after the search for “cat”. What should the page show?

choices.label: An error, because responses arrived out of order
Results for “cat”, ignoring the late “ca” response
Results for “ca”, because it arrived last
Both result lists merged

questions.explanation: Render a response only if its query matches what is in the box now, or cancel the older request. Showing whichever arrived last is exactly the bug; an error punishes the user for network timing; and merging mixes in results for a query nobody is asking any more.

questions.prompt: Your team wants to show success before the server confirms. For which action is that acceptable?

choices.label: Starring a restaurant as a favourite
Showing a UPI payment as completed
Confirming the last Tatkal seat on a train
Cancelling an order the kitchen may have started

questions.explanation: A favourite rarely fails, harms nobody if it is briefly wrong and rolls back cleanly. A payment can be declined by the bank and a Tatkal seat can be taken by someone else a second earlier, and the user acts on the result, so both must wait for the server. A cancellation may be refused once cooking starts, so promising it early misleads the user.

questions.prompt: A user types “paneer” at a steady 150 ms per key, then stops. The search box has a 300 ms debounce. How many search requests are sent?

choices.label: Six, one for each key pressed
One, about 300 ms after the last key
Three, one every 300 ms while typing
None until the user presses Enter

questions.explanation: Debounce restarts its 300 ms timer on every key, and keys arrive every 150 ms, so the timer expires only after the last one: one request. One per key is no debounce at all; a request every 300 ms while typing is throttling, a different technique; and a debounced box searches by itself without Enter.

questions.prompt: Order an optimistic “like” update.

items.label: Update the count on screen
Server responds
Send the request
On failure, roll back the count and tell the user

questions.explanation: Show the change first, then send it, then reconcile. On failure the count goes back and the user is told why; a silent rollback looks like a glitch and makes people tap again.

questions.prompt: Updating a shared to-do list item’s “done” checkbox.
constraints: Other users may edit the same list

approaches.label: Wait for the server before ticking the box
Update locally and never confirm
Optimistic update with rollback, then refresh from the server

rationaleOptions.label: Local-only updates are fine because the server will catch up
The box ticks instantly and is corrected on the rare failure
Refetching reconciles changes made by other users

rationaleConflicts.r3: Without sending and confirming, the server never learns of the change.

questions.explanation: Low-risk toggles suit optimistic updates as long as failures roll back and the list is refreshed. Waiting for the server makes a checkbox feel broken on a 2-second mobile round trip, and never confirming means a failed write or another user’s change goes unnoticed.

flashcards.back: UI state lives in the page; server state is a cached copy of data owned elsewhere.
Track the latest request; cancel or ignore older ones.

flashcards.front: When are optimistic updates a bad idea?
flashcards.back: When the user must trust the result, such as payments.

sources.title: MDN: Using the Fetch API (cancelling requests)

mechanism.title: How client code keeps a copy of server data honest
steps: Classify state before choosing where to keep it. UI state (open panels, form drafts, scroll position) is owned by the page. Server state (records, lists, counts) is owned by the server; the page only holds a snapshot that ages from the moment it arrives.

For server state, the useful questions are: what is the key for this data (for example user 42’s profile), how long is the copy fresh, when is it refetched (on focus, on reconnect, after a mutation), and who else reads it.
One cache entry per key, shared by every view, avoids copies drifting apart. After a change, update or invalidate that entry, and every view that reads it shows the new value.

Requests can overlap and complete in any order. Keep an identifier for the latest request per key, and cancel older ones (browsers provide an abort mechanism for in-flight requests) or discard their responses when they arrive.

Optimistic updates write the expected result into the cache immediately, send the request, and on failure restore the previous value and tell the user. Pessimistic (confirmed) updates show progress and change the screen only after the server agrees.
Conditional requests (ETag and If-None-Match) make refetching cheap: unchanged data returns a 304 with no body, so refreshing on focus does not have to cost a full download.

useWhen: Optimistic updates for small, reversible actions where speed matters.
A single shared cache keyed by resource for server data used in several views.
avoidWhen: Avoid optimistic updates for payments, irreversible actions or anything with complex server-side rules.
Avoid duplicating server data into many independent component states.

numbers.title: How many requests debouncing saves
assumptions: A user types a 12-character query at about 5 characters per second
Without debouncing, one request per keystroke
Debounce: send 300 ms after typing pauses (an example value)
steps: Without debouncing: 12 requests, most for partial words.
Typing gaps are about 200 ms, below 300 ms, so the debounce fires once at the end.
With debouncing: 1 request (plus any during longer pauses).
That is roughly a 90% cut in requests and in out-of-order responses to handle.
numbers.result: Debouncing turns a dozen requests into about one; cancellation handles the few that still overlap.

india.title: Request cancellation in the platform
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The DOM standard defines an abort signal, documented on MDN, that lets a page cancel an in-flight request. Search boxes and typeahead components use it to cancel the previous request when a new query starts, which both saves bandwidth and removes the out-of-order response problem at its source. The same signal can cancel timers and event listeners tied to a view that has closed.

pitfalls.trap: “The latest response is always for the latest request.”
pitfalls.say: “Responses can arrive out of order; I track the latest request and ignore or cancel older ones.”

pitfalls.trap: “Make every update optimistic for speed.”
pitfalls.say: “Only for low-risk, reversible actions; payments and deletes wait for the server.”

takeaways: UI state is the page’s; server state is a cached copy that goes stale.
Keep one cache entry per resource and invalidate it on change.
Debounce and cancel to avoid out-of-order responses.
Optimistic updates suit small, reversible actions only.

interactive.title: Which results appear?
interactive.prompt: A search box sends a request on every keystroke and renders whichever response arrives. The user types “ca”, then “cat”. The “ca” request takes 900 ms; the “cat” request takes 200 ms.

choices.label: “cat” results flash, then are replaced by “ca” results
choices.feedback: Right: the slow “ca” response lands last and overwrites the correct results.

choices.label: Only “cat” results, because it was sent last
choices.feedback: Send order does not decide arrival order.

choices.label: Only “ca” results, because it was sent first
choices.feedback: “cat” arrives first and is shown briefly before being overwritten.

interactive.reveal: Render only responses that match the current query, and cancel superseded requests. Debouncing reduces how often this happens but does not remove it.

seeAlso.why: Cache invalidation strategies on the server side
State machines that make UI states explicit

title: Service Workers and Offline
objectives: Explain where a service worker sits and what it can intercept
Pick a caching strategy per kind of request
Update a service worker without breaking users

cards.title: A programmable proxy in the browser
cards.body: A service worker is a script the browser runs separately from the page. Once installed, it can intercept the page’s network requests for its scope and answer from a cache, from the network, or both. That is what makes offline pages and instant repeat loads possible.

cards.title: Misconception: a service worker replaces HTTP caching
cards.body: The HTTP cache still works underneath. The service worker’s own cache is controlled entirely by your script: nothing expires unless you delete it. A careless cache-first rule can keep serving an old file indefinitely.

cards.title: The service worker lifecycle
cards.body: A new version does not take over pages the old one controls straight away.
steps: Register: the page asks the browser to install the script
Install: cache the files the app shell needs
Waiting: the new version waits while old pages are open
Activate: delete old caches; start controlling pages
Fetch: intercept requests from controlled pages

cards.title: Three strategies cover most requests
cards.body: Cache first suits versioned static files. Network first, falling back to cache, suits pages and API reads that should be fresh when possible. Stale-while-revalidate answers from cache immediately and refreshes the copy in the background, for data where slightly old is acceptable.

cards.title: Trap: caching the HTML cache-first
cards.body: If the app shell HTML is served cache-first, users keep loading the old shell, which references old asset names, until the service worker itself updates. Serve HTML network-first (or revalidate it), and reserve cache-first for hashed assets.

cards.title: Edge case: service worker scope
cards.body: A service worker controls only pages under the path it was served from: a worker at /app/sw.js controls /app/ by default and cannot control /. To control a wider scope, serve the script from that path or send the Service-Worker-Allowed response header. Mis-scoped workers explain many “offline works on some pages only” reports.

questions.prompt: What can a service worker do that a normal page script cannot?

choices.label: Read the DOM of every open tab
Intercept the page’s network requests and answer them
Bypass HTTPS requirements
Run before the browser downloads any HTML for a first-ever visit

questions.explanation: A service worker is a proxy for its scope. It cannot touch any page’s DOM (it posts messages instead), it requires HTTPS rather than bypassing it, and it is installed by a page, so a first-ever visit downloads the HTML normally.

questions.prompt: Which strategy suits app.3f9a1c.js?

choices.label: Never cache
Network first
Network only
Cache first

questions.explanation: The hash in the name changes whenever the content does, so a cached copy can never be stale: cache first is safe and instant. Network first spends a round trip on a file that cannot change, and never caching or network only make repeat and offline loads slow or impossible.

questions.prompt: You deploy a new service worker. Users have the site open in a tab. When does the new version control that tab by default?

choices.label: Immediately, even in the middle of the user’s session
Once every tab on the old version has closed
Only after the browser itself is restarted
Not until users clear their cache

questions.explanation: By default the new worker installs, then waits until no tab is controlled by the old one, so a page is never served by two versions; one reload of the only open tab is not enough, because the old page is still alive while the new one loads. A browser restart or clearing the cache is not what the lifecycle waits for, and sites can opt in to taking over sooner.

questions.prompt: A restaurant list may be a few minutes old, but it must appear at once even on a weak 3G signal. Which strategy fits?

choices.label: Network only, with a spinner until the list arrives
Cache first, keeping the copy until the next deploy
Stale-while-revalidate
Network first, waiting 10 s before using the cache

questions.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate shows the cached list at once and refreshes it in the background, so the next view is fresh. Network only leaves a spinner on 3G, cache first until the next deploy can show a list that is days old, and network first with a 10-second timeout makes a weak signal feel broken.

questions.prompt: Order the service worker lifecycle.

items.label: Wait while old pages are open
Handle fetch events
Activate and clean old caches
Register
Install and cache the shell

questions.explanation: Install and activate are separate so updates are safe.

questions.prompt: Offline support for a field-inspection app used where signal is patchy.
constraints: Data must reach the server eventually

approaches.label: Cache API responses forever, cache first
Cache the app shell, store submissions in IndexedDB, and send them when back online
Network only, with an error message offline

rationaleOptions.label: Queued submissions are sent when the connection returns
The shell and forms work with no signal
Caching API responses forever keeps the data correct

rationaleConflicts.r3: Cached responses never update, so inspectors would see outdated data.

questions.explanation: Offline-first apps cache the shell, queue writes locally and sync later.

flashcards.front: Where does a service worker sit?
flashcards.back: Between the page and the network, for requests in its scope.

flashcards.front: Why does a new version wait?
flashcards.back: So pages are not controlled by two versions at once; it activates when old pages close.
Cache first.

mechanism.title: How a service worker handles requests and updates
steps: A service worker is registered by a page for a scope (a path prefix). It runs on its own thread with no DOM access, only in secure contexts (HTTPS or localhost), and the browser can stop it when idle and start it again for the next event.
On install, it usually opens a named cache and stores the files the app shell needs. If any of those fail to download, installation fails and the previous version stays in charge.

After install, the new version waits until no pages are controlled by the old one. Then it activates, which is the moment to delete caches from old versions. A page can ask the waiting worker to take over sooner, but then it must be ready for a version change mid-session.

For each request in scope, the fetch handler decides what to return: a cached response, a network response, or a combination such as network with a timeout falling back to cache. Requests it does not handle go to the network as usual (through the HTTP cache).

Writes made offline need their own handling: store them (for example in IndexedDB) and replay them when the connection returns, either when the page sees it is online again or through a background sync event where the browser supports it.
The browser checks for an updated service worker script on navigation and periodically. Serving the worker script itself with a short cache lifetime ensures users get updates promptly.

useWhen: Offline-capable apps and repeat-visit speed for apps people return to often.
Cache first for hashed assets; network first or stale-while-revalidate for HTML and data.
avoidWhen: Avoid cache-first for HTML or unversioned files; users can be stuck on old versions.
Avoid caching personal API responses without a plan for logout and expiry.

numbers.title: Repeat-visit load with a cached shell
assumptions: App shell: HTML 30 KB plus 600 KB of assets (example)
Mobile link 2 Mbit/s with 150 ms RTT (example)
Shell cached by the service worker
steps: Without the cache: about 630 KB × 8 = 5,040 kbit ÷ 2,000 kbit/s ≈ 2.5 s of transfer plus round trips.
With cache-first assets: the 600 KB comes from disk, typically in tens of milliseconds.
Network-first HTML still costs a round trip (150 ms) plus 30 KB (0.12 s) when online.
Offline, the HTML falls back to the cached copy, so the app still opens.
numbers.result: Caching the shell turns a multi-second repeat load into roughly one round trip plus local reads, and keeps the app usable offline.

india.title: The service worker lifecycle as documented
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: web.dev’s article on the service worker lifecycle, by Chrome engineers, explains why a new worker waits: if two versions controlled pages at the same time, one page could load assets cached by another version and break. It describes the skip-waiting option and its risk, and recommends cleaning old caches in the activate step, which is the pattern this lesson follows.

pitfalls.trap: “The service worker will keep users up to date.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if I design it to: HTML network-first, hashed assets cache-first, and old caches cleaned on activate.”

pitfalls.trap: “Offline just means caching GET requests.”
pitfalls.say: “Writes made offline must be stored and replayed when the connection returns.”

takeaways: A service worker intercepts requests in its scope and decides cache or network.
New versions install, wait, then activate.
Cache first for hashed files; network first or stale-while-revalidate for HTML and data.
Offline writes need a local queue and a replay.

interactive.title: Why do users see the old version?
interactive.prompt: You deploy a fix. Users with the site open in a tab keep seeing the old version even after reloading once. The service worker serves HTML cache-first.

choices.label: The new worker is waiting, and the old one keeps serving the cached HTML
choices.feedback: Right: the waiting worker cannot take over while the old one controls open pages.

choices.label: The CDN has not updated yet
choices.feedback: Possible in general, but the cache-first HTML in the service worker is enough to explain it.

choices.label: Browsers cache HTML for 24 hours by default
choices.feedback: There is no such fixed default; the service worker’s own cache rule is the cause.

interactive.reveal: Serve HTML network-first, keep the worker script’s HTTP cache short, and clean old caches on activate. Optionally prompt users to reload when a new version is waiting.

seeAlso.why: Where client-side caches fit among other cache layers

title: DOM Events: Capture, Bubbling and Delegation
objectives: Trace an event through its capture, target and bubble phases
Use one delegated listener instead of one per element
Tell stopping propagation apart from cancelling the default action

cards.title: An event travels down the tree, then back up
cards.body: When you click a button inside a list inside the page, the browser builds a path from the window down to the button. The event first visits each ancestor going down (capture), then the button itself (target), then each ancestor again going up (bubble). A listener on any element on that path can react.

cards.title: Worked example: one listener for a 1,000-row table
cards.body: A table has 1,000 rows, each with Edit, Delete and Share buttons. One listener per button means 3,000 registrations, plus 3 more for every row added later.
