cards.title: Worked example: how flakiness compounds
cards.body: A suite has 500 tests, each failing spuriously one run in a thousand. The chance a run is clean is 0.999 to the power 500, about 0.61, so about 39% of runs fail with no code change. At 1,000 such tests it drops to about 37% clean. A tiny per-test flake rate makes a big suite unreliable, which is why each flaky test must be fixed or quarantined quickly.

cards.title: Trap: waiting with fixed sleeps
cards.body: A test that waits two seconds for a result is slow when the app is fast and flaky when the machine is busy. Wait for a condition instead: the element appears, the request completes, the text changes, with a timeout as a safety net. Also isolate data per test, fake the clock for time-based logic, stub third-party services at the network boundary and disable animations.

questions.prompt: Where should the rule “quantity must be between 1 and 99” be tested most thoroughly?

choices.label: End-to-end tests in a real browser covering each boundary value separately
Unit tests of the validation rule, plus one component test of the message
A visual test of the form with an invalid quantity
Manual testing before each release

questions.explanation: Boundary cases are cheap and precise as unit tests, and one component test proves the message is wired up. End-to-end tests per boundary are slow; screenshots cannot check logic; manual checks do not scale.

questions.prompt: A refactor renames CSS classes, and 40 component tests fail though the page looks and works the same. What change prevents this?

choices.label: Find elements by role, label and accessible name
Snapshot the full markup of each component
Add test-only data attributes to each element
Run the tests only after a manual review

questions.explanation: Role and name queries match how users and assistive technology find controls, so markup changes do not break them. Markup snapshots break on any change; test-only attributes help stability but do not check accessibility; a manual review before running does not stop the queries from breaking.

questions.prompt: An end-to-end test fails about once in 50 runs, only on the CI server, at a step that waits 2 seconds for a list to load. What is the best fix?

choices.label: Raise the wait to 10 seconds
Retry the full suite on the CI server whenever any test fails
Delete the test because it is unreliable
Wait until the list’s items are present, with a timeout

questions.explanation: Waiting for the condition makes the test as fast as the app and tolerant of slow machines. Longer sleeps slow the suite and still fail sometimes, blanket retries hide real bugs, and deleting loses coverage.

questions.prompt: Which problem can only an end-to-end test in a real browser catch?

choices.label: A tax calculation rounding 0.5 the wrong way
An error message rendering under the wrong field after validation
A production build that serves the wrong API base URL
A function returning the wrong date format

questions.explanation: Configuration and wiring across the built app, the network and the backend only show up end to end. Rounding and formatting are unit concerns, and message placement is a component test.

questions.prompt: Order the response to a newly flaky test.

items.label: Find the cause: timing, shared state, order or external calls
Quarantine it so it no longer blocks merges
Fix it and return it to the blocking suite
Reproduce it by running it repeatedly or under load

questions.explanation: Stop the damage, reproduce, find the root cause, then restore the test; quarantine must not become a graveyard.

questions.prompt: A suite has 500 tests and each fails spuriously in 0.1% of runs, independently. About what percentage of runs pass with no spurious failure?
questions.workedAnswer: 0.999⁵⁰⁰ ≈ e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.61, so about 61% of runs are clean
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the expected number of flakes per run is 500 × 0.001 = 0.5, so a clean run is far from guaranteed.

flashcards.back: The lowest one that can catch the problem; end to end only for critical journeys.
By role, label and accessible name, like users and assistive technology.
500 tests at 0.1% each: about 61% of runs clean.
Wait for a condition with a timeout.

mechanism.title: How the layers fit together
steps: Unit tests run pure logic in milliseconds: formatting, validation, reducers, calculations. They give precise failures and cover edge cases cheaply, but they cannot see rendering, browser behaviour or how pieces are wired together.

Component and integration tests render a piece of the interface in a simulated document or a real browser, interact with it through events, and assert on what appears. Network calls are stubbed at the boundary with realistic responses, ideally generated from the same schema the API uses so the stubs cannot drift. This layer catches most interface bugs at a fraction of end-to-end cost.

Contract tests check that the client and the API agree on requests and responses without running both together. End-to-end tests drive a real browser through the built app against a deployed backend; they catch configuration, routing, authentication and cross-service problems, and they are the slowest and least stable layer, so they cover a few critical journeys.

Visual regression tests take screenshots at fixed viewport sizes and compare them with approved images, catching layout and styling regressions that assertions miss. They need stable fonts, data and animations to avoid noise. Automated accessibility checks run in component or end-to-end tests, but they find only part of the problems, so manual keyboard and screen reader checks are still needed.

Flakiness is non-determinism: timing, shared state between tests, dependence on test order, real time and time zones, randomness and external services. Each source has a fix: wait for conditions, create data per test, fake the clock, seed randomness, stub external calls. Track flaky tests, quarantine them out of the blocking path, and fix them, because the failure probability compounds with suite size.

useWhen: Any front end with more than one developer or frequent releases.
Critical journeys such as sign-up and payment, which need end-to-end coverage.
avoidWhen: Avoid testing every edge case end to end; push it down a layer.
Avoid fixed sleeps and tests that share data or depend on order.

rows: Wiring, configuration, real browser and backend

numbers.title: What flakiness and runtime cost
assumptions: 500 tests, each with a 0.1% spurious failure rate
steps: Clean run probability: 0.999⁵⁰⁰ ≈ 0.61, so about 39% of runs fail spuriously.
Halving every flake rate to 0.05%: 0.9995⁵⁰⁰ ≈ 0.78 clean.
End-to-end runtime: 200 × 20 s = 4,000 s, about 67 minutes on one worker.
On 8 workers: 4,000 ÷ 8 = 500 s, about 8 minutes if tests are independent.
numbers.result: Small per-test flake rates compound; parallelism only works for isolated tests.

india.title: Flakiness at scale
india.label: Publicly reported (Google Testing Blog, 2016)
india.body: In a 2016 post on the Google Testing Blog, Google reported that about 1.5% of all test runs across its corpus produced a flaky result, meaning the same code both passed and failed, and that almost 16% of its tests showed some level of flakiness. It described mitigations such as re-running failed tests, marking known flaky tests to fail only after three consecutive failures, and tracking flakiness to find causes.

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s cover every validation rule end to end.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d unit-test the rules and keep end to end for the journey.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add a two-second wait so it passes.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d wait for the element or request instead.”

pitfalls.trap: “It’s flaky, just re-run it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d quarantine and fix it; flakes compound across the suite.”

takeaways: Test each behaviour at the lowest layer that can catch it.
Keep end-to-end tests for a few critical journeys.
Find elements by role and accessible name.
Per-test flakiness compounds: 500 × 0.1% leaves 61% clean runs.
Replace sleeps with conditions; isolate data and clocks.

interactive.title: How often does the suite go red?
interactive.prompt: A team has 500 tests. Each one, independently, fails spuriously in 1 run out of 1,000 even when the code is fine. Predict how often a full run fails with no real bug.

choices.label: About 0.1% of runs, the same as one test
choices.feedback: That is the rate for one test; across 500 tests the chances add up.

choices.label: About 39% of runs
choices.feedback: Right: 0.999 to the power 500 is about 0.61, so 39% of runs have at least one spurious failure.

choices.label: About 5% of runs
choices.feedback: That would need a flake rate of about 0.01% per test, ten times lower.

interactive.reveal: Expected flakes per run are 500 × 0.001 = 0.5, so a clean run is barely more likely than not. Fix or quarantine flaky tests as soon as they appear.

seeAlso.why: Where these tests run in a CI/CD pipeline
Accessible names that user-style queries rely on
State machines whose transitions are easy to unit-test
Unit, integration and contract tests for the services the UI calls

title: The Cascade, Specificity and Cascade Layers
objectives: Predict which declaration wins using origin, layers, specificity and order
Compute selector specificity, including :is, :not, :where and inline styles
Organise a stylesheet with cascade layers so utilities and overrides win without !important

cards.title: When two rules disagree
cards.body: Most elements match several rules that set the same property. The cascade compares the competing declarations step by step, moving to the next step only on a tie: origin and importance, then cascade layer, then specificity, then order of appearance. So the later declaration wins only when origin, layer and specificity are all equal. Styles set directly in an element’s style attribute sit between importance and layers, beating any selector. Knowing the order turns “why is my style ignored?” into a lookup.

cards.title: The cascade’s tie-breakers in order
cards.body: Each step only matters if all earlier steps tie.
steps: Origin and importance: user-agent, user and author styles; !important reverses their order
Inline style attribute beats any selector in the same origin and importance
Cascade layer: for normal rules, later layers win and unlayered styles beat all layers
Specificity: compare (IDs, classes and attributes and pseudo-classes, types and pseudo-elements)
Order of appearance: the later declaration wins

cards.title: Worked example: comparing specificity
cards.body: Count three columns. nav .menu > li.active a:hover has 0 IDs; .menu, .active and :hover make 3 in the class column; nav, li and a make 3 in the type column: (0, 3, 3). #sidebar a scores (1, 0, 1) and wins, because columns compare left to right and one ID beats any number of classes. Combinators and the universal selector add nothing. :is() and :not() take their most specific argument; :where() always adds zero.

cards.title: Layers: decide the winner by intent, not selector weight
cards.body: Declare the order once: @layer reset, base, components, utilities. A rule in utilities beats a rule in components whatever their specificity, so a one-class utility can override a component styled with an ID. Styles outside any layer beat all layered styles, which lets older or third-party CSS be wrapped in a low layer. For !important declarations the layer order reverses, so an important reset in the first layer beats everything later.

cards.title: Trap: fighting with !important
cards.body: Adding !important to win one battle starts an arms race: the next override needs !important and higher specificity, and so on. Important declarations also reverse the layer order, which surprises people. Fix the structure instead: lower the specificity of component selectors, often with :where(), and put overrides in a later layer.

cards.title: Edge case: inherited values have no weight
cards.body: Properties such as color and font-family inherit from the parent when no rule sets them on the element. An inherited value loses to any rule that targets the element itself, even the browser’s own styles: #article { color: green } does not colour a link inside it, because the user-agent rule for links sets its colour directly. Set the property on the element, or use the inherit keyword in a rule that matches it.

questions.prompt: Which selector has the highest specificity?

choices.label: .card .title .icon .label
main article section p span
#promo a
:where(#promo) .card a

questions.explanation: #promo a is (1, 0, 1). Four classes are (0, 4, 0), five types are (0, 0, 5), and :where() contributes zero, leaving (0, 1, 1). One ID outranks any number of classes.

questions.prompt: Layers are declared as base, components, utilities. A utility rule .mt-0 sets margin-top: 0; a component rule #hero .heading sets margin-top: 2rem. Both are normal declarations. Which applies?

choices.label: margin-top: 2rem, because the component selector is more specific
margin-top: 0, because utilities is a later layer
Whichever rule appears later in the file
Neither; conflicting layers cancel the property

questions.explanation: Layer order is compared before specificity, so the later layer wins for normal declarations. Specificity and source order only break ties within the same layer.

questions.prompt: A third-party widget’s stylesheet is unlayered, and the site’s own styles are all in layers. The widget’s rules keep overriding the site’s. Why?

choices.label: Third-party stylesheets are treated as user-agent styles
The widget’s selectors are more specific than the site’s
Unlayered normal styles beat styles in any layer
Layers apply only to stylesheets on the same origin

questions.explanation: Unlayered author styles form an implicit final layer. Importing the widget’s stylesheet into a low layer with @import and a layer name puts it below the site’s layers.

questions.prompt: An element has style="color: red" and a stylesheet rule #main p { color: blue }. Both are normal declarations. Which colour wins?

choices.label: Blue, because the ID selector is more specific
Blue, if the stylesheet loads after the HTML containing the attribute
Whichever was declared later in the document
Red, because the style attribute beats any selector

questions.explanation: Inline style attributes are ranked above all selectors in the same origin and importance; only !important author rules (or higher origins) beat them.

questions.prompt: Order the cascade’s tie-breakers from first applied to last.

items.label: Specificity
Origin and importance
Order of appearance
Cascade layer
Inline style attribute

questions.explanation: Each later step only decides when everything before it ties.

questions.prompt: How many class-column components (classes, attributes and pseudo-classes) does nav .menu > li.active a:hover[href] have?
assumptions: Types and combinators are not counted in this column
The attribute selector [href] counts as a class-level component
questions.explanation: Sanity check: three type selectors (nav, li, a) go in the third column, which only matters if the first two tie.

flashcards.back: Origin and importance, inline style, layer, specificity, order of appearance.
IDs; classes, attributes and pseudo-classes; types and pseudo-elements.
:where() adds zero; :is() takes its most specific argument.
Beat all layered normal styles; important declarations reverse the layer order.

sources.title: MDN: Introduction to the CSS cascade
W3C: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5

mechanism.title: How the browser picks one value
steps: For each element and property, the browser collects every declaration from every stylesheet that matches. If none exists, the value is inherited from the parent for inherited properties, or set to the property’s initial value. If several exist, the cascade sorts them and the winner becomes the cascaded value.

The first criterion is origin and importance. Normal declarations rank user-agent, then user, then author styles, with author winning. Important declarations reverse that: important user-agent beats important user, which beats important author, so users with accessibility style sheets can override sites. Transitions and animations also have their own positions in this ranking.

Within an origin and importance, declarations in an element’s style attribute beat those from selectors. Then come cascade layers. Normal declarations in later-declared layers beat earlier ones, and unlayered declarations beat all layers. Important declarations reverse the order, so important rules in the earliest layer win. Layers can be nested and created by importing a stylesheet into a named layer.

Next is specificity, compared as three numbers: ID selectors; class selectors, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes; type selectors and pseudo-elements. Columns compare left to right without carrying, so (1, 0, 0) beats (0, 15, 0). :is(), :not() and :has() take the specificity of their most specific argument; :where() is always zero, which makes it useful for low-weight base styles that are easy to override.

The final tie-breaker is order of appearance: the declaration that comes later in the combined stylesheets wins. Shorthands set all their longhands, so a later background shorthand resets an earlier background-image. Inheritance is separate from the cascade: an inherited value applies only when no declaration targets the element itself.

useWhen: Design systems where components, themes and utilities must override each other predictably.
Sites mixing their own CSS with third-party or legacy stylesheets.
avoidWhen: Avoid raising specificity or adding !important to win a conflict.
Avoid styling components with ID selectors that are hard to override.

rows: Each override needs even higher specificity
Later layers win regardless of selectors
Unlayered styles still beat all layers

numbers.title: Scoring two selectors
assumptions: Both in the same layer, both normal declarations
steps: A: IDs 0; classes .menu and .active plus :hover = 3; types nav, li, a = 3: (0, 3, 3).
B: IDs 1; classes 0; types a = 1: (1, 0, 1).
Compare the first column: 1 beats 0, so B wins without looking further.
Wrap A in :where() and it scores (0, 0, 0), so any single class overrides it.
numbers.result: Specificity is compared column by column; one ID outranks any number of classes, and :where() resets weight to zero.

india.title: What the specification defines
india.label: Official specification (W3C)
india.body: The W3C CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5 specification defines the cascade sort order as origin and importance, context, element-attached styles, layers, specificity and order of appearance, and introduces the @layer rule. It specifies that unlayered styles are treated as the final layer for normal declarations, and that the order of layers is reversed for important declarations. MDN documents the same order with examples.

pitfalls.trap: “Make the selector more specific to win.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d put the override in a later layer instead of escalating specificity.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add !important, it always wins.”
pitfalls.say: “Important flips the layer order and starts an arms race; I’d fix the structure.”

pitfalls.trap: “The parent is green, so the link should be green.”
pitfalls.say: “Inherited values lose to any rule on the link itself, including the browser’s.”

takeaways: The cascade sorts by origin and importance, inline style, layer, specificity, then order.
Specificity compares IDs, then classes, then types, without carrying.
Later layers win regardless of specificity; unlayered styles win over layers.
Use :where() for low-weight defaults and layers for overrides, not !important.

interactive.title: Which colour does the link get?
interactive.prompt: The site declares @layer base, components. Inside the components layer: #nav a.link { color: red }. Outside any layer, an old stylesheet has a { color: blue }. Both are normal declarations and both match the same link.

choices.label: Red, because its selector is far more specific
choices.feedback: Specificity is compared only within the same layer; the layer decides first.

choices.label: Blue, because unlayered styles beat layered ones
choices.feedback: Right: unlayered normal styles act as a final layer, so a plain type selector beats the layered rule.

choices.label: Whichever stylesheet loads last
choices.feedback: Order of appearance is the last tie-breaker, after layers and specificity.

interactive.reveal: Move legacy and third-party CSS into an early layer, for example by importing it into a legacy layer listed first, so the site’s own layers can override it.

seeAlso.why: The layout properties these cascade rules usually decide
Where style calculation sits in the rendering pipeline
Media queries that add conditional rules to the cascade

title: Third-Party Scripts: Cost and Containment
objectives: Count what a third-party script costs in connections, main-thread time, layout shift and risk
Load third parties late, behind facades, or in sandboxed frames instead of directly in the page
Govern tags with owners, budgets and measurement so the page does not slowly fill up

cards.title: Someone else’s code, with your page’s powers
cards.body: Analytics, ads, chat widgets, video players, A/B testing and tag managers run in your page with the same rights as your own script. They can read the page, every field the user types into, and any cookie not marked HttpOnly, and they can change what the page shows. They also compete for the network and the main thread. Each one is a performance and security decision, usually made by someone outside the front-end team.

cards.title: Worked example: a new origin on the critical path
cards.body: A synchronous script tag in the head loads from a vendor’s origin. Before any byte arrives, the browser needs DNS, TCP and TLS 1.3, about three round trips: at 80 ms each, 240 ms. The request itself adds another round trip, so the first byte arrives after about 320 ms, while the parser waits. If the vendor is slow or down, the page waits until the request times out. Loading it async removes the parser wait; deferring it until after load removes it from the first view.

cards.title: Containment options, weakest to strongest
cards.body: Pick by how much the script needs and how much you trust it.
steps: Load async or after the page is interactive instead of blocking the parser
Show a facade, such as a video thumbnail, and load the real widget on click
Self-host pinned versions with an integrity hash and restrict them with a policy
Run untrusted widgets in a sandboxed iframe on a separate origin
Move analytics collection to your own server endpoint where possible

cards.title: Facades: load the heavy thing on intent
cards.body: A video embed or chat widget can pull hundreds of kilobytes of script on every page view, though most visitors never press play or open the chat. A facade is a lightweight look-alike, such as a thumbnail with a play button or a chat bubble, that loads the real widget when the user interacts. Lighthouse flags embeds that could use facades.

cards.title: Trap: the tag manager as a back door
cards.body: A tag manager lets marketing add scripts without a deploy. That is useful, and it also means code reaches production without review, testing or performance budgets. Give every tag an owner and a purpose, review new tags like code, set a budget for main-thread time and bytes, and remove tags whose campaigns have ended.

cards.title: Edge case: when a vendor is down
cards.body: A vendor outage should cost a feature, not the page. Scripts loaded async or after load fail on their own; a synchronous script in the head or a render-blocking stylesheet from the vendor can blank the page until the browser gives up. Test it by blocking each third-party origin in the browser’s developer tools and checking that the page still renders and works.

questions.prompt: A landing page embeds a video player that downloads about 500 KB of script, and about 5% of visitors press play. What is the best change?

choices.label: Show a thumbnail facade and load the player on click
Preload the player script so it is ready when visitors press play
Move the embed lower on the page
Compress the page’s images more heavily

questions.explanation: A facade spares 95% of visitors the download and main-thread work. Preloading makes it start sooner for everyone, moving it lower may not delay the script, and image compression does not touch the player cost.

questions.prompt: Why can an analytics script read what users type into a payment form on the same page?

choices.label: Browsers grant scripts from trusted vendors extra rights
The vendor’s cookies give it access to the form
Analytics scripts run in a separate process with page access
Every script in the page runs with the page’s own privileges

questions.explanation: Scripts in a page share its origin and access, whatever their source. Cookies and processes are not the reason; there is no trusted-vendor tier. Sensitive fields belong in isolated frames or pages with few scripts.

questions.prompt: The vendor of a synchronous script in the page’s head has an outage, and the page stays blank for about 20 seconds. What prevents this?

choices.label: A preconnect hint so the vendor’s connection opens earlier
Loading the script async or after load, so the parser does not wait
Serving the page’s HTML from a CDN closer to users
A service worker that caches the page’s HTML for repeat visits

questions.explanation: Non-blocking loading makes the vendor’s failure cost only its own feature. Preconnect cannot help when the vendor is down, a closer CDN speeds the HTML but not the vendor’s script, and caching the HTML still leaves the parser waiting on the script.

questions.prompt: Main-thread time from tags grew by 400 ms over a year, one tag at a time. Which practice stops this?

choices.label: Owners, a review for new tags and a main-thread budget
Moving the tag manager to the bottom of the page
Letting each team add tags it needs without review
Asking the vendors to make their scripts faster

questions.explanation: Governance turns slow growth into decisions: every tag has an owner, new ones are reviewed, and a budget forces trade-offs. Position helps little, unreviewed tags are the cause, and vendors control their own code.

questions.prompt: Order an audit of the third parties on a page.

items.label: Remove unused tags and assign owners to the rest
List every third-party request and the tag that triggered it
Defer, facade or sandbox what remains, then set a budget
Measure each one’s bytes, main-thread time and blocking behaviour

questions.explanation: Inventory, measure, remove and assign, then contain and keep a budget so it stays fixed.

questions.prompt: A vendor script sits on an origin the browser has never contacted, 80 ms away. Name lookup, connection and encryption setup cost one round trip each. How long until the script request itself can leave the browser?
assumptions: Nothing about the origin is cached
Each setup step costs one full round trip
questions.workedAnswer: DNS 80 + TCP 80 + TLS 80 = 240 ms before the request; the response adds at least one more round trip
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a cold connection to a new origin costs a quarter of a second before any data, which is why third parties on the critical path hurt.

flashcards.back: The same as your own script: page, input and non-HttpOnly cookies.
A lightweight stand-in that loads the real widget on interaction.
Block its origin in developer tools; the page should still work.
Owners, review for new tags, a main-thread and byte budget.

sources.title: Chrome for Developers: Lazy load third-party resources with facades
MDN: The iframe element and its sandbox attribute

mechanism.title: Where third-party cost comes from and how to contain it
steps: Network cost comes first. Each new origin needs DNS, a TCP connection and a TLS handshake before its first request; scripts then often fetch more scripts, pixels and configuration from further origins. A synchronous script blocks the parser until it downloads and runs, so a slow vendor delays the whole page and a down vendor can blank it.

Main-thread cost follows. Third-party code is parsed, compiled and run on the same thread as your own, and it often adds listeners for scroll, clicks and visibility. On mid-range phones this lengthens tasks and raises interaction latency. Ads and embeds inserted without reserved space also cause layout shifts.

Loading strategy is the first lever. Load scripts async, or defer non-essential ones until after the page is interactive or the first user interaction. Use preconnect only for the one or two origins on the critical path. Replace heavy embeds such as video players, maps and chat with facades that load the real thing on intent. Reserve space for ads and embeds so they do not shift content.

Isolation is the second lever. Anything in the page shares its origin and powers. A sandboxed iframe on a separate origin limits what a widget can do: without allow-same-origin it runs in an opaque origin, and capabilities such as scripts, forms and popups must be granted one by one. A Content Security Policy limits where scripts and data can go, and self-hosting a pinned version with an integrity hash stops silent changes.

Governance is the third lever, because third parties accumulate. Keep an inventory of every tag with an owner and purpose, review new tags for privacy, security and performance, set budgets for bytes and main-thread time, and test pages with each vendor blocked. Field monitoring segmented by page shows when a newly added tag causes a regression.

useWhen: Pages with analytics, ads, embeds, chat, A/B testing or tag managers.
Checkout, login and account pages where scripts can read sensitive input.
avoidWhen: Avoid synchronous third-party scripts in the head.
Avoid running untrusted widgets in the main page when a sandboxed frame would do.

columns: What the vendor can still do
rows: Blocks parsing; outage can blank the page

numbers.title: What a cold third-party origin costs
assumptions: DNS, TCP and TLS 1.3 at one round trip each
A vendor script of 150 KB compressed (illustrative)
steps: Connection setup: 3 × 80 ms = 240 ms before the request.
Request and first byte: one more round trip, about 320 ms in total.
Transfer at 5 Mbit/s: 150 × 8 ÷ 5,000 = 0.24 s more.
If synchronous, the parser waits about 560 ms plus execution time; async moves that off the critical path.
numbers.result: One synchronous vendor script can cost over half a second of first view on a mobile connection before it runs a line of code.

india.title: A third-party script host changes owner
india.label: Publicly reported (Sansec, 2024)
india.body: Many sites loaded a browser polyfill directly from the cdn.polyfill.io domain. In February 2024 the domain and its project account were sold to a new owner, and in June 2024 the security firm Sansec reported that the script served from it had been altered to redirect some mobile visitors to scam and betting sites, on more than 100,000 sites that embedded it. The domain’s registrar suspended it days later. Because the file was generated per browser, an integrity hash could not have pinned it; the durable fixes were self-hosting a reviewed copy or removing a polyfill modern browsers no longer needed.

pitfalls.trap: “The vendor is reputable, so their script is safe.”
pitfalls.say: “It runs with our page’s powers; I’d limit it, pin it or sandbox it.”

pitfalls.trap: “Preconnect to all our vendors.”
pitfalls.say: “Only the one or two on the critical path; the rest load later.”

pitfalls.trap: “Marketing owns the tags, not us.”
pitfalls.say: “Tags ship code to our users; I’d set owners, reviews and a budget.”

takeaways: Third-party scripts run with your page’s full powers.
Load them async or after interaction, never synchronously in the head.
Use facades for heavy embeds and sandboxed frames for untrusted widgets.
Keep payment and login pages nearly free of third parties.
Govern tags with owners, reviews and budgets.

interactive.title: How should the chat widget load?
interactive.prompt: A support chat widget adds about 300 KB of script and several new origins. About 2% of visitors open the chat, mostly on help pages. The widget also appears on the checkout page.

choices.label: Load it in the head on every page so it is ready
choices.feedback: Every visitor pays the network and main-thread cost for a feature 2% use, and an outage can block the page.

choices.label: A chat-bubble facade that loads the widget on click, and no widget on checkout
choices.feedback: Right: the cost moves to the 2% who want it, and checkout keeps few scripts near card fields.

choices.label: Load it async on every page, including checkout
choices.feedback: Better than blocking, but 98% of visitors still download and run it, and it can read checkout input.

interactive.reveal: Load heavy widgets on intent, and keep sensitive pages free of scripts that do not need to be there.

seeAlso.why: Policies and integrity hashes that restrict third-party code
Preconnect, preload and lazy loading
Supply-chain risk in the code you ship

title: UI State Machines: Making Impossible States Impossible
objectives: Spot impossible combinations created by independent boolean flags
Model a component as explicit states, events and transitions
Use the model to ignore invalid events, such as a second submit, and to drive tests

cards.title: Boolean soup
cards.body: A data panel tracks isLoading, isError and hasData as three separate flags. Three booleans allow 2³ = 8 combinations, but only four are meaningful: idle, loading, success and error. The other four, such as loading and error at once, are bugs waiting to happen: a spinner over an error message, or stale data shown as fresh. Each new flag doubles the combinations again.

cards.title: Misconception: a state machine needs a library
cards.body: A state machine is just three things: a single variable holding the current state, a list of events, and a table saying which event moves which state where. A switch over the state, or a lookup table, is enough. Libraries add visual tools and nested states, but the idea is a design discipline, not a dependency.

cards.title: A payment button as a state machine
cards.body: Each state lists the events it accepts; others are ignored.
steps: idle: on submit, go to submitting and send the request
submitting: on success go to paid; on failure go to failed; ignore submit
failed: on retry go to submitting; show the error
paid: terminal; ignore submit and retry
Data lives with its state: the error message only in failed, the receipt only in paid

cards.title: Worked example: the double charge
cards.body: If the only guard is a disabled button that appears on the next render, a fast double click can fire two submit handlers first, sending two payment requests. In a state machine, every click is sent to the machine as an event, the first one moves idle to submitting as it is processed, before any render, and submitting has no transition for submit, so the second click does nothing. Pair it with an idempotency key so even a retry after a timeout cannot charge twice.

cards.title: Trap: keeping data in states where it is meaningless
cards.body: If the error message is a separate field, it survives into the next success and is shown with fresh data. Attach data to the state that owns it: the error only exists in failed, the results only in success, and the previous results in a refreshing state if you want to keep showing them while reloading. Then showing stale data becomes a choice you write down, not an accident.

cards.title: Edge case: states that run in parallel
cards.body: A video player is playing or paused, and independently muted or unmuted, and fullscreen or not. Modelling every combination as one flat list gives 2³ = 8 states that are hard to maintain. Statecharts, introduced by David Harel in the 1980s, allow parallel regions and nested states, so each concern stays a small machine of its own.

questions.prompt: A form tracks isSubmitting, isSuccess and isError as separate booleans. How many combinations can the code represent, and how many are valid?

choices.label: 8 combinations, about 4 valid
3 combinations, all valid
6 combinations, about 3 valid
4 combinations, about 2 valid

questions.explanation: Three independent booleans give 2³ = 8 combinations. Only idle, submitting, success and error make sense; the rest are impossible states that the code can still reach.

questions.prompt: A payment button sometimes sends two requests on a double click. What does a state machine change?

choices.label: It debounces the click by a fixed delay
It hides the button with a style rule right after the first click event
In submitting, the submit event has no transition, so it is ignored
It retries the request until one of them succeeds

questions.explanation: The first event moves to submitting at once, and the state does not accept submit. A fixed delay can be beaten by a slow render, styles do not stop queued events, and retries risk more charges.

questions.prompt: After a failed load and a successful retry, an old error banner still shows above the new data. What is the root cause?

choices.label: The retry request returned cached data that still contained the old error
The error lived in a separate field instead of in the failed state
The banner component was rendered twice
The server sent the error and the data together

questions.explanation: Data attached to the state that owns it disappears when the state changes. A separate error field survives transitions unless every code path remembers to clear it.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a finite state machine for a UI component?

choices.label: A set of flags that any handler can change
A record of each event the user has triggered since the page loaded
A cache entry per key, shared by all views
One current state and a table of transitions per event

questions.explanation: The machine holds a single current state, and each event either maps to a transition or is ignored. Flags are what it replaces; an event log and a cache are different tools.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to turn a component’s flags into a state machine.

items.label: Attach data to the states that own it
List the events: user actions and responses
Write a test for each transition
List the states the user can actually see
For each state, decide which events it accepts and where they lead

questions.explanation: Start from what users see, add the events, fill the transition table, move data into states, then test each transition.

questions.prompt: A component has four independent boolean flags. How many combinations of their values can the code represent?
assumptions: Each flag is true or false independently
questions.explanation: Sanity check: typically only a handful of those are valid states, which is why a single state variable is safer.

flashcards.back: n flags give 2ⁿ combinations, most of them invalid states.
One current state, events, and a transition table; other events are ignored.
In the state that owns it: the error only in failed, results only in success.
Statecharts: parallel regions and nested states.

sources.title: W3C: State Chart XML (SCXML): State Machine Notation for Control Abstraction
ACM HOPL III: Statecharts in the Making, a Personal Account (David Harel)

mechanism.title: How explicit states remove a class of bugs
steps: Interface code often grows one flag at a time: a loading flag, then an error flag, then a refreshing flag. Each handler flips the flags it knows about. With n flags the code can represent 2 to the power n combinations, and nothing stops it reaching the invalid ones. Bugs appear as screens that show two things at once or carry leftovers from an earlier state.

A finite state machine replaces the flags with one value naming the current state, such as idle, loading, success or failure. Events, such as a user submit or a server response, are sent to the machine. A transition table says, for each state, which events it accepts and which state comes next; an event with no entry for the current state is ignored. Rendering is a function of the current state.

Data travels with states. In a typed language this is a tagged union: the success variant carries results, the failure variant carries an error, and the loading variant may carry the previous results if the design keeps them visible. Code cannot read results in the failure state because they do not exist there. Side effects, such as sending a request or moving focus, are attached to transitions, so they run exactly when the state changes.

Because the machine ignores events it does not expect, races become explicit decisions. A second submit while submitting is ignored. A response that arrives after the user cancelled finds the machine in idle, where it has no transition, so it is dropped. For overlapping requests, the state can hold the id of the request it is waiting for and accept only that response.

Bigger interfaces need structure. Statecharts, introduced by David Harel and standardised in notation such as the W3C’s SCXML, add nested states that share transitions, parallel regions for independent concerns, and guards on transitions. The model doubles as documentation and a test plan: one test per transition and one per ignored event covers the component’s behaviour.

useWhen: Components with asynchronous work: forms, uploads, payments, wizards, media players.
Flows where a double action or a late response would cause real damage.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple toggles where one boolean is the whole state.
Avoid one flat machine for independent concerns; use parallel regions.

rows: Yes, 2 to the power n combinations
Fewer; data can still be left over
State machine with data in states
A transition table to write and maintain

numbers.title: Counting the states
assumptions: A panel with flags isLoading, isError, hasData and isRefreshing
Valid screens: idle, loading, success, refreshing with old data, failure
steps: Representable combinations: 2⁴ = 16.
Valid states: 5, so 11 of the 16 combinations are bugs the code can reach.
As a machine: one variable with 5 values, so 0 invalid states.
Tests: one per transition, for example 8 transitions plus 3 ignored events = 11 tests for full coverage of behaviour.
numbers.result: A single state variable shrinks 16 representable combinations to the 5 that are real.

india.title: The notation behind statecharts
india.label: Official specification (W3C) and public history
india.body: The W3C’s State Chart XML recommendation defines a standard notation for state machines with nested and parallel states, events, guards and actions, based on Harel statecharts. In his paper for the ACM History of Programming Languages conference in 2007, David Harel describes how statecharts grew out of specifying the behaviour of complex reactive avionics systems, where flat state diagrams became unmanageable.

pitfalls.trap: “Add another flag for the refreshing case.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d add a refreshing state, so it cannot combine with error.”

pitfalls.trap: “Disable the button after the click to stop double submits.”
pitfalls.say: “The state should ignore submit while submitting; disabling is only the visual.”

pitfalls.trap: “Clear the error at the start of every handler.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d keep the error inside the failed state, so it disappears with it.”

takeaways: n independent flags allow 2 to the power n combinations; most are bugs.
Model one current state, events and a transition table.
Unexpected events are ignored, which removes double submits and late responses.
Keep data inside the state that owns it.
Use statecharts for nested and parallel concerns.

interactive.title: What happens to the late response?
interactive.prompt: A search panel is a state machine with states idle, searching and results. The user searches for “lamp”, then presses Cancel before the response arrives, which moves the machine back to idle. Two seconds later the response for “lamp” arrives.

choices.label: The lamp results appear, since the request succeeded
choices.feedback: That is what flag-based code often does; the machine is no longer searching.

choices.label: The panel shows an error for the cancelled request
choices.feedback: There is no transition from idle on a response, so nothing renders.

choices.label: It is ignored: idle has no transition for a response
choices.feedback: Right: the event arrives in a state that does not accept it, so the machine drops it.

interactive.reveal: Explicit states make late events harmless by default. Cancel the request too, to save the work, but correctness no longer depends on it.

seeAlso.why: Client state, caching and stale responses that machines make explicit
Optimistic updates, which add pending and rolled-back states
Idempotency keys that back up a double-submit guard on the server

title: Money in Code: Minor Units, Rounding and Currency
objectives: Carry amounts as integer minor units with a currency code, in storage and in JSON
Round once, at a stated step, with a stated rule, and allocate remainders so splits add up
Convert currencies with a recorded rate, and make money endpoints reject a reused key with a changed amount

cards.title: Amounts on the wire and in the database
cards.body: A binary double cannot hold 0.1 exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, and many JSON parsers, including JavaScript’s, read every number as a double. Store money as an integer count of the currency’s minor unit (₹499.99 is 49,999 paise) or as a fixed-scale decimal, and send it the same way: {"amount": 49999, "currency": "INR"}, or a decimal string such as "499.99". The ISO 4217 code says how many minor digits to use: INR and USD have 2, JPY has 0, and KWD has 3.

cards.title: Worked example: splitting ₹100 three ways
cards.body: ₹100 is 10,000 paise, and 10,000 ÷ 3 is 3,333 with 1 paisa left over. Rounding each share to ₹33.33 charges ₹99.99 in total, so one paisa vanishes from the books. Instead give everyone the floor (3,333) and hand the leftover units out one at a time by a fixed rule, such as to the payer first: 3,334 + 3,333 + 3,333 = 10,000. The shares differ by at most one paisa and always add up.

cards.title: From request to stored amount
cards.body: The amount is made exact at the edge and rounded only where a rule says so.
steps: The request carries {"amount": "499.99", "currency": "INR"}
Look up INR’s minor digits in ISO 4217: 2
Parse the string exactly into 49,999 paise; reject a third decimal place
Apply tax or discounts in integers and exact decimals, rounding once with the named mode
Store 49,999 with INR; format as ₹499.99 only when displaying

cards.title: Rounding and conversion: choose the rule and the moment
cards.body: Two decisions change totals. The mode: half-up turns 2.5 into 3, while half-even (banker’s rounding) turns 2.5 into 2 and 3.5 into 4, which removes the upward bias over millions of roundings. The moment: three items at ₹10.10 with 18% tax give 3 × ₹1.82 = ₹5.46 if tax is rounded per line, but ₹5.45 if it is computed once on ₹30.30. Currency conversion follows the same rule: multiply the source minor units by the rate in exact decimal, round once into the target’s minor units, and store the rate and source amount alongside the result.

cards.title: Trap: a retry that changes the amount
cards.body: Idempotency keys stop a retried payment from charging twice, but only if the server checks that the retry is the same request. If a client bug reuses the key for a ₹5,000 payout after a ₹500 one, replaying the stored ₹500 result hides the bug, and running the new request breaks the key’s promise. Store a hash of the request body with the key, replay only when it matches, and reject a mismatch with an error. The IETF Idempotency-Key draft suggests 422 Unprocessable Content for this case, and Stripe’s API, for example, also returns an error when a key is reused with different parameters.

questions.prompt: Which JSON body is safest for a payment amount sent to an API?

choices.label: {"amount": 49999, "currency": "INR"}
{"amount": 499.99, "currency": "INR"}

questions.explanation: a: a JSON number like 499.99 is read as a double by many parsers, and the currency is missing. b: correct, an integer count of paise is exact in every parser up to 2⁵³, and the code says what the unit is. c: a formatted display string depends on locale (“1,234.50” or “1.234,50”) and has to be parsed by guesswork. d: the currency helps, but the amount is still a float on the way in.

questions.prompt: An API stores amounts for INR and JPY accounts as integer minor units. What must travel with each amount?

choices.label: The exchange rate on the day it was created
Its ISO 4217 currency code
A flag saying whether it was rounded
How many decimals the app displays

questions.explanation: a: a rate is needed only when converting, not to know what the stored number means. b: correct, the code tells you the unit, and INR has 2 minor digits while JPY has 0, so 500 means ₹5.00 or ¥500. c: a rounding flag does not say what the unit is. d: display settings vary by screen; the currency code is the stable fact.

questions.prompt: ₹100 is split between 3 people in paise. Which result keeps the books balanced?

choices.label: 3,333 paise each, writing off the extra paisa
3,333.33 paise each, kept as decimals
3,334 paise each, the payer covering 2 more

questions.explanation: a: the books are short by one paisa on every split. b: correct, floors plus one leftover unit handed out by a fixed rule sum to exactly 10,000. c: a paisa cannot be charged in thirds, so this only postpones the rounding. d: charging 10,002 paise collects more than the bill.

questions.prompt: Half-even (banker’s) rounding is applied to ₹2.5 and ₹3.5, rounding to whole rupees. What are the results?

choices.label: 3 and 4
2 and 4
2 and 3
3 and 3

questions.explanation: a: that is half-up, which always rounds .5 upwards. b: correct, half-even rounds .5 to the nearest even digit, so the ups and downs cancel out over many values. c: that is half-down or truncation. d: that is half-odd, a rarely used mode.

questions.prompt: A client retries POST /payouts with the same Idempotency-Key, but the amount has changed from ₹500 to ₹5,000. What should the server do?

choices.label: Pay ₹5,000, since the latest request wins
Replay the stored ₹500 result as a success
Reject it: the key belongs to another request
Pay the ₹4,500 difference as a top-up

questions.explanation: a: running a new request under an old key breaks the promise that one key means one operation. b: the client believes ₹5,000 went out when only ₹500 did, and the bug stays hidden. c: correct, a key names one request; comparing a stored hash of the body exposes the client bug at once. d: inventing a top-up guesses at intent and moves money nobody asked for.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for charging an INR card for a $12.99 price.

items.label: Multiply exactly: 1,299 × 83.2715 = 108,169.6785 paise
Parse “12.99” USD into 1,299 cents
Store 108,170 INR with the rate and the 1,299 USD source amount
Fetch the USD-to-INR rate and record it with its time
Round once, half-even, to 108,170 paise

questions.explanation: Parse into exact units first, use one recorded rate, keep full precision through the multiplication and round only at the end, then store enough to repeat and explain the conversion later.

questions.prompt: An app splits ₹100 bills three ways, rounds each share to ₹33.33 and drops the leftover paisa. It does 200,000 such splits a day. How many rupees go unaccounted for each day?
assumptions: One paisa is lost per split
questions.explanation: Sanity check: that is about ₹7.3 lakh a year of drift from one rounding rule, which reconciliation will flag even though each single split looks fine.

flashcards.front: How should money travel and be stored?
flashcards.back: As integer minor units (or a decimal string or fixed-scale decimal) plus an ISO 4217 currency code.
2 and 4: .5 goes to the even neighbour, so bias cancels out.
Reject it: a key names one request, so a changed body is a client bug, not a retry.

sources.title: RFC 8259: JSON, section 6 on numbers and interoperability
IETF draft: The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field
Martin Fowler: Money (Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture)

mechanism.title: How money stays exact from request to storage
steps: Parse money at the edge into an exact type. A request carrying “499.99” or 49999 with “INR” becomes 49,999 minor units with the code INR, using the number of minor digits that ISO 4217 lists for the currency; a value with more decimals than the currency allows is rejected, not rounded silently. From then on, adding and subtracting are integer operations, which are exact.

Multiplication and division are where rounding enters: tax, discounts, interest, conversion and splits. Each produces a fraction of a minor unit that has to be rounded. Do it once, at a step you name (per line or per invoice), with a mode you name (half-up, half-even), and keep the unrounded rate or price in the record so the calculation can be repeated and explained later.

Splits need allocation, not rounding. Dividing 10,000 paise three ways gives three floors of 3,333 and a remainder of 1. Hand the remainder out one unit at a time by a deterministic rule, such as largest fractional part first or a fixed party order. The same rule, applied on refund, reverses each share exactly, so a partially refunded group bill does not leave a stray paisa behind.

Conversion uses one recorded rate. Fetch the rate once for the operation, keep it as an exact decimal with enough digits (often 6 or more), multiply the source minor units by it, and round once into the target’s minor units. Store the source amount and currency, the rate, its source and time, and the result, so a refund can reverse the same conversion rather than using today’s rate by accident.

Endpoints that move money are idempotent and strict about it. The idempotency key is stored with a hash of the request body and the result, in the same transaction as the money write. A matching retry gets the stored result; a mismatched body under the same key is rejected. The bookkeeping itself, balanced ledger rows and reconciliation, is an architecture topic of its own; this lesson stops at the API and the stored amount.

useWhen: Any system that charges, refunds, splits, converts or reports money.
Public payment and payout APIs, where clients in many languages parse your amounts.
avoidWhen: Avoid floats for money anywhere, including JSON payloads and analytics totals that finance will compare.
Avoid converting with a fresh rate on refund; reuse the rate stored with the original charge.

rows: Needs the currency to know the unit
Scale must cover rates and tax
Totals drift by fractions of a paisa

numbers.title: Per-line or per-invoice tax rounding
steps: Per line: ₹10.10 × 0.18 = ₹1.818, which rounds to ₹1.82.
Three lines: 3 × ₹1.82 = ₹5.46 of tax.
Per invoice: ₹30.30 × 0.18 = ₹5.454, which rounds to ₹5.45.
The two rules differ by 1 paisa on this invoice; across many invoices the gap adds up and must match what the tax return reports.
numbers.result: Neither rule is wrong; mixing them is. Pick the one the rules or contract require and use it in invoices, credit notes and reports alike.

india.title: Paise, GST lines and a dollar price
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: an Indian marketplace shows ₹499.99 on screen but its API sends 49999 with INR and stores the same. Tax on each invoice is computed either per line or on the invoice total, and the business picks one rule and applies it to invoices, credit notes and refunds so the totals reconcile with its tax filings. For a seller who prices in dollars, checkout converts once with a stored rate and keeps both amounts, so a refund a month later returns exactly what was charged. Retried payment calls carry an idempotency key, and a key reused with a different amount is rejected and logged as a client bug.

pitfalls.trap: “A double is precise enough for rupees.”
pitfalls.say: “Doubles cannot hold 0.1 exactly; I’d carry paise as integers with the currency code, in JSON too.”

pitfalls.trap: “Round each share and the totals will work out.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d allocate the remainder by a fixed rule so the shares always sum to the bill.”

takeaways: Carry money as integer minor units with an ISO 4217 code, on the wire and at rest.
Round once, at a named step, with a named mode.
Convert with one recorded rate and keep it with the result.
Reject an idempotency key reused with a different body.

interactive.title: Splitting ₹100 three ways
interactive.prompt: A bill-split feature computes 100 ÷ 3 in floating point, rounds each share to two decimals and charges three cards. What does finance see when it adds up the charges for this bill?

choices.label: ₹99.99 charged against a ₹100 bill
choices.feedback: Right: each share rounds down to ₹33.33, and the leftover paisa belongs to nobody.

choices.label: Exactly ₹100, since the rounding cancels out
choices.feedback: All three shares round the same way, so nothing cancels; the error is one paisa every time.

choices.label: ₹100.02, since each share rounds up
choices.feedback: 33.333… is below the halfway point, so half-up rounding takes it down, not up.

interactive.reveal: Work in paise and allocate: 10,000 ÷ 3 gives three floors of 3,333 and a remainder of 1, which goes to one person by a fixed rule. The shares become 3,334, 3,333 and 3,333 and always add up to the bill.

seeAlso.why: Idempotency keys are what stop a retried payment from posting twice
How numbers are encoded in JSON and other formats decides whether amounts survive the trip
Double-entry ledgers record every money movement as balanced entries, in the minor units this lesson stores

title: Long-Running Operations in APIs
objectives: Accept slow work with 202 Accepted and a status resource the client can poll
Keep polling cheap and retries safe with Retry-After, callbacks and idempotency keys
Support cancellation, failure states and expiry of operations and their results

cards.title: Hand back a ticket, not a held connection
cards.body: Generating a 2 GB export can take four minutes. Holding the HTTP request open that long fails in ordinary ways: proxies and load balancers close idle connections (60 seconds is a common default), mobile networks drop, and every waiting request holds a server connection. Instead, accept the work, queue it and reply 202 Accepted with a Location header such as /operations/op_81. The client polls that URL until the operation finishes, then fetches the result.

cards.title: Life of an operation
cards.body: The status resource is the record of where the work stands.
steps: POST /exports with an Idempotency-Key; reply 202 and Location: /operations/op_81
A worker picks it up: status moves from queued to running, with progress
The client polls the status URL, waiting as long as Retry-After says
Finished: status done with a link to the result, or failed with an error
The operation and its result expire after a stated time, such as 7 days

cards.title: Worked example: what polling costs
cards.body: 50,000 exports a day, each running about 4 minutes. If clients poll every second, that is 240 polls each, or 12M status requests a day for 50,000 jobs. Polling every 10 seconds cuts it to 1.2M. Backing off instead (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s, then every 30 s) needs only about a dozen polls per job, around 600,000 a day. Send Retry-After on each status reply so the server, not the client, sets the pace.

cards.title: Callbacks alongside the status URL
cards.body: A webhook on completion saves clients from polling at all, but webhooks get lost: the receiver is down, a firewall blocks it, or a retry gives up. Keep the status URL as the record and treat the callback as a hint that it is worth checking now. Sign callbacks so the receiver can tell they came from you, and include only the operation id, so a forged or replayed callback reveals nothing.

cards.title: Trap: a retried POST starts a second job
cards.body: The client’s POST times out before the 202 arrives, so it retries, and two exports run. Require an Idempotency-Key on the POST and return the same operation id for a repeat. Also plan for the unhappy endings: a cancel request moves the operation to cancelling and then cancelled, workers check for it between chunks, a worker that stops sending heartbeats gets its operation retried or marked failed, and done, failed and cancelled are final.

questions.prompt: An endpoint starts a report that takes about 3 minutes to build. What should the first response be?

choices.label: 200 OK, sent once the report finishes
202 Accepted with a status URL
201 Created with an empty report body
504 Gateway Timeout, asking for a retry

questions.explanation: a: the connection must stay open for 3 minutes, and proxies may close it first. b: correct, the work is accepted and the client gets somewhere to check on it. c: 201 says the resource exists now, which it does not. d: a 504 tells the client something failed, and a retry would start the work again.

questions.prompt: How should a server tell clients how often to poll an operation’s status?

choices.label: Close the connection when a client polls too soon
Reply 429 to every poll until the work is done
Document a fixed 1-second interval for all
Send a Retry-After header on each status reply

questions.explanation: a: closing connections looks like a network error and invites fast retries. b: 429 to well-behaved clients turns normal polling into errors. c: a fixed 1-second interval creates heavy load for long jobs. d: correct, the server can lengthen the wait for long jobs or under load.

questions.prompt: A status URL says “running” for hours because the worker crashed. What fixes this?

choices.label: Clients poll more often so they notice sooner
A heartbeat timeout that retries or marks it failed
The status endpoint returns 500 while a job runs
Status records are deleted after one hour

questions.explanation: a: polling faster just reads the same stale status more often. b: correct, a worker that stops heartbeating has its operation retried or moved to failed, so clients get a final state. c: a 500 tells the client the status service broke, not the job. d: deleting the record leaves the client with a 404 and no explanation.

questions.prompt: A POST /exports times out before the 202 arrives, and the client retries with the same Idempotency-Key. What should happen?

choices.label: A second export starts under a new id
The server replies 409 with no id
The server returns the same operation id
The first export is cancelled and restarted

questions.explanation: a: that is the duplicate the key exists to prevent. b: a 409 leaves the client unable to find the job it started. c: correct, the client gets the status URL of the export that is already running. d: restarting wastes the work already done.

questions.prompt: Why keep a status URL when you also send a completion webhook?

choices.label: Webhooks cannot carry the result’s location
Status URLs are needed to authenticate
Clients must poll before a webhook is sent
Webhooks can be lost; the URL is the record

questions.explanation: a: a webhook can carry a link, but it may never arrive. b: authentication is separate from how status is reported. c: clients that get webhooks need not poll at all on the happy path. d: correct, a client that missed the callback can still find out the result.

questions.prompt: Order a long-running export from the client’s side.

items.label: See status done with a result link
POST with an Idempotency-Key
Download the result before it expires
Poll, waiting as long as Retry-After says
Receive 202 and the status URL

questions.explanation: The key makes the first step safe to retry, and the expiry on the result is why the last step has a deadline.

questions.prompt: 30,000 operations a day each run about 5 minutes, and clients poll every 2 seconds. Roughly how many status polls is that per day?
assumptions: Each operation is polled from start to finish
questions.explanation: Design implication: a Retry-After of 30 s cuts this to 300,000 polls a day, and a completion webhook cuts it to almost none for clients that can receive one.

flashcards.back: 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing at a status resource.
Retry-After on each status reply, client backoff, and optional webhooks.
done (with a result link), failed (with an error) or cancelled.

mechanism.title: How an API runs work that outlasts a request
steps: The client sends the request with an Idempotency-Key. The server validates it, checks the key and stores a new operation record, with an id, a status of queued, the request parameters and an expiry time, in the same transaction that enqueues the job. It replies 202 Accepted, a Location header pointing at /operations/{id}, and a small body with the id and status. If the key was seen before, it returns the existing operation instead.

A worker takes the job, marks the operation running and updates progress as it goes, such as rows exported or a percentage. It sends heartbeats while it works. A supervisor looks for running operations whose heartbeat has stopped, then retries them if the work is idempotent or marks them failed with a reason, so no client polls a dead job forever.

Clients poll the status URL. Each reply says the status and carries a Retry-After header, short at first and longer for jobs known to be slow or when the system is busy. Clients back off between polls and stop at a final state. Clients that can receive webhooks register a callback URL and get a signed notification on completion, but the status resource remains the record they can always check.

The operation ends in one final state. done includes a link to the result, often a short-lived signed URL to a file in object storage. failed includes a machine-readable error code and a message. cancelled follows a cancel request: the API marks the operation cancelling, the worker checks for that between chunks, cleans up and marks it cancelled. A final state never changes again.

Operations and results do not live forever. The API documents how long they are kept, for example 7 days, after which the status URL returns 404 or 410 and the result file is deleted. A cleanup job enforces this. The documented limit lets clients plan, and it stops storage from growing without bound as millions of old exports pile up.

useWhen: Exports, reports, media processing and other work that takes more than a few seconds.
Requests whose duration varies widely and can exceed proxy timeouts.
avoidWhen: Avoid it for work that reliably finishes within about a second; a direct reply is simpler.
Avoid polling every second with no Retry-After; it creates load out of nothing.

numbers.title: Held connections versus a ticket
assumptions: Each export takes 240 s to build
steps: Synchronous: by Little’s law, concurrent requests = arrival rate × time = 1 × 240 = 240 connections held open.
Each held connection also needs a worker waiting on it, and any proxy with a 60 s idle timeout will cut them first.
Asynchronous: 1 × 0.05 s = 0.05 connections busy on average for the requests themselves.
The 240 builds still run, but on queue workers whose number you choose, not on request threads.
numbers.result: A ticket moves long work off the request path, where it no longer holds connections or depends on proxy timeouts.

india.title: Bank statements and tax data exports
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: Illustrative: an accounting app lets a firm download twelve months of transactions for all its clients ahead of the tax filing deadline. The export can take several minutes and many firms ask in the same week. The API returns 202 with a status URL, sends Retry-After of 15 seconds and then longer, and notifies the firm’s webhook when the file is ready. The result link expires after seven days, and a retried request with the same idempotency key returns the export already running instead of starting another.

pitfalls.trap: “We just raised the load balancer timeout to 10 minutes.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d return 202 with a status URL, so long work does not depend on any proxy timeout.”

pitfalls.trap: “The webhook tells them when it is done.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d keep a status URL as the record too, because callbacks can be lost.”

takeaways: Reply 202 with a status URL for work that outlasts a request.
Use Retry-After and backoff to keep polling cheap; add signed callbacks.
Require an idempotency key so a retried POST does not start a second job.
Define final states, heartbeats, cancellation and expiry.

interactive.title: A slow PDF behind a load balancer
interactive.prompt: An endpoint builds PDFs synchronously. Most take 20 s, but large ones take 90 s. The load balancer closes connections idle for 60 s. What do users with large PDFs see?

choices.label: A timeout error while the server keeps building the PDF
choices.feedback: Right: the load balancer gives up at 60 s, but the work continues and its result has nowhere to go.

choices.label: The PDF, just after a longer wait
choices.feedback: The connection is closed at 60 s, before the reply exists.

choices.label: A 202 response that the load balancer adds for them
choices.feedback: Load balancers do not convert slow requests into asynchronous ones.

interactive.reveal: The user gets an error, retries and starts a second 90-second build. Return 202 with a status URL, build in a worker, and the timeout stops mattering.

seeAlso.why: The work behind a 202 runs as a background job on a queue
Idempotency keys make the starting POST safe to retry
Completion callbacks are webhooks and should be signed and retried the same way
Account deletion across services is a long-running operation with a status

title: Testing a Service: Unit, Integration and Contract Tests
objectives: Match unit, integration, contract and end-to-end tests to the risks they catch
Test data access against a real database instead of a mock that agrees with you
Keep tests fast and repeatable by controlling time, randomness and shared state

cards.title: Match the test to the risk
cards.body: Unit tests check pure logic, such as a price or tax calculation, in milliseconds. Integration tests run your code against real dependencies, above all the database, and catch wrong SQL, missing migrations and violated constraints, in about a second each. Contract tests check that your API still gives each consumer the fields and types it relies on. End-to-end tests drive a whole user journey across services; they are slow and fail for unrelated reasons, so keep a few for the critical paths.

cards.title: Worked example: the bug a mock agreed with
cards.body: A sign-up handler relies on a unique constraint on email and turns the database’s unique-violation error into a 409. The unit test mocks the repository to “throw a duplicate error”, and passes. In production the driver reports the violation with a different error code from the one the handler checks, so users get a 500. Only a test against a real database, started fresh in a container and migrated with the real migrations, exercises the constraint and the actual error the driver returns.

cards.title: A consumer-driven contract test
cards.body: Each consumer states what it relies on; the provider checks it on every build.
steps: The consumer records the requests it sends and the response fields it reads
Those expectations are published as a contract file
The provider’s build replays each request against the real provider
A removed field or changed type fails the provider’s build, before release
Both sides deploy knowing they still agree

cards.title: Flaky tests come from hidden inputs
cards.body: A test that sometimes fails usually reads something it does not control: the clock, random numbers, test order, data left by another test, or a real network call. Pass in a clock the test can set, seed random generators, give each test its own data (a rolled-back transaction or unique ids), and wait for a condition rather than a fixed sleep. Flakiness adds up: 400 tests that each fail 0.5% of the time make 1 − 0.995⁴⁰⁰ ≈ 86% of runs go red.

cards.title: Trap: chasing coverage instead of risks
cards.body: 90% line coverage can still miss the concurrent double booking, the migration that locks a table, the timeout path and the retried request. Coverage shows which lines ran, not whether the failure cases were checked. List the ways the service can fail, such as a dependency timeout, a duplicate request, a partial write or a bad input, and write a test for each one.

questions.prompt: Which test best catches a wrong tax calculation for a cart?

choices.label: An end-to-end test run through the browser
A contract test against the payments API
A unit test of the price function
A load test at expected peak traffic

questions.explanation: a: it could catch it, slowly, and a failure would not say which part was wrong. b: a contract checks the shape of calls between services, not the arithmetic. c: correct, pure logic is best tested directly with many cases, including rounding edges. d: load tests measure capacity, not correctness.

questions.prompt: A test with a mocked database passes, but production returns 500 on duplicate sign-ups. What would have caught it?

choices.label: More unit tests around the mocked handler
A higher line-coverage threshold in CI
Running the same suite twice in a row
An integration test on a real database

questions.explanation: a: more tests against the same mock repeat the same wrong assumption. b: the lines already ran; coverage cannot see the wrong error mapping. c: a deterministic test passes twice just as easily. d: correct, a real database raises the real constraint error and exposes the mapping bug.

questions.prompt: A provider team renames a JSON field. With consumer-driven contract tests, what fails first?

choices.label: The provider’s own build
The consumer’s production traffic
The consumer’s unit tests
A nightly end-to-end run

questions.explanation: a: correct, the provider replays each consumer’s expectations and the missing field fails its build before release. b: that is what happens without contracts. c: the consumer’s tests use its own stub of the provider, which still has the old field. d: an end-to-end run might notice later, if it covers that field.

questions.prompt: A test checks that a token “expires in 1 hour” and fails a few times a week, always near midnight. What is the right fix?

choices.label: Retry the test up to three times in CI
Inject a clock the test can control
Raise the test’s timeout to one hour
Run the suite only during working hours

questions.explanation: a: retries hide the flakiness and the bug it may point to. b: correct, the code reads time from a clock the test sets, so the result no longer depends on when it runs. c: the failure is about dates, not slowness. d: avoiding midnight hides a real date-boundary bug that users will hit.

questions.prompt: Tests pass one at a time but fail when the suite runs in random order. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The CI machine has too little memory
A race inside the test framework itself
Shared state left behind by another test
The database is too slow under parallel load

questions.explanation: a: memory pressure fails tests regardless of order. b: possible but rare; suspect your own tests first. c: correct, one test leaves data or settings that another depends on or trips over; isolate each test’s data. d: slowness causes timeouts, which do not depend on order.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an isolated database integration test.

items.label: Begin a transaction for this test
Roll back so the next test starts clean
Start a fresh database, for example in a container
Run the code and check the rows it wrote
Apply the real migrations

questions.explanation: Real migrations prove the schema, and the rollback gives every test the same starting point without rebuilding the database.

questions.prompt: A suite has 300 tests and each fails at random 0.2% of the time, independently. Roughly what percent of runs fail at least once?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: nearly half the runs go red with no real bug, so people stop trusting the suite; each flaky test is worth fixing.

flashcards.front: What does an integration test catch that a unit test misses?
flashcards.back: Wrong SQL, missing migrations and real constraint errors from the actual database.
Consumers publish what they rely on; the provider’s build checks it before release.
Time, randomness, test order, shared data and real network calls.

sources.title: Martin Fowler: The Practical Test Pyramid
Martin Fowler: Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests

mechanism.title: How a backend test suite is put together
steps: Start from risks, not layers. List what can go wrong: business rules computed wrongly, queries that return the wrong rows, a migration that breaks old data, an API change that breaks a consumer, a dependency that times out, a request that is retried. Each risk points at the cheapest kind of test that can catch it, and that kind is the one to write.

Pure logic gets unit tests: functions that take values and return values, with no database or network. Keep business rules in such functions where you can, because they can then be tested with hundreds of cases, including rounding edges and empty inputs, in well under a second. Mocks belong at the boundary of this code, and only for things that are slow or outside your control.

Data access gets integration tests against the real database engine, the same version as production, started fresh for the test run, often in a container, and built with the real migrations. Each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back, or uses its own unique ids, so tests do not see each other’s data. These tests catch the bugs mocks cannot: SQL errors, constraint errors, wrong isolation assumptions and slow queries.

Service boundaries get contract tests. Each consumer records the requests it makes and the parts of the response it reads; the provider’s pipeline replays them on every build. A provider can then remove a field nobody reads without fear, and is stopped from removing one that someone does. A small number of end-to-end tests cover the journeys that would cost the most to break, such as sign-up and checkout.

Everything runs on every change, so speed and determinism matter. Time, randomness and identifiers are passed in so tests can fix them. Waits poll for a condition with a timeout instead of sleeping. Tests that turn out to be flaky are quarantined and fixed quickly, because a suite that fails at random teaches people to ignore red builds, and then real failures get ignored too.

useWhen: Any service that will be changed by more than one person over time.
Services with consumers in other teams, where contracts prevent surprise breakage.
avoidWhen: Avoid mocking the database to test queries; the mock agrees with whatever you assumed.
Avoid a large end-to-end suite as the main safety net; it is slow and fails for unrelated reasons.

numbers.title: A CI budget of 10 minutes
assumptions: 2,000 unit tests at about 5 ms each
200 integration tests at about 300 ms each
20 end-to-end tests at about 30 s each
steps: Integration: 200 × 0.3 s = 60 s.
End-to-end: 20 × 30 s = 600 s, ten times the other two combined.
