A join key needs a foreign key and a typed index. Totals used in reports need a numeric type. A status with allowed values needs a constraint, which a typed column gives you directly.

questions.prompt: A service must keep each webhook body unchanged so it can verify the sender’s signature later. Which PostgreSQL type fits?

choices.label: jsonb, because it is the faster type
json or text, which keep the original text
jsonb with a GIN index on the body
A typed column for each field in the body

questions.explanation: A signature covers the exact bytes. json and text keep whitespace, key order and duplicates as received. jsonb normalises the document, so re-serialising it gives different bytes and the signature check fails; an index does not change that. Splitting into columns loses the original text too. A jsonb copy can sit alongside for querying.

questions.prompt: WHERE attrs @> '{"brand": "Acme"}' scans 5 million rows of a jsonb column. Which index serves it?

choices.label: A B-tree index on the whole attrs column
A hash index on attrs
A GIN index on attrs
An expression index on (attrs->>'colour')

questions.explanation: GIN indexes the keys and values inside each document, which is what containment needs. A B-tree or hash index on the whole value helps only when matching the entire document. An expression index on colour serves queries on colour, not brand.

questions.prompt: WHERE data->>'qty' > '5' returns orders with qty 7 but not qty 12. Why?

choices.label: ->> returns text, so the values compare as strings
JSON numbers above 9 are stored as floating point
The GIN index skips numbers with two digits
qty 12 rows were written before the index existed

questions.explanation: As text, '12' sorts before '5' because '1' < '5'. Cast with (data->>'qty')::int > 5. JSON numbers are not converted to floats at 10. GIN does not serve this text comparison at all, and an index never changes which rows match, only how they are found.

questions.prompt: A 100 KB jsonb document holds a counter that is updated 50 times a second, and each update rewrites the whole document. About how many GB a day are rewritten, before compression?
questions.formula: document size × updates per second × seconds per day
questions.explanation: Design implication: moving the counter to its own column or row cuts this to a few bytes per update. 5 is the per-second figure in MB, and 43.2 drops a factor of ten.

questions.prompt: Lookups filter on attrs->>'sku_ref' = $1 and then sort by that same key. Which index fits best?

choices.label: A GIN index on the whole attrs document
A B-tree expression index on (attrs->>'sku_ref')
A hash index on the attrs column as a whole
A block-range index on attrs, which stays very small

questions.explanation: An expression B-tree stores one extracted value per row, serves equality and can return rows in key order. GIN serves containment and key-existence across all keys, is larger, and cannot provide ordering. A hash index on the whole document matches only identical documents. Block-range indexes suit values that follow physical row order, which JSON keys rarely do.

questions.prompt: A payments service stores events from 12 payment providers. Each has its own fields, but every event has an amount, currency, status and merchant.

approaches.label: All JSON
approaches.description: One jsonb column per event, nothing else

approaches.label: Hybrid
approaches.description: Typed columns for amount, currency, status and merchant; jsonb for the rest

approaches.label: All columns
approaches.description: A column for every field any provider has ever sent

rationaleOptions.label: Typed shared fields get constraints, foreign keys and exact sums
Putting everything in JSON makes reports just as fast
New provider fields land in JSON without a migration
A column per field keeps the schema complete and simple

rationaleConflicts.r3: Hundreds of mostly-null columns and a migration for every new provider field are neither simple nor complete for long.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Reports must extract and cast every value from JSON, and nothing enforces types or allowed values on them.

questions.explanation: Give the fields you report and enforce on real columns, and let JSON absorb the parts that vary.

flashcards.back: Variable, read-together data; not join keys, totals or constrained fields
jsonb: parsed, indexable, normalised; json: original text, reparsed each use
Cast before numeric or date comparisons
Rewrites the whole document; keep hot fields in columns

mechanism.title: How a database stores and searches JSON
steps: On insert the document is validated. PostgreSQL json keeps the text; jsonb and MySQL JSON parse it into a binary form with keys and values that can be found without reparsing.
Path operators read inside the document: ->, ->> and #> in PostgreSQL, ->, ->> and JSON_EXTRACT in MySQL. Extracted values are JSON or text until cast.

Indexes work on what you extract or on the document as a whole. An expression index stores one extracted value per row, like any B-tree. A GIN index stores every key and value as separate entries pointing to the rows that contain them.
Large documents are compressed and stored out of line. Reading one key still loads the whole value, and changing one key usually writes a whole new copy.
Nothing checks the shape of the document unless you add rules: CHECK constraints on extracted values, JSON schema validation in MySQL, or checks in the application.

Statistics are thinner inside documents. The planner knows a lot about a typed column but little about a key buried in JSON, so estimates for filters on JSON keys are rougher; an expression index or a generated column gives the planner statistics on that key too.

useWhen: Attributes that vary by row and are read with it
Keeping an external payload as received
Prototyping a field before it earns a real column
Sparse optional settings
avoidWhen: Join keys and foreign keys
Fields in reports, sums and constraints
Counters and fields that change many times a second
Data that every query reads key by key

numbers.title: The cost of a hot counter inside a document
assumptions: Illustrative; before compression and log overhead
steps: Per second: 100,000 bytes × 50 = 5 MB.
Per day: 5 MB × 86,400 ≈ 432 GB written as new row versions.
Moved to an 8-byte column: 8 × 50 × 86,400 ≈ 35 MB a day of changed values, plus fixed per-row overhead.
Old versions must also be cleaned up, which adds more work for the larger design.
numbers.result: Hot fields belong outside large documents; the saving here is roughly ten-thousand-fold in changed bytes.

india.title: PostgreSQL JSON documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual explains that json stores an exact copy of the input text that processing functions must reparse, while jsonb is stored in a decomposed binary format that is slightly slower to input but significantly faster to process and supports indexing. It also notes that jsonb does not preserve whitespace, key order or duplicate keys, keeping the last value when keys repeat.

pitfalls.trap: Putting join keys in JSON
pitfalls.say: Promote them to typed columns with foreign keys

pitfalls.trap: Comparing ->> results without casting
pitfalls.say: Cast to the right type, or the comparison is textual

pitfalls.trap: A GIN index for a one-key equality lookup
pitfalls.say: An expression B-tree is smaller and supports ordering

takeaways: Hybrid design: typed columns for the core, JSON for what varies
jsonb for querying; json or text only to keep the original bytes
Index what you query: GIN for containment, expression indexes for one key
Cast extracted values, and keep fast-changing fields out of documents

interactive.title: Duplicate keys in jsonb
interactive.prompt: The text {"plan": "basic", "plan": "pro"} is inserted into a PostgreSQL jsonb column. What is read back?

choices.label: {"plan": "basic", "plan": "pro"}
choices.feedback: That is what json (not jsonb) would return, keeping the input text.

choices.label: {"plan": "basic"}
choices.feedback: jsonb keeps the last value for a repeated key, not the first.

choices.label: {"plan": "pro"}
choices.feedback: Right: jsonb keeps only the last value for a duplicate key.

interactive.reveal: jsonb normalises documents: duplicate keys collapse to the last one, whitespace and key order are not kept. If exact input matters, store it as json or text.

seeAlso.why: GIN and other inverted indexes, which jsonb containment queries use
Document databases, the NoSQL family built around JSON-like records
Evolving JSON payload schemas without breaking readers

title: Stack, Heap and Memory Allocation
objectives: Say what lives on a thread’s stack and what lives on the heap
Explain what an allocator does between your program and the kernel
Recognise fragmentation and choose arenas or pools for short-lived objects

cards.title: Two places a value can live
cards.body: Each thread has a stack: a contiguous region where every function call pushes a frame holding its locals and return address, and every return pops it. Allocating there is just moving a pointer, and it is freed automatically on return, but the size is fixed when the thread starts (commonly 1 to 8 MB, depending on the platform and settings). The heap is shared by all threads and holds data of any size whose lifetime is not tied to one call; an allocator has to find space for it and take it back later.

cards.title: Worked example: how deep can recursion go?
cards.body: A recursive walk is fine on a balanced tree and crashes on a degenerate one.
steps: Assume an 8 MB stack (8,388,608 bytes) and 200-byte frames (illustrative)
Frames that fit: 8,388,608 ÷ 200 ≈ 41,900 nested calls
A balanced tree of 1 million nodes is about 20 levels deep: 20 frames, no problem
A degenerate tree (a linked list in disguise) of 1 million nodes needs 1 million frames, about 200 MB: the thread runs into the guard page below its stack and the process gets a segmentation fault
Fix: replace recursion with a loop and an explicit stack stored on the heap, which can grow to any size

cards.title: What sits between malloc and the kernel
cards.body: An allocator asks the kernel for large regions (by moving the program break or mapping pages) and carves them into blocks. Most allocators round small requests up to a size class, keep free lists per class, and give each thread a small cache so common allocations need no lock. Very large requests are usually mapped directly and handed back to the kernel when freed; small freed blocks normally stay inside the process for reuse.

cards.title: Misconception: freeing memory shrinks the process
cards.body: After a program frees most of its objects, its resident memory often stays near the peak. The allocator keeps freed small blocks for the next request, and it can only return a page to the kernel when every block on it is free. Resident size is therefore a high-water mark shaped by the allocator, not a live count of the data in use.

cards.title: Trap: fragmentation in a process that runs for weeks
cards.body: When objects of many sizes and lifetimes are mixed, freed blocks leave holes between long-lived ones. Total free space can be large while no single hole fits the next request, so the allocator asks the kernel for more and resident memory creeps up with no leak in the code. Group objects that die together in an arena or pool, reuse buffers of fixed sizes, and compare live data with resident memory before hunting for a leak.

questions.prompt: A function fills a local array and returns a pointer to it. Callers sometimes see garbage. Why?

choices.label: The heap allocator frees local arrays as the function exits
The array was in the returned function’s frame, which later calls reuse
The kernel unmaps that stack page as soon as the call returns
Local arrays become read-only once their function has returned

questions.explanation: Locals live in the function’s stack frame; after the return that memory is reused by the next call, so the pointer now aims at whatever is written there. The heap allocator never manages locals, the kernel does not unmap stack pages on every return (the stack region stays mapped), and nothing makes the memory read-only. Return a heap allocation or let the caller pass in the buffer.

questions.prompt: A batch job frees 2 GB of small objects at the end of each run, yet its resident memory stays near the 2.5 GB peak. What is the usual reason?

choices.label: Freed blocks stay in the allocator for reuse
Freed pages move into the page cache but stay counted as the process’s
The kernel zeroes freed pages slowly, a batch at a time
The stack keeps a copy of every object the job allocated

questions.explanation: Allocators keep small freed blocks in their free lists and can return a page only when all of it is free, so resident memory behaves like a high-water mark. Heap pages do not turn into page cache, zeroing is not what holds them, and stacks hold frames, not copies of heap objects.

questions.prompt: Live data stays at 1 GB, but over a week resident memory climbs from 1.2 GB to 3 GB. Heap profiles show no growing object type. Which explanation fits?

choices.label: The main thread’s stack grows a little with each request
Log files read by the process count as its resident heap
Freed holes are too small or scattered to reuse
The translation buffer keeps more entries as uptime grows

questions.explanation: Fragmentation grows resident memory without growing live data: free space exists but in pieces that do not fit new requests. Stacks are fixed-size and reused, cached file pages are not part of the heap, and the TLB is a small fixed-size CPU cache that has nothing to do with resident memory.

questions.prompt: A recursive tree walk works on balanced trees but crashes with a segmentation fault on a 1-million-node degenerate tree. What is the robust fix?

choices.label: Catch the fault and retry the walk on a fresh thread
Split the walk across more threads running at once
Raise the heap size limit for the process
Use a loop with an explicit stack kept on the heap

questions.explanation: The crash is stack exhaustion: one frame per level, a million levels. A heap-allocated work stack grows as needed. Retrying overflows again, more threads each have their own small stack and the walk is still deep, and the heap limit does not affect the thread’s stack size. Raising the stack size also works but only moves the limit.

questions.prompt: A thread’s stack is 1 MB (1,048,576 bytes) and each recursive call uses a 256-byte frame. About how many nested calls fit?
assumptions: The whole stack is available for these frames
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a few thousand levels is plenty for balanced structures (a billion-node balanced tree is about 30 deep) but not for input-shaped recursion such as a long linked list or deeply nested JSON from users.

questions.prompt: Order what a typical allocator does for a small allocation, from the cheapest path to the most expensive.

items.label: If the cache is empty, refill it from the shared free lists under a lock
Round the size up to its size class
If those are empty too, ask the kernel for more pages
Take a free block from this thread’s cache for that class

questions.explanation: Size class, then the lock-free thread cache, then the shared lists, then a system call; most allocations stop at the second step.

flashcards.back: Stack: per thread, frames freed on return, fixed size. Heap: shared, any size and lifetime, managed by an allocator.

flashcards.front: Why doesn’t resident memory drop after free?
flashcards.back: Allocators keep freed blocks for reuse and can return a page only when all of it is free.
Free memory split into holes that do not fit new requests, so the process grows without a leak.

mechanism.title: How memory is handed out inside a process
steps: A thread’s stack is reserved when the thread starts. The main thread’s size usually comes from a resource limit (RLIMIT_STACK, often 8 MB on Linux); other threads get a size chosen by the thread library or the caller. An unmapped guard page sits below it, so running off the end faults immediately instead of silently overwriting other memory.

Each call pushes a frame with arguments that do not fit in registers, saved registers, locals and the return address. Allocation and freeing are a single pointer adjustment, which is why stack data is effectively free, and why it cannot outlive the call that created it.

The heap is managed by an allocator library in user space. It obtains memory from the kernel in large chunks, splits it into size classes (for example 16, 32, 48 bytes and up), and keeps free lists for each. Per-thread caches serve most requests without locks; only refills and returns touch shared structures.

Large blocks follow a different path: above a threshold (128 KB by default in the GNU C library, adjusted dynamically) allocations are mapped directly from the kernel and unmapped on free, so they return memory at once. Small blocks are carved out of shared regions and return memory only when whole pages or the top of the heap become free.

Fragmentation is the gap between the memory a process holds and the memory its live objects need. External fragmentation is free space split into unusable holes; internal fragmentation is space wasted by rounding a request up to its size class, such as a 33-byte request in a 48-byte class.

Arenas (also called regions or bump allocators) serve a group of objects that die together, such as everything built while handling one request: allocation is a pointer bump and the whole arena is reset at once. Pools of fixed-size objects avoid fragmentation for one hot type. Garbage-collected runtimes solve the same problem differently, often by moving live objects together.

useWhen: Use the stack for small, call-scoped data and the heap for anything large or longer-lived.
Use arenas or pools when many objects share a lifetime or a size.
avoidWhen: Avoid recursion whose depth is set by user input.
Avoid reading resident memory alone as proof of a leak; compare it with live data.

rows: Nothing inside can outlive the arena
One size per pool; idle memory stays reserved

numbers.title: What a per-request arena saves
assumptions: 10,000 requests a second, each making 2,000 small allocations that all die when the request ends (illustrative)
About 50 ns per malloc and free pair on a general-purpose allocator and about 2 ns per arena bump (illustrative orders of magnitude)
steps: Allocations: 10,000 × 2,000 = 20 million a second.
General allocator: 20,000,000 × 50 ns = 1.0 CPU-second per second, a whole core spent on allocation.
Arena: 20,000,000 × 2 ns = 0.04 CPU-seconds per second, plus one reset per request.
Freeing is free with the arena, and because each request reuses the same memory, fragmentation from these objects disappears.
numbers.result: For short-lived, same-lifetime objects an arena turns about one core of allocator work into about 4% of a core; measure your own allocator before assuming the gap.

india.title: How one C library returns memory to the kernel
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The mallopt(3) manual page documents the GNU C library allocator’s thresholds. Requests at or above M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KB by default, adjusted dynamically) are served with mmap, which the page notes has the advantage that such blocks can always be released back to the system independently. Smaller blocks come from the heap, which is trimmed only from its top when more than M_TRIM_THRESHOLD bytes are free there, which is why a few long-lived small objects can pin a large heap in place.

pitfalls.trap: “Memory didn’t drop after we freed everything, so we have a leak.”
pitfalls.say: “Allocators keep freed blocks; I’d compare live heap size with resident memory to tell a leak from fragmentation.”

pitfalls.trap: “Recursion is fine, the stack is huge.”
pitfalls.say: “It is a few MB per thread; if input controls the depth I’d use an explicit heap-allocated stack.”

takeaways: Stacks are per thread, fixed in size and freed on return.
Allocators keep freed small blocks, so resident memory is a high-water mark.
Fragmentation grows a process without a leak.
Arenas and pools make same-lifetime or same-size objects cheap.

interactive.title: Speed up an allocation-heavy parser
interactive.prompt: A service parses each 50 KB request body into thousands of tiny objects and drops them all when the response is sent. A profile shows 30% of CPU inside malloc and free. Which change removes the most of that cost?

choices.label: Allocate the request’s objects from a per-request arena and reset it after the response
choices.feedback: Right: allocation becomes a pointer bump and freeing is one reset for the whole request.

choices.label: Give every worker thread a larger stack
choices.feedback: The objects live on the heap; stack size does not change what malloc costs.

choices.label: Add more worker threads so allocation runs in parallel
choices.feedback: More threads multiply the allocator work and can add contention on shared free lists.

interactive.reveal: Objects that are born and die together are the ideal case for an arena: no per-object free, no fragmentation, and allocation cost close to zero. The catch is discipline: nothing built in the arena may be kept after the reset.

seeAlso.why: Virtual memory explains where heap and stack pages physically come from
Garbage collectors solve the same freeing problem automatically
Memory leaks in long-lived pages: when reachable objects never die

title: Garbage Collection: Throughput, Pauses and Heap Size
objectives: Explain how a tracing collector decides what is garbage
Relate allocation rate, live data and heap size to how often collections run
Choose between throughput and pause time, and read a pause’s effect on tail latency

cards.title: Reachable means alive
cards.body: A tracing garbage collector starts from roots (thread stacks, registers and globals), follows every reference it finds, and marks what it reaches. Anything unmarked can never be used again, so its memory is reclaimed. The program never calls free; the price is that the collector must periodically do this work, and at some points it must stop or coordinate with the program’s threads to get a consistent picture.

cards.title: Why most collectors split the heap by age
cards.body: In typical programs most objects die young: request buffers, temporary strings, iterators. A generational collector allocates into a small young area and collects it often; survivors are copied into an older area that is collected rarely. Copying only the few survivors is cheap, so young collections cost roughly in proportion to live data, not to garbage.

cards.title: Worked example: heap size sets the collection rate
cards.body: Headroom above live data is what the allocator can fill before the next collection.
steps: A service allocates 500 MB/s and keeps 1 GB of live data (illustrative)
With a 2 GB heap the headroom is 1 GB: a collection every 1 GB ÷ 500 MB/s = 2 s
With a 4 GB heap the headroom is 3 GB: a collection every 6 s, three times less often
Each collection still has to trace about the same 1 GB of live data, so total GC work per second falls about threefold
Below about 1.2 GB the headroom approaches zero and the process collects almost continuously, then fails with out-of-memory

cards.title: Trap: a heap limit larger than the container
cards.body: A runtime that sizes its heap from the machine’s memory, or a heap flag copied from a bigger host, can let the heap grow past the container’s memory limit. The collector sees plenty of room and defers work, then the kernel kills the process for exceeding its cgroup limit, with no out-of-memory error from the runtime at all. Set the heap limit below the container limit, leaving room for thread stacks, native buffers and the runtime itself.

cards.title: Misconception: a concurrent collector has no cost
cards.body: Concurrent collectors do most marking while the program runs, so pauses shrink to milliseconds. The work does not vanish: they spend CPU on background threads, add small checks (barriers) to reference writes or reads, and need extra headroom because the program keeps allocating during a cycle. If allocation outruns the collector, it falls back to a long stop-the-world collection.

questions.prompt: Objects X and Y point at each other, and no stack frame or global variable refers to either. Under a tracing collector, what happens to the pair?

choices.label: Keeps both, since each still has a reference count of one
Frees both, because neither can be reached from a root
Frees one and keeps the other to preserve a single reference
Moves both into the old generation for a later decision

questions.explanation: Tracing works from roots, so a cycle that no root reaches is garbage no matter how its members point at each other. Keeping them because of a nonzero count is how plain reference counting behaves, which is exactly why it leaks cycles. Freeing only one is not a rule any collector uses, and promotion depends on surviving collections, not on cycles.

questions.prompt: Why is a young-generation collection usually fast even when the young area was full of objects?

choices.label: Young objects are smaller, so tracing each one costs less
The young area is collected only when the program is idle
Its cost tracks the few survivors, not the dead objects
Young collections skip the roots and scan the heap linearly

questions.explanation: A copying young collection touches only what is still alive; dead objects are reclaimed by reusing the whole area. Object size matters little, collections run when the young area fills rather than when idle, and roots are always where tracing begins.

questions.prompt: A service collects every 0.5 seconds and spends 25% of CPU in the collector. Live data is steady at 1.8 GB in a 2 GB heap. What is the best first step?

choices.label: Raise the heap limit to give real headroom above live data
Call the collector by hand after every request
Add more collector threads and keep the heap size
Lower the young area so each collection has less to do

questions.explanation: With 0.2 GB of headroom the program fills it almost immediately, so collections run back to back, each tracing 1.8 GB. More headroom spaces them out. Collecting by hand adds collections, more threads spread the same excess work, and a smaller young area makes collections even more frequent.

questions.prompt: A service has a 150 ms p99 target. The collector pauses for 300 ms about every 10 seconds, and requests take 20 ms otherwise. Which effect should you expect?

choices.label: No effect on p99, since pauses are rare compared with requests
Only the request running during the pause is slowed
About 3% of requests are delayed, so p99 breaks the target
The p50 rises to about 300 ms while the p99 stays fine

questions.explanation: About 3% of requests (300 ms out of every 10 s) arrive during a pause, and their extra waits spread evenly from 0 to 300 ms. The slowest 1% of all traffic is the worst third of that group, which waits more than 200 ms, so p99 is about 220 ms and breaks the 150 ms target. Every request in flight or arriving is delayed, not just one, and the median is unaffected because 97% of requests miss the pause.

questions.prompt: A service allocates 400 MB/s, live data is 1.2 GB, and the heap limit is 3.2 GB. Roughly how many seconds pass between collections?
assumptions: Collections start when the heap is full
questions.explanation: Design implication: only the headroom above live data buys time, so doubling a heap that is mostly live data can multiply the interval many times over, while the same doubling on a mostly empty heap barely matters.

questions.prompt: Choose a collector setup for a payments API.
constraints: 16 GB heap with 6 GB of live data
Spare CPU of about 20% on each node

approaches.label: A low-pause concurrent collector
approaches.description: Marks while the program runs; pauses of a few milliseconds

approaches.label: A throughput collector
approaches.description: Stops the program for each collection; least total CPU spent

approaches.label: Disable collection and restart nodes nightly
approaches.description: Avoids all collections until memory runs out

rationaleOptions.label: Pauses must stay well below the 50 ms target
The spare CPU can pay for background marking and barriers
Throughput collectors use the least CPU, so they are best here
Restarts remove the need for headroom

rationaleConflicts.r3: Least CPU matters less than pauses that can exceed 50 ms when tracing a large heap stop-the-world.
rationaleConflicts.r4: At normal allocation rates 16 GB fills in minutes, not a day, so the process would run out long before the restart.

questions.explanation: The binding constraint is tail latency, and the node has CPU to spare, so trading CPU for short pauses is the right exchange. A throughput collector is the right choice for batch jobs where only total time counts.

flashcards.front: What does a tracing GC keep?
flashcards.back: Everything reachable from roots (stacks, registers, globals); the rest is garbage, cycles included.
(heap limit − live data) ÷ allocation rate.
Throughput: least CPU, longer stop-the-world pauses. Low-pause: short pauses, more CPU and headroom.

sources.title: Fundamentals of garbage collection (.NET), Microsoft Learn
HotSpot Virtual Machine Garbage Collection Tuning Guide, Oracle

mechanism.title: What a collector does during one cycle
steps: Allocation is a pointer bump in a thread-local buffer inside the young area, so creating an object is about as cheap as using a stack. When the young area fills, a young collection is triggered.

The collector finds roots: references held in every thread’s stack frames and registers and in global variables. To read thread stacks consistently, threads are brought to safe points, which is the part of a pause that grows with the number of threads.

Marking follows references from the roots. References from old objects into the young area are tracked by a write barrier (a small check on each reference store), so a young collection does not need to scan the whole old area.

Survivors are copied into a survivor area or promoted to the old generation after surviving several collections, and the young area is reused from empty. Its cost depends on survivors, which is why short-lived garbage is nearly free.

Old-generation collections are rarer and larger. Concurrent collectors mark the old area while the program runs and compact it piece by piece; throughput collectors stop all threads and do it in parallel, which finishes sooner but pauses longer.
If the program allocates faster than a concurrent cycle can reclaim, or headroom runs out, the collector falls back to a full stop-the-world collection, often the longest pause the service ever sees.

useWhen: Use a throughput collector for batch jobs where only total run time matters.
Use a low-pause collector when tail latency has a target and the node has CPU to spare.
avoidWhen: Avoid running with the heap barely above live data; collections become constant.
Avoid heap limits at or above the container memory limit.

rows: Short young pauses, rare longer ones
Tight latency targets on large heaps
None, but cascading frees can stall
Deterministic cleanup; cycles need extra handling

numbers.title: How heap size changes GC cost
assumptions: Allocation of 1.2 GB/s, 1.5 GB of live data (illustrative)
Each collection costs about the same because it traces the same live data
steps: 2 GB heap: headroom 0.5 GB, so a collection every 0.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 0.42 s, about 2.4 a second.
4 GB heap: headroom 2.5 GB, so a collection every 2.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 2.1 s, about 0.48 a second.
Ratio: 2.4 ÷ 0.48 = 5 times fewer collections for twice the memory.
If one collection costs 100 ms of CPU, GC drops from about 240 ms to about 48 ms of CPU per second.
numbers.result: Doubling the heap here cuts collector CPU about fivefold because headroom grows from 0.5 GB to 2.5 GB; memory is the cheapest GC tuning knob when live data is close to the limit.

india.title: Generations in a managed runtime
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Microsoft’s documentation for the .NET garbage collector describes three generations. Generation 0 holds short-lived objects such as temporary variables and is collected most frequently; objects that survive move to generation 1, a buffer between short- and long-lived objects, and then to generation 2 for long-lived data. Because a collection can release memory in one generation rather than across the whole managed heap, most collections stay small and fast, which is the same idea used by most generational collectors.

pitfalls.trap: “We have GC pauses, so let’s call the collector manually.”
pitfalls.say: “Manual collections add work; I’d first check headroom above live data and the allocation rate.”

pitfalls.trap: “Average latency is fine, so GC isn’t a problem.”
pitfalls.say: “Pauses hit a small share of requests, so I’d check p99 and pause logs, not the average.”

takeaways: Reachable from roots means alive; cycles are collected.
Time between collections is headroom divided by allocation rate.
Pauses hurt the tail, not the average.
Keep the heap limit below the container limit.

interactive.title: Spend memory or CPU?
interactive.prompt: Live data is 1.5 GB in a 2 GB heap and the service allocates 1.2 GB/s. You can raise the heap to 4 GB. How does the number of collections change?

choices.label: About 5 times fewer collections
choices.feedback: Right: headroom grows from 0.5 GB to 2.5 GB, so the interval grows fivefold.

choices.label: About 2 times fewer, matching the heap
choices.feedback: The heap doubles, but only the space above live data buys time, and that grows fivefold.

choices.label: About the same, since live data has not changed
choices.feedback: Live data sets the cost of each collection, not how often they happen.

interactive.reveal: Interval = (heap − live) ÷ allocation rate: 0.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 0.42 s before and 2.5 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 2.1 s after. Each collection traces the same 1.5 GB, so total collector CPU falls by about the same factor.

seeAlso.why: Manual allocation and fragmentation are the problem a collector automates
Container memory limits decide how big the heap may safely be
Pauses show up as p99 misses against a latency SLO

title: CPU Caches, Locality and False Sharing
objectives: Explain why memory access patterns can change speed tenfold or more
Estimate the cost of cache misses from rough latencies
Spot and fix false sharing between threads

cards.title: Memory moves in 64-byte lines
cards.body: The CPU never reads a single byte from main memory; it fetches a whole cache line, 64 bytes on most current processors, into a hierarchy of caches. A hit in the smallest cache takes around a nanosecond, while a trip to main memory takes on the order of 100 ns (rough figures that vary by machine). Programs are fast when the next data they need is already in a line they fetched, and slow when each access lands somewhere new.

cards.title: Worked example: an array against a linked list
cards.body: Same 10 million values, same sum, very different memory traffic.
steps: 10 million 4-byte integers in an array occupy 40 MB in consecutive lines
The hardware prefetcher sees the sequential pattern and streams lines ahead: at about 10 GB/s the sum takes about 4 ms
The same values in a linked list whose nodes are scattered across the heap cost roughly one cache miss per node
10,000,000 misses × about 80 ns ≈ 0.8 s, around 200 times slower for the same arithmetic
Lesson: contiguous layouts and predictable access often matter more than the operation count (all latencies illustrative)

cards.title: Keeping lines coherent across cores
cards.body: Each core has its own small caches, so when one core writes a line, copies held by other cores must be invalidated before the write completes. The hardware does this automatically, which keeps memory consistent, but every write to a line another core is using turns into traffic between cores. Data written by one thread and read by many is cheap only if writes are rare.

cards.title: Trap: false sharing between per-thread counters
cards.body: Eight threads each increment their own counter, and the counters sit next to each other in an array. There is no shared variable in the code, yet the program scales worse than a single thread, because all eight counters share one 64-byte line and every increment steals that line from the other cores. Pad or align each hot per-thread value to its own line, or keep it in a local variable and combine at the end.

cards.title: Misconception: fewer instructions always run faster
cards.body: An algorithm that does fewer operations but jumps around memory can lose to one that does more work on contiguous data. Binary search over a sorted array of a few thousand keys often beats a tree with the same keys, and scanning a small array can beat a hash lookup. Compare candidates by memory accesses and measure on realistic sizes before trusting the operation count.

questions.prompt: A loop reads one byte, skips 63, reads the next byte, and so on through a large buffer. Compared with reading every byte, roughly how much memory traffic does it cause?

choices.label: One sixty-fourth of the traffic, matching the bytes it reads
Half the traffic, because the prefetcher skips alternate lines
About the same traffic, since each read pulls a full line
Twice the traffic, because each skipped line is fetched twice

questions.explanation: Memory moves in 64-byte lines, so touching one byte per line still fetches every line: the bytes skipped were transferred anyway. Traffic would drop to a sixty-fourth only if bytes moved individually, prefetchers fetch more lines rather than fewer, and nothing fetches a line twice in a single forward pass.

questions.prompt: Eight threads each increment a separate counter in an array of eight 8-byte longs. Throughput drops as threads are added. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The counters share one cache line, so cores keep stealing it
Separate counters need a lock, and the threads wait on it
Eight threads exceed what the scheduler can run on eight cores
Integer increments are slow when several cores run them together

questions.explanation: Eight 8-byte counters fill exactly one 64-byte line, so each write invalidates the line in seven other caches. No lock is involved because the variables are distinct, eight threads on eight cores is a normal fit, and an increment on a line the core already owns is fast.

questions.prompt: A two-dimensional grid is stored row by row. A loop sums it column by column, with the column as its outer loop. What usually speeds it up the most?

choices.label: Using a smaller integer type for the loop counters
Running the column loop on several threads
Swapping the loops so the row index changes slowest
Storing the grid as one row array per thread instead

questions.explanation: Walking a row-major grid column by column jumps a full row between accesses, so nearly every read is a new line. Swapping the loops makes accesses sequential and lets the prefetcher stream lines. Counter types barely matter, threads multiply the same miss pattern, and per-thread row arrays do not fix the access order.

questions.prompt: A configuration object is read by every request on 32 cores and rewritten once a minute. A hit counter beside it is written by every request. Which change helps the most?

choices.label: Copy the configuration into each thread on every request
Make the configuration read-only and reload it in place
Put a lock around reads of the configuration object
Move the hit counter to its own line or make it per-core

questions.explanation: Reads of a line that nobody writes are cheap on every core; the problem is the counter, whose constant writes invalidate the line holding the configuration too. Copying on every request adds work, the configuration is already effectively read-only, and a lock adds a contended write on every read.

questions.prompt: A lookup does 5 million random accesses into a 4 GB table, and each one misses every cache and costs about 100 ns. Roughly how many milliseconds do the accesses take?
assumptions: Each access costs a full memory round trip
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the same 5 million accesses hitting the first-level cache at about 1 ns would take about 5 ms, so layout and locality can matter a hundredfold. Real CPUs overlap some independent misses, so measure before relying on the exact figure.

questions.prompt: Order these from fastest to slowest typical access latency.

items.label: Main memory
First-level cache
Local SSD read
Last-level (shared) cache

questions.explanation: Roughly 1 ns, tens of nanoseconds, about 100 ns, then tens to hundreds of microseconds for a solid-state disk.

flashcards.back: 64 bytes on most current CPUs; memory always moves a line at a time.
Threads write different variables on the same line, so cores keep invalidating each other.
Pad or align hot per-thread data to separate lines, or accumulate locally and combine.

mechanism.title: What happens on a memory access
steps: The CPU translates the virtual address, then checks its first-level data cache, typically tens of kilobytes per core with a latency of a few cycles.
On a miss it checks the second-level cache (per core, hundreds of kilobytes to a few megabytes) and then the shared last-level cache (several to tens of megabytes), each larger and slower.

If every cache misses, the request goes to main memory, costing on the order of 100 ns, enough time for hundreds of simple instructions. The whole 64-byte line containing the address comes back and is placed in the caches.

Prefetchers watch access patterns. Sequential or constant-stride access is detected and future lines are requested before they are needed, which is why scanning an array runs near memory bandwidth rather than at miss latency.

When a core writes a line, the coherence protocol invalidates copies in other cores. A later read by another core must fetch the line from the writer, which costs tens of nanoseconds and serialises cores that write the same line.

Dependent loads (following a pointer to get the next address) cannot be overlapped, so a pointer-chasing structure pays the full miss latency at each step, while independent loads in an array can be in flight together.

useWhen: Use contiguous arrays and structure layouts that match the access order of hot loops.
Use per-thread or per-core accumulators, padded to a line, for counters written on every operation.
avoidWhen: Avoid pointer-heavy structures in hot paths over large data sets.
Avoid placing frequently written fields next to fields that many threads read.

rows: Random access into a large table
Batch, sort or partition by key
Use arrays or allocate nodes together

numbers.title: What false sharing costs a counter loop
assumptions: About 1 ns per increment on a line the core owns; about 50 ns when the line must be fetched from another core (illustrative orders of magnitude)
steps: Padded counters: 100,000,000 × 1 ns = 0.1 s per thread, all threads in parallel.
Shared line, worst case: each increment pays about 50 ns, so 100,000,000 × 50 ns = 5 s per thread.
The 8-thread run takes about 5 s instead of 0.1 s, slower than one thread doing all 800 million increments alone (0.8 s).
Padding each counter to 64 bytes uses 8 × 64 = 512 bytes instead of 64, a negligible cost.
numbers.result: False sharing can make a parallel loop about 50 times slower than its padded version and slower than running it on one thread; 448 extra bytes of padding remove it.

india.title: Finding false sharing with a profiler
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Microsoft’s Visual Studio documentation describes false sharing as threads updating different variables that sit on the same cache line, which forces the line to bounce between cores even though no data is actually shared. Its profiler can flag the hot field and the competing threads; the usual fix it shows is padding or reorganising the structure so each thread’s frequently written data occupies a separate cache line.

pitfalls.trap: “Each thread has its own variable, so there’s no contention.”
pitfalls.say: “Distinct variables can still share a 64-byte line; I’d check layout and pad hot per-thread fields.”

pitfalls.trap: “The tree does fewer comparisons, so it must be faster.”
pitfalls.say: “For small data the array may win on cache misses; I’d benchmark both at real sizes.”

takeaways: Memory moves in 64-byte lines.
A miss to main memory costs around 100 ns, roughly a hundred times a first-level hit.
Contiguous, predictable access lets prefetching hide latency.
Writes to a shared line serialise cores, even for distinct variables.

interactive.title: Why does adding threads slow it down?
interactive.prompt: Four threads each count matching records in their quarter of an array, storing the running count in results[threadIndex], an array of four 8-byte integers. One thread takes 2 s; four threads take 3 s.

choices.label: The four counts share a cache line, so every increment bounces it between cores
choices.feedback: Right: four 8-byte slots fit in one 64-byte line, and each write invalidates the other three caches.

choices.label: The array of records is too large to split across four threads
choices.feedback: Each thread reads its own contiguous quarter, which is the ideal parallel pattern.

choices.label: The threads need a lock around results, and they are waiting on it
choices.feedback: Each thread writes only its own slot, so no lock is needed or used.

interactive.reveal: Count in a local variable inside each thread and write results[threadIndex] once at the end, or pad each slot to 64 bytes. Either makes the four threads independent, and the run should approach 0.5 s.

seeAlso.why: Virtual memory and the TLB sit just in front of the caches
Atomics and contended counters pay the same line-transfer cost
Moving a thread to another core leaves its warm cache behind

title: Atomics, Compare-and-Swap and Memory Ordering
objectives: Use atomic operations and compare-and-swap loops correctly
Explain why compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations, and how acquire and release prevent it
Recognise the ABA problem and contention limits of lock-free code

cards.title: One indivisible step
cards.body: An atomic operation reads and updates a memory location so that no other thread can see it half done. Atomic increments, exchanges and compare-and-swap (CAS) are single hardware instructions on common CPUs. CAS takes an address, an expected value and a new value: it writes the new value only if the location still holds the expected one, and reports whether it succeeded. Almost every lock-free structure is built from it.

cards.title: Worked example: a CAS retry loop
cards.body: Updating a shared maximum without a lock.
steps: Read the current maximum: 40
Compute the new value locally: this thread saw 57, so the new maximum is 57
CAS(max, expected 40, new 57); meanwhile another thread already stored 52, so the CAS fails and returns 52
Recompute with the fresh value: 57 is still larger, so try CAS(max, 52, 57), which succeeds
If the fresh value had been 60, the loop would stop without writing: never overwrite a newer value blindly

cards.title: Why a plain flag is not enough
cards.body: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations when a single thread cannot tell the difference, so another thread can see a ready flag set before the data it guards. A release store on the flag guarantees that earlier writes become visible first; an acquire load on the flag guarantees that later reads see them. Paired together they publish data safely, which is what a mutex does for you on lock and unlock.

cards.title: Trap: the ABA problem
cards.body: A lock-free stack pops by reading the top node A and its next pointer, then CASing the top from A to next. If, in between, another thread pops A, pops B, and pushes A back, the CAS still sees A and succeeds, installing a pointer to B, which was freed. Equal values do not mean nothing changed. Counters (tagged pointers) or deferred freeing schemes such as hazard pointers or epochs prevent it.

cards.title: Misconception: lock-free means fast under contention
cards.body: Every successful atomic write needs exclusive ownership of its cache line, so 32 cores hammering one atomic counter queue up for that line just as they would for a lock, and failed CAS attempts waste work on top. Lock-free code guarantees that some thread always makes progress; it does not make a contended location scale. Shard hot counters per core and sum them when read.

questions.prompt: A thread increments a shared counter with a CAS loop: read v, compute v + 1, CAS(counter, v, v + 1). What must happen when the CAS fails?

choices.label: Write v + 1 with a plain store, since the CAS already checked
Give up, because another thread has done the increment
Wait for the other thread to finish, then retry the same CAS
Read the current value again, recompute, and retry the CAS

questions.explanation: A failure means another thread changed the counter after this thread read it, so the computed value is stale and must be recomputed from the fresh one. A plain store would overwrite the other update, giving up loses this increment, and retrying with the old expected value can never succeed.

questions.prompt: A producer writes a record and then sets ready = true with ordinary, non-atomic writes. A consumer on another core loops until ready is true and reads the record. Which outcome is possible?

choices.label: The consumer sees ready but reads an old or partial record
Nothing bad: writes always become visible in program order
The record is safe, but ready may flip back to false later
The consumer reads the record twice and double counts it

questions.explanation: Without release and acquire ordering, the compiler or CPU may make the flag visible before the record, so the consumer can read stale data. Program order is not guaranteed across cores. Nothing writes false again, so the flag cannot flip back, and the consumer reads the record once; the danger is reading it too early.

questions.prompt: A lock-free stack uses CAS on the top pointer. Under heavy load it sometimes returns a node that was already freed. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: CAS is not atomic on the machine’s pointer size
The top changed from A and back to A between the read and CAS
Two threads pushed at once and both CAS operations succeeded
The stack grew larger than the CPU cache could hold

questions.explanation: That is the ABA problem: the CAS compares only the pointer value, so a node that was popped and pushed back looks unchanged while its next pointer is stale. Pointer-width CAS is atomic on mainstream CPUs, two CAS operations on the same expected value cannot both succeed, and cache size affects speed, not correctness.

questions.prompt: A request counter is a single atomic integer incremented by every request on 64 cores. Profiling shows time spent on that increment. What is the best fix?

choices.label: Replace the atomic with a mutex around a plain integer
Use a CAS loop instead of an atomic add instruction
Keep a counter per core and sum them when read
Mark the counter volatile so it skips the CPU cache

questions.explanation: The cost is 64 cores taking turns owning one cache line. Per-core counters keep each line local, and the rare reader adds them up. A mutex has the same single hot line plus waiting, a CAS loop adds failed retries, and volatile does not bypass the cache or make increments atomic.

questions.prompt: Under contention each CAS attempt succeeds with probability 0.25, independently. On average, how many attempts does one update take?
questions.explanation: Design implication: wasted attempts grow as the success rate falls, so at 5% success each update takes 20 tries; reducing sharing helps far more than tuning the loop.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of safely publishing a record from one thread to another.

items.label: Producer sets the ready flag with a release store
Consumer reads the record’s fields
Producer writes every field of the record
Consumer reads the ready flag with an acquire load and sees true

questions.explanation: Release after the writes, acquire before the reads: everything written before the release is visible after the matching acquire.

flashcards.back: Write new only if the location still holds expected; report success. Retry with a fresh read on failure.
Release store publishes earlier writes; an acquire load that sees it makes them visible to later reads.
A value changes and changes back, so CAS succeeds on stale assumptions; use tags or deferred freeing.

mechanism.title: What an atomic operation does in hardware
steps: To perform an atomic read-modify-write, the core must own the cache line exclusively. If another core holds a copy, the coherence protocol invalidates it first, which takes tens of nanoseconds when the line is elsewhere.
While the core owns the line, it performs the read and the write without letting any other core access the line in between, so the operation appears indivisible to every thread.
Compare-and-swap returns whether the location held the expected value. Software builds loops on top: read, compute, CAS, and on failure use the value just returned to recompute.

Separately, compilers reorder and cache values in registers, and CPUs let loads overtake stores and buffer writes. Single-threaded results stay the same, but other cores may observe operations in a different order.

Ordering constraints (release, acquire, or full barriers) limit that reordering. A release store keeps earlier memory operations before it; an acquire load keeps later operations after it. Locks include both, which is why code using a mutex correctly needs no explicit barriers.

Lock-free structures must also reclaim memory safely: a node removed by one thread may still be read by another. Schemes such as hazard pointers or epoch-based reclamation delay freeing until no thread can hold a reference, which also prevents ABA on reused nodes.

useWhen: Use atomics for counters, flags and single-word state shared between threads.
Use CAS loops when an update depends on the current value and must not lose concurrent changes.
avoidWhen: Avoid hand-written lock-free structures where a mutex or a tested library structure would do.
Avoid relying on ordinary variables for signalling between threads.

rows: Exclusion plus ordering for a whole section

numbers.title: When a shared counter stops scaling
assumptions: Each atomic increment on a contended line costs about 50 ns while the line moves between cores (illustrative)
Per-core counters cost about 1 ns per increment (illustrative)
steps: One contended line serves increments one at a time: 1 ÷ 50 ns = 20 million increments a second in total, however many cores try.
A service doing 50 million increments a second cannot be served by that line at all.
With per-core counters each core handles its own: 64 cores × (1 ÷ 1 ns) leaves the counter far from any limit.
Reading the total sums 64 values, about 64 cache misses, which is fine for a metrics scrape every few seconds.
numbers.result: A single contended atomic caps the whole machine at roughly 20 million updates a second in this example; sharding by core removes the cap at the cost of a slower, rare read.

india.title: How the Linux kernel documents memory ordering
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel’s memory-barriers document explains that CPUs and compilers may reorder memory accesses, and that without barriers one CPU can observe another’s stores in a different order than they were issued. It describes acquire and release operations as one-way barriers and shows the classic message-passing pattern: write the data, then publish a flag with release semantics, and read the flag with acquire semantics before reading the data.

pitfalls.trap: “It’s atomic, so it’s thread-safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Each atomic is safe alone; invariants across several fields still need a lock or careful ordering.”

pitfalls.trap: “Lock-free will fix the contention.”
pitfalls.say: “A single hot line still serialises cores; I’d shard the counter per core first.”

takeaways: CAS writes only if the value is unchanged; on failure, re-read and recompute.
Use release to publish and acquire to read published data.
Equal values do not prove nothing changed: beware ABA.
A hot atomic serialises cores; shard it.

interactive.title: Is this flag safe?
interactive.prompt: Thread A fills a buffer and then sets done = true as an atomic store with relaxed ordering. Thread B loops until an atomic relaxed load of done returns true, then reads the buffer.

choices.label: Unsafe: relaxed ordering lets B see done before the buffer
choices.feedback: Right: relaxed atomics only make the flag itself indivisible; they do not order the buffer writes.

choices.label: Safe: any atomic flag orders the memory around it
choices.feedback: Only acquire, release or stronger orderings constrain surrounding accesses.

choices.label: Safe on every CPU because stores are never reordered
choices.feedback: Compilers can reorder too, and some CPUs reorder stores freely.

interactive.reveal: Make the store a release and the load an acquire. Then everything A wrote before setting done is guaranteed visible to B once B sees done = true, on every CPU and compiler.

seeAlso.why: Mutexes give you atomicity and ordering in one tool
Atomics pay the cache-line transfer cost described there
Lock-free code avoids deadlock but brings its own failure modes

title: cgroups: CPU Throttling and Memory Limits
objectives: Explain how a CPU quota is enforced per period and why it causes latency spikes
Distinguish CPU weights from CPU limits, and memory.high from memory.max
Predict what counts against a container’s memory limit

cards.title: What a container limit really is
cards.body: A container is ordinary processes placed in a control group (cgroup), a kernel object that accounts for and limits resources for every process inside it. CPU can be shared by weight, which only matters when CPUs are busy, or capped by a quota: a number of CPU-microseconds the group may use in each period, 100 ms by default. Memory has a soft throttle point (memory.high) and a hard limit (memory.max).

cards.title: Worked example: a 2-CPU limit with 16 busy threads
cards.body: Quota is spent in wall-clock time across all threads at once.
steps: Limit: 2 CPUs, which is 200 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period
16 threads become runnable together at the start of a period on a 32-core machine
They burn 16 CPU-ms per millisecond, so the 200 ms quota is gone after 200 ÷ 16 = 12.5 ms
Every thread in the group is then throttled for the remaining 87.5 ms of the period
A request needing 13 ms of work now takes over 100 ms, although average CPU use looks far below the limit

cards.title: Requests, weights and limits are different knobs
cards.body: A CPU weight (what an orchestrator’s CPU request usually sets) decides how contended CPU is divided and never stops a group from using idle cores. A CPU quota (what a CPU limit sets) is a hard cap enforced even when the machine is idle. Many teams set requests for fair placement and leave CPU limits off or generous for latency-sensitive services, because throttling hurts tail latency even when there is spare capacity.

cards.title: Trap: files in a memory-backed directory count as memory
cards.body: Writing a large file into a tmpfs directory (such as an in-memory scratch volume or /dev/shm) uses memory charged to the container. So do page cache pages for files the container reads and writes, though clean cache can be reclaimed. A job that writes 3 GB of temporary files to a memory-backed volume inside a 4 GB limit can be killed while its own heap is small. Put large scratch data on disk-backed storage.

cards.title: Misconception: the memory limit is enforced like a heap limit
cards.body: At memory.high the kernel throttles the group and reclaims its memory aggressively, so the process slows down rather than failing. At memory.max, if reclaim cannot free enough, the kernel’s OOM killer terminates a process in the group with SIGKILL. The program gets no allocation error and cannot clean up; it simply disappears, and the orchestrator reports it as killed for out-of-memory.

questions.prompt: A service with a 1-CPU limit averages 40% CPU, yet its p99 latency jumps to over 100 ms every few seconds. What should you check first?

choices.label: Whether its throttled time counters are rising
Whether the node has fewer physical cores than containers
Whether its memory limit is lower than its CPU limit
Whether the load average on the node is above one

questions.explanation: Averages hide bursts: a burst of parallel threads can spend a whole period’s quota in a few milliseconds and then wait for the next period, which the cgroup reports in its throttling counters. Packing more containers than cores is normal with weights, memory and CPU limits are not compared, and node load average reflects every container, not this group’s quota.

questions.prompt: A container has a CPU request of 1 and no CPU limit on an otherwise idle 8-core node. How much CPU can it use?

choices.label: Exactly one CPU, because the request is enforced as a cap
Up to all 8 cores while nothing else wants them
Half a CPU until the scheduler measures its real usage
None until another container on the node is also running

questions.explanation: A request becomes a weight that only divides contended CPU, so on an idle node the container can use every core. It is a limit, not a request, that sets a hard quota. Nothing starts at half a CPU or waits for a neighbour to run.

questions.prompt: A worker with a 2 GB memory limit and a 400 MB heap is killed for out-of-memory while extracting a 1.8 GB archive into an in-memory scratch volume. Why?

choices.label: The heap grew briefly to 2 GB while reading the archive
The archive’s compressed bytes were counted twice by the kernel
Files in the memory-backed volume count against the limit
Extraction raised the CPU usage, which lowered the memory cap

questions.explanation: tmpfs pages are memory, charged to the container, so 1.8 GB of files plus a 400 MB heap exceeds 2 GB. Nothing suggests a heap spike, compressed input is not double counted, and CPU usage never changes the memory limit.

questions.prompt: What happens when a container’s memory usage reaches memory.max and the kernel cannot reclaim enough?

choices.label: The next allocation returns an error the program can handle
The container is paused until memory is freed elsewhere
Its pages are moved to the node’s other containers
A process in the group is killed with SIGKILL

questions.explanation: The cgroup OOM killer picks a process in the group and sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, so there is no cleanup and the exit code is 137. Allocations typically succeed until the pages are touched, so there is no handleable error; there is no pausing, and memory is never moved to other containers.

questions.prompt: A container’s quota is 100 ms of CPU per 100 ms period (1 CPU). Eight threads start running together on a large machine. After how many milliseconds is the quota used up?
assumptions: All 8 threads run in parallel on separate cores
The period starts when they start
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the group is then throttled for 87.5 ms of every 100 ms period, which is why a parallel burst in a small container shows long stalls even though the average CPU use is only one core.

questions.prompt: Order what happens as a container’s memory use keeps growing towards its limits.

items.label: Usage reaches memory.max and reclaim cannot free enough
Usage passes memory.high and the group is throttled under heavy reclaim
The OOM killer sends SIGKILL to a process in the group
The kernel reclaims clean page cache and swaps if allowed

questions.explanation: Throttle and reclaim first, then the hard limit, then the kill; memory.high slows a group down, only memory.max kills.

flashcards.back: CPU time allowed per period (default period 100 ms); when spent, the whole group waits for the next period.
Request: weight for contended CPU and placement. Limit: hard quota, enforced even on an idle node.
high: throttle and reclaim, no kill. max: hard limit; the OOM killer sends SIGKILL.

sources.title: Control Group v2, Linux kernel documentation
Resource Management for Pods and Containers, Kubernetes

mechanism.title: How the kernel enforces CPU and memory limits
steps: Every process belongs to one cgroup in a hierarchy. Controllers enabled for that group (cpu, memory, io, pids) charge the group for what its processes use and apply its limits.

For CPU, the cpu.weight file sets a relative share used only when CPUs are contended. The cpu.max file holds a quota and a period, such as 200000 100000, meaning 200 ms of CPU per 100 ms: two CPUs’ worth.

The scheduler deducts run time from the group’s quota as any of its threads run on any core. When the quota hits zero, all the group’s threads are taken off the CPU until the next period refills it. The cpu.stat file counts how many periods were throttled and the total throttled time.
For memory, every page the group’s processes allocate, including page cache for files they touch, tmpfs files and kernel memory such as socket buffers, is charged to the group.

Above memory.high the kernel throttles allocations and reclaims aggressively; this never invokes the OOM killer. Reaching memory.max forces reclaim, and if that fails, the OOM killer picks a process within the group and kills it.

Runtimes that size thread pools or heaps from the machine instead of the cgroup will oversubscribe: 64 threads under a 2-CPU quota burn the quota quickly, and a heap sized for 64 GB will be killed at a 4 GB limit.

useWhen: Use CPU requests (weights) for every container so the scheduler places and shares fairly.
Use memory limits everywhere, with heap and buffer settings sized below them.
avoidWhen: Avoid tight CPU limits on latency-sensitive services with bursty parallel work.
Avoid large scratch files on memory-backed volumes inside a small memory limit.

columns: Effect when the node is idle
rows: SIGKILL from the OOM killer, exit 137

numbers.title: How a CPU limit stretches one burst
assumptions: A request fans out to 20 threads, each needing 15 ms of CPU, on a machine with plenty of idle cores (illustrative)
The container’s limit is 2 CPUs: 200 ms per 100 ms period
steps: Total CPU needed: 20 × 15 ms = 300 ms.
Period 1: 20 threads use 20 CPU-ms per ms, so the 200 ms quota is gone at 10 ms; each thread has done 10 ms and needs 5 ms more.
Throttled until the period ends at 100 ms; period 2 refills 200 ms and the remaining 100 ms of work takes 5 ms.
The request finishes at about 105 ms. Without the limit it would finish at 15 ms; with a 3-CPU limit (300 ms quota) it would finish within the first period, at 15 ms.
numbers.result: A CPU limit that is ample on average turned a 15 ms burst into a 105 ms response, seven times slower; size limits for peak parallelism or rely on requests alone.

india.title: How the kernel documents memory.high
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel’s cgroup v2 documentation describes memory.high as a throttle limit: when a group’s usage goes over it, the group’s processes are throttled and put under heavy reclaim pressure, and going over the high limit never invokes the OOM killer. It describes memory.max as the hard limit, where the OOM killer is invoked if usage cannot be reduced. Kubernetes’ resource documentation adds that CPU limits are enforced by throttling, while a container exceeding its memory limit may be killed.

pitfalls.trap: “CPU averages 40% of the limit, so the limit isn’t a problem.”
pitfalls.say: “Quotas are enforced per 100 ms period; I’d check throttled periods in cpu.stat.”

pitfalls.trap: “It was OOM killed, so the heap leaked.”
pitfalls.say: “The cgroup counts page cache, tmpfs and native memory too; I’d break down memory.stat first.”

takeaways: A CPU limit is a quota per 100 ms period, spent across all threads at once.
Parallel bursts get throttled even when average use is low.
Requests set weights; limits set hard caps.
memory.max kills with SIGKILL; tmpfs and page cache count too.

interactive.title: How long does the burst take?
interactive.prompt: A container limited to 2 CPUs (200 ms per 100 ms period) gets a request that fans out to 20 threads of 15 ms CPU work each. The node has 32 idle cores.

choices.label: About 105 ms, because the quota runs out at 10 ms and the rest waits for the next period
choices.feedback: Right: 200 ms of quota covers 10 ms on 20 threads; the last 5 ms each runs after the refill at 100 ms.

choices.label: About 15 ms, because 32 idle cores can run all 20 threads
choices.feedback: Idle cores do not help once the group’s quota is spent.

choices.label: About 150 ms, because 300 ms of work at 2 CPUs takes 150 ms
choices.feedback: That assumes smooth use of two CPUs; quota is spent in parallel bursts and refilled only at period boundaries.

interactive.reveal: Throttling is all-or-nothing per period, so the finish time is set by period boundaries, not by average CPU. Fewer threads, a higher limit or no limit would all finish within the first period.

seeAlso.why: The scheduler that enforces quotas and weights
Orchestrators set these cgroup values from requests and limits
An OOM kill arrives as SIGKILL with exit code 137

title: File Descriptors and Resource Limits
objectives: Explain what a file descriptor is and what consumes one
Size a process’s descriptor limit from its connections and files
Diagnose “too many open files” and descriptor leaks

cards.title: A small integer for every open thing
cards.body: A file descriptor is an index into a process’s table of open kernel objects: files, sockets, pipes, event queues, timers. Every open, accept, socket, pipe or epoll call returns the lowest free number, and close frees it. Each process has a limit on how many it may hold (RLIMIT_NOFILE, commonly 1,024 by default for the soft limit on many Linux systems), and the whole system has a global limit too.

cards.title: Worked example: how many clients fit under the limit?
cards.body: A proxy uses two descriptors per client: one inbound, one to the backend.
steps: Soft limit: 1,024 descriptors
Already used: 24 for standard streams, log files, listening sockets and the event queue
Clients that fit: (1,024 − 24) ÷ 2 = 500
Raising the soft limit to 65,536 gives (65,536 − 24) ÷ 2 = 32,756 clients
Client 501 fails at accept with EMFILE: a per-process error, not a sign that the machine is out of memory

cards.title: Trap: a descriptor leak looks like a capacity problem
cards.body: A code path that opens a file or connection and returns early on an error without closing it leaks one descriptor each time. Nothing fails for days; then accept and open start returning EMFILE and the service stops taking traffic, and a restart “fixes” it. Watch the count of open descriptors per process, release them in a finally or scoped block, and treat a count that climbs steadily under flat traffic as a leak.

cards.title: Misconception: an EMFILE error goes away on its own
cards.body: An event loop that hits EMFILE on accept leaves the pending connection in the listen queue. With level-triggered readiness, the listening socket stays readable, so the loop wakes immediately, fails accept again, and spins at full CPU while doing nothing useful. Back off or temporarily stop watching the listening socket, and some servers keep one spare descriptor to accept and immediately close the excess connection.

cards.title: Descriptors survive fork and exec unless told not to
cards.body: A child created by fork gets copies of all the parent’s descriptors, and they stay open across exec unless marked close-on-exec. A helper program launched by a server can then hold the server’s listening socket or database connections, so the port stays busy after the server exits and connections never close. Open descriptors with the close-on-exec flag by default.

questions.prompt: Which of these does NOT use up a file descriptor in the process that calls it?

choices.label: Accepting a new TCP connection
Creating a pipe to a child process
Allocating a 1 MB buffer on the heap
Creating an epoll instance to watch sockets

questions.explanation: Heap memory is managed by the allocator and never appears in the descriptor table. Accept returns a new socket descriptor, a pipe returns two descriptors (one for each end), and an epoll instance is itself a descriptor.

questions.prompt: A proxy starts failing new connections with “Too many open files” at about 500 clients. Memory and CPU are fine. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The kernel ran out of memory for socket buffers
The soft descriptor limit of 1,024 is used at two per client
The listen backlog is full, so the kernel resets new clients
The system-wide file table limit for all users was reached

questions.explanation: Two descriptors per proxied client reach a 1,024 soft limit at about 500 clients, and the error name says so. Socket buffer exhaustion shows different errors, a full backlog drops or resets connections without “too many open files”, and the system-wide table gives ENFILE (“too many open files in system”), not the per-process EMFILE.

questions.prompt: Open descriptors for a service rise by about 300 an hour under steady traffic and drop to normal after each restart. Which code is the most likely culprit?

choices.label: An error path that returns before closing a file it opened
A cache that holds parsed objects in memory without a limit
A thread pool that keeps its idle worker threads alive
A logger that writes every request to one open file

questions.explanation: A leak grows with the number of times the faulty path runs and resets on restart. An unbounded cache leaks memory, not descriptors; idle threads hold no descriptors of their own; and a logger writing to one open file uses one descriptor for its whole life.

questions.prompt: After accept fails with EMFILE, an event-loop server pins a core at 100% CPU and serves nothing. Why?

choices.label: The kernel retries the failed accept in a busy loop
The rejected client keeps retrying faster and faster
The listener stays readable, so the loop wakes and fails again
The error disables the event queue and falls back to polling

questions.explanation: The pending connection is still queued, so a level-triggered event loop is told again and again that the listener is ready, and each accept fails at once. The kernel does not retry for you, the client is just waiting in the queue, and EMFILE does not disable the event queue.

questions.prompt: A proxy has a limit of 4,096 descriptors, uses 40 for itself, and needs 2 per client. How many clients can it serve at once?
assumptions: Every client holds both descriptors for the whole session
No other files are opened per request
questions.explanation: Sanity check: forgetting the backend connection doubles the estimate to about 4,056, so count every descriptor a request holds (upstream connections, temporary files) and leave headroom for bursts.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to confirm and fix a suspected descriptor leak.

items.label: Compare the growth with traffic to see if it climbs under flat load
Find the code path that opens that kind and add a guaranteed close
Track open descriptor counts for the process over time
List what the open descriptors point to and find the dominant kind

questions.explanation: Measure, correlate with load, classify what is leaking, then fix the path that opens it.

flashcards.back: A per-process integer naming an open kernel object: file, socket, pipe, event queue.
EMFILE: this process hit its limit. ENFILE: the whole system’s file table is full.
A flag that closes a descriptor when the process execs, so children don’t inherit sockets or files.

mechanism.title: What happens when a process opens something
steps: The process calls open, socket, accept, pipe or a similar call. The kernel creates or finds the kernel object (an open file description holding the offset and flags, or a socket).

The kernel then picks the lowest unused number in the process’s descriptor table and points that slot at the object. If the table already holds as many entries as the soft RLIMIT_NOFILE allows, the call fails with EMFILE.

Separately, the system tracks the total number of open files across all processes; when that global limit is reached, calls fail with ENFILE, which points at the whole machine rather than one process.

Duplicating a descriptor (dup, or fork copying the table) makes two numbers point at one open file description, which shares the file offset. The object is released only when the last descriptor referring to it is closed.
At exec, descriptors marked close-on-exec are closed and the rest stay open in the new program. Libraries that open descriptors without the flag leak them into every child process.
The soft limit can be raised by the process up to the hard limit; only a privileged process can raise the hard limit. Service managers and container runtimes set both when they start the process.

useWhen: Raise the soft limit for servers that hold many connections, and size it from clients × descriptors per client.
Open descriptors with close-on-exec unless a child must inherit them.
avoidWhen: Avoid raising limits to hide a leak; the count will reach any limit eventually.
Avoid a tight accept retry loop after EMFILE.

rows: Raise the soft limit or fix the leak
Find the process holding the most
Child kept the listener without close-on-exec
Close in finally or a scoped block

numbers.title: Sizing the limit for a connection-heavy service
assumptions: Target: 20,000 concurrent clients through a proxy (illustrative)
Per client: 1 inbound socket and 1 upstream socket; 50 fixed descriptors; 25% headroom for bursts and slow closes
steps: Descriptors for clients: 20,000 × 2 = 40,000.
Add fixed descriptors: 40,000 + 50 = 40,050.
Round up to the next common setting: 65,536, which also leaves room for sockets lingering after close.
numbers.result: A 20,000-client proxy needs a descriptor limit around 50,000; the 1,024 default would cap it at about 500 clients.

india.title: What the manual says about running out
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The accept(2) manual page lists two distinct errors: EMFILE when the per-process limit on the number of open file descriptors has been reached, and ENFILE when the system-wide limit on the total number of open files has been reached. The getrlimit(2) page describes RLIMIT_NOFILE as one greater than the maximum descriptor number the process may open, and explains that an unprivileged process may raise its soft limit only up to its hard limit.

pitfalls.trap: “We get ‘too many open files’, so the disk is full.”
pitfalls.say: “It means the descriptor limit; I’d count open descriptors and check if they grow under flat load.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just set the limit to a million.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d size it from clients × descriptors each, and fix any leak first.”

takeaways: Every file, socket, pipe and event queue uses a descriptor.
EMFILE is per process; ENFILE is system-wide.
A steady climb under flat traffic is a leak.
Use close-on-exec so children don’t inherit descriptors.

interactive.title: What happens at client 501?
