interactive.prompt: A proxy runs with the default soft limit of 1,024 descriptors, uses 24 of its own, and opens one inbound and one upstream socket per client. Clients keep arriving.

choices.label: Accept fails with EMFILE once about 500 clients are connected
choices.feedback: Right: (1,024 − 24) ÷ 2 = 500 clients use every remaining descriptor.

choices.label: The kernel raises the limit automatically when it is reached
choices.feedback: Limits never grow by themselves; the process or its service manager must raise the soft limit.

choices.label: New clients succeed but the oldest connections are closed
choices.feedback: The kernel never closes existing descriptors to make room.

interactive.reveal: Size the limit from clients × descriptors per client plus headroom. Also make the event loop handle EMFILE without spinning, by backing off or pausing the listener until descriptors are free.

seeAlso.why: Every descriptor is created and used through system calls
Event loops watch descriptors for readiness
Pooled connections each hold a descriptor for their whole life

title: Amdahl’s Law: How Far More Cores Go
objectives: Compute the speedup limit set by the serial part of a job
Explain why contention can make extra cores slow a job down
Decide between more cores, less serial work, or a bigger problem size

cards.title: The serial part sets the ceiling
cards.body: If a fraction p of a job’s work can run in parallel and the rest must run one step at a time, then on N cores the speedup is 1 ÷ ((1 − p) + p ÷ N). As N grows the parallel term shrinks towards zero, so the speedup can never exceed 1 ÷ (1 − p). With 95% parallel work the ceiling is 20 times, whether you have 64 cores or 6,400.

cards.title: Worked example: 95% parallel, more and more cores
cards.body: Each doubling of cores buys less than the one before.
steps: 1,000 cores: 1 ÷ (0.05 + 0.00095) ≈ 19.6 times, almost at the ceiling of 20
Going from 8 to 32 cores quadruples the hardware for about 2.1 times the speed
Cost per job (cores × time) rises by about 1.9 times, so the extra speed is paid for in efficiency

cards.title: Trap: contention makes the curve bend back down
cards.body: Amdahl’s law assumes the serial part stays fixed. Real systems also pay for coordination: a lock, a shared counter or a cache line that every core touches costs more as cores are added, because they queue for it. Past some point throughput falls as cores increase. If adding cores makes a job slower, look for a shared hot spot before buying hardware.

cards.title: Misconception: Amdahl says big machines are pointless
cards.body: Amdahl’s law fixes the problem size. Gustafson’s observation is that people usually grow the problem with the machine: more data, finer models, more users. If the serial part stays roughly constant while the parallel part grows, more cores keep paying off. The useful question is whether your workload is a fixed task you want sooner, or a growing one you want to keep up with.

cards.title: Where serial time hides
cards.body: Serial work is not only code that runs on one thread. Reading an input file before splitting it, merging results at the end, waiting on one database connection, holding a global lock, or a single coordinator handing out tasks all count. Measure how the job’s time splits before parallelising, and shrink the largest serial step first: halving a 10% serial part raises the ceiling from 10 to 20 times.

questions.prompt: A job is 90% parallel. What is the most speedup any number of cores can give it?

choices.label: About 9 times, the parallel share over the serial share
As much as the number of cores you add to the job
10 times, since 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9) is the ceiling
About 1.1 times, the inverse of the parallel share

questions.explanation: The serial 10% always takes its full time, so the job can never finish faster than one tenth of the original: 10 times. Nine is the ratio of parallel to serial work, not the limit; unlimited scaling ignores the serial part; and 1 ÷ 0.9 is what you get by mixing up which share is serial.

questions.prompt: A batch job runs in 40 s on 8 cores and in 55 s on 32 cores. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: The serial part grew because more cores were added
Threads contend for a shared lock or hot cache line
Amdahl’s law predicts slowdowns past 8 cores
The operating system can schedule at most 8 threads

questions.explanation: Amdahl’s law only flattens the curve; a job getting slower with more cores means coordination costs grow with core count, usually a contended lock, atomic or cache line. The serial code itself did not change, Amdahl never predicts a slowdown, and schedulers run far more than 8 threads.

questions.prompt: Analytics runs over 10 times more data each year on 10 times more cores. Run time stays about the same. Which idea explains why scaling still pays off?

choices.label: The serial share shrinks as the parallel work grows
Amdahl’s ceiling rises in proportion to the core count
Cache misses fall as more data is processed in total
More cores lower the time spent in each serial step

questions.explanation: This is Gustafson’s scaled speedup: if serial work stays roughly fixed while parallel work grows with the data, the serial share falls and more cores stay useful. Amdahl’s ceiling depends on the serial share, not on cores; more data usually means more misses, not fewer; and serial steps by definition do not speed up with cores.

questions.prompt: A pipeline spends 20 s reading input on one thread and 80 s processing in parallel on 4 cores. Which change shortens it the most?

choices.label: Doubling to 8 cores for the processing step
Splitting the input read across 4 threads
Raising the priority of the processing threads
Running the processing on faster, single-core hardware

questions.explanation: Now: 20 + 80 ÷ 4 = 40 s. Eight cores give 20 + 10 = 30 s. A 4-way parallel read gives 5 + 20 = 25 s, assuming storage keeps up. Priority does not create CPU time on an otherwise idle machine, and one fast core loses the 4-way parallel step.

questions.prompt: A job is 80% parallel. What speedup do 4 cores give?
assumptions: The serial 20% does not speed up
Parallel work splits perfectly across cores
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the ceiling for this job is 1 ÷ 0.2 = 5 times, and 4 cores already reach half of it, so another 4 cores add only about 1.3 times more (from 2.5 to 3.3).

questions.prompt: A nightly report takes 90 minutes and must finish in 45. Choose the change.
constraints: Profile: 60 minutes reading files through one thread, 30 minutes of parallel scoring on 8 cores
Storage can serve about six times the current read rate
Budget allows a larger machine or a week of engineering

approaches.label: Parallelise the file reading
approaches.description: Split input reads across several threads or processes

approaches.label: Move to a 32-core machine
approaches.description: Quadruple the cores for the scoring step

approaches.label: Tune the scoring code for 20% gains
approaches.description: Optimise the parallel step’s inner loop

rationaleOptions.label: The 60-minute serial read alone is longer than the 45-minute budget
Storage headroom means a 6-way read could take about 10 minutes
Quadrupling the cores quarters the whole run time
Faster scoring code fixes the serial bottleneck

rationaleConflicts.r3: Only the scoring step speeds up: 60 + 30 ÷ 4 = 67.5 minutes, still over budget.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Scoring is the parallel part; 20% off it gives 60 + 24 = 84 minutes.

questions.explanation: With a 6-way read the job takes about 10 + 30 = 40 minutes, inside the target with no new hardware, while 32 cores still leave it at 67.5. When the serial part is the biggest slice, attack it first.

flashcards.back: Speedup = 1 ÷ ((1 − p) + p ÷ N); ceiling 1 ÷ (1 − p).

flashcards.front: Why can more cores make a job slower?
flashcards.back: Coordination costs (locks, shared lines) grow with cores and can outweigh the extra work done.
Grow the problem with the machine; a fixed serial part becomes a smaller share.

sources.title: Amdahl, Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities (1967)

mechanism.title: Where parallel speedup goes
steps: Split the job’s single-core time T into a serial part s × T and a parallel part p × T, with s + p = 1.
On N cores the parallel part ideally takes p × T ÷ N while the serial part still takes s × T, so the run time is T × (s + p ÷ N) and the speedup is 1 ÷ (s + p ÷ N).
As N grows, p ÷ N approaches zero and the speedup approaches 1 ÷ s. Half the ceiling is reached at N = p ÷ s cores (19 cores for 95% parallel); after that each extra core buys less.

Real systems add a coordination cost that grows with N: threads queue for locks, cores fight over cache lines, and coordinators hand out work one task at a time. Models such as the universal scalability law add these terms, and they make throughput peak and then fall.
Gustafson’s scaled speedup holds run time fixed instead of problem size. If the serial part stays constant while parallel work grows with N, the speedup is about s + p × N, which keeps growing.
In practice, profile the split first, shrink the largest serial step (I/O, merging, global locks), remove shared hot spots, and only then add cores, measuring throughput at each size.

useWhen: Use Amdahl’s law to estimate the ceiling before buying cores or rewriting for parallelism.
Use it to rank optimisations: shrinking serial work raises the ceiling itself.
avoidWhen: Avoid scaling up a job that slows down as cores are added; find the contention first.
Avoid assuming linear speedup in capacity plans.

rows: Parallel share is large and cores are idle-free
Serial share is already a large slice
Time rises as cores are added

numbers.title: Is 4 times the cores worth it?
assumptions: Cost is proportional to cores × run time
steps: Speed gain: 12.55 ÷ 5.93 ≈ 2.1 times for 4 times the cores.
Cost per job: 2.55 ÷ 1.35 ≈ 1.89 times higher.
numbers.result: Quadrupling cores for a 95% parallel job gives about 2.1 times the speed at about 1.9 times the cost per job; halving the 5% serial part instead would raise the 32-core speedup to about 18.

india.title: Where the law comes from
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Gene Amdahl presented the argument in 1967 at the AFIPS Spring Joint Computer Conference, in a paper titled “Validity of the single processor approach to achieving large scale computing capabilities”, arguing that a fixed share of sequential housekeeping work limits what parallel hardware can deliver. In 1988 John Gustafson’s “Reevaluating Amdahl’s law” in Communications of the ACM argued that in practice the problem size grows with the machine, so measured speedups on large parallel computers can far exceed the fixed-size prediction.

pitfalls.trap: “Doubling cores will halve the run time.”
pitfalls.say: “Only the parallel part halves; I’d measure the serial share and compute the real speedup.”

pitfalls.trap: “More cores made it slower, so the machine is bad.”
pitfalls.say: “That points to contention; I’d profile locks and shared state before scaling.”

takeaways: Speedup is capped at 1 ÷ serial share.
Each doubling of cores buys less than the last.
Contention can make extra cores slow a job down.
Shrinking serial work raises the ceiling; more cores never do.

interactive.title: Is triple the cores worth it?
interactive.prompt: A job has 10 s of serial setup and 90 s of perfectly parallel work on one core. Slide the core count and watch what each extra core buys.
interactive.takeaway: 10 cores give 19 s (5.3 times faster); 30 cores give 13 s, only 1.46 times better again for triple the hardware, and no number of cores beats 10 s. Cutting the setup from 10 s to 5 s on 10 cores gives 14 s, almost as fast as 30 cores, without any new hardware.

seeAlso.why: Scheduling decides how threads share the cores in the formula
Locks are the most common source of serial time
Capacity plans should not assume linear scaling

title: Green Threads, Coroutines and Async Runtimes
objectives: Explain how a runtime multiplexes many lightweight tasks onto a few OS threads
Compare stackful and stackless designs and what each costs
Spot the calls that block a carrier thread and stall unrelated tasks

cards.title: Many tasks, few kernel threads
cards.body: Kernel threads are scheduled by the operating system and each reserves its own stack, so a process with tens of thousands of them pays for memory and context switches. Lightweight tasks (green threads, virtual threads, coroutines) are scheduled by a runtime in user space instead: it runs many tasks on a small pool of OS threads, called carriers, and switches between tasks when one waits for I/O, timers or a channel. This is M:N scheduling.

cards.title: Stackful or stackless
cards.body: A stackful task has its own small, growable stack, so it can pause anywhere inside ordinary nested calls and code looks blocking. A stackless coroutine is compiled into a state machine that saves only the variables live across each suspension point; it can pause only where the code marks a suspension (an await), and every caller up the chain must be async too. Stackless tasks are usually smaller; stackful ones avoid splitting the code into two colours.

cards.title: Worked example: one blocking call stalls everyone
cards.body: Four carrier threads run 10,000 tasks.
steps: A task calls a file or DNS function that blocks in the kernel instead of yielding to the runtime
Its carrier thread is now stuck in the kernel and cannot run any other task
If four tasks do this at once, all four carriers are blocked and 9,996 ready tasks wait, even though the CPU is idle
Latency spikes for unrelated requests until a blocking call returns
Fix: use the runtime’s non-blocking version, or hand blocking work to a separate pool sized for it

cards.title: Trap: holding a lock across a suspension point
cards.body: A task takes an ordinary mutex, then awaits a network call while holding it. The task is suspended, but the lock stays held, and another task on the same carrier that wants it blocks the carrier itself, which can deadlock a single-threaded runtime. Some runtimes also pin a lightweight task to its carrier while it holds a monitor lock. Release locks before suspending, or use a lock provided by the runtime that suspends instead of blocking.

cards.title: Misconception: lightweight tasks make CPU work faster
cards.body: Lightweight tasks make waiting cheap, not computing. A hundred thousand tasks each waiting on a socket cost little, but CPU-bound tasks still need cores, and a task that computes for 200 ms without reaching a suspension point delays every other task on its carrier in runtimes that switch only cooperatively. Move long computation to a worker pool sized to the core count, or yield periodically.

questions.prompt: A server handles 50,000 mostly idle connections. Why do lightweight tasks suit it better than one kernel thread per connection?

choices.label: The kernel runs lightweight tasks at a higher priority
Each waiting task costs a few kilobytes, not a full thread stack
Lightweight tasks run on more cores than the machine has
Lightweight tasks skip the system calls that I/O needs

questions.explanation: A suspended task keeps only a small stack or state machine and no kernel thread, so idle connections are cheap and the runtime avoids kernel context switches. The kernel does not see tasks at all, so it gives them no priority; they cannot use more cores than exist; and I/O still goes through system calls, just non-blocking ones.

questions.prompt: A service on an async runtime with 4 carrier threads stalls for seconds at a time while CPU stays low. Each stall coincides with slow responses from a legacy file share. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The runtime’s scheduler has too many tasks in its queue
The file share answers slowly, so the network stack retries
The runtime switches tasks too often, wasting time
Blocking file reads tie up all four carrier threads

questions.explanation: Calls that block in the kernel hold the carrier, and four slow reads at once leave no carrier free, so everything stops while the CPU idles. Long queues are normal and cheap, retries would show up as network errors rather than total stalls, and task switching is fast and would raise CPU, not lower it.

questions.prompt: A team moves from stackless coroutines to stackful virtual threads. What do they gain?

choices.label: Ordinary blocking-style code can suspend inside nested calls
Each task uses less memory than a stackless state machine
Tasks can now run CPU-bound work faster than before
The kernel can schedule each task directly on a core

questions.explanation: A stackful task saves its whole stack, so any function can suspend without marking every caller async. Stackless state machines are usually smaller, not larger; CPU-bound work runs at the same speed; and the kernel still schedules carriers, not tasks.

questions.prompt: On a single-threaded cooperative runtime, one request handler resizes an image for 300 ms without any await. What do other requests see?

choices.label: Nothing, because each task runs on a separate core
A small slowdown spread evenly across all tasks
A stall of up to 300 ms, since nothing else can run
An error, because the runtime cancels long-running tasks

questions.explanation: Cooperative runtimes switch only at suspension points, so a 300 ms computation holds the only carrier for 300 ms. Tasks do not get their own cores, the delay is not spread out because there is no preemption, and runtimes do not cancel tasks for running long.

questions.prompt: A server keeps 100,000 lightweight tasks alive, each using about 4 KB of stack or state. Roughly how many megabytes do they take?
assumptions: Only task stacks or state are counted
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the same 100,000 connections on kernel threads with 64 KB committed each (illustrative) would need about 6.4 GB, sixteen times more, before counting context-switch costs.

questions.prompt: Order what a runtime does when a task reads from a socket that has no data yet.

items.label: The carrier thread picks the next ready task and runs it
The task calls the runtime’s read, which tries a non-blocking read and gets “would block”
When the event queue reports the socket readable, the task is made ready and later resumed
The runtime registers the socket with the event queue and suspends the task

questions.explanation: Try, park, run something else, resume on readiness: the carrier never sleeps while other tasks are ready.

flashcards.back: Many user-space tasks multiplexed by a runtime onto a few OS (carrier) threads.
Stackful: own growable stack, suspend anywhere. Stackless: state machine, suspend only at marked awaits.
Blocking system calls, long CPU work without yielding, or locks held across a suspension.

mechanism.title: How a runtime multiplexes tasks
steps: The runtime starts a pool of carrier threads, often one per core, each with a run queue of ready tasks. Idle carriers can steal tasks from busy ones to balance load.
A task runs on a carrier until it reaches a suspension point: an I/O call that would block, a timer, a channel or lock operation, or an explicit yield.

At a suspension, the runtime saves the task’s state (its small stack, or the state machine’s fields), registers interest with the kernel’s readiness mechanism such as epoll, and moves on to the next ready task on the same carrier.
One or more poller threads wait on the event queue. When a socket becomes readable or a timer fires, the matching task is put back on a run queue.
Calls the runtime cannot make non-blocking, such as some file system operations or name lookups, are passed to a separate blocking pool, or the runtime adds a carrier temporarily to compensate.

Some runtimes can preempt a task that runs too long; others are purely cooperative. In either case, code that blocks the carrier inside the kernel, or holds it through a lock, removes that carrier from service for everyone.

useWhen: Use lightweight tasks for many concurrent, mostly waiting operations such as connections and calls to other services.
Use a separate pool sized to the cores for CPU-heavy work.
avoidWhen: Avoid blocking system calls on carrier threads.
Avoid holding ordinary locks across a suspension point.

rows: Tens of KB to MB of stack
Memory and context switches at high counts
Blocking or pinned calls stall carriers

numbers.title: What a blocked carrier costs
assumptions: 4 carrier threads serving 1,500 requests a second at 2 ms of CPU each (illustrative)
A 1% minority of requests calls a blocking lookup that takes 100 ms
steps: CPU needed: 1,500 × 2 ms = 3 CPU-seconds per second, 75% of four carriers.
Blocking time: 1,500 × 1% × 100 ms = 1.5 carrier-seconds per second spent stuck in the kernel.
Demand on carriers becomes 3 + 1.5 = 4.5 carrier-seconds per second against 4 available, 112% of capacity, so queues grow without bound.
Moving the lookups to a separate blocking pool takes the carriers back to 3 of 4, 75% busy, and the queues drain.
numbers.result: A blocking call on just 1% of requests pushes the carriers from 75% to 112% of capacity here; keep blocking work off carriers.

india.title: How one runtime documents pinning
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Oracle’s documentation for Java virtual threads explains that a virtual thread is mounted on a platform carrier thread and unmounted when it blocks, freeing the carrier to run another virtual thread. It cannot be unmounted while pinned: when it runs code inside a synchronized block or method, or runs a native method or foreign function. The documentation notes that pinning does not make an application incorrect but can hinder scalability. From JDK 24 (JEP 491), synchronized code no longer pins; native methods and foreign functions still do.

pitfalls.trap: “We switched to async, so it scales now.”
pitfalls.say: “Waiting got cheap; I’d still check for blocking calls and long CPU work on the carriers.”

pitfalls.trap: “A mutex is fine inside an async function.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if it’s released before any await; otherwise I’d use the runtime’s async lock.”

takeaways: A runtime runs many tasks on a few carrier threads.
Stackful tasks suspend anywhere; stackless ones only at awaits.
Blocking calls and held locks stall a carrier for every task on it.
Lightweight tasks make waiting cheap, not CPU work.

interactive.title: Why did the whole service freeze?
interactive.prompt: An async service runs on 2 carrier threads. Two requests arrive that each call a library function doing a blocking DNS lookup that takes 5 s because the resolver is down. Hundreds of other requests are queued.

choices.label: Both carriers are blocked in the kernel, so no task runs for 5 s
choices.feedback: Right: blocking calls hold their carriers, and only two exist.

choices.label: Only the two lookup requests wait; the others continue normally
choices.feedback: That would be true only if the lookups yielded to the runtime or ran on a separate pool.

choices.label: The runtime preempts the lookups after a time slice and moves on
choices.feedback: A thread blocked in a system call cannot be preempted by a user-space runtime.

interactive.reveal: Run blocking calls on a dedicated blocking pool or use a non-blocking resolver. Then the two lookups wait on their own threads while the carriers keep serving everyone else.

seeAlso.why: Event loops and readiness are the layer under every runtime
Choosing processes, threads or async I/O for a service
Kernel threads are what carrier threads are made of

title: Diagnosing a Slow Machine: Load, CPU Time and iowait
objectives: Check utilisation, saturation and errors for each resource in a fixed order
Read load average, CPU time categories and steal time correctly
Tell a CPU-bound, I/O-bound and memory-starved machine apart

cards.title: A checklist beats guessing
cards.body: For every resource (CPUs, memory, disks, network, and limits such as descriptors or a cgroup quota) ask three questions: how busy is it (utilisation), is work queueing for it (saturation), and is it reporting errors. Working through the list in the same order each time finds the bottleneck faster than staring at whichever graph looks worst, and it rules resources out as well as in.

cards.title: Misconception: load average is CPU usage
cards.body: On Linux the load average counts tasks that are runnable or in uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting for disk or a network file system), averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. A load of 16 on a 16-core machine can mean every core is busy, or that the CPUs are idle and 16 threads are stuck waiting for a slow disk. Compare load with core count and then look at CPU time categories before deciding which one it is.

cards.title: Worked example: three machines with a load of 12
cards.body: Same number, three different problems, on 8-core machines.
steps: Machine A: CPU 98% user time, run queue about 12: CPU-bound, four threads always waiting for a core
Machine B: CPU 85% idle and iowait, 10 threads in disk wait: I/O-bound, more cores would not help
Machine C: CPU 30% user, 40% steal: a virtual machine whose host is giving its CPU time to other tenants
Each needs a different fix: more CPU or less work for A, faster or fewer I/Os for B, a different host or instance size for C
The load average alone could not tell them apart; CPU categories and per-resource saturation could

cards.title: Trap: reading iowait as a busy CPU
cards.body: iowait is time a CPU sat idle while at least one task was waiting on disk I/O. It is idle time with a label, not work. High iowait means storage is the thing to look at, and it can drop to zero when an unrelated CPU-heavy job starts, even though the disk is just as slow. Check the disks’ own utilisation and queue length rather than trusting iowait’s size.

cards.title: Steal time and memory pressure
cards.body: On a virtual machine, steal time is time the guest wanted to run but the hypervisor ran something else; persistent steal means the instance is not getting the CPU it was sold or has used up burst credits. Memory problems look different again: little free memory is normal because of page cache, but rising major page faults, swap activity or reclaim stalls mean the working set no longer fits.

questions.prompt: A 16-core database server shows a load average of 20, but CPU is 80% idle. What is the most likely situation?

choices.label: The load counter is stale and should be ignored
Many threads are blocked waiting for disk I/O
Twenty processes are using a core at full speed
The server has more cores than the load can use

questions.explanation: Linux counts tasks in uninterruptible sleep, typically disk waits, in the load average, so a high load with idle CPUs points at storage. The counter is live, twenty CPU-bound processes would show the CPUs busy, and spare cores do not raise the load.

questions.prompt: A server’s iowait falls from 40% to 5% after a CPU-heavy batch job starts on it. Disk latency is unchanged. What happened?

choices.label: The batch job warmed the page cache, so disk waits stopped
The CPUs became fast enough to hide the disk latency
Idle time once labelled iowait is now used by the batch job
The kernel lowered the disk’s priority behind the CPU work

questions.explanation: iowait is idle CPU time while I/O is outstanding; once the CPUs have other work, that time becomes busy time instead, even though disk waits continue. A warmer cache would have reduced disk latency, faster CPUs do not change storage, and nothing reprioritised the disk.

questions.prompt: A virtual machine’s latency doubled overnight. Its own CPU usage is unchanged at 45%, but steal time rose from 1% to 30%. Which action addresses the cause?

choices.label: Tune the application’s thread pool size downward
Move to another host or a non-burstable instance type
Add swap so the guest can use more memory
Increase the guest’s disk read-ahead setting

questions.explanation: Steal time is CPU the hypervisor withheld, from noisy neighbours or exhausted burst credits, so the fix is outside the guest. Thread pool tuning, swap and disk read-ahead change nothing about how much CPU the host grants.

questions.prompt: A web host is slow. CPU is 35% busy with no throttling, disks are 5% busy, and memory shows 200 MB free of 32 GB, most of the rest as page cache. What should you check next?

choices.label: Network and limits such as descriptors and connection pools
Free memory, since 200 MB is dangerously low
The CPUs again, because 35% hides a saturated core
The disks again, because 5% is suspiciously low

questions.explanation: CPU, disk and memory look healthy: page cache is reclaimable, so low free memory is normal. Moving on to the remaining resources, network and software limits, is how the checklist works. A single saturated core is possible, but per-core figures would be checked as part of CPU, which showed no saturation here.

questions.prompt: A single-threaded process is pinned at 100% of one core on a 16-core machine. Roughly what overall CPU utilisation does the machine report?
assumptions: Overall utilisation is averaged across all cores
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a machine-wide 6% can hide a process that is completely CPU-bound, so check per-core and per-thread figures before calling the CPU idle.

questions.prompt: Choose the next step for a slow reporting server.
constraints: One disk at 100% utilisation with a queue of 30 requests

approaches.label: Investigate the disk workload
approaches.description: Find what issues the I/O and reduce or spread it

approaches.label: Upgrade to a 16-core machine
Raise the process priority
approaches.description: Give the reporting process more scheduler share

rationaleOptions.label: High load with mostly iowait means threads wait on storage
A saturated disk with a deep queue is the bottleneck
A load of 14 on 8 cores shows the CPUs are overloaded
More scheduler share speeds up waiting threads

rationaleConflicts.r3: Most of the load is threads in disk wait, and the CPUs are 80% idle or waiting.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Threads blocked on I/O are not waiting for a CPU, so priority does nothing for them.

questions.explanation: Every signal points at the disk: saturation (queue of 30), utilisation (100%) and load made of disk waits. Find the queries or jobs driving the I/O, add caching or indexes, or move to faster storage.

flashcards.back: For each resource check Utilisation, Saturation (queueing) and Errors.

flashcards.front: What does Linux load average count?
flashcards.back: Runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (often disk waits).
iowait: idle CPU while I/O is pending. Steal: time the hypervisor gave your vCPU to someone else.

mechanism.title: A repeatable pass over one slow machine
steps: Start with the symptom and the time it began, so later metrics can be compared with a normal period rather than judged in isolation.
CPU: overall and per-core utilisation; time split into user, system, iowait, steal and idle; run queue length or load against core count; and, in containers, throttled periods.
Memory: available memory (counting reclaimable cache), major page faults, swap in and out, and reclaim or pressure-stall figures. Low free memory alone is not a problem.
Disks: utilisation, queue depth and average latency per device. A device near 100% busy with a growing queue is saturated, whatever the CPU says.
Network: throughput against link capacity, retransmits and drops. Then software limits: descriptor counts, connection pools, thread pools and locks, which saturate without any hardware graph moving.
For each resource note utilisation, saturation and errors, move on when it is clean, and stop at the first resource that is saturated; then confirm by relieving it and watching the symptom.

useWhen: Use the same checklist on every incident so nothing is skipped under pressure.
Use CPU categories and per-device figures to explain a high load average.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating machine-wide CPU percentage as proof the CPU is fine.
Avoid reading low free memory or high iowait as the cause by itself.

rows: Available memory, swap and page faults

numbers.title: Reading one snapshot
assumptions: An 8-core VM over one minute: 0.9 runnable tasks per core on average, CPU time 40% user, 5% system, 15% iowait, 25% steal, 15% idle (illustrative)
steps: Runnable work: 0.9 × 8 ≈ 7 tasks, about one per core, so the run queue alone looks fine.
Work the guest got done: 40% + 5% = 45% of its CPU time.
Time it wanted but did not get: 25% steal, more than half as much again as the 45% of work actually done.
iowait of 15% is idle time; disks need checking, but steal is the larger loss.
numbers.result: Here a quarter of the VM’s CPU time is withheld by the host; fixing that (a different host or instance) is worth more than tuning the application.

india.title: Where the numbers come from
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The proc_loadavg(5) manual page describes the first three fields of /proc/loadavg as the number of jobs in the run queue (state R) or waiting for disk I/O (state D), averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. The proc_stat(5) page lists the CPU time categories in /proc/stat, including iowait, which it notes is not reliable, and steal, the time spent in other operating systems when running in a virtualised environment.

pitfalls.trap: “Load is 20, so we need more CPUs.”
pitfalls.say: “Load includes disk waits; I’d check CPU idle and disk queues before adding cores.”

pitfalls.trap: “Free memory is only 200 MB, we’re out of RAM.”
pitfalls.say: “Page cache is reclaimable; I’d look at available memory, swap and major faults.”

takeaways: Check utilisation, saturation and errors for every resource in order.
Linux load includes disk waits, not just CPU demand.
iowait is idle time; check the disks directly.
Steal time means the host, not your code, is taking the CPU.

interactive.title: What kind of slow is this?
interactive.prompt: A 4-core VM is slow. Load average is 4.2, CPU shows 50% user, 2% iowait, 45% steal and 3% idle. Disks are 10% busy.

choices.label: The host is withholding CPU from this VM
choices.feedback: Right: 45% steal means the guest wanted to run and the hypervisor did not let it.

choices.label: The application is CPU-bound and needs optimising
choices.feedback: User time is only 50%; nearly as much time is stolen as is used.

choices.label: The disk is saturated and threads wait for it
choices.feedback: iowait is 2% and disks are 10% busy, so storage is not the issue.

interactive.reveal: The load is about one per core and the guest is barely idle, yet half its CPU time is stolen. Moving to a dedicated or larger instance, or checking burst credits, addresses it; profiling the application would not.

seeAlso.why: Run queues and scheduling explain what load measures
Container throttling is another hidden CPU limit to check
Start from the SLI that broke, then walk the resources

title: Memory-Mapped Files and Zero-Copy I/O
objectives: Explain how mapping a file differs from reading it into a buffer
Count the copies in a read-then-write path and what sendfile or splice remove
Know when mmap is the wrong tool, especially for databases and changing files

cards.title: A file that looks like memory
cards.body: mmap maps a range of a file into the process’s address space. Nothing is read at first; touching a page causes a page fault, and the kernel loads that page from the page cache, reading it from disk if needed. Reads and writes then go straight to page cache pages, with no read or write call and no copy into a private buffer. Several processes mapping the same file share the same physical pages.

cards.title: Worked example: counting copies when serving a file
cards.body: A server sends a 1 GB file to a client.
steps: Disk to page cache: done by the device with DMA, no CPU copy
read(): the CPU copies 1 GB from the page cache into the program’s buffer
write() to the socket: the CPU copies 1 GB from the buffer into socket buffers, then the network card sends it with DMA
Total: 2 GB of CPU copying and two system calls per chunk
sendfile(): the kernel moves page cache pages to the socket directly; no data passes through user space, and with gather-capable network cards no CPU copy remains

cards.title: Trap: a mapped file shrinks under you
cards.body: If another process truncates a file while you have it mapped, touching a page that is now past the end of the file raises SIGBUS, which by default kills the process. With read you would simply get a short read. Map only files you control, or that change by appending in a way you coordinate, and treat log files or user uploads that may be truncated as read-call territory.

cards.title: Misconception: mmap is always faster than read
cards.body: Each first touch of a page costs a page fault, and mapping, unmapping and updating page tables have their own costs, especially when many threads share the mapping. For one sequential pass over a large file, read with a large buffer often matches or beats mmap. mmap helps most for random access to data that stays hot and for sharing read-only data between processes.

cards.title: Why many databases avoid mmap for writes
cards.body: With a writable shared mapping, the kernel decides when dirty pages are written back, so the program cannot guarantee that its log reaches disk before the data pages it describes, which is the ordering crash recovery depends on. I/O errors arrive as signals rather than return codes, and page eviction is outside the program’s control. Engines that manage their own buffer pool and call write and fsync keep that control.

questions.prompt: A process maps a 10 GB file and reads 100 random pages from it. Roughly how much is read from disk, assuming nothing is cached?

choices.label: All 10 GB at the moment mmap is called
Only the pages touched, plus any read-ahead
Nothing, since mapped files live in RAM
Half the file, chosen by the kernel up front

questions.explanation: mmap only sets up the mapping; pages are loaded on first touch through page faults, and the kernel may read a little extra ahead. Nothing is loaded at map time, mapped data still comes from disk the first time, and there is no fixed share loaded up front.

questions.prompt: A file server uses read into a buffer and then write to the socket. CPU profiles show most time copying memory. What change removes those copies?

choices.label: Use a larger buffer so there are fewer read calls
Read the file with direct I/O to skip the page cache
Send from the page cache with sendfile or splice
Compress the file before writing it to the socket

questions.explanation: sendfile and splice move data from the page cache to the socket inside the kernel, so the two copies through user space disappear. A larger buffer reduces calls but not bytes copied, direct I/O lets the disk write straight into the user buffer but still copies from it into the socket, and compression adds CPU work.

questions.prompt: A log indexer maps active log files. Occasionally it dies with SIGBUS right after the logs are rotated by truncation. Why?

choices.label: The mapped pages were reclaimed and could not be reloaded
The file grew past the size of the mapping it had created
Two processes mapped the file and corrupted each other
It touched pages past the new end of the truncated file

questions.explanation: Accessing a mapped page beyond the end of the file raises SIGBUS, and truncation moved the end. Clean pages are simply reloaded from the file when needed; growth past the mapping just leaves the new data unmapped; and shared mappings see the same pages consistently.

questions.prompt: Why do many database engines avoid writing their data files through a shared memory mapping?

choices.label: Mapped writes cannot be made durable with any call
The kernel chooses when dirty pages reach disk
Mapped files are limited to the size of physical memory
Writes through a mapping skip the page cache entirely

questions.explanation: Crash recovery needs the log to reach disk before the data pages it describes, and with a writable mapping the kernel can write back any dirty page at any time. Mapped writes can be flushed with msync; files larger than RAM can be mapped; and mapped writes go to page cache pages, they do not skip them.

questions.prompt: A server sends 2 GB/s of files using read and write. Roughly how many GB/s of CPU memory copying does switching to sendfile remove, assuming a gather-capable network card?
assumptions: Disk and network transfers use DMA, not the CPU
read and write each copy every byte once
questions.explanation: Sanity check: at roughly 5 to 10 GB/s of copy bandwidth per core (illustrative), 4 GB/s is about half a core or more, plus extra cache pollution, which is why file servers and proxies use zero-copy paths.

questions.prompt: A server sends an uncached file to a client with read and then write. Put the movements of its bytes in order.

items.label: write copies them from that buffer into the socket’s send buffer
The disk controller transfers the bytes into the page cache by DMA
The network card fetches them from the send buffer by DMA
read copies them from the page cache into the program’s buffer

questions.explanation: Two DMA transfers and two CPU copies; sendfile keeps the bytes in the kernel and drops both CPU copies.

flashcards.back: Maps file pages into the address space; data is loaded on first touch via page faults.

flashcards.front: Copies in read + write to a socket?
flashcards.back: Two CPU copies through user space; sendfile or splice remove them.
Raised when touching a mapped page past the file’s current end, for example after truncation.

mechanism.title: What the kernel does for mapped and zero-copy I/O
steps: mmap creates a virtual memory area describing a file range and its permissions. No data moves and no physical pages are assigned yet.

On first access the CPU faults. The kernel finds the page in the page cache, or reads it from disk (often with read-ahead), then installs a page table entry pointing at that page-cache page and retries the instruction.

For shared mappings, writes dirty the page-cache page directly; the kernel’s write-back later writes it to disk, or msync forces it. Private mappings copy a page on its first write so changes stay in the process.
With read and write, the kernel copies between the page cache and a user buffer, and again into socket buffers. Each copy touches every byte through the CPU caches.

sendfile passes page-cache pages to the socket inside the kernel. With network cards that can gather from scattered pages, the card reads the data directly and the CPU never copies it; splice offers the same idea between pipes and other descriptors.

Zero-copy paths only work when the kernel can send the bytes as they are. If the application must transform them, such as encrypting TLS in user space or compressing, the data has to pass through user space, unless the kernel performs that work (for example kernel TLS).

useWhen: Use mmap for random reads of large, stable files and for sharing read-only data between processes.
Use sendfile or splice for serving unchanged file bytes to sockets.
avoidWhen: Avoid mmap for files that other processes may truncate.
Avoid writable mappings where you must control the order of writes to disk.

rows: Small files or data that must change
One, from the user buffer to the socket

numbers.title: Copy cost at file-server scale
assumptions: A server sends 1.25 GB/s, a 10 Gbit/s link at full rate (illustrative)
About 8 GB/s of memory copy per core (illustrative)
steps: read + write: 2 copies × 1.25 GB/s = 2.5 GB/s of CPU copying.
At 8 GB/s per core that is 2.5 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.31 of a core, before counting system calls and cache misses.
With sendfile and a gather-capable card: 0 GB/s of CPU copying, leaving system call and TCP costs.
At 100 Gbit/s (12.5 GB/s) the read + write path would need 25 GB/s of copying, about 3 cores just moving bytes.
numbers.result: Zero-copy saves about a third of a core at 10 Gbit/s and about three cores at 100 Gbit/s in this example; the faster the link, the more it matters.

india.title: What the manual pages promise
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The sendfile(2) manual page states that because the copying is done within the kernel, sendfile is more efficient than the combination of read and write, which would require transferring data to and from user space. The mmap(2) page lists SIGBUS for an attempted access to a page of the buffer that lies beyond the end of the mapped file, and SIGSEGV for a write into a region mapped read-only, the two signals a mapped-file reader must be prepared for.

pitfalls.trap: “mmap is zero-copy, so it’s always fastest.”
pitfalls.say: “It saves a copy but adds page faults; for one sequential pass I’d benchmark read with a large buffer.”

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s mmap the data file and let the OS handle durability.”
pitfalls.say: “The kernel picks the write-back order; I’d keep a log written with write and fsync.”

takeaways: mmap loads pages on first touch and shares them with the page cache.
read + write costs two CPU copies; sendfile can cost none.
Truncating a mapped file turns accesses into SIGBUS.
Writable mappings give up control of write-back order.

interactive.title: Which path for a static file server?
interactive.prompt: A server sends large, unchanging video files over plain HTTP at 40 Gbit/s and is CPU-bound. Profiles show time in memory copies and system calls.

choices.label: Send each file with sendfile so the bytes never enter user space
choices.feedback: Right: the kernel hands page-cache pages to the socket with no user-space copies.

choices.label: Map each file and write from the mapping to the socket
choices.feedback: This removes one copy, but the copy into socket buffers remains and page faults are added.

choices.label: Read with a 16 MB buffer to cut the number of system calls
choices.feedback: Fewer calls, but both copies of every byte remain.

interactive.reveal: At 40 Gbit/s (5 GB/s) read + write copies 10 GB/s, more than a core of pure copying. sendfile removes it; if the files must be encrypted, kernel TLS keeps the zero-copy path where the platform supports it.

seeAlso.why: The page cache is what both mmap and sendfile operate on
Page faults and page tables make mapped files possible
Why databases control write order with a log and fsync

title: Service-to-Service Authentication: mTLS and Workload Identity
objectives: Explain why network location is not an identity
Describe what mutual TLS proves and what it leaves to authorisation
Design short-lived, automatically rotated workload certificates

cards.title: Being inside the network is not an identity
cards.body: Many systems trust any request that comes from an internal address. Then one compromised container, laptop on the VPN or misrouted load balancer can call every internal service. Zero trust, as NIST SP 800-207 describes it, removes that implicit trust: each request is authenticated and authorised on its own, wherever it comes from. Firewalls and private subnets still help, but they limit where traffic can reach. They do not prove who sent it.

cards.title: Mutual TLS: both sides show a certificate
cards.body: In ordinary TLS only the server proves who it is. In mutual TLS (mTLS) the server also asks for a client certificate, and the client proves it holds the matching private key during the handshake. The receiver checks that the certificate chains to a CA it trusts for workloads. It then reads the identity from the certificate, usually a URI such as spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api in the subject alternative name. That identity becomes the input to an access policy.

cards.title: Worked example: payments calls the ledger
cards.body: The payments service must create ledger entries. Nothing else may.
steps: The platform verifies the payments workload (which cluster, namespace and service account it runs as) and issues a 24-hour certificate naming it
Payments opens TLS to the ledger and checks the ledger’s certificate chains to the internal CA and names the ledger
The ledger asks for a client certificate, verifies the chain and the key proof, and reads the identity spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api
The ledger’s policy allows that identity to POST /entries and nothing else; every other identity gets 403
Payments renews at about half the lifetime, so a failed renewal leaves 12 hours to fix it before anything breaks

cards.title: Misconception: mTLS is authorisation
cards.body: mTLS answers “which workload is calling?” It does not answer “may it do this?”. A ledger that accepts any certificate from the internal CA still lets a compromised reporting service write entries. Pair mTLS with a per-endpoint policy keyed on the workload identity. The certificate also names the service, not the customer. When the end user matters, pass their identity separately as a signed, short-lived token, and check both.

cards.title: Trap: long-lived certificates nobody rotates
cards.body: A two-year certificate installed by hand fails twice. Its private key stays useful to a thief for months, and one day it expires and takes the service down because nobody remembered. Short lifetimes (hours to days) with automatic issuance and renewal fix both. Alert when any certificate is within a quarter of its lifetime of expiry and has not renewed. Keep the CA’s own key in a KMS or HSM, because whoever holds it can mint any identity.

questions.prompt: An attacker gets code running in one container of a cluster whose services trust any request from an internal address. What can it most likely do?

choices.label: Call internal services as if it were any trusted caller
Little, because internal traffic is already encrypted with TLS
Read only the files of the container it compromised
Reach the internet but none of the internal services

questions.explanation: Trust based on source address means any foothold inside inherits that trust. Encryption hides traffic from eavesdroppers but does not authenticate the sender. A foothold is not confined to its own files when the network itself grants access, and egress rules do not stop east-west calls.

questions.prompt: In mutual TLS, what does the server learn that ordinary TLS does not tell it?

choices.label: That the connection is encrypted in both directions
The client’s identity, proven with its private key
Which end user is behind the calling service
That the client’s code has not been modified

questions.explanation: The extra step is the client certificate and the proof of its private key. Ordinary TLS already encrypts both directions. The certificate names the workload, not the end user, and it says nothing about whether the workload’s code was tampered with.

questions.prompt: The ledger accepts mTLS from any certificate signed by the internal workload CA. What is still missing?

choices.label: A second handshake for each request
Longer RSA keys in each workload certificate
Rules for which identities may call which endpoints
Encryption of the request body inside the TLS tunnel

questions.explanation: Authentication without authorisation lets every workload with a certificate call every endpoint. Extra handshakes, bigger keys and body encryption add cost but still let a compromised service make calls it should not.

questions.prompt: A fleet of 2,000 workloads uses 24-hour certificates, each renewed at half its lifetime. How many certificates does the CA issue per hour?
questions.workedAnswer: Each workload renews every 12 hours, so 2,000 / 12 ≈ 167 issuances per hour, about 4,000 a day.
questions.explanation: Design implication: renewing at half life doubles issuance compared with renewing at expiry (83 per hour), but leaves time to recover from a failed renewal.

questions.prompt: Order how a workload gets and uses its identity.

items.label: The workload presents it in an mTLS handshake
The platform verifies where the workload runs (attestation)
The workload renews the certificate before it expires
The platform issues a short-lived certificate naming the workload
The receiver checks the chain and maps the identity to a policy

questions.explanation: Identity is issued only after the platform has checked what the workload is. It is then used and checked, and renewed before expiry.

questions.prompt: Renewal is automated either way. Why prefer 24-hour service certificates over 2-year ones?

choices.label: Short certificates make each handshake faster
Clients refuse internal certificates older than a day
Revocation lists only work for short certificates
A stolen private key stops being useful within a day

questions.explanation: Short lifetimes limit how long a stolen key works without relying on revocation, which clients often check poorly. Handshake speed does not depend on lifetime. No client rule rejects day-old certificates, and revocation lists apply to any lifetime.

flashcards.back: Implicit trust based on network location: each request is authenticated and authorised.

flashcards.front: What extra thing does mTLS prove?
flashcards.back: The client holds the private key for a certificate naming its identity.
A stolen key expires quickly, and automated renewal is exercised all the time.

mechanism.title: How workload identity works end to end
steps: Attest: before issuing anything, the platform checks facts it controls, such as the node, the cluster, the namespace and the service account. Do not trust anything the workload merely claims about itself.

Issue: a workload CA signs a short-lived certificate whose subject alternative name carries a structured identity (for example a SPIFFE ID). The private key is generated on the workload and never leaves it.

Authenticate: every connection uses mTLS. Each side checks the peer’s chain against the workload trust bundle and reads the peer identity. A sidecar proxy or a library can do this so application code stays simple.
Authorise: a policy maps caller identity to allowed operations, such as payments may POST /entries on the ledger. Deny by default, and keep policies in version control with review.

Propagate the user: when a request acts for a customer, forward a signed, short-lived user token alongside the service identity. The receiver checks both: is this service allowed, and is this user allowed?
Rotate and observe: renew at about half the lifetime, alert on renewal failures and near-expiry certificates, and log the caller identity for every denied request.

useWhen: Many services call each other inside a cluster or across clouds
Compliance or a past incident demands proof of which service made each call
avoidWhen: A single service with one database and no internal callers, where the cost outweighs the gain
Calls from customers’ browsers, which should use user tokens rather than client certificates

rows: Any foothold inside inherits the trust
Keys leak, rarely rotate and are copied between services
Which workload holds the private key
Needs a CA, rotation and an authorisation policy
Which service the issuer vouched for
Bearer token: replayable until it expires unless bound to the connection

numbers.title: What short lifetimes cost the CA
assumptions: About 5 ms of CA signing time per certificate (illustrative)
steps: Issuance: 2,000 × 2 renewals a day = 4,000 certificates a day, or about 167 an hour
Signing load: 4,000 × 5 ms = 20 seconds of CA work per day, which is negligible
Exposure: a stolen key works for at most 24 hours, against up to 730 days for a 2-year certificate
Failure budget: renewing at half life leaves 12 hours to notice and fix a broken renewal before outages start
numbers.result: The CA load is trivial, and the window in which a stolen key is useful shrinks by a factor of about 700.

india.title: NIST SP 800-207 tenets of zero trust
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture, 2020) lists tenets that match this design. All communication is secured regardless of network location. Access to each resource is granted per session. Access is decided by dynamic policy that includes the identity of the requester. Authentication and authorisation are dynamic and strictly enforced before access is allowed. Google’s BeyondProd paper describes the same idea applied to its own production services: mutual authentication between services, and service identity in place of network location.

pitfalls.trap: Accepting any certificate from the internal CA as permission to call anything
pitfalls.say: mTLS tells me who is calling. A deny-by-default policy per endpoint tells me whether they may.

pitfalls.trap: Hand-installed certificates with multi-year lifetimes
pitfalls.say: Automate issuance and renew at half life, so expiry is routine instead of an outage.

pitfalls.trap: Dropping the end user’s identity at the first internal hop
pitfalls.say: Forward a signed user token so downstream services can still enforce per-customer rules.

takeaways: Network location limits reach; it does not prove identity
mTLS proves which workload holds a key, and a policy decides what it may do
Short-lived, automatically renewed certificates shrink the value of a stolen key
Carry the end user’s identity separately from the service identity

interactive.title: Who gets in?
interactive.prompt: The ledger requires mTLS from the internal CA, and its policy lets only the payments identity POST /entries. An attacker controls the reports service, which has a valid certificate for its own identity.

choices.label: Reports connects, but POST /entries is refused by policy
choices.feedback: Right: authentication succeeds and authorisation denies it.

choices.label: Reports can post entries because its certificate is valid
choices.feedback: A valid certificate only says who it is; the policy does not list reports.

choices.label: Reports can post entries after copying the payments certificate
choices.feedback: The certificate is public. Without the payments private key the handshake fails.

interactive.reveal: Identity plus a deny-by-default policy contains a compromised service to what it was already allowed to do.

seeAlso.why: The TLS handshake that mTLS extends with a client certificate
Secrets managers issue short-lived credentials using the same workload identity
Private networking limits reach, which complements identity checks

title: Encryption at Rest and Envelope Encryption
objectives: Say what storage encryption protects against and what it does not
Explain envelope encryption with data keys and a KMS
Plan key rotation and crypto-shredding without re-encrypting everything

cards.title: What encryption at rest protects, and what it does not
cards.body: Disk, volume and database storage encryption protect against someone who gets the bytes without going through your system. Examples are a stolen or discarded drive, a snapshot shared to the wrong account, or a backup tape left in a taxi. They do not protect against an attacker who queries through the application or holds its database credentials. The storage layer decrypts for every authorised read, so it decrypts for them too. To protect a field from people with database access, encrypt it in the application with a key the database cannot use.

cards.title: Envelope encryption: a key for the data, a key for the key
cards.body: Generate a random data key (DEK), encrypt the data locally with an AEAD cipher such as AES-256-GCM, then ask the key management service (KMS) to encrypt the DEK under a key-encryption key (KEK) that never leaves the KMS. Store the wrapped DEK next to the ciphertext. To read, send the wrapped DEK to the KMS, get the plaintext DEK back and decrypt locally. Bulk data never crosses the network to the KMS. That matters because KMS calls take small inputs: AWS KMS Encrypt accepts up to 4,096 bytes, and Cloud KMS up to 64 KiB.

cards.title: Worked example: encrypting a 2 GB backup
cards.body: A nightly database backup must be unreadable to anyone who copies the file but lacks KMS permission.
steps: Ask the KMS for a new 256-bit data key; it returns the key in plain form and wrapped under the backup KEK
Encrypt the backup locally in chunks with AES-256-GCM, using a unique nonce for each chunk
Write the wrapped data key, a few hundred bytes, into the backup header
Erase the plain data key from memory once the backup is written
To restore, the KMS unwraps the key only after checking the caller’s permission, and it logs the call

cards.title: Misconception: rotating the master key means re-encrypting all data
cards.body: When a KMS rotates a KEK, it creates a new key version and keeps the old versions to unwrap DEKs they protected. New DEKs are wrapped under the new version. Optionally you re-wrap old DEKs, which means rewriting a few hundred bytes per object, not the object itself. Re-encrypting the data is needed only when a DEK itself may have been exposed. Rotation therefore limits how much data any one key version protects, at almost no cost.

cards.title: Trap: the key stored next to the data
cards.body: Encrypting a column while keeping the key in the same database, or in a config file in the repository, means one leak hands over both. Keep KEKs in a KMS or HSM with an access policy separate from the data’s, and audit every unwrap. The reverse danger is just as real: deleting a KEK destroys every DEK it wrapped. KMSs make you schedule deletion with a waiting period (AWS KMS: 7 to 30 days) so a mistake can be cancelled.

questions.prompt: The cloud provider encrypts a database volume at rest. An attacker steals the app’s database password. What does the volume encryption do for you?

choices.label: It blocks the queries, since the attacker lacks the disk key
Little: the database decrypts rows for any valid login
It returns rows still encrypted, so they are unreadable
It forces a second login using the KMS key

questions.explanation: Storage encryption is transparent to authorised readers. A valid database login is an authorised reader, so the queries succeed and return plain rows. The disk key is used by the storage layer, not requested from clients, and the KMS is not involved in each SQL login.

questions.prompt: Why encrypt a 2 GB file with a local data key instead of sending the file to the KMS?

choices.label: A local key is stronger than a key held in the KMS
Local encryption removes the need to store any key
KMS calls take small inputs, and bulk data stays local
The data key can then be stored unwrapped beside the file

questions.explanation: KMS encrypt calls are limited to kilobytes, and shipping gigabytes to a central service would be slow and costly. Key strength is the same, since both are 256-bit. You still store the data key, but wrapped by the KMS, never unwrapped next to the data.

questions.prompt: The KMS rotates its master key every year. What happens to data encrypted three years ago?

choices.label: It must be re-encrypted before the rotation can finish
It becomes unreadable, which is the point of rotating
It stays readable, since old key versions unwrap old data keys
It is quietly re-encrypted in place by the storage layer

questions.explanation: Rotation adds a version and keeps the old ones for decryption. Nothing is re-encrypted unless you choose to re-wrap the data keys. Making old data unreadable is what key deletion does, not rotation.

questions.prompt: Each customer’s records are encrypted under that customer’s own data key. One customer asks to be erased, but copies sit in 40 backups. What does destroying their key do?

choices.label: Makes their records in all 40 backups unreadable
Shrinks the backups by removing their records
Has no effect until each backup is restored and edited
Also destroys other customers’ data in those backups

questions.explanation: Crypto-shredding makes the ciphertext useless wherever it is, without touching the backups. The bytes are still there, so the backups do not shrink. Other customers use different keys and are unaffected.

questions.prompt: A service writes 50 million objects a day and requests a new data key from the KMS for each. On average, how many KMS calls per second is that?
questions.workedAnswer: 50,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 579 calls per second on average, and peaks will be higher.
questions.explanation: Design implication: that load can approach a provider’s request quotas, so batch objects under one data key or cache data keys briefly with strict limits.

questions.prompt: Order a read of an envelope-encrypted record.

items.label: Decrypt the record locally with the returned data key
Send the wrapped data key to the KMS
Erase the plain data key from memory
Load the ciphertext and its wrapped data key
The KMS checks the caller’s permission and logs the request

questions.explanation: The KMS sees only the small wrapped key and decides whether to unwrap it. The bulk decryption happens locally.

flashcards.front: What does disk encryption not stop?
flashcards.back: Anyone who reads through the application or with valid database credentials.
Encrypt data with a local data key; encrypt that key under a KMS key that never leaves the KMS.
Destroying a key so every copy of the data it protected becomes unreadable.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5: Key Management

mechanism.title: Layers of encryption at rest and how keys flow
steps: Choose the threat first. Storage encryption covers lost media and stray snapshots. Application-level (field) encryption also covers database administrators, SQL injection that reads raw columns, and leaked database credentials, because the database never holds the key.

Generate a fresh data key per object, per file or per tenant, using the KMS or a CSPRNG. Encrypt with an AEAD cipher and a unique nonce, and bind context (such as the record id) as associated data so ciphertext cannot be swapped between rows.
Wrap the data key under a KEK in the KMS. The KEK’s access policy names which workloads may unwrap, and every unwrap is logged, which gives you an audit trail of who read what.
Rotate KEKs on a schedule. The KMS keeps old versions for unwrapping, so rotation is cheap. Re-wrap DEKs if policy requires, and re-encrypt data only if a DEK was exposed.
Choose the key granularity on purpose. One DEK per customer enables crypto-shredding: destroying it erases that customer’s data everywhere, including in backups you cannot edit.

Plan for KMS outages and costs. Cache unwrapped DEKs in memory for minutes, with a cap on how many objects each may encrypt. Treat KEK deletion as a destructive change: disable first, watch for failures, and only then schedule deletion.

useWhen: Data with legal or contractual protection, or held for many tenants
You need per-customer erasure that reaches backups
avoidWhen: Public or easily regenerated data, where key management adds risk without benefit
You would have to keep the KEK beside the data, which adds complexity without separation

rows: Anyone reading through the database or app
Database admins and leaked DB credentials
A compromised app server that can unwrap keys
The whole server side, including the operator
Lost keys, and features such as server-side search

numbers.title: KMS calls for 50 million objects a day
assumptions: One data key per object, or one per batch of 1,000 objects
Peak traffic about 3 times the average (illustrative)
steps: Per object: 50,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 579 calls per second to KMS, on average
At a 3× peak that is about 1,740 calls per second, which can hit request quotas and adds a network round trip to every write
Per batch of 1,000: 579 / 1,000 ≈ 0.58 calls per second, about 50,000 calls a day
Trade-off: one key then protects 1,000 objects, so crypto-shredding a single object is no longer possible
numbers.result: Batching data keys cuts KMS traffic about 1,000-fold. Pick the batch boundary to match what you may need to erase on its own, such as one customer.

india.title: AWS KMS and Google Cloud KMS on envelope encryption
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The AWS KMS documentation defines envelope encryption as encrypting plaintext with a data key and then encrypting the data key under another key. Its Encrypt operation accepts at most 4,096 bytes with a symmetric key, which is why bulk data is encrypted locally. Google Cloud’s guidance says Cloud KMS was designed to manage key-encryption keys, so its Encrypt and Decrypt input is capped at 64 KiB. It recommends generating data keys locally and storing them wrapped next to the data they protect. AWS requires a waiting period of 7 to 30 days before a KMS key is actually deleted.

pitfalls.trap: Claiming the database is safe because “it is encrypted at rest”
pitfalls.say: Storage encryption covers lost media. For people with database access I need field encryption with a key the database cannot use.

pitfalls.trap: Deleting an old KMS key to tidy up
pitfalls.say: Disable it first and watch for failures; deletion destroys every data key it wrapped.

pitfalls.trap: Reusing a nonce with AES-GCM because the key is per object
pitfalls.say: A per-object key with a fresh random nonce per encryption avoids nonce reuse, which would break GCM.

takeaways: Storage encryption protects media, not data read through the system
Envelope encryption keeps bulk data local and keys in the KMS
KEK rotation is cheap because old versions keep unwrapping
Per-customer data keys make erasure reach backups through crypto-shredding

interactive.title: What does deleting the key do?
interactive.prompt: An engineer schedules deletion of the KMS key that wraps every data key for the orders database, thinking it is unused. The waiting period is 30 days.

choices.label: If nobody cancels, all order data becomes unreadable for good
choices.feedback: Right: every data key it wrapped can no longer be unwrapped.

choices.label: Orders stay readable, because the data keys are cached
choices.feedback: Caches expire within minutes; after that, nothing can unwrap the data keys.

choices.label: The KMS re-wraps the data keys under a default key
choices.feedback: No KMS does this. Deletion is final once the waiting period ends.

interactive.reveal: Disable the key first and alert on decryption failures during the waiting period; that turns a silent disaster into a cancelled change.

seeAlso.why: AEAD and key types underpin the data keys used here
Secrets managers and KMSs share the same access-policy and audit model
Backups need a key strategy, or a restore can fail when you need it

title: Defending Login: Credential Stuffing, Lockouts and Enumeration
objectives: Recognise credential stuffing and why per-IP limits miss it
Choose throttling and step-up challenges over hard lockouts
Remove account-enumeration leaks from login, sign-up and reset flows

cards.title: Credential stuffing replays passwords that work elsewhere
cards.body: People reuse passwords, and billions of username and password pairs from other sites’ breaches circulate. In credential stuffing an attacker replays those pairs against your login, usually one attempt per account, spread across thousands of IP addresses. Only a small fraction succeed. The figures here are illustrative: 0.5% of 10 million attempts is still 50,000 accounts taken over. Because each address and each account sees only a few attempts, limits keyed only on IP or only on account barely notice.

cards.title: Hard lockouts hand attackers a denial of service
cards.body: Locking an account for a day after five failures stops guessing against that account. It also lets anyone who knows a username lock its owner out, and a script can do that to every user. Prefer per-account throttling that grows the delay with each failure, then a step-up check such as a second factor or a bot challenge, plus a notification to the owner. NIST SP 800-63B-4 caps consecutive failed attempts on one account at 100 before stronger measures. That figure is a ceiling, not a target.

cards.title: Worked example: layered limits on one login endpoint
cards.body: A consumer app with 20 million accounts wants to slow attacks without locking out real users.
steps: Per source address or network: about 20 attempts per minute, which slows single noisy sources
Per account: after 5 failures add a growing delay or a challenge; after 100 consecutive failures require recovery
Across the site: watch the failure ratio, since a jump from 10% to 60% failed logins signals a stuffing run
On every new or changed password: reject ones found in breach corpuses, and force a reset for accounts whose current password is exposed
Offer MFA and passkeys, which make a correct password alone insufficient

cards.title: Misconception: “Wrong password” is a helpful message
cards.body: If the login says “No such user” for one input and “Wrong password” for another, it confirms which accounts exist. Status codes, redirects and response times leak the same thing. A server that skips the slow password hash for unknown users answers in milliseconds instead of a quarter of a second. Return one message and status, and hash a dummy password when the user is missing. Sign-up and reset leak too, so say “If an account exists, we have sent a link”.

cards.title: Trap: a CAPTCHA as the only defence
cards.body: Challenges raise the cost per attempt, but paid solving services and automation get through many of them cheaply. They also hurt accessibility, and they do nothing once the attacker holds a correct password. Use challenges as one layer, triggered by risk signals such as a new device, a burst of failures or a flagged network. Behind them, put MFA, breached-password checks and alerts on unusual success patterns.

questions.prompt: Failed logins jump to 400,000 an hour from 30,000 addresses. Each attempt pairs a different username with a different password, and about 0.5% succeed. What is happening?

choices.label: Credential stuffing with pairs leaked from another site
Password spraying: one common password tried on many accounts
Brute force: many guesses aimed at a single account
A broken password hash rejecting real users after a deploy

questions.explanation: Distinct username and password pairs with a small success rate are the signature of replayed breach data. Spraying reuses the same few passwords across accounts. Brute force concentrates on one account. A broken hash would make real users fail, not make strangers succeed.

questions.prompt: Why is “lock the account for 24 hours after 5 failures” risky for a public consumer app?

choices.label: Anyone who knows a username can lock its owner out
It lets attackers guess without limit once the lock ends
Locking an account resets its MFA enrolment
It slows the password hash for the other users

questions.explanation: The control punishes the account owner for an attacker’s actions, and it can be scripted across many usernames. Five guesses a day is a tight limit, not an unlimited one. Lockout state is unrelated to MFA enrolment and to hashing cost.

questions.prompt: Login answers in 5 ms for unknown usernames and in 250 ms for wrong passwords, with identical text. What leaks?

choices.label: The password hash, through the error text
Which usernames exist, through the timing
The salt, through the size of the response
Nothing useful, because the messages match

questions.explanation: Only known users go through the slow hash, so timing separates them. Hash a dummy password for unknown users. The text, size and salt are not exposed here; matching messages are not enough when timing differs.

questions.prompt: An attacker replays 10 million leaked pairs, and 0.5% are valid on your site (an illustrative rate). How many accounts are taken over if none use MFA?
questions.explanation: Design implication: small percentages of huge lists add up. MFA stops most of these takeovers, because a correct password alone is no longer enough.

questions.prompt: Order the responses as failed attempts pile up on one account.

items.label: Require a bot challenge or a second factor
Allow attempts at normal speed
Notify the owner and require recovery at the hard limit
Add a short delay that grows with each failure

questions.explanation: Escalate friction gradually, so real users who mistype are barely slowed while sustained guessing becomes expensive.

questions.prompt: When should a site check passwords against a list of breached passwords?

choices.label: When one is set or changed, and optionally at login
Once a year, by scanning the stored password hashes
Only after the owner reports the account hacked
Only for administrator accounts

questions.explanation: NIST requires checking new passwords against compromised lists. Checking at login lets you force a reset when a current password turns up in a new breach. Slow, salted hashes cannot be scanned in bulk, waiting for a report is too late, and stuffing targets ordinary users.

questions.prompt: A shopping app sees nightly stuffing runs from residential IP addresses. Support complains that the current lockout policy blocks real customers.
constraints: Attempts spread over tens of thousands of addresses
One or two attempts per account

approaches.label: Risk-based challenges, breached-password resets and optional MFA
Stricter per-IP limits of 5 attempts per hour
Lock each account after 2 failures

rationaleOptions.label: Distributed attempts slip under per-IP and per-account limits
Challenges only on risk keep friction low for real customers
Tighter IP limits stop attacks from residential addresses
Lockouts stop stuffing because each pair is tried once

rationaleConflicts.r3: Each address sends only a few attempts, and residential ranges are shared with real customers.
rationaleConflicts.r4: With one attempt per account a lockout never triggers, but it does lock out real users.

questions.explanation: Stuffing is distributed and low-and-slow, so defend with signals across the whole site and with factors beyond the password.

flashcards.back: Stuffing replays leaked pairs; spraying tries a few common passwords on many accounts.
They let anyone lock a known user out; throttle and step up instead.

flashcards.front: How do you stop timing enumeration?
flashcards.back: Same message and status, and hash a dummy password when the user does not exist.

sources.title: OWASP Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet
NIST SP 800-63B: Authentication and Lifecycle Management

mechanism.title: How a layered login defence works
steps: Measure first: record each attempt with account, source network, device signals and outcome. Without a failure-ratio baseline you cannot tell a stuffing run from a busy evening.
Rate-limit on several keys at once: source address, network block, account and the whole site. Each key catches a different attack shape, and none catches them all.

Escalate per account instead of locking. Add a growing delay, then a challenge or second factor, and notify the owner. Keep a hard ceiling (NIST: at most 100 consecutive failures) that leads to recovery, not a timed lock anyone can trigger.
Make responses uniform: the same message, status and similar timing for unknown users, wrong passwords and locked accounts. Apply the same rule to sign-up and password reset.

Check passwords against breach corpuses when they are set, and at login if you can do it privately (for example with a k-anonymity range query that sends only a hash prefix). Force a reset when a match appears.
Remove the password’s value: offer MFA and passkeys, and prompt users towards them after a risky login. A replayed password then fails at the second step.

useWhen: Any public login, sign-up or reset endpoint
