SERVFAIL only from validating resolvers, often after a key or provider change.

sources.title: RFC 4033: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements
RFC 5452: Measures for Making DNS More Resilient against Forged Answers
RFC 7858: DNS over Transport Layer Security (TLS)

mechanism.title: Where DNS can be attacked and what each defence covers
steps: A device’s stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which asks root, top-level and authoritative servers. Classic DNS sends each of these as unencrypted, unsigned UDP, so there are two places to attack: the hop from the device to its resolver, and the hops from the resolver to authoritative servers.

An attacker on the network path, such as a hostile Wi-Fi hotspot, can read queries and answer them first. An attacker off the path must guess the transaction ID and source port; RFC 5452’s randomisation makes that a guess among billions, but a successful forgery is cached for its TTL and served to every user of that resolver.

DNSSEC lets the zone owner sign each set of records. The resolver checks the signature with the zone’s key, the key against a DS record signed by the parent, and so on to the root key. A forged or altered answer fails the check, and the resolver returns SERVFAIL rather than a lie, so DNSSEC protects every hop, but only for signed zones and validating resolvers.

DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS wrap the device-to-resolver hop in TLS. The local network can no longer read or change queries, and DoH looks like any other HTTPS traffic on port 443. The resolver still sees every query, so the choice of resolver becomes a privacy decision, and internal names only work if the encrypted resolver is the company’s own.

Each defence has an operational cost. DNSSEC needs keys rolled and signatures refreshed, or the zone goes dark for validating users. Encrypted DNS moves queries away from network operators’ resolvers, which can break internal names and filtering unless devices are pointed at the right resolver.

useWhen: Signing a zone whose answers attackers would profit from changing, such as a bank or payment domain.
Encrypting DNS for devices that use untrusted networks such as public Wi-Fi.
avoidWhen: Avoid enabling DNSSEC without automated signing and monitoring of expiry.
Avoid sending managed laptops’ DNS to a public resolver when internal names matter.

rows: Forged or altered answers on any hop
Reading or altering the device-to-resolver hop
The resolver itself, and unsigned answers it fetches

numbers.title: How long a poisoned answer lasts
assumptions: A forged A record is accepted with a TTL of 86,400 s (the attacker chooses it; illustrative)
The resolver serves 50,000 users who visit the site about twice a day (illustrative)
steps: The forged answer stays cached for up to 86,400 s, a whole day.
Lookups served from cache in that day: 50,000 × 2 = 100,000.
Every one of them goes to the attacker’s address unless the resolver’s cache is flushed.
With DNSSEC validation, the forged record fails its signature check and is never cached.
numbers.result: One accepted forgery can misdirect a resolver’s whole user base for as long as the attacker’s TTL; validation stops it at the door.

india.title: Government domains and DNSSEC in India
india.label: Public example
india.body: Public DNSSEC checking tools such as DNSViz let anyone inspect whether a domain, for example a government or bank domain under .in or .gov.in, publishes signed records and a DS record at its parent. A user on a validating resolver who looks up a signed domain gets SERVFAIL rather than an altered answer if the signatures fail. Teams running such domains in India, as anywhere, need automated signing and expiry monitoring, because a missed rollover makes the domain unreachable only for users of validating resolvers, which makes the outage look partial and confusing.

pitfalls.trap: “We use DoH, so our DNS is authenticated.”
pitfalls.say: “DoH encrypts the hop to the resolver; whether answers are authentic depends on DNSSEC and on trusting that resolver.”

pitfalls.trap: “Some users can’t reach us; it must be their ISP.”
pitfalls.say: “If only validating resolvers fail, I’d check our DNSSEC chain first: DS records, key rollover and signature expiry.”

takeaways: Plain DNS accepts the first matching reply; random IDs and ports make blind forgery hard, not impossible.
DNSSEC signs answers so resolvers can reject forgeries; it encrypts nothing.
DoT and DoH encrypt the device-to-resolver hop; the resolver still sees every name.
Broken DNSSEC chains show up as SERVFAIL for validating resolvers only.

interactive.title: Who can reach the domain?
interactive.prompt: A company moves its domain to a new DNS provider that does not sign zones, but forgets to remove the DS record the old, signing provider had published at the parent. What happens next?

choices.label: Nothing changes for anyone
choices.feedback: Validating resolvers still find the DS record, expect signatures, and reject the new unsigned answers.

choices.label: Users of validating resolvers get SERVFAIL; others are fine
choices.feedback: Right: the parent says the zone is signed, the new answers have no valid signatures, so validators refuse them, while non-validating resolvers never check.

choices.label: Every user gets the old provider’s addresses
choices.feedback: Once caches expire, resolvers ask the new provider; the problem is that validators reject its answers, not that old ones persist.

choices.label: Browsers show a certificate warning
choices.feedback: Certificates are checked after the lookup; here the lookup itself fails for validating users, so the browser never reaches the site.

interactive.reveal: DNSSEC failures are partial outages: only users behind validating resolvers break. Remove or update the DS record at the parent before switching to a provider that signs differently or not at all, and wait out its TTL.

seeAlso.why: How resolvers walk the DNS hierarchy and cache answers
TLS, which DoT and DoH use to encrypt queries
DNS in system design: TTLs, failover and steering

title: Mobile and Wi-Fi Networks: The Last Mile
objectives: Explain why wireless links add jitter and loss that wired links do not
Account for radio wake-up time and battery cost when designing mobile traffic
Keep sessions alive across network changes and short NAT timeouts

cards.title: Air is a shared, noisy medium
cards.body: On Wi-Fi, every device on a channel takes turns: a sender listens, waits a random back-off if the air is busy, and transmits only when it is clear. Frames that are corrupted by interference are retried by the radio itself, invisibly to TCP, so loss often shows up as extra delay instead. Signal strength sets the data rate, so a phone at the edge of coverage both sends slowly and takes airtime from everyone else. Wireless latency therefore varies far more than a cable’s.

cards.title: What happens when an idle phone sends a request
cards.body: On cellular networks, the radio has to wake before data can move.
steps: The phone has been idle, so its radio is in a low-power state with no channel to the network
The app sends a request; the radio first negotiates a connection with the cell tower
Only then do the DNS lookup, TCP and TLS handshakes and the request itself go out
After the reply, the radio stays in a high-power state for several seconds in case more data comes
It then drops back to idle, and the next request pays the wake-up again

cards.title: Worked example: chatty requests on a sleepy radio
cards.body: Spreading small requests out keeps waking the radio and keeping it awake.
steps: Assume a wake-up of 100 ms, a round trip of 80 ms and a high-power tail of 5 s after each burst (illustrative figures; real values vary by network)
An app sends 6 analytics pings, one every 20 s: each pays 100 ms + 80 ms = 180 ms and keeps the radio awake 5 s
Radio awake time: 6 × 5 s = 30 s, plus six wake-ups
Batched into one request at the end: one wake-up, one round trip, one 5 s tail
Awake time falls from about 30 s to about 5 s, a sixth, for the same data
cards.note: Result. On mobile, the number of separate bursts matters more than the bytes. Batch background work, piggyback on requests the user is already waiting for, and let the platform schedule deferrable uploads.

cards.title: When the network changes under a connection
cards.body: Walking out of Wi-Fi range moves a phone to cellular and gives it a new IP address. A TCP connection is identified by its addresses and ports, so every open connection dies and must be rebuilt, including TLS. QUIC (RFC 9000) identifies connections by connection IDs instead, so a client can migrate an open connection to the new path after validating it. Either way, apps should treat a network change as normal: retry idempotent requests and resume uploads from the last confirmed byte.

cards.title: Trap: keep-alives tuned for a data centre
cards.body: Mobile operators often place many users behind carrier-grade NAT, whose idle timers can be short: RFC 4787 asks for at least 2 minutes for UDP and RFC 5382 for over 2 hours for established TCP, but some carrier devices use much shorter timers in practice. A long-lived connection with no traffic for longer than the timer silently loses its mapping, and the next message from the server is dropped. Sending a keep-alive every few seconds keeps it, but also keeps the radio awake and drains the battery. Use the platform’s push service for wake-ups, and keep-alives near, not far below, the timer.

cards.title: Misconception: more bars means a fast connection
cards.body: Signal strength is only one factor. A crowded cell or a busy Wi-Fi channel shares its capacity among everyone on it, so full bars at a stadium can still mean seconds of latency. Large buffers in the radio network can add hundreds of milliseconds under load. Measure from real devices, split latency by network type, and design for the slow tail: small first responses, compressed payloads and timeouts that allow for wireless variance.

questions.prompt: Why does Wi-Fi loss often show up as extra latency rather than as TCP retransmissions?

choices.label: TCP turns off loss detection on Wi-Fi links
The radio retries corrupted frames itself before TCP notices
Wi-Fi frames are larger than Ethernet frames
Access points queue every packet until the signal improves

questions.explanation: Link-layer retries hide most losses from TCP but take airtime, which adds delay. TCP has no special Wi-Fi mode; frame size does not explain it; and access points do not hold packets indefinitely waiting for signal.

questions.prompt: The first request after a phone sits idle is slower than the next few. What adds the extra time?

choices.label: The radio must connect to the network before sending
The phone’s CPU is in a power-saving mode
The server’s connection pool has gone cold
The cell tower has to fetch the phone’s profile first

questions.explanation: An idle radio first sets up a channel with the tower, which costs time before any packet moves. CPU wake is microseconds by comparison; a cold server pool would affect all clients, not one phone after idling; and the tower does not fetch a profile per request.

questions.prompt: An app sends a small analytics event every 15 seconds in the background. What change saves the most battery?

choices.label: Compress each event to half its size
Switch the events from TCP to UDP
Batch events and send them together less often
Send each event to a nearer server

questions.explanation: Each separate burst wakes the radio and keeps it in high power for seconds, so fewer bursts matter most. Halving tiny payloads saves little; UDP still wakes the radio; and a nearer server shortens a round trip but not the awake tail.

questions.prompt: A user walks from Wi-Fi onto cellular in the middle of a large upload over TCP. What happens?

choices.label: The upload continues on the new network unchanged
The phone keeps its Wi-Fi IP address on cellular
The upload waits until Wi-Fi returns, then resumes
The connection breaks, because its address changed

questions.explanation: TCP connections are bound to their addresses, so a new IP means a new connection; the app should resume from the last confirmed byte. Seamless continuation needs QUIC migration or a multipath transport; and phones get a new address on each network.

questions.prompt: A chat app keeps an idle connection to its server, and messages sometimes never arrive after a few minutes of silence. What is a likely cause?

choices.label: The carrier NAT dropped the idle mapping
The server ran out of file descriptors
The phone’s DNS cache expired
The server’s TLS session ticket expired

questions.explanation: An idle mapping that times out means the server’s next packets are dropped at the NAT. File-descriptor exhaustion would refuse new connections; DNS is not used on an open connection; and a session ticket matters only when a new connection resumes TLS.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when an idle phone makes a request.

items.label: The radio stays in high power for a few seconds
The radio is idle with no channel to the tower
The radio drops back to idle
DNS, handshakes and the request go out
The radio connects to the network

questions.explanation: Wake, send, linger, sleep. Every separate burst repeats the whole cycle.

questions.prompt: A radio stays awake 5 s after each burst. An app sends 12 separate bursts an hour; batched, it would send 2. How many seconds of awake tail per hour does batching save?
assumptions: Bursts far enough apart that tails do not overlap
questions.explanation: Sanity check: from 60 s to 10 s of tail per hour, a sixth, without changing how much data is sent.

flashcards.back: Shared airtime, random back-offs and link-layer retries that turn loss into delay.
After a burst the cellular radio stays in high power for seconds; fewer bursts save battery.
A new IP breaks TCP connections; QUIC can migrate with connection IDs; apps must resume.

sources.title: RFC 9000: QUIC, section 9 on connection migration
RFC 3481: TCP over Second and Third Generation Wireless Networks
RFC 4787: NAT Behavioral Requirements for Unicast UDP

mechanism.title: What the wireless hop does to your traffic
steps: On Wi-Fi, devices share a channel and take turns. Each sender listens before it transmits and waits a random back-off when the air is busy, and the receiver acknowledges each frame. A corrupted frame is resent by the radio, so the transport above sees a delay rather than a loss, and a weak device using a low data rate takes more airtime from everyone.

On cellular networks, the phone’s radio moves between states. In idle it saves power but has no channel; before sending it must negotiate one with the network, which takes time. After traffic ends it lingers in a high-power state for a few seconds in case more data follows, then drops back. Each separate burst therefore costs a wake-up delay and a tail of battery use.

Radio networks buffer heavily to ride out fading and scheduling, so latency under load can grow by hundreds of milliseconds, and loss-based congestion control fills those buffers. Round-trip times are both higher and more variable than on wired paths, which stretches timeouts and makes the slow tail of requests much longer than the median.

Moving between networks changes the device’s IP address. TCP connections, named by addresses and ports, break and must be rebuilt with fresh handshakes. QUIC names connections with connection IDs so a client can validate a new path and keep going; multipath transports can use both networks at once.

Mobile operators often put subscribers behind carrier-grade NAT. Idle mappings expire, after which inbound packets for that flow are dropped. Apps that need server-initiated messages either keep mappings alive with periodic traffic, at a battery cost, or rely on the platform’s push channel, which shares one connection across all apps.

useWhen: Designing APIs and sync for phone apps on cellular or public Wi-Fi.
Setting timeouts, retries and keep-alives for clients on wireless links.
avoidWhen: Avoid frequent background polling on mobile when a push channel exists.
Avoid timeouts tuned for data-centre round trips on wireless clients.

rows: Each pays wake-up and round trips

numbers.title: A screen that makes five calls in a row
assumptions: Wake-up 100 ms, round trip 80 ms on cellular (illustrative)
Five dependent API calls on one warm connection
steps: Sequential calls: 100 ms wake-up + 5 × (80 + 20) ms = 600 ms.
One combined call that returns everything: the five 20 ms steps take 5 × 20 = 100 ms, so 100 + 80 + 100 = 280 ms, if the server runs the five steps itself.
On Wi-Fi with a 20 ms round trip and no wake-up: 5 × 40 = 200 ms versus 20 + 100 = 120 ms.
The combined call saves 320 ms on cellular but only 80 ms on Wi-Fi.
numbers.result: Round trips cost four times more on cellular here, so collapsing dependent calls matters most where users are on mobile.

india.title: Designing for patchy mobile coverage
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: A delivery app used by riders across Indian cities sees phones move between 4G, 5G, weak signal under flyovers and shop Wi-Fi many times a shift. Its order screen originally made five calls in a row; it is changed to one call that returns the whole screen. Location updates are batched every 30 seconds instead of sent every 5, proof-of-delivery photos upload in resumable chunks so a network change does not restart them, and new orders arrive through the platform push service rather than a polling loop.

pitfalls.trap: “The API is fast; our server time is 20 ms.”
pitfalls.say: “On cellular each round trip and radio wake-up dominate; I’d measure end-to-end latency on real devices by network type.”

pitfalls.trap: “Send a keep-alive every 10 seconds so messages always arrive.”
pitfalls.say: “That keeps the radio awake and drains the battery; I’d use the platform push channel and keep-alives near the NAT timeout.”

takeaways: Wireless links share airtime and retry frames, turning loss into jitter.
Cellular radios pay a wake-up and a high-power tail per burst; batch to save both.
A network change gives a new IP and breaks TCP; resume or use QUIC migration.
Carrier NAT drops idle mappings; prefer push channels to frequent keep-alives.

interactive.title: Which costs more battery?
interactive.prompt: Two versions of an app send the same 60 small background events an hour. Version A sends each event as it happens, roughly once a minute. Version B batches them and sends once every 15 minutes. Assume a cellular radio that stays in high power for 5 seconds after each burst. Which drains the battery more, and roughly how much awake tail does each spend per hour?

choices.label: They cost the same, since the data is identical
choices.feedback: The bytes are the same, but the number of separate bursts is not, and each burst keeps the radio awake for the tail.

choices.label: A, with about 300 s of tail against about 20 s for B
choices.feedback: Right: A has 60 bursts × 5 s = 300 s of tail; B has 4 bursts × 5 s = 20 s, about one fifteenth.

choices.label: B, because its batches are larger
choices.feedback: Larger batches take a little longer to send, but they wake the radio 4 times instead of 60, so B spends far less time awake.

interactive.reveal: On mobile, count bursts, not bytes. Batch deferrable work, send it with requests the user already triggered, and let the operating system schedule background sync.

seeAlso.why: Latency versus bandwidth, which explains why round trips dominate on mobile
HTTP/3 and QUIC, which can migrate connections across networks
NAT and its idle timers, which carrier networks apply to every user

title: Watching the Network: Counters, Flow Records and Probes
objectives: Choose between interface counters, flow records and active probes for a monitoring question
Turn counters into rates correctly and see what averages hide
Scale sampled flow data and know what sampling cannot see

cards.title: Three lenses on one network
cards.body: Interface counters, read by SNMP or streaming telemetry, say how many bytes, packets, errors and drops each port saw: cheap, always on, but blind to who sent what. Flow records (NetFlow, IPFIX, sFlow, cloud VPC flow logs) summarise conversations: addresses, ports, bytes and whether a rule accepted or rejected them. Active probes send real traffic, a TCP connect or an HTTP request from where users are, and measure what they get. Each answers a different question; packet capture is for the cases none of them settle.

cards.title: From a counter to a utilisation graph
cards.body: Counters only ever go up; rates come from differences between readings.
steps: Every 60 s the collector reads the port’s received-bytes counter
It subtracts the previous reading: 4.5 GB arrived in that minute
Rate = 4.5 × 10⁹ bytes × 8 ÷ 60 s = 600 Mbit/s
On a 10 Gbit/s port that plots as 6% utilisation for the minute
If the counter wrapped or the device rebooted in between, the difference is wrong and must be discarded

cards.title: Worked example: the burst a one-minute average hides
cards.body: Short bursts at line rate overflow switch buffers while the average looks calm.
steps: A replication job sends 2 GB into a 10 Gbit/s port in one burst: 2 × 8 = 16 Gbit, which takes 1.6 s at line rate
Other traffic on the port averages 1 Gbit/s
One-minute average: (16 + 60 × 1) Gbit ÷ 60 s ≈ 1.27 Gbit/s, about 13% utilisation
During those 1.6 s the port was full, and anything else arriving was queued or dropped
The output-drops counter rose by thousands in that minute, while the utilisation graph stayed flat
cards.note: Result. Utilisation averaged over a minute can read 13% while the port drops packets. Alert on drop and discard counters, and use finer intervals or switch buffer telemetry where bursts matter.

cards.title: Sampling: seeing the big flows cheaply
cards.body: Recording every packet on a busy router is too costly, so sFlow and sampled flow export look at 1 packet in N and scale up. With 1-in-2,048 sampling, 500 sampled packets from one source mean about 500 × 2,048 ≈ 1 million packets. That is accurate for large flows, which is what top-talker reports and DDoS detection need, but a short connection with 20 packets is usually not sampled at all. For per-connection questions, use unsampled flow logs or a capture.

cards.title: Trap: a green ping while users are failing
cards.body: An ICMP ping from inside the data centre proves one path carries ICMP. Users may come through another network, the load balancer may answer pings while the application port is closed, and ICMP is often treated differently by routers. Probe what users do: a TCP connect and an HTTP request to the real port, from several outside locations and networks, and record latency percentiles, not only success.

cards.title: Misconception: high utilisation is the alarm
cards.body: A link at 85% that never drops packets is doing its job; a link at 20% that drops during bursts is hurting users. Errors (corrupted frames, usually cabling or optics) and discards (full queues) are the signals that something is wrong. Pair them with flow records to see who caused the traffic, and with probes to see what users felt.

questions.prompt: An outbound bill doubled overnight. Which data tells you which hosts and destinations caused it?

choices.label: Interface byte counters on the internet router
Flow records with addresses, ports and bytes
An HTTP probe from three outside locations
The error counters on each switch port

questions.explanation: Flow records attribute bytes to conversations. Interface counters confirm the total but not who sent it; probes measure user experience, not volume; and error counters point to faulty links, not traffic sources.

questions.prompt: A 32-bit byte counter on a 10 Gbit/s port running at line rate wraps how often?

choices.label: About every 3.4 seconds
About every 34 seconds
About every 5.7 minutes
About every 57 minutes

questions.explanation: 2³² bytes × 8 ÷ 10¹⁰ bit/s ≈ 3.4 s, so polling every minute misses many wraps; 64-bit counters exist for this. 34 s is the wrap time at 1 Gbit/s, 5.7 minutes at 100 Mbit/s and 57 minutes at 10 Mbit/s, as RFC 2863 lists.

questions.prompt: A storage port averages 15% over each minute, yet its output-drop counter climbs during replication. What is happening?

choices.label: The counters are misreporting and should be reset
The link is faulty and corrupting frames
The port needs a longer polling interval
Short bursts at line rate overflow the port’s buffer

questions.explanation: Bursts of a second or two fill the queue while the minute’s average stays low. Resetting counters only hides the evidence; corrupted frames raise the error counter, not drops; and a longer interval smooths the bursts even more.

questions.prompt: With 1-in-1,000 packet sampling, which question can you answer reliably?

choices.label: Which sources send the most traffic through this router
Whether one specific 10-packet connection was blocked
The exact byte count of every customer’s session
Which packets carried a given customer’s password

questions.explanation: Large flows produce many samples, so top talkers are estimated well. A 10-packet connection is probably never sampled; sampled totals are estimates, not exact bills; and flow data has no packet contents.

questions.prompt: Which probe best tells you whether customers can use a public API?

choices.label: A ping to the load balancer from a server next to it
A check of the API servers’ CPU usage
An HTTPS request to a real endpoint from several networks
A count of open connections on the load balancer

questions.explanation: Testing the real protocol from outside measures what customers experience. A nearby ping skips DNS, TLS, the application and the user’s path; CPU and connection counts are internal signals that can look normal during an outage.

questions.prompt: Order how a collector turns a byte counter into a utilisation value.

items.label: Multiply by 8 and divide by the interval in seconds
Read it again at the end
Divide by the port speed to get utilisation
Read the counter at the start of the interval
Subtract, discarding the result if the counter wrapped or reset

questions.explanation: Two readings, a safe difference, bits per second, then a share of the port speed.

questions.prompt: A router samples 1 packet in 2,048. Over five minutes it records 350 sampled packets from one source. About how many thousand packets did that source send?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about 2,400 packets a second, a heavy talker, which is the kind of flow sampling estimates well; a source with 20 packets would usually show none.

flashcards.back: Counters: how much and drops per port; flows: who talked to whom; probes: what users experience.
Line-rate microbursts that overflow buffers; watch drop and discard counters.
Multiply samples by N; good for big flows, blind to small ones.

sources.title: RFC 2863: The Interfaces Group MIB, section 3.1.6 on counter size
RFC 7011: IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol
Google SRE book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

mechanism.title: How network monitoring data is produced
steps: Every switch, router and host interface keeps counters: bytes and packets in and out, errors and discards. They only increase, from boot, and a collector reads them every so often by SNMP or receives them by streaming telemetry. A rate is the difference between two readings divided by the time between them.

Counter size and polling interval set what you can see. A 32-bit byte counter wraps every few seconds on a 10 Gbit/s port, so fast interfaces use 64-bit counters. A long interval averages away bursts, so a port can drop packets in a two-second burst while showing low utilisation for the minute.

Routers and cloud networks can also export flow records. A flow is a set of packets sharing addresses, ports and protocol; the exporter keeps a byte and packet count per flow and sends a summary when the flow ends or a timer expires. Cloud flow logs add whether a security rule accepted or rejected the traffic.

On busy devices, flow export or sFlow samples one packet in N and scales up. Large flows yield many samples and good estimates; small flows may not be seen at all. Sampled data is right for top talkers, capacity planning and attack detection, not for proving whether one short connection happened.

Active probes complete the picture: synthetic TCP connects, DNS lookups and HTTP requests sent on a schedule from outside locations, recording success and latency percentiles. They measure the user’s view across every layer, while counters and flows explain why it changed.

useWhen: Alerting on drops, errors and probe latency for the paths users depend on.
Attributing traffic and cost to hosts, services and destinations.
avoidWhen: Avoid alerting on utilisation alone without drop counters.
Avoid using sampled flow data to prove whether a single short connection happened.

rows: How much, and were packets dropped
Who talked to whom, how much, accepted or rejected
Packet contents; small flows when sampled
Can users connect, and how fast

numbers.title: Polling interval against burst visibility
assumptions: A 10 Gbit/s port with 1 Gbit/s of background traffic
steps: During the burst the port carries 10 Gbit/s for 2 s.
Averaged over 10 s: (2 × 10 + 8 × 1) ÷ 10 = 2.8 Gbit/s, 28% utilisation.
Averaged over 60 s: (2 × 10 + 58 × 1) ÷ 60 = 1.3 Gbit/s, 13% utilisation.
Averaged over 300 s: (2 × 10 + 298 × 1) ÷ 300 ≈ 1.06 Gbit/s, under 11%.
numbers.result: The same full-rate burst reads 28%, 13% or under 11% depending on the interval; only the drop counter shows it every time.

india.title: Monitoring a payments gateway during a sale
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: An online retailer in Hyderabad runs a flash sale, and customers report failed payments while the dashboards show network utilisation at 30%. The team adds the output-drop counters of the links to its payment provider, which jump during each burst of checkout traffic. VPC flow logs show that retries from one misconfigured service account for a third of the bytes, and synthetic HTTPS checks from several Indian cities record latency percentiles that line up with the drops. Fixing the retry storm and spreading the traffic over another link clears the failures before the next sale.

pitfalls.trap: “The link is only at 30%, so the network is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “A minute’s average hides bursts; I’d check the drop and discard counters for that link first.”

pitfalls.trap: “Ping works, so the service is up.”
pitfalls.say: “Ping tests one path for ICMP; I’d probe the real HTTPS endpoint from outside networks.”

takeaways: Counters show volume and drops, flows show who, probes show what users feel.
Rates come from counter differences; use 64-bit counters on fast ports.
Averages hide line-rate bursts; alert on drops and discards, not utilisation alone.
Sampled flows estimate big flows well and miss small ones.

interactive.title: Is the link the problem?
interactive.prompt: Video uploads to an office file server stall for a few seconds several times an hour. The switch port to the server shows 12% average utilisation on a 5-minute graph, no errors, and an output-drop counter that rises by a few thousand each time a stall is reported. What is the best reading?

choices.label: The link is fine: 12% is far from full
choices.feedback: The average is low, but the drop counter rising with each stall says the port’s queue is overflowing during short bursts.

choices.label: The link is faulty and corrupting frames
choices.feedback: Corrupted frames would raise the error counter, which is zero; drops without errors mean a full queue, not a bad cable.

choices.label: Bursts overflow the port’s buffer while the average stays low
choices.feedback: Right: several hosts uploading at once briefly exceed the port speed, the queue overflows and TCP backs off, which users feel as stalls.

choices.label: The file server is too slow to accept data
choices.feedback: A slow server would shrink its receive window and slow senders, but it would not make the switch drop packets on the way to it.

interactive.reveal: Utilisation averages hide line-rate bursts. Correlate drop counters with the complaints, then add capacity to that port, spread the uploads or give the bursty traffic its own queue.

seeAlso.why: Debugging one failing connection, after monitoring shows where to look
Packet loss and queueing delay, which drop counters reveal
Cloud networks, whose flow logs record accepted and rejected traffic

title: Connection Tracking and Stateful Firewalls
objectives: Explain how a stateful firewall lets replies back in without explicit rules
Write stateless rules that allow return traffic on ephemeral ports
Size a connection-tracking table and recognise when it overflows

cards.title: Remembering who started the conversation
cards.body: A stateful firewall keeps a table of connections it has seen. When a host inside sends a SYN to a server, the firewall records the addresses, ports and protocol, so the reply SYN-ACK is matched to that entry and let in, with no rule for inbound traffic needed. NAT relies on the same table. A stateless filter, such as a cloud network ACL, checks each packet against its rules alone, so return traffic needs its own allow rule.

cards.title: One connection through a tracking table
cards.body: The entry is created by the first packet and removed by a timer.
steps: A client at 10.0.1.5:51234 sends a SYN to 203.0.113.9:443; the outbound rule allows it
The firewall creates an entry for that five-tuple in state NEW
The SYN-ACK comes back, matches the entry, and the state becomes ESTABLISHED
Every later packet in either direction matches the entry and is let through without re-checking each rule
After FIN and ACK the entry lingers for a timeout (Linux defaults to 120 s for TIME_WAIT), then is deleted

cards.title: Worked example: how a busy proxy fills the table
cards.body: Short connections keep occupying entries well after they close.
steps: A proxy opens 3,000 new short connections a second to backends
Each closed connection keeps its entry for 120 s in TIME_WAIT (the Linux default)
Entries held by closed connections: 3,000 × 120 = 360,000
Plus open connections: 3,000 a second each lasting about 1 s, so about 3,000 more
If the table maximum is 262,144, it fills, and the kernel logs “table full, dropping packet”
cards.note: Result. About 363,000 entries against a limit of 262,144, so new connections are dropped at random and look like network loss. Raise the limit with memory to match, shorten the TIME_WAIT timeout, reuse connections, or skip tracking for traffic that does not need it.

cards.title: Stateless rules need the return path spelled out
cards.body: A network ACL that allows inbound TCP 443 to a web subnet must also allow the outbound replies, which go to the client’s ephemeral port, anywhere from 1,024 to 65,535 depending on the client’s system. The same applies in reverse: servers in the subnet calling out need an inbound rule for the ephemeral ports of the replies. Forgetting this makes connections hang at the handshake, because SYNs arrive but SYN-ACKs are dropped.

cards.title: Trap: asymmetric routes through stateful firewalls
cards.body: A stateful firewall must see both directions of a connection. If the request goes out through firewall A and the reply comes back through firewall B, B has no entry and drops the reply as unsolicited. This happens with two internet links, failover pairs that do not share state, or routes that changed mid-connection. Keep both directions on the same device, synchronise state between pairs, or use stateless filtering where paths can differ.

cards.title: Edge case: idle established connections forgotten
cards.body: Entries expire when idle. Linux keeps an established TCP entry for 5 days by default, but cloud firewalls and NAT gateways often time out idle connections in minutes. A database connection idle overnight then sends its next query into a firewall that has forgotten it, and the packet is dropped or reset. Enable TCP keep-alives shorter than the shortest idle timeout on the path, or let the pool close idle connections first.

questions.prompt: A security group allows outbound HTTPS and has no inbound rules. Why do replies from the web server still arrive?

choices.label: Replies from port 443 are exempt from filtering by design
The group tracks the connection and admits its replies
Security groups only filter traffic between subnets
The client retries until a reply slips through

questions.explanation: Stateful filters remember the outbound connection and allow its return traffic. Port 443 replies have no special exemption; security groups filter at each interface, not only between subnets; and retries do not get past a filter that drops them.

questions.prompt: A network ACL allows inbound TCP 443 to a web subnet, and clients hang during the handshake. What is missing?

choices.label: An outbound rule for replies to the clients’ ephemeral ports
An inbound rule for port 80 as a fallback
An outbound rule for port 443 to the clients
A larger connection-tracking table on the ACL

questions.explanation: A stateless ACL needs replies allowed explicitly, and they go to each client’s ephemeral port. Port 80 is a different service; replies leave from 443 but go to the client’s port, so a rule for destination 443 does not match; and stateless ACLs keep no tracking table.

questions.prompt: A busy proxy host starts dropping new connections at random, and the kernel log says the connection-tracking table is full. What is the most direct fix?

choices.label: Raise the listen backlog on each backend server
Move the proxy’s backend traffic from TCP to UDP
Lower the TCP SYN retry count on the proxy host
Raise the table limit or shorten the closed-entry timeout

questions.explanation: The table holds entries for closed connections too, so either more room or shorter TIME_WAIT tracking helps, along with connection reuse. The backlog is on another host; UDP flows are tracked as well; and fewer retries make failures quicker, not rarer.

questions.prompt: A site with two internet links and a firewall on each sees some connections fail at random. Requests leave via one link, and replies sometimes return via the other. Why do they fail?

choices.label: The second link has a smaller MTU
Packets reordered between links are discarded by TCP
The second firewall has no entry for the connection
The replies arrive with the wrong destination port

questions.explanation: Each stateful firewall sees only one direction, so the second drops replies it never saw requested. MTU differences break large packets, not random connections; TCP reorders packets rather than discarding them; and the ports are correct.

questions.prompt: A connection pool’s first query after a quiet night hangs, then fails. A cloud firewall sits between the app and the database. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The database dropped all its indexes overnight
The firewall expired the idle connection’s entry
The app’s DNS cache pointed to an old address
TCP slow start reset the idle connection

questions.explanation: Idle entries expire, so the next packet on the old connection matches nothing and is dropped. Indexes do not vanish overnight; an open connection does not use DNS; and slow start restart lowers the window but does not drop packets.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a TCP connection’s entry in a tracking table.

items.label: The SYN-ACK matches it and it becomes ESTABLISHED
FIN and ACK move it to a closing state
The first SYN creates an entry in state NEW
A timeout expires and the entry is deleted
Later packets match the entry and skip the rule list

questions.explanation: Created by the first packet, confirmed by the reply, removed by a timer after the close.

questions.prompt: A host opens 2,000 short connections a second, and each closed connection stays in the tracking table for 120 s. About how many thousand entries do closed connections hold?
questions.explanation: Design implication: closed connections can dominate the table; halving the TIME_WAIT timeout or reusing connections halves the entries without adding memory.

flashcards.back: Stateful remembers connections and admits replies; stateless checks each packet, so replies need rules.
New connections drop at random; entries include closed connections waiting out their timeout.
A stateful firewall that sees only the reply drops it as unsolicited.

sources.title: AWS: Control subnet traffic with network access control lists
RFC 6335: IANA procedures for port numbers
RFC 5382: NAT Behavioral Requirements for TCP

mechanism.title: How connection tracking decides what to let through
steps: A stateful firewall, a NAT device or a host with connection tracking looks at the first packet of a flow and checks it against the rule list. If the rules allow it, it creates an entry keyed by the five-tuple: source and destination address and port, and protocol.

Each later packet is looked up in a hash table first. A packet that matches an entry in either direction is allowed, typically by one early rule for established traffic, without checking the rest of the list, which is both faster and what lets replies in. Packets that match nothing and are not allowed as new connections are dropped as unsolicited.

The entry tracks state. For TCP it follows the handshake and close; for UDP, which has no handshake, it treats a reply within a timeout as part of the flow. Every state has a timer: on Linux, established TCP entries last 5 days of idleness by default, closing ones about 2 minutes, unreplied UDP 30 seconds.

The table has a fixed maximum, set by memory. Entries for closed connections count until their timers end, so a host making thousands of short connections a second can fill it. When it is full, new connections are dropped, which looks like random packet loss to the applications.

Stateless filters, such as cloud network ACLs, keep no table. They are cheaper and immune to table exhaustion and asymmetric paths, but every allowed conversation needs rules in both directions, including the replies to ephemeral ports.

useWhen: Protecting hosts and subnets with default-deny inbound rules while allowing replies.
Running NAT, which needs a table to map replies back.
avoidWhen: Avoid stateful firewalls on paths where requests and replies can take different routes.
Avoid tracking very high rates of short connections without sizing the table and timeouts.

rows: Loses NAT and stateful checks for that traffic

numbers.title: Sizing a tracking table for a gateway
assumptions: A NAT gateway host handles 5,000 new connections a second (illustrative)
Closed entries held 120 s; typical connection lasts 10 s
About 300 bytes of memory per entry (illustrative)
steps: Closed connections: 5,000 × 120 = 600,000 entries.
Open connections: 5,000 × 10 = 50,000 entries.
Total ≈ 650,000; with 30% headroom, a limit of about 850,000 entries.
Memory: 850,000 × 300 bytes ≈ 255 MB, affordable on a gateway host.
numbers.result: Closed connections are over 90% of the table here; the timeout matters more than the open-connection count.

india.title: Opening a branch application to the cloud
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: A hospital chain in Chennai moves its appointment system to a cloud network. The web tier’s security group allows HTTPS from the internet, and replies work automatically. A network ACL added later for the subnet allows only inbound 443, and patients’ booking pages hang until an outbound rule for ephemeral ports 1,024 to 65,535 is added. Months later, the reporting job that opens thousands of short database connections every second fills the NAT host’s tracking table at month end; connection pooling cuts the rate and the drops stop.

pitfalls.trap: “The ACL allows 443, so HTTPS works.”
pitfalls.say: “A stateless ACL also needs the replies allowed, to the clients’ ephemeral ports.”

pitfalls.trap: “Random drops at peak must be the network.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check the host’s connection-tracking count against its limit; a full table drops new connections at random.”

takeaways: Stateful filters remember connections and admit their replies; stateless ones need rules both ways.
Replies go to the client’s ephemeral port, so stateless rules must allow that range.
Tracking entries outlive closed connections; size the table from rate × timeout.
Both directions must pass the same stateful device, or replies are dropped.

interactive.title: Where did the replies go?
interactive.prompt: Servers in a private subnet call a payment API on the internet. The subnet’s network ACL allows all outbound traffic and inbound traffic only on port 443. Calls time out after the SYN is sent. Why?

choices.label: The payment API blocks the servers’ addresses
choices.feedback: It might drop packets too, but the ACL here drops every reply anyway, which explains the timeouts without assuming anything about the API.

choices.label: The ACL drops the replies, which arrive on ephemeral ports
choices.feedback: Right: replies come back to the servers’ ephemeral ports, not 443, and a stateless ACL has no memory that the servers asked.

choices.label: Outbound HTTPS needs a separate rule for port 443 on the API side
choices.feedback: Outbound is already allowed for all traffic; the missing piece is inbound replies.

choices.label: The servers need public addresses to receive replies
choices.feedback: Private servers can reach the internet through NAT; replies come back through it, then hit the ACL.

interactive.reveal: Stateless rules must describe both directions. Allow inbound TCP on the ephemeral range from the API’s addresses, or rely on the stateful security group and keep the ACL broad.

seeAlso.why: NAT, which uses the same connection table
Ephemeral ports, which return traffic is addressed to
Security groups and network ACLs in cloud networks

title: Prepared Statements and Plan Caching
objectives: Explain what preparing a statement saves and what it changes
Recognise when a cached generic plan is wrong for some parameter values
Use prepared statements safely with poolers and schema changes

cards.title: Parse once, run many times
cards.body: Every SQL statement is parsed, checked against the catalog, planned and then executed. A prepared statement sends the SQL once with parameter markers, such as WHERE customer_id = $1, and later executions send only the values. That saves repeated parsing and, if the plan is reused, repeated planning. It also keeps values out of the SQL text, which is the main defence against SQL injection. Many drivers prepare statements for you; the behaviour below applies whether you prepare explicitly or not.

cards.title: Worked example: what planning costs at high query rates
cards.body: Planning is cheap per query but adds up when the same statements run thousands of times a second.
steps: Assume 20,000 queries a second and 0.2 ms of planning each (illustrative)
Planning time: 20,000 × 0.2 ms = 4,000 ms of CPU every second
That is about 4 CPU cores spent only on planning
With reused plans, planning drops to near zero for those statements
Execution time is unchanged; only the repeated parse and plan work is saved

cards.title: Generic plans and custom plans
cards.body: A custom plan is made for the actual values of one execution. A generic plan is made once for any values and reused. PostgreSQL makes custom plans for the first five executions of a prepared statement, then switches to the generic plan if its estimated cost is not much higher than the average custom plan. The plan_cache_mode setting (PostgreSQL 12 and later) can force either behaviour. SQL Server compiles a plan for the parameter values seen at first compilation, caches it, and reuses it for later values; this is called parameter sniffing.

cards.title: When one plan does not fit every value
cards.body: Skewed data breaks the one-plan assumption. If 0.1% of orders are cancelled and 90% are delivered, WHERE status = $1 wants an index lookup for 'cancelled' and a sequential scan for 'delivered'. A generic or first-sniffed plan picks one and is badly wrong for the other, so the same query is fast for some users and slow for others. Fixes include forcing custom plans or recompiling just that statement, separate statements for the rare and common cases, and, in SQL Server 2022, parameter-sensitive plan optimisation, which caches several plans for one statement.

cards.title: Trap: varying SQL text defeats the cache
cards.body: Plans are cached by statement text. Gluing values into the SQL makes every statement new, so nothing is reused and injection becomes possible. IN lists of varying length do the same quietly: IN ($1), IN ($1, $2) and so on are different statements. In PostgreSQL, = ANY($1) with an array parameter keeps one statement for any length. Identifiers such as a sort column cannot be parameters; choose them from a fixed allowlist in code.

cards.title: Edge case: poolers and schema changes
cards.body: A prepared statement lives on one server connection. Behind a pooler in transaction mode, the next transaction may run on another connection, where the statement does not exist; poolers either track statements per connection or need session mode. PgBouncer 1.21 and later tracks protocol-level prepared statements when max_prepared_statements is set, but not SQL PREPARE. Schema changes invalidate cached plans, which are replanned on next use. In PostgreSQL, a prepared SELECT * whose result columns change after an ALTER TABLE fails with "cached plan must not change result type" and has to be prepared again.

questions.prompt: An app runs the same lookup 5,000 times a second with different ids. What does preparing it save?

choices.label: Execution time for each index lookup
Network time for returning the rows
Repeated parsing, and planning if the plan is reused
Disk reads, because the prepared statement caches the rows it returns

questions.explanation: Preparing moves parse and analysis to once per connection, and a reused plan skips planning as well. The index lookup itself runs on every execution. Result rows still cross the network. Prepared statements cache plans, not data; the buffer pool caches pages either way.

questions.prompt: Planning takes 0.3 ms per statement, and a service sends 15,000 statements per second. How many processor cores does planning alone occupy?
assumptions: 1 core = 1,000 ms of CPU per second
questions.formula: queries per second × planning ms ÷ 1,000 ms per core
questions.explanation: Design implication: on a 16-core server that is over a quarter of the CPU, which plan reuse could give back to execution. 45 and 0.45 move the decimal point by one place in either direction.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL prepared query by status ran five times for “delivered”, which matches 90% of rows. From the sixth run, calls for “cancelled” (0.1% of rows) are slow. What happened?

choices.label: Its statistics expired after five runs and were not rebuilt
It switched to a generic plan chosen for typical values
Its pages were evicted from the buffer pool
The connection reached a per-statement execution limit

questions.explanation: The first five runs got custom plans for a common value, so the generic plan, estimated for an average value, looked no costlier and was adopted. Rare values then get that one plan, which can read far more than they need. plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan for that statement or session restores per-value planning. Had the first five runs been for rare values, their cheap custom plans would have kept the generic plan out. Statistics do not expire per run. Eviction would slow the first runs too. There is no limit on how often a statement may execute.

questions.prompt: In SQL Server, a procedure first ran for a customer with 2 million orders and cached a scan plan. Small customers are now slow. What fixes it at the source?

choices.label: Restart the server every night to clear the cache
Add memory so the large scan plan runs from cached pages instead
Recompile that statement per call, or plan for typical values
Rebuild every index on the orders table weekly

questions.explanation: The cached plan suits the first value it saw. A recompile hint on that statement, an OPTIMIZE FOR hint, or parameter-sensitive plan optimisation in SQL Server 2022 match the plan to the values. A restart only clears the cache until the next unlucky first call. More memory makes a wrong scan somewhat cheaper but still wrong. Rebuilding indexes may trigger recompiles by chance, not reliably.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a prepared statement on one connection.

items.label: Server parses and stores the statement
Server picks a custom or cached plan and executes
Client sends SQL with parameter markers to prepare
Rows go back and the statement stays for the next values
Client sends values for one execution

questions.explanation: Parsing happens once, at prepare time; each execution supplies values, chooses a plan and runs. The statement lives until the connection closes or it is deallocated.

questions.prompt: After adding a transaction-mode pooler, some requests fail with “prepared statement does not exist”. Why?

choices.label: The pooler strips parameter markers from statements
The transaction ran on a different server connection
The database deletes prepared statements after each commit
Statements expire after a fixed number of seconds

questions.explanation: The statement was prepared on one server connection, and the next transaction was given another. Use a pooler that tracks prepared statements per connection, session mode, or unnamed per-execution statements. Poolers forward parameter markers unchanged. Prepared statements survive commits and have no time limit; they end with the connection or an explicit DEALLOCATE.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL report query filters by region with a parameter. One region holds 70% of rows; the other 40 regions are small. It runs about 50 times a minute, and planning takes 2 ms.

approaches.label: Force a generic plan
Force custom plans
Inline the values
approaches.description: Build the SQL text with the region in it

rationaleOptions.label: Each run is planned for its own region, so small ones use the index
One generic plan suits every region equally well
At 50 runs a minute, 2 ms of planning is negligible
Inlining values is safe if quotes are escaped

rationaleConflicts.r3: The large region wants a scan and the small ones want an index; no single plan fits both.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Escaping is fragile and also makes every statement new text; parameters with custom plans keep safety and fit.

questions.explanation: Plan reuse pays off at thousands of executions a second. At 50 a minute, planning each run costs almost nothing and avoids the wrong plan.

flashcards.back: SQL sent once with parameter markers; later runs send only values
One plan for any value versus one plan per execution
SQL Server caches the plan for the first values it sees
May need custom plans, recompiles or separate statements

sources.title: SQL Server: Parameter sensitive plan optimization
OWASP: SQL injection prevention cheat sheet

mechanism.title: How a statement goes from text to a cached plan
steps: Parse: the SQL text becomes a tree, and names are resolved against the catalog. Preparing does this once and stores the result under a statement name on that connection.
Bind: each execution supplies parameter values. They are never parsed as SQL, so a value such as ' OR 1=1 -- is just a string.
Plan: the planner estimates costs with the statistics it has. For a custom plan it uses the actual values; for a generic plan it uses average selectivity.
Reuse: the engine decides whether to keep the generic plan. PostgreSQL compares its estimate with the custom plans so far; SQL Server reuses the first compiled plan until something invalidates it.
Invalidate: schema changes, new statistics or cache pressure throw plans away, and the next execution plans again.

Measure before tuning. Query statistics show how often each statement runs and its average time; if planning is a small share of that time, plan reuse is not where the gain is, and per-value plans are the safer default for skewed queries.

useWhen: High-rate, short queries where planning is a real share of the time
Every query that takes user input, for safety
Batch jobs that run one statement many times
Drivers and poolers that support prepared statements
avoidWhen: Do not force generic plans on queries over skewed columns
Do not build SQL text from values, even for speed
Do not rely on named prepared statements behind a pooler that does not track them
Do not leave IN lists of varying length when an array parameter exists

rows: Depends on the first value seen

numbers.title: When plan reuse matters
assumptions: Planning 0.2 ms, execution 0.3 ms per query
steps: Share of time in planning: 0.2 ÷ (0.2 + 0.3) = 40%.
At 10,000 queries a second, planning is 10,000 × 0.2 ms = 2 seconds of CPU per second, about 2 cores.
A report taking 2 s with 2 ms of planning: planning is 0.1% of the time.
A wrong plan that turns 2 s into 60 s costs far more than any planning it saved.
numbers.result: Reuse plans for fast, frequent queries; plan each time for slow or skewed ones.

india.title: PostgreSQL PREPARE documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual for PREPARE explains that a prepared statement can be executed with a generic plan or a custom plan, and that by default the first five executions use custom plans; a generic plan is then used if its estimated cost is not much higher than the average of the custom plans. It also documents plan_cache_mode for overriding this choice.

pitfalls.trap: “Prepared statements are always faster”
pitfalls.say: They save parsing and planning, but a generic plan can be far slower for skewed values

pitfalls.trap: Clearing the plan cache to fix a slow query
pitfalls.say: Fix why one plan does not fit: custom plans, recompiles or separate statements

pitfalls.trap: Named statements behind a transaction pooler
pitfalls.say: Use pooler support, session mode, or unnamed statements

takeaways: Preparing saves parse and plan work and keeps values out of SQL text
PostgreSQL may switch to a generic plan after five custom ones; SQL Server reuses the first sniffed plan
Skewed data needs per-value plans for the affected statements
Keep statement text stable: array parameters, allowlisted identifiers

interactive.title: The sixth execution
interactive.prompt: A PostgreSQL prepared statement has run five times with custom plans, using default settings. What happens on the sixth execution?

choices.label: It always makes another custom plan
choices.feedback: Only if the generic plan looks clearly more expensive, or custom plans are forced.

choices.label: It may switch to a generic plan if its estimate is close enough
choices.feedback: Right: the generic plan is used if its estimated cost is not much higher than the average custom plan.

choices.label: The statement is deallocated and must be prepared again
choices.feedback: Prepared statements last until the connection closes or they are deallocated explicitly.

interactive.reveal: From the sixth run, PostgreSQL compares the generic plan’s estimate with the custom plans so far. For skewed columns that comparison can pick a plan that is wrong for rare values.

seeAlso.why: How the planner estimates cost, the input to every cached plan
Connection pool modes and why session state may not follow you
Injection, and why parameters rather than escaping are the defence

title: Bulk Loading and Batched Writes
objectives: Explain where per-row overhead comes from in row-by-row writes
Choose bulk paths and batch sizes that load quickly and can resume
Handle indexes, constraints and retries during large loads

cards.title: Where the time goes in row-by-row writes
cards.body: Inserting one row per statement pays fixed costs every time: a network round trip, parsing, and, with autocommit, a commit that waits for the log to be flushed to disk. For a single row these costs dwarf the work of storing it. Batching shares them: many rows per statement, many statements per transaction, or a bulk-load command that streams rows. The aim is to spend time on storing data rather than on waiting.

cards.title: Worked example: one million rows, three ways
cards.body: Illustrative figures: 1 ms round trip, about 1 ms per commit flush.
steps: Row by row with autocommit: 1,000,000 round trips and commits, about 2 ms each, so roughly 2,000 s, over half an hour
Batches of 1,000 rows per statement and commit: 1,000 round trips and commits, about 2 s of waiting plus the insert work
Streaming bulk load (COPY in PostgreSQL, LOAD DATA in MySQL): one statement, rows streamed, parsed in bulk
Batch sizes beyond a few thousand give little more speed but larger transactions
The insert work itself, writing rows and index entries, stays the same in every case

cards.title: Bulk paths and batch sizes
cards.body: Engines provide fast paths for loading: COPY FROM in PostgreSQL, LOAD DATA in MySQL, BULK INSERT and bcp in SQL Server. Without them, multi-row INSERT … VALUES statements, or the driver's batch API, cut round trips. Batches of roughly hundreds to a few thousand rows usually capture most of the gain. Each batch should be its own transaction, so a failure loses one batch rather than the whole load, and the job should record the last key it committed so it can resume.

cards.title: Indexes, constraints and statistics during loads
cards.body: Every index adds work to every inserted row, and foreign keys and triggers add checks. For a new or empty table, load the data first and build the indexes afterwards, which is much faster than maintaining them row by row. For a live table, keep the indexes, because queries need them, and load in modest batches. After a large load, update statistics (ANALYZE in PostgreSQL) so the planner knows how big the table now is.

cards.title: Trap: one giant transaction
cards.body: Loading 50 million rows in one transaction looks tidy: all or nothing. But a failure near the end rolls everything back and starts over, the transaction holds its locks for the whole time, and replicas apply the change as one large burst, so they lag. In MVCC engines, a long transaction can also hold back the cleanup of dead rows across the database. Load in committed batches instead, into a staging table if the data must appear all at once, then switch over in one short step.

cards.title: Edge case: a retried batch inserts duplicates
cards.body: A batch commits, but the acknowledgement is lost to a timeout, so the job retries and inserts the same rows again. Give every incoming row a natural or idempotency key with a unique constraint, and insert with "do nothing on conflict" (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING in PostgreSQL, INSERT IGNORE or ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE in MySQL). Alternatively, load into a staging table and merge from it, which also lets you validate rows before they touch the real table.

questions.prompt: A job inserts 2 million rows one per statement. The round trip to the database is 0.5 ms and everything else is ignored. About how many seconds does it spend on round trips?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about 17 minutes of pure waiting. In batches of 1,000 rows it would be 2,000 round trips, about 1 s. 1,000,000 is the same total left in milliseconds, and 2,000 s uses a 1 ms round trip.

questions.prompt: Batching cut a load from 40 minutes to 3. Why not put all 5 million rows in one statement?

choices.label: Throughput keeps doubling with batch size, so one statement is fastest
Databases accept only 1,000 rows in any transaction
Gains flatten, while memory, lock time and the cost of a failure grow
Large statements skip the write-ahead log and risk losing data

questions.explanation: Once fixed costs are shared across a few thousand rows, larger batches add little speed but use more memory, hold locks longer and make a retry redo everything. Throughput does not keep doubling. Transactions have no general 1,000-row limit. Large statements are logged like small ones.

questions.prompt: A new empty table will receive 200 million rows and needs 5 indexes. What order is usually fastest?

choices.label: Create the indexes first so the load can use them
Load the rows, then build the indexes
Load half, build the indexes, load the rest
Load in random key order to spread the writes

questions.explanation: Building an index from complete data sorts once and writes pages sequentially; maintaining it during the load inserts entries one at a time into random places. Inserts do not use indexes to go faster. Building halfway only adds the slow path for the second half. Random order makes index maintenance worse, not better.

questions.prompt: A nightly job loads 30 million rows into a live table in one 3-hour transaction. What is the biggest risk?

choices.label: The database caps a transaction at 1 hour
A failure late in the run rolls everything back
Rows become visible to readers one at a time
Its rows are not written to the log until commit

questions.explanation: All-or-nothing means a failure at 2 h 50 min wastes the run and the retry may miss the window. Long transactions also hold locks, make replicas lag and delay cleanup. There is no general time cap. Readers see none of the rows until commit. Changes are logged as they are made, not only at commit.

questions.prompt: Order a staged import of a supplier file into a live products table.

items.label: Merge into products in batches, doing nothing on key conflicts
Stream the file into an empty staging table
Drop the staging table
Validate rows and remove duplicates in staging
Update the table statistics

questions.explanation: Staging takes the fast bulk path without touching live data, validation happens before anything reaches products, and batched merges keep transactions short. Statistics are refreshed once the data has landed, and staging is removed last.

questions.prompt: A batch times out, is retried, and the table ends up with two copies of 5,000 rows. What prevents this?

choices.label: A longer timeout on each batch so replies arrive in time
Fewer rows per batch
A unique key on the rows, with insert-if-absent
Retrying only when the database is idle

questions.explanation: The first attempt had committed; only the reply was lost. With a unique key and “do nothing on conflict”, a retry inserts nothing it has already stored. Longer timeouts and smaller batches make lost replies rarer but cannot rule them out. Retry timing does not change whether the first attempt committed.

questions.prompt: Every night, 30 million rows from a partner must land in a live orders table before 06:00. The job sometimes fails halfway.

approaches.label: One transaction
approaches.description: Load everything, commit once at the end

approaches.label: Row by row
Committed batches
approaches.description: Batches of about 5,000 rows, each committed, with the last key recorded

rationaleOptions.label: Each batch commits, so a failure loses minutes of work, not hours
A single transaction is safest because it can be retried
Short transactions keep locks and replica lag small
Row-by-row inserts are easiest to resume

rationaleConflicts.r3: A retried single transaction repeats all of the work and may miss the window again.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Row-by-row inserts resume easily but pay a round trip and commit per row: hours for 30 million rows.

questions.explanation: Batches share the per-row costs, keep transactions short, and with a recorded key the job picks up where it stopped.

flashcards.back: Round trip, parse and commit flush; batching shares them
COPY (PostgreSQL), LOAD DATA (MySQL), BULK INSERT (SQL Server)
Load first, build indexes after, then update statistics
Unique key plus insert-if-absent, or staging and merge

mechanism.title: What happens to each row in a load
steps: The client sends the row, alone or in a batch. Each message pays a round trip, so the number of messages, not the number of rows, sets the network cost.
The server parses the statement and plans it. A bulk command or a multi-row statement does this once for many rows.
The row is written to a table page and one entry is added to each index. This is the real work, and it is the same however the rows arrive.
Constraints and triggers run: unique checks, foreign-key lookups, defaults. Each adds reads per row.
At commit, the log is flushed to disk. Committing every row pays one flush per row; committing every few thousand rows pays one per batch.

Afterwards, the planner still believes the old table size until statistics are refreshed, and replicas must replay every change. A load is finished when queries plan well against the new data and replicas have caught up, not when the last batch commits.

useWhen: Imports, backfills and migrations of more than a few thousand rows
Initial loads into new tables
Nightly partner or warehouse feeds
Event ingestion that can buffer for a moment
avoidWhen: Do not load millions of rows row by row with autocommit
Do not run a multi-hour load in one transaction on a live primary
Do not drop indexes on a live table that queries depend on
Do not retry batches without a unique key or a merge step

numbers.title: Choosing a batch size
assumptions: 1 ms round trip and commit wait per batch
0.02 ms of insert work per row
steps: Batch of 1: 1 + 0.02 = 1.02 ms per row.
Batch of 100: (1 + 100 × 0.02) ÷ 100 = 0.03 ms per row, about 34 times faster.
Batch of 10,000: (1 + 10,000 × 0.02) ÷ 10,000 = 0.0201 ms per row, barely better than 1,000.
numbers.result: Most of the gain arrives by a few hundred to a thousand rows; beyond that, larger batches only grow transactions.

india.title: PostgreSQL “Populating a database” guide
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual recommends turning off autocommit and doing all inserts in one transaction or a few, using COPY rather than INSERT, removing indexes and foreign-key constraints before loading a new table and recreating them afterwards, and running ANALYZE afterwards so the planner has up-to-date statistics. It also suggests raising maintenance_work_mem temporarily to speed up index creation, and notes that these steps matter most for one-time loads into new tables rather than routine inserts into live ones.

pitfalls.trap: “Bigger batches are always faster”
pitfalls.say: Gains flatten after a few thousand rows while risk keeps growing

pitfalls.trap: Dropping indexes on a live table to load faster
pitfalls.say: Only for new or offline tables; live queries need them

pitfalls.trap: Retrying after a timeout without a key
pitfalls.say: The first attempt may have committed; use insert-if-absent

takeaways: Per-row cost is mostly round trips and commits; batching shares them
Use bulk commands where possible, and batches of hundreds to thousands otherwise
New tables: load, then index, then analyse
Commit in batches, record progress, and make retries idempotent

interactive.title: Growing the batch size
interactive.prompt: A load uses batches of 1, then 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 rows. How does throughput change?

choices.label: It rises steeply at first, then flattens out
choices.feedback: Right: once fixed costs are shared across many rows, the per-row work dominates.

choices.label: It rises in proportion to the batch size every time
choices.feedback: Per-row insert work stays, so the speed-up cannot keep growing in proportion.

choices.label: It peaks at 10 rows and falls after that
choices.feedback: Batches of hundreds or thousands are usually much faster than 10.

interactive.reveal: Batching removes waiting, not work. When waiting is a small share of the time, larger batches mainly make transactions longer and failures costlier.

seeAlso.why: Transactions and commits, the unit each batch should be
Why each commit waits for the write-ahead log flush
Backfills during live schema migrations

title: Using a Table as a Job Queue: SKIP LOCKED and Its Limits
objectives: Claim jobs from a table safely with several workers
Choose between holding a lock and taking a lease while a job runs
Recognise when a table queue should become a broker or a log

cards.title: Why use a table as a queue
cards.body: Many applications already have a relational database, and their background jobs are born inside a database transaction: "send the receipt for this order". Putting the job in a jobs table, in the same transaction as the order, means the job exists if and only if the order committed, with no second system to keep in step. A typical jobs table has an id, a status, a run_at time, an attempt count, a lease expiry and the job's payload.

cards.title: Worked example: two workers claim jobs without colliding
cards.body: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets each worker lock different rows instead of waiting for each other.
steps: Worker A: SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'ready' AND run_at <= now() ORDER BY run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
A locks 10 rows. Worker B runs the same query, skips A’s locked rows and gets the next 10
Without SKIP LOCKED, B would wait for A's locks; with a plain SELECT, both could take the same rows
Each worker sets status = 'running' and lease_until = now() + 5 minutes on its rows, then commits, so row locks last milliseconds
After the work, the worker deletes the job or marks it done; if it crashes, the lease expires and another worker can claim it

cards.title: Hold the lock, or take a lease
cards.body: One style keeps the transaction open while the job runs, holding the row lock. It is simple, and a crash releases the lock, so the job becomes available again. But each running job holds a connection and an open transaction for its whole duration, which in MVCC engines also holds back cleanup. The other style commits a claim with a lease expiry and works outside any transaction. It suits jobs longer than a second or two, but needs the claim query to take back expired leases and the finishing step to check that the worker still owns the job. SKIP LOCKED is available in PostgreSQL 9.5 and later, MySQL 8.0 and Oracle; SQL Server offers the READPAST hint for a similar effect.

cards.title: Indexes and churn
cards.body: A queue table is small but very busy: every job is inserted, updated at least once and then deleted. A partial index such as ON jobs (run_at) WHERE status = 'ready' keeps the claim query reading only ready jobs. In PostgreSQL each update and delete leaves a dead row version, so vacuum must keep pace. A long-running transaction anywhere in the database stops that cleanup, dead entries pile up in the queue index, and claim queries that used to take a millisecond start scanning thousands of dead entries.

cards.title: Trap: read first, then update
cards.body: A worker runs SELECT … WHERE status = 'ready' LIMIT 1, then UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running' WHERE id = 42. Two workers can read job 42 in the same instant, both update it, and both run it. Make the claim one atomic step: lock with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside the claiming statement, or use a conditional UPDATE … WHERE id = 42 AND status = 'ready' and treat zero affected rows as "someone else got it". Even then, jobs can run twice after a lease expires, so job handlers must be idempotent.

cards.title: Edge case: when a table queue reaches its limits
cards.body: Each job costs several writes on the primary: insert, claim and delete, each with index updates and log records. Thousands of jobs a second compete with the application’s own writes and keep vacuum busy. A table queue also hands each job to one worker and then forgets it. If many independent consumers must each read every event, or events must be replayed later, or ordering per key matters at high volume, a log such as Kafka or a dedicated broker fits better, often fed from the database through an outbox.

questions.prompt: Two workers sometimes run the same job. Each reads a ready job with a plain SELECT, then updates its status. What is the cause?

choices.label: Both read the row before either update committed
The jobs table lacks a primary key on id
The workers use different isolation levels
The status index is out of date until vacuum runs

questions.explanation: A plain SELECT takes no lock, so both see job 42 as ready and both update it. Claim with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a conditional update that checks the status. A primary key does not stop two updates of the same row. Isolation levels differing does not create the race; it exists at Read Committed for both. Index maintenance is not deferred to vacuum.

questions.prompt: Worker A has locked 10 ready jobs with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. Worker B runs the same query. What does B get?

choices.label: B waits until A commits, then gets the same 10
B gets an error saying the rows are locked
B gets the next 10 unlocked ready jobs
B gets A’s 10 rows, but as read-only copies

questions.explanation: SKIP LOCKED leaves out rows that cannot be locked immediately, so B moves on to other ready jobs at once. Waiting is the behaviour without SKIP LOCKED; an error is what NOWAIT does. Locked rows are not returned in any form.

questions.prompt: In a lease design, a worker crashes 2 minutes into a job whose lease lasts 5 minutes. What happens to the job?

choices.label: It is rolled back and becomes ready again at once for any worker
It stays running until the lease expires, then can be reclaimed
It is lost for good unless an operator resets its status by hand
The database restarts it on another worker

questions.explanation: The claim was committed, so nothing rolls back. After lease_until passes, the claim query treats it as available. Immediate release happens only in the hold-the-lock style, where the crash ends the transaction. The lease exists precisely so the job is not lost. Databases do not run jobs.

questions.prompt: A queue processes 2,000 jobs a second. Each job is inserted, updated once when claimed, and deleted when done. About how many million row writes a day does that add?
assumptions: 3 row writes per job: insert, claim, delete
questions.formula: jobs per second × writes per job × seconds per day
questions.explanation: Design implication: each of those writes also updates indexes and the log, and in PostgreSQL leaves dead versions for vacuum, so the queue can rival the application’s own write load. 172.8 counts only the inserts, and 6 is the per-second figure in thousands.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a job in a lease-based table queue.

items.label: Do the work outside any transaction
Insert the job in the same transaction as the order
Delete the job only if this worker still holds the lease
Claim it with SKIP LOCKED and set a lease expiry
Commit the claim so the row lock is released

questions.explanation: The job is born with the business change, claimed atomically, and committed quickly; the work happens without an open transaction, and the final step checks ownership so a worker whose lease expired does not delete someone else’s claim.

questions.prompt: Which new requirement is the clearest sign to move from a jobs table to a log or broker?

choices.label: Jobs must be created atomically with the order
Five services must each read every order event, and replay it
About 50 jobs a second must now be processed by the workers
Failed jobs should be retried three times before giving up
