questions.explanation: Many independent consumers reading the same events, with replay, is what logs are built for; a jobs table hands each job to one worker and deletes it. Atomic creation is the main strength of a table queue. 50 jobs a second is modest for a table. Retries are a column and a WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: An online shop on one PostgreSQL primary sends about 200 emails a minute after orders commit. No email may be sent for an order that rolled back.

approaches.label: Broker publish
approaches.description: Commit the order, then publish to a message broker

approaches.label: Jobs table
approaches.description: Insert a job in the order transaction; workers claim with SKIP LOCKED

approaches.label: Polling orders
approaches.description: Workers scan all orders every minute for unsent emails

rationaleOptions.label: The job commits or rolls back with the order
Publishing after commit is atomic with the order
SKIP LOCKED lets several workers share the queue without collisions
Scanning all orders each minute stays cheap as the shop grows

rationaleConflicts.r3: If the process dies between commit and publish, the email is never sent; a broker needs an outbox to be atomic.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A full scan grows with every order ever placed, while the work per minute stays the same.

questions.explanation: At a few emails a second a jobs table is ample, and it gives atomicity for free. Revisit it when volume or fan-out grows.

flashcards.back: Jobs commit or roll back with the business change
Lock rows you can get now, skip the rest; workers never collide
Committed claim with an expiry; expired leases are reclaimed
High churn, fan-out to many consumers, replay: use a log or broker

sources.title: MySQL: Locking reads (NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED)

mechanism.title: How workers share a jobs table
steps: A producer inserts a row with status ready and a run_at time, inside the same transaction as the change that caused it. If that transaction rolls back, the job never existed.

A worker runs a claim query: ready rows due now, in run_at order, a small LIMIT, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. The engine walks the index, tries to lock each row, and skips any row another transaction holds.
The worker marks its rows running with a lease expiry and commits. Its locks are released within milliseconds, so other workers are never blocked for the length of a job.
The worker does the job, then deletes the row or marks it done, checking that it still owns the lease. On failure it increments attempts and sets a later run_at, a simple form of backoff.
The claim query also picks up running rows whose lease has expired, which is how work from crashed workers is recovered. Because that can run a job twice, handlers must be idempotent.

Cleanup keeps the table healthy. Done rows are deleted or moved to a history table, vacuum reclaims dead versions, and the partial index on ready jobs stays small as long as nothing holds back that cleanup for long.

Tens to a few hundred jobs a second
Teams that want one fewer system to run
Delayed jobs with a run_at time
avoidWhen: Thousands of jobs a second on a busy primary
Many consumers that each need every event
Replaying old events
Strict ordering per key at high volume

rows: No, can lose jobs on crash
Outbox table relayed to a broker
Yes, via the broker or log

numbers.title: What a table queue costs the primary
assumptions: Insert, claim update and delete per job
Two indexes on the jobs table
steps: Row writes: 500 × 3 = 1,500 a second.
Index writes: each insert adds 2 index entries and, when the claim changes an indexed column, the update adds more; roughly 1,500 to 3,000 a second.
Dead row versions left for vacuum: 500 × 2 = 1,000 a second, 86.4 million a day.
At 5,000 jobs a second all of this is ten times larger, which is where a broker starts to pay for itself.
numbers.result: A table queue is cheap at hundreds of jobs a second and an increasingly heavy tenant on the primary beyond that.

india.title: PostgreSQL SELECT documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual explains that with SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped. It warns that skipping locked rows gives an inconsistent view of the data, so the option is not suitable for general-purpose work, but notes that it can be used to avoid lock contention when multiple consumers access a queue-like table.

interactive.title: One job, two workers
interactive.prompt: Only one job is ready. Worker A has claimed it with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and has not committed yet. Worker B runs the same claim query. What happens?

choices.label: B waits for A to commit, then gets nothing
choices.feedback: SKIP LOCKED never waits for row locks; that is the point of it.

choices.label: B gets no rows, immediately
choices.feedback: Right: the only ready row is locked, so it is skipped and B sees an empty result at once.

choices.label: B gets the same job and both run it
choices.feedback: B cannot lock a row A holds, and SKIP LOCKED leaves it out.

interactive.reveal: Empty results are normal for a queue worker: it sleeps briefly or waits for a notification, then asks again.

title: Finding Slow Queries: Statement Statistics and Slow Logs
objectives: Rank queries by total load rather than by single slow runs
Read statement statistics to tell a bad plan from too much work
Go from a statement fingerprint to a verified fix

cards.title: Two views of query load
cards.body: Statement statistics group executions of the same query shape and keep running totals: calls, total and mean time, rows and pages read. PostgreSQL has the pg_stat_statements extension, MySQL the performance_schema statement digest tables, and SQL Server the Query Store. A slow query log records individual executions above a time threshold, with their actual text: log_min_duration_statement in PostgreSQL, slow_query_log with long_query_time in MySQL. Statistics show where the load is; the log shows concrete examples to investigate.

cards.title: Worked example: the slowest query is not the biggest problem
cards.body: Rank by total time, which is calls × mean time, because that is what the server spends.
steps: Query A: a monthly report, mean 2 s, 100 calls an hour: 200 s an hour
Query B: a product lookup, mean 5 ms, 200,000 calls an hour: 1,000 s an hour
B uses five times the server time of A, though each call is 400 times faster
Cutting B to 1 ms saves 800 s an hour; making A instant saves at most 200 s
Sort by mean time to find what annoys one user; sort by total time to find what loads the server

cards.title: Reading a statistics row
cards.body: Each row describes one normalised statement, with constants replaced by parameters. Look at rows per call: a high number suggests missing filters or pagination. Compare pages read from storage with pages found in cache: many reads point to a missing index or a working set larger than memory. In MySQL, rows examined against rows sent shows how much was read to produce the answer; 2,000,000 examined for 20 sent is a scan doing an index’s job. Mean time hides outliers, so check the maximum or the standard deviation as well.

cards.title: From fingerprint to fix
cards.body: Take the top statements by total time. Get a real example with real values from the slow log or the application, run it under EXPLAIN with actual timings and buffer counts, and compare estimated rows with actual rows at each step. Fix the cause: an index, a rewrite, fresher statistics, or less work requested. Then compare the statement’s statistics over the same length of time before and after. PostgreSQL’s auto_explain module can log the plans of statements slower than a threshold, which helps when a plan changes only sometimes.

cards.title: Trap: the slow log shows only slow queries
cards.body: With long_query_time or log_min_duration_statement at 1 second, a server can run at 90% CPU and log nothing, because the load comes from millions of 5 ms queries. Logging every statement on a busy server is not the answer either: it adds I/O and can slow the database. Use statement statistics for the overall picture, keep the slow-log threshold for outliers, and sample if you need full text for fast queries.

cards.title: Edge case: fast on average, slow sometimes
cards.body: A statement averages 3 ms but users report occasional 4-second waits. Statistics that include the maximum or the deviation show it; the plan usually does not. Common causes are waiting for a lock held by another transaction, a cache miss after a restart or failover, and a plan that changes for some parameter values. Check wait events and lock waits for the slow moments (pg_stat_activity in PostgreSQL, performance_schema in MySQL), not only the plan.

questions.prompt: A statement has a mean time of 40 ms and runs 50,000 times an hour. How many seconds of server time does it use per hour?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 2,000 s of work in a 3,600 s hour means this statement alone keeps more than half a core busy on average. 200 and 20,000 slip the decimal point by one place.

questions.prompt: Which statement should you tune first to reduce database load?

choices.label: Mean 8 s, 30 calls a day
Mean 12 ms, 400,000 calls a day
Mean 900 ms, 200 calls a day
Mean 1 ms, 100,000 calls a day

questions.explanation: Totals: 30 × 8 s = 240 s; 400,000 × 12 ms = 4,800 s; 200 × 0.9 s = 180 s; 100,000 × 1 ms = 100 s. The 12 ms statement carries twenty times the load of the 8-second one. Slow single runs matter for those users, but they are not where the server spends its time.

questions.prompt: CPU sits at 90%, but the slow log, set to 1 second, has been empty all day. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: The slow log is broken and needs a restart
The load comes from many queries under 1 second
CPU is used by the log writer itself
Queries only count as slow while waiting on disk

questions.explanation: Millions of fast statements can saturate a server without any single one crossing the threshold; statement statistics would show them. An empty log at a 1 s threshold is normal. Writing an empty log costs nothing. Time in the log is wall time, whether spent on CPU, disk or locks.

questions.prompt: A MySQL slow log entry shows rows_examined 2,000,000 and rows_sent 20. What does that suggest?

choices.label: The result was too large to send quickly
A filter is not served by an index
The network dropped most of the rows
The query cache returned old rows

questions.explanation: Reading two million rows to return 20 is a scan where an index lookup should be; check the plan and the filter columns. 20 rows is a small result. Rows sent counts what the server produced, not what arrived. MySQL 8.0 removed the query cache.

questions.prompt: Order a query-tuning pass.

items.label: Run EXPLAIN with actual timings and buffers
Compare statistics over an equal window afterwards
Sort statement statistics by total time
Fix the cause: index, rewrite or statistics
Get a real example with its actual values

questions.explanation: Pick by load, examine a concrete execution, change one thing, and confirm with the same measurement you started from. Run EXPLAIN with actual execution on writes only inside a transaction you roll back, or on a copy.

questions.prompt: A lookup averages 3 ms, yet users sometimes wait 4 seconds for it. Its plan looks fine. What should you check next?

choices.label: Whether the query needs a covering index
Lock waits and wait events at the slow moments
Whether the table should be partitioned
Whether the mean includes the planning time

questions.explanation: A good plan with rare long waits usually means the statement waited for something: a row lock, a cold cache, or a connection. Wait events and lock views show which. A covering index or partitioning changes typical speed, not rare 4-second stalls. Whether planning is counted cannot turn 3 ms into 4 s.

questions.prompt: A team wants production query monitoring on a primary that serves 20,000 statements a second.
constraints: See where total load comes from

approaches.label: Log every statement
approaches.description: Set the slow-log threshold to zero

approaches.label: Statistics plus a threshold
approaches.description: Statement statistics, a slow log at about 500 ms, sampled plan logging

approaches.label: Ad hoc only

rationaleOptions.label: Aggregated statistics show total load per statement at low cost
Logging every statement has no measurable overhead
A threshold log captures the text and values of outliers
Complaints reliably point to the statements causing load

rationaleConflicts.r3: At 20,000 statements a second, full logging writes a large stream of text and can slow the server itself.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Users notice slow pages, not the fast queries that together use most of the server.

questions.explanation: Aggregate everything cheaply, log only what is slow, and add plans for the outliers.

flashcards.back: calls × mean time; rank by it to reduce load
Normalised queries with running totals: calls, time, rows, pages
Individual executions over a threshold, with real values
A large ratio means reading far more than you return

sources.title: SQL Server: Monitoring performance with the Query Store

mechanism.title: How statement statistics are collected
steps: When a statement finishes, the engine computes a fingerprint of its normalised text, with literal values replaced by parameters, so WHERE id = 7 and WHERE id = 9 count as one statement.
It adds the execution’s numbers to that statement’s running totals: one more call, the elapsed time, rows returned, pages found in cache and pages read from storage.

Totals live in shared memory with a fixed number of entries. When there are more distinct statements than entries, the least-used are discarded, which is another reason to avoid statements whose text varies.
Totals grow from the last reset. To compare before and after a fix, take a snapshot, wait an equal period, and subtract, or reset at a known time.
Separately, the slow log writes one entry per execution above the threshold, with the full text and values, and in MySQL rows examined and sent.
Neither source shows why a statement waited. Lock views and wait-event sampling fill that gap and should be read alongside them when times vary widely.

Managed services and monitoring tools usually read these same views on a schedule and chart the differences, so the numbers on a dashboard are deltas of the totals described here, not a separate measurement.

useWhen: Before any tuning work, to choose what to tune
After a release, to spot statements whose cost rose
Capacity planning, to see which statements grow with traffic
Incident reviews, to find the statement behind a spike
avoidWhen: Do not tune by mean time alone
Do not log every statement on a busy primary
Do not compare totals over windows of different length
Do not trust a plan from EXPLAIN without actual timings

rows: Total load per statement, rows, pages
Real text and values of slow runs
Where one execution spent its time
What a session is waiting for now

numbers.title: Ranking by load
assumptions: Three statements from one hour of statistics
steps: Search: 120,000 calls × 15 ms = 1,800 s.
Checkout: 8,000 calls × 60 ms = 480 s.
Export: 12 calls × 30 s = 360 s.
Halving search saves 900 s an hour, more than removing the other two entirely.
numbers.result: The statement to tune first is the one with the largest calls × mean, which is often a fast one.

india.title: PostgreSQL pg_stat_statements documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual describes pg_stat_statements as a module that tracks planning and execution statistics of all SQL statements executed by a server. It explains that statements are combined into one entry when they have the same query structure, with constants replaced by parameter symbols, and lists columns such as calls, total_exec_time, mean_exec_time, rows, and shared blocks hit and read.

pitfalls.trap: Tuning the slowest single query first
pitfalls.say: Rank by total time to cut load

pitfalls.trap: Setting the slow log to zero in production
pitfalls.say: Use statistics for totals and a threshold log for outliers

pitfalls.trap: Declaring victory from one fast run
pitfalls.say: Compare statistics over equal windows before and after

takeaways: Statement statistics show total load; slow logs show examples
Rank by calls × mean time
Rows per call, pages read and rows examined point to the cause
Check waits when a good plan is sometimes slow

interactive.title: Two lookups, one entry?
interactive.prompt: An app runs SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 7 and then SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 9. How does pg_stat_statements record them?

choices.label: As two entries, one per id value
choices.feedback: Constants are replaced before grouping, so the values do not create separate entries.

choices.label: As one entry with calls = 2
choices.feedback: Right: both normalise to WHERE id = $1 and share one row of totals.

choices.label: Not at all, because they are too fast to record
choices.feedback: Every completed statement is counted, however fast.

interactive.reveal: Grouping by query shape is what makes the totals useful: a million lookups for different ids add up to one line you can rank.

title: Estimating Table and Index Size
objectives: Estimate bytes per row, including the engine’s per-row overhead
Estimate index size from entry width and how full pages are
Turn table size into disk, memory and recovery-time plans

cards.title: Why estimate size before you have the data
cards.body: Size drives several decisions at once: whether the working set fits in memory, how much disk to provision, and how long a backup restore, a replica rebuild or a full-table migration will take. A rough estimate made from the schema and expected row counts is usually within a factor of two, which is enough to tell a 50 GB table from a 5 TB one. The method is the same everywhere: bytes per row, rows per page, pages per table, then the same for each index.

cards.title: Worked example: 500 million orders in PostgreSQL
cards.body: Illustrative schema: id bigint, customer_id bigint, created_at timestamptz, total numeric, status smallint, plus a short note.
steps: Column data: about 70 bytes per row on average, including the variable-length total and note
Per-row overhead: a 23-byte tuple header padded to 24, plus a 4-byte line pointer in the page, so about 28 bytes
Per row: about 100 bytes, so 500,000,000 × 100 bytes ≈ 50 GB for the table
Primary key index on a bigint: about 20 bytes per entry, with leaf pages about 90% full, so 500,000,000 × 20 ÷ 0.9 ≈ 11 GB
Two more indexes of similar width: about 33 GB of indexes in total, two-thirds the size of the table

cards.title: Where the overhead comes from
cards.body: Every engine adds bytes to each row. In PostgreSQL the tuple header is 23 bytes and each row also has a 4-byte line pointer; values are aligned, so a boolean followed by a bigint wastes 7 bytes of padding, and ordering columns from widest to narrowest avoids it. A NULL takes a bit in a null bitmap, not the column’s width. InnoDB stores each row in the clustered primary-key index with a 5-byte record header and two hidden fields, a 6-byte transaction id and a 7-byte roll pointer, and every secondary index entry carries the primary key. Pages are 8 KB by default in PostgreSQL and 16 KB in InnoDB, each with its own header.

cards.title: Indexes and how full their pages are
cards.body: An index entry holds the key, a pointer to the row and a small header. For an 8-byte key in PostgreSQL that is about 20 bytes, including the line pointer. How full the pages are matters as much as entry width. Keys that always arrive in increasing order fill leaf pages up to the fill factor, 90% by default for PostgreSQL B-trees. Random inserts split pages, which then sit about two-thirds to three-quarters full on average, so the same index can be a third larger. Updates and deletes leave further free space until it is reused or the index is rebuilt.

cards.title: Trap: counting only the column bytes
cards.body: Adding up column widths gives the smallest number you will ever see. Per-row overhead often adds 20 to 40% for narrow rows; indexes commonly add half the table size or more; free space and dead rows add more. Then the database is copied: a primary with two replicas holds three copies, backups add more, and the write-ahead log and temporary files need room. A disk plan built from raw column bytes can be short by a factor of five or more.

cards.title: Edge case: measure a sample instead of trusting the formula
cards.body: Variable-length values, compression and fill patterns are hard to predict. Load a representative sample, say a million realistic rows, build the planned indexes, and measure. In PostgreSQL, pg_relation_size, pg_indexes_size and pg_total_relation_size report the sizes; in MySQL, information_schema.TABLES reports data_length and index_length. Scale the measurement by the expected row count; if your formula and the sample differ by more than about 30%, trust the sample and find out why.

questions.prompt: A table will hold 200 million rows with about 92 bytes of column data each, plus 28 bytes of per-row overhead. About how many GB will the table take, before indexes?
assumptions: 92 bytes of data + 28 bytes overhead per row
Ignore page headers and free space
questions.explanation: Sanity check: overhead alone is 200 million × 28 bytes = 5.6 GB, nearly a quarter of the total. 18.4 forgets the overhead, and 2.4 drops a factor of ten.

questions.prompt: An index has 300 million entries of about 20 bytes each, and its leaf pages are about 90% full. About how many GB does it take?
questions.formula: entries × bytes per entry ÷ fill fraction
questions.explanation: Design implication: with random inserts the pages would be nearer 70% full, about 8.6 GB, so the insert pattern matters as much as the key width. 6 ignores the free space in each page, and 5.4 multiplies by 0.9 instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A PostgreSQL table’s columns are, in order: is_active boolean, id bigint, is_deleted boolean, created_at timestamptz. How can it be made smaller?

choices.label: Change both booleans to smallint so they align better
Put the 8-byte columns first, then the booleans
Store created_at as text instead
Set the table fill factor to 100 so pages are packed full

questions.explanation: Each 8-byte value must start on an 8-byte boundary, so a boolean before it wastes 7 bytes of padding, twice here: the data takes 32 bytes instead of 18. The whole row is then padded to a multiple of 8, so with the 23-byte header each row shrinks from 56 to 48 bytes. smallint is wider than boolean and still needs padding. Text timestamps are larger. 100 is already the default table fill factor.

questions.prompt: An index built fresh last year is now 40% larger, though the table’s row count barely changed. Keys are random UUIDs. What explains it?

choices.label: B-tree depth grows with the age of the index
Each entry gains a timestamp as it ages
Page splits from random inserts left pages partly empty
The index now stores every old row version forever

questions.explanation: A fresh build packs pages to the fill factor. Random inserts since then split full pages into half-empty ones, and deletes leave gaps, so the average page holds fewer entries. A rebuild packs them again. Depth grows with the number of entries, not age. Entries do not gain timestamps. Dead entries are cleaned up over time rather than kept forever.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a storage estimate for a new table.

items.label: Add per-row overhead and alignment padding
Add each planned index the same way
List the columns and their average widths
Multiply for replicas and add headroom for growth and logs
Multiply by rows, allowing for page fill

questions.explanation: Each step builds on the one before: row width, then rows, then indexes on top of the table, and only then the copies and headroom that turn database size into disk to buy.

questions.prompt: Tables and indexes total 400 GB on the primary. There are two replicas, and you want 30% headroom on each server. How much disk is needed across the three?

choices.label: About 520 GB
About 1,200 GB
About 1,560 GB
About 1,800 GB

questions.explanation: 400 GB × 1.3 = 520 GB per server, and three servers need 1,560 GB. 520 GB covers only the primary. 1,200 GB has three copies but no headroom. 1,800 GB adds 50% headroom rather than 30%. Backups are stored separately on top of this.

questions.prompt: A team must order disks for a new service. The schema is designed, but no production data exists, and the estimate must be within about 30%.

approaches.label: Column-width sum
approaches.description: Add the column widths and multiply by rows

approaches.label: Copy a similar system
approaches.description: Use the size of another team’s database

approaches.label: Formula checked by a sample
approaches.description: Estimate with overhead and indexes, then load a realistic sample and measure

rationaleOptions.label: The formula covers overhead, page fill and every index
Column widths alone come within 30% for most tables
A measured sample catches compression and variable widths the formula misses
Another system’s size transfers well because databases are similar

rationaleConflicts.r3: Raw column bytes leave out row overhead, indexes and free space, which together can double the size.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Row counts, widths and indexes differ between systems, so their sizes do not transfer.

questions.explanation: A formula gives the structure of the answer and a sample checks it; together they are reliable enough to buy hardware.

flashcards.back: Column data + per-row header + line pointer + padding
entries × entry width ÷ page fill fraction
Sequential inserts pack pages; random inserts leave them about 70% full
Tables + indexes, × copies, + headroom, then measure a sample

mechanism.title: How rows and index entries fill pages
steps: Storage is divided into fixed pages: 8 KB in PostgreSQL, 16 KB in InnoDB. Each page has a header, then rows or index entries, then free space.

Each row carries a header with visibility and layout information. In PostgreSQL that is 23 bytes plus a 4-byte pointer from the page’s item array; InnoDB uses a record header plus hidden transaction fields.

Values are stored in column order and aligned to their natural boundaries, so the order of columns changes how much padding a row needs. NULLs cost a bit, and long values may be compressed or moved out of line.
Index entries hold the key and a row pointer (PostgreSQL) or the primary key (InnoDB secondary indexes). They are packed into leaf pages up to a fill factor and split when full.
The table and its indexes grow with inserts and with dead versions left by updates and deletes until cleanup reuses the space. Rebuilding packs pages again.
Estimates therefore come in layers: raw data, then overhead, then page fill, then indexes, then copies. Each layer is simple, and missing any one of them is the usual source of large errors.

useWhen: Choosing server memory and disk
Predicting restore and replica rebuild times
Deciding whether to partition or archive
Comparing schema options, such as key types
avoidWhen: Do not plan disk from raw column widths
Do not assume an index is small because its key is
Do not ignore replicas, backups and log space
Do not trust an estimate you could measure with a sample

numbers.title: From table size to recovery time
assumptions: Restore speed: about 200 MB a second
steps: Copy time: 80,000 MB ÷ 200 MB/s = 400 s, about 7 minutes.
Index rebuilds after a logical restore can take as long again or longer.
Replaying a day of logs to reach the right moment adds more time.
At 8 TB the copy alone is about 11 hours, which may be longer than the business can wait.
numbers.result: Size sets recovery time, so a table that grows tenfold needs its recovery plan revisited too.

india.title: PostgreSQL page layout documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual documents the page layout: a 24-byte page header, an array of 4-byte item identifiers pointing to items, free space, and the items themselves. It states that every table row begins with a fixed-size header occupying 23 bytes on most machines, followed by an optional null bitmap, and that values are aligned according to their type.

pitfalls.say: Add overhead, indexes, copies and headroom; measure a sample

pitfalls.trap: Booleans and bigints mixed at random
pitfalls.say: Order columns widest first in PostgreSQL to avoid padding

pitfalls.trap: Estimating an index as key bytes × rows
pitfalls.say: Add the entry header and divide by how full the pages are

takeaways: Bytes per row = data + header + pointer + padding
Index size = entries × entry width ÷ page fill
Indexes often add half the table size or more

interactive.title: Space taken by NULL
interactive.prompt: A PostgreSQL row has a nullable 8-byte bigint column, and it is NULL in this row. How much space does that column use in the row?

choices.label: 8 bytes, the same as any bigint
choices.feedback: NULL values are not stored as data at all.

choices.label: One bit in the row’s null bitmap
choices.feedback: Right: a NULL is recorded as a bit, and no bytes are reserved for the value.

choices.label: 4 bytes for a NULL marker

interactive.reveal: Sparse nullable columns are cheap in PostgreSQL. The bitmap appears only in rows that contain a NULL, and it is part of the header area.

title: Timeouts and Guardrails Inside the Database
objectives: Explain why client timeouts do not stop work on the server
Set statement, lock and idle-transaction limits per workload
Handle what a timeout leaves behind in a transaction

cards.title: The database needs its own limits
cards.body: A client timeout ends the client's wait; it does not necessarily stop the query. The server may keep running it until it finishes or notices the connection is gone, using CPU, I/O and locks for an answer nobody will read. Server-side limits stop that work. PostgreSQL has statement_timeout, lock_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and, from version 17, transaction_timeout. MySQL has max_execution_time for SELECT statements and innodb_lock_wait_timeout, 50 seconds by default. SQL Server has SET LOCK_TIMEOUT. Together they put a ceiling on how much one session can hold.

cards.title: Worked example: abandoned queries pile up
cards.body: Illustrative figures: 20 requests a second hit a query that suddenly takes 60 seconds; clients give up after 5 seconds and retry once.
steps: Each request runs the query twice: the first attempt and one retry
Without a server limit, each attempt runs the full 60 s, so about 20 × 2 × 60 = 2,400 queries are running at once
That is far beyond the connection limit and CPU, so every other query slows down too
With statement_timeout = 5 s, each attempt stops at 5 s: about 20 × 2 × 5 = 200 at once
Users still see errors, but the database stays up for everyone else while the slow query is fixed

cards.title: Choosing values per workload
cards.body: One global value rarely fits. A web request with a 2-second deadline wants a statement limit at or just under that deadline, because work after the deadline is wasted. A nightly report may legitimately run for 20 minutes. Set limits per role, per database or per transaction (SET LOCAL in PostgreSQL), and give long jobs their own role or a replica. Keep lock_timeout short, a few seconds, for web traffic and schema changes, so a blocked statement fails fast instead of queueing behind a lock.

cards.title: Idle sessions that hold things
cards.body: A session that opened a transaction and then waits on the application, say for an external API call, holds its locks and its snapshot while doing nothing. Other writers queue behind its locks, and in MVCC engines cleanup cannot remove row versions it might still see. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout in PostgreSQL ends such sessions after a set time. The better fix is in the code: do slow external calls before or after the transaction, never inside it. Separate settings close sessions that are idle outside a transaction, such as idle_session_timeout in PostgreSQL 14 and later or wait_timeout in MySQL.

cards.title: Trap: relying on the client timeout alone
cards.body: An application sets a 3-second timeout in its driver and assumes no query can run longer. When the timeout fires, the driver stops waiting; depending on the driver, it may or may not send a cancel request, and the server may keep working. Retries then add more copies of the same expensive query. Set a matching limit on the server as well, and make retries back off.

cards.title: Edge case: what a timeout leaves behind
cards.body: Engines differ in how much a timeout undoes. In PostgreSQL, a statement cancelled by statement_timeout inside a transaction puts the whole transaction into an aborted state: later statements fail until you roll back. In MySQL, innodb_lock_wait_timeout by default rolls back only the statement that waited, and the transaction stays open with its earlier changes; innodb_rollback_on_timeout changes that to a full rollback. Either way, the application must decide: roll back and retry the whole transaction, which must be safe to repeat, or report the failure.

questions.prompt: A client’s 3-second timeout fires while its query runs. The server has no statement limit. What happens to the query?

choices.label: It is cancelled on the server at the same moment
It is rolled back and retried by the database
It may keep running until it ends or the server notices
It is paused until the client reconnects

questions.explanation: The timeout ends the client’s wait. Unless the driver sends a cancel, the server keeps executing until it finishes or detects the closed connection, often when it tries to send results. Databases do not retry statements on their own, and there is no pause-and-resume for a disconnected client.

questions.prompt: Requests arrive at 30 per second, and each starts a query that now takes 40 seconds on the server. With no server-side limit, about how many of these queries are running at the same moment?
questions.formula: arrival rate × time each one runs (Little’s law)
questions.workedAnswer: 30 per second × 40 s = 1,200 running at once
questions.explanation: Design implication: a 4-second statement limit would cut that to 30 × 4 = 120, and the server stays usable while the slow query is fixed. 120 is that capped figure, and 30 is the arrival rate, not the number running.

questions.prompt: A session opened a transaction, updated a row, then waited 10 minutes on an external API. Which setting ends such sessions?

choices.label: statement_timeout
lock_timeout
idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
TCP keepalive on the connection

questions.explanation: The session is idle inside a transaction, which is exactly what this setting limits; it ends the session and releases its locks. statement_timeout applies while a statement runs, and none is running. lock_timeout limits waiting for a lock, not holding one. Keepalives detect dead connections, and this one is alive.

questions.prompt: In MySQL with default settings, a statement fails with a lock wait timeout midway through a transaction. What has been undone?

choices.label: Only that statement; earlier changes remain
The whole transaction, back to its start
Nothing; the statement keeps waiting
The whole session, which is disconnected

questions.explanation: By default InnoDB rolls back just the statement that timed out; the transaction is still open with its earlier changes, and the application must decide to roll back or continue. innodb_rollback_on_timeout makes it a full rollback. The statement does stop waiting, and the connection remains open.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a statement inside a transaction hits statement_timeout. Order what follows in a well-behaved application.

items.label: The transaction is now aborted; further statements fail
It retries the whole transaction with backoff, if safe to repeat
The statement is cancelled with an error
The application issues ROLLBACK

questions.explanation: After the error, the transaction cannot continue in PostgreSQL; rolling back clears it, and only a whole-transaction retry can redo the work consistently. Retrying just the failed statement would fail again with “current transaction is aborted”.

questions.prompt: An API has a 2-second deadline for each request. What statement limit fits its database role?

choices.label: 30 seconds, to be safe
None, so slow queries still finish
About 1.5 to 2 seconds
50 ms, for every role in the database

questions.explanation: Work that continues past the request deadline is wasted, so the limit should sit at or just under it. 30 seconds lets abandoned queries run 15 times longer than anyone waits. No limit is the pile-up case. 50 ms for every role would break legitimate reports and migrations.

questions.prompt: One PostgreSQL database serves an API with a 2-second deadline and nightly reports that take up to 20 minutes.
constraints: Protect the API from runaway queries

approaches.label: One global limit of 2 s
No limits
approaches.description: Rely on client timeouts and monitoring

approaches.label: Limits per role
approaches.description: API role 2 s; report role 30 minutes, ideally on a replica

rationaleOptions.label: Each workload gets a limit that matches its own deadline
A single global value is easiest and fits both
Reports keep running, but away from the API’s connections
Client timeouts already stop server work

rationaleConflicts.r3: A 2-second global limit kills every report; a 20-minute one protects nothing for the API.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A client timeout ends the wait, not necessarily the query on the server.

questions.explanation: Per-role settings cost one ALTER ROLE each and let both workloads have limits that make sense.

flashcards.back: Stops waiting; the server may keep working
Caps how long one statement may run on the server
Caps how long a statement may wait for a lock
Holds locks and snapshot; limit it and keep external calls outside

sources.title: MySQL: InnoDB startup options and system variables

mechanism.title: What each guardrail measures and what it does when it fires
steps: A statement limit starts a timer when a statement begins. If the statement is still running when it expires, the server cancels it and returns an error; locks it took are released when the transaction ends.
A lock-wait limit starts a timer only while a statement waits for a lock. It turns an indefinite queue into a fast, clear failure, which matters most for schema changes and hot rows.

An idle-in-transaction limit measures time between statements inside an open transaction. When it fires, the server ends the session, which rolls the transaction back and frees its locks and snapshot.
A transaction limit, where available, caps the whole transaction however its time is split between statements and idle gaps.
Idle-session and connection limits close connections that have done nothing for a long time, protecting the connection count rather than locks.
The application sees an error in every case. It must roll back if the engine has not, decide whether the transaction is safe to retry, and back off so retries do not recreate the overload.

useWhen: Every role used by interactive traffic
Schema migrations on busy tables (short lock waits)
Applications that call external services near transactions
Shared databases with mixed workloads
avoidWhen: Do not set one global limit for very different workloads
Do not set statement limits longer than anyone waits
Do not retry immediately and without limit after a timeout
Do not treat a guardrail as the fix for a slow query

numbers.title: Why limits keep an incident small
steps: No limit: 50 × 30 = 1,500 queries would need to run at once, five times the connection limit.
New connections are refused and healthy requests fail too.
With a 2 s limit: 50 × 2 = 100 at once, a third of the connections.
Only the affected endpoint fails, and the rest of the application keeps working.
numbers.result: A server-side limit turns a database-wide outage into one failing endpoint.

india.title: PostgreSQL client connection defaults
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The PostgreSQL manual documents statement_timeout as aborting any statement that takes more than the specified time, lock_timeout as aborting any statement that waits longer than the specified time while attempting to acquire a lock, and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout as terminating any session that has been idle within an open transaction for longer than the specified time. It advises against setting statement_timeout globally in postgresql.conf because it would affect all sessions, which is the reason to set it per role or per session instead.

pitfalls.trap: “The driver timeout protects the database”
pitfalls.say: It protects the caller; set server-side limits too

pitfalls.trap: One timeout for API and reports
pitfalls.say: Set limits per role or per transaction

pitfalls.trap: Calling an external API inside a transaction
pitfalls.say: Move the call outside; limit idle-in-transaction time as a backstop

takeaways: Client timeouts end the wait, not necessarily the work
Statement, lock-wait and idle-transaction limits each cap a different resource
Match each limit to the deadline of the workload using it
After a timeout, roll back and retry the whole transaction, with backoff

interactive.title: After the timeout
interactive.prompt: In PostgreSQL, inside BEGIN, an UPDATE is cancelled by statement_timeout. The application then runs SELECT 1 in the same transaction. What happens?

choices.label: It returns 1; only the UPDATE failed
choices.feedback: That is closer to MySQL’s default for lock-wait timeouts; PostgreSQL aborts the transaction.

choices.label: It fails: the transaction is aborted until ROLLBACK
choices.feedback: Right: every statement fails with “current transaction is aborted” until the transaction ends.

choices.label: The UPDATE is retried automatically first
choices.feedback: The database never retries statements on its own.

interactive.reveal: Code that catches a timeout must end the transaction before doing anything else on that connection, and connection pools should reset sessions they get back in this state.

seeAlso.why: Deadlines across services, which database limits should match
Locks and long transactions, which lock and idle limits contain
Connection limits and pools, which runaway queries exhaust

title: Read-Write Locks and Lock Granularity
objectives: Decide when a read-write lock beats a plain mutex
Raise a lock’s throughput ceiling by shortening or splitting critical sections
Avoid writer starvation and upgrade deadlocks

cards.title: Many readers or one writer
cards.body: A read-write lock lets any number of threads hold it for reading at once, or exactly one thread hold it for writing. It helps when reads are frequent, writes are rare and the read section is long enough to matter. Every reader still updates a shared count when it enters and leaves, so for very short sections the lock’s own bookkeeping can cost more than the work it protects.

cards.title: Worked example: one lock caps the whole service
cards.body: A cache protected by a single mutex.
steps: Each lookup holds the lock for 2 µs (illustrative)
Only one thread can be inside at a time, so the cache serves at most 1 ÷ 2 µs = 500,000 lookups a second, however many cores there are
Split the cache into 16 shards by key hash, each with its own lock
With keys spread evenly and enough cores, the ceiling rises towards 16 × 500,000 = 8 million lookups a second
Shortening the section to 1 µs (no allocation or logging inside it) doubles every one of those ceilings

cards.title: Trap: writers that never get in
cards.body: Many read-write locks prefer readers: a new reader may enter while a writer is waiting, as long as another reader holds the lock. Under steady read traffic there is always some reader inside, so the writer waits indefinitely and the data it should update goes stale. Choose a lock that blocks new readers once a writer queues, or keep read sections short enough that gaps appear.

cards.title: Misconception: you can upgrade a read lock in place
cards.body: Two threads each hold the read lock and both decide to write. Each asks for the write lock while still holding its read lock, each waits for the other reader to leave, and neither ever will: a deadlock. Release the read lock, take the write lock, and re-check the condition, since another thread may have changed it in between, or use a lock with an explicit single-upgrader mode.

cards.title: Finer locks bring new rules
cards.body: Splitting one lock into many raises throughput but makes operations that span several shards harder. Moving an item between two shards needs both locks, and taking them in different orders in different threads can deadlock, so always lock shards in a fixed order such as by index. Operations over every shard, like a total count, either lock all of them in order or accept a value that is only approximately consistent.

questions.prompt: A configuration map is read on every request and rewritten once an hour. Each read copies a few fields in about 50 ns. Which lock choice should you test first?

choices.label: A read-write lock, since reads vastly outnumber writes
A plain mutex, or an immutable snapshot swapped on change
A spin lock, since the hourly write must finish fast
No lock, because readers do not modify the map

questions.explanation: With a 50 ns read section, the read-write lock’s shared reader count becomes the bottleneck, so a mutex is often as fast; swapping in a new immutable snapshot removes locking from reads entirely. The read-write lock seems right by ratio but loses on bookkeeping. A spin lock does nothing for readers, and with no lock, readers can see a half-written map during the hourly change.

questions.prompt: A metrics store uses a read-write lock. Under heavy dashboard traffic, the writer that records new data falls minutes behind. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The writer has a lower thread priority than readers
Readers hold the lock longer than the writer does
New readers keep entering while the writer waits
The write lock is recursive and blocks itself

questions.explanation: A reader-preferring lock admits new readers whenever another reader is inside, so with constant reads the writer starves. Thread priority does not change lock admission, longer reads only matter because readers overlap without gaps, and a recursive lock does not block its own holder.

questions.prompt: Two threads hold the same read lock. Each then requests the write lock without releasing its read lock. What happens?

choices.label: Both block forever, each waiting for the other to leave
The first to ask gets the write lock, the other waits
Both get the write lock, because they already hold it
The lock converts both reads into one shared write

questions.explanation: A write lock needs every reader gone, and each thread is a reader the other is waiting on, so neither proceeds. Asking first does not help because the other reader is still inside, write locks are never shared, and no lock merges two readers into a writer.

questions.prompt: A shared hash map is protected by one mutex and profiles show threads waiting on it. Which change usually raises throughput the most?

choices.label: Replace the mutex with a read-write lock of the same scope
Add more threads so that more of them reach the lock
Use a fair lock so waiting threads take turns in order
Shard the map by key hash, each shard with its own lock

questions.explanation: Independent locks per shard let operations on different keys run in parallel, multiplying the ceiling. A read-write lock helps only if reads dominate and are long, more threads lengthen the queue, and a fair lock orders waiting threads without letting more of them in at once.

questions.prompt: Every request holds one global lock for 4 µs. What is the most requests per second the service can complete, however many cores it has?
assumptions: The lock is held only during the 4 µs section
Handing the lock over costs nothing
questions.explanation: Sanity check: real handovers between cores add hundreds of nanoseconds, so the practical ceiling is lower; plan to stay well under it, or shorten and split the section.

questions.prompt: A thread holding a read lock discovers it needs to modify the data. Order the safe steps.

items.label: Acquire the write lock
Make the change if it is still needed, then release the write lock
Release the read lock
Re-check the condition that made the write necessary

questions.explanation: Never wait for the write lock while holding the read lock, and re-check after acquiring because another writer may have acted in the gap.

flashcards.front: When does a read-write lock help?
flashcards.back: Many readers, rare writes, and read sections long enough to outweigh the shared reader count.
1 ÷ time the lock is held per operation, regardless of core count.
Two readers both wait for the write lock while holding their read locks.

mechanism.title: How a read-write lock admits threads
steps: The lock keeps a count of active readers, a flag for an active writer, and usually a count of waiting writers, often packed into one word changed with atomic operations.
A reader may enter if no writer holds the lock; depending on the policy it may also have to wait if a writer is queued. Entering increments the reader count, and leaving decrements it.
A writer may enter only when the reader count is zero and no other writer holds the lock. Waiting threads sleep and are woken when the state changes.

Because every reader writes the shared count, readers on many cores still fight over one cache line. For short sections that traffic, not the waiting, sets the cost, which is why sharded counters or copy-on-write snapshots often beat a read-write lock.
Policies differ: reader preference maximises read throughput but can starve writers; writer preference blocks new readers once a writer waits, so writers progress but reads stall briefly.
Granularity is a separate choice: one lock over everything is simple and safe; per-shard or per-object locks raise throughput, at the cost of lock ordering rules for multi-object operations.

useWhen: Use a read-write lock when reads dominate and each read section does real work, such as walking a structure.
Use sharding when operations touch independent keys.
avoidWhen: Avoid read-write locks around tiny read sections; measure against a mutex.
Avoid upgrading a held read lock in place.

rows: Memory for old copies still in use

numbers.title: What sharding buys
assumptions: Lookups hold the lock for 2 µs; the service needs 3 million lookups a second (illustrative)
Keys are spread evenly by hash
steps: One lock: ceiling 1 ÷ 2 µs = 500,000 a second, six times too few.
Shards needed at the ceiling: 3,000,000 ÷ 500,000 = 6.
Running each shard at no more than 50% of its ceiling keeps waits short: 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12 shards.
Round up to 16 shards, a power of two that lets the shard be picked with a bit mask of the hash.
numbers.result: Sixteen shards give a combined ceiling of 8 million lookups a second, leaving the needed 3 million at under 40% of capacity.

india.title: What the manual says about writer starvation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux manual page for pthread_rwlockattr_setkind_np describes the reader-preference setting, which is the default in the GNU C library: a reader receives the lock even if a writer is waiting, and as long as there are readers, the writer will be starved. It also notes that the writer-preference setting is ignored by that library, because supporting recursive read locks would make it deadlock, and offers a non-recursive writer-preferring mode instead.

pitfalls.trap: “Reads outnumber writes, so a read-write lock is faster.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if read sections are long; I’d benchmark it against a mutex and a snapshot swap.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add cores to get past the lock.”
pitfalls.say: “A lock caps throughput at 1 ÷ hold time; I’d shorten or shard it.”

takeaways: Read-write locks help long reads with rare writes.
A lock’s ceiling is one divided by its hold time.
Reader-preferring locks can starve writers.
Never upgrade a read lock while holding it; release, lock, re-check.

interactive.title: Will the read-write lock help?
interactive.prompt: A service’s hot path takes a mutex around a 30 ns hash map lookup. Reads are 99% of operations. A teammate proposes switching to a read-write lock.

choices.label: Probably not: the shared reader count costs about as much as the lookup
choices.feedback: Right: every reader still writes one shared line, so short sections gain little or nothing.

choices.label: Yes, roughly a hundred times faster because readers run in parallel
choices.feedback: Readers overlap only after each has updated the shared count, which is the expensive part here.

choices.label: No, read-write locks are only for reads served from disk
choices.feedback: They work for any data; the issue here is the tiny section, not where the data lives.

interactive.reveal: Measure before switching. For tiny read sections, sharding the map or publishing an immutable copy that readers access without a lock usually beats both a mutex and a read-write lock.

seeAlso.why: Mutual exclusion and why shared data needs a lock at all
Lock ordering prevents deadlocks when you split locks
Atomics explain why a shared reader count is costly

title: How Locks Wait: Spinning, Sleeping and Futexes
objectives: Explain why an uncontended lock needs no system call
Choose between spinning and sleeping from how long a lock is held
Recognise lock convoys and spinning on a preempted holder

cards.title: The fast path stays in user space
cards.body: Modern mutexes are built on a futex (fast user-space mutex): an integer in shared memory changed with atomic instructions. Taking a free lock is one compare-and-swap, with no system call. Only when the lock is already held does the waiter ask the kernel to put it to sleep on that address, and only when someone is waiting does the unlocker ask the kernel to wake one. Uncontended locking therefore costs tens of nanoseconds.

cards.title: Spin or sleep?
cards.body: A waiting thread can spin, retrying the atomic operation in a loop, or sleep in the kernel until woken. Sleeping and waking costs a pair of system calls and a context switch, on the order of microseconds, while spinning costs nothing extra if the lock frees within a few hundred nanoseconds. Most library mutexes spin briefly and then sleep, which suits both short and long hold times.

cards.title: Worked example: pick by hold time
cards.body: Rough costs on one machine (illustrative).
steps: Sleep and wake round trip: about 5 µs of CPU and latency
Lock held for 200 ns: spinning waits about 200 ns; sleeping would cost about 25 times more
Lock held for 1 ms: spinning burns 1 ms of a core doing nothing; sleeping costs 5 µs and frees the core for other work
Unknown or variable hold time: spin for roughly the cost of a sleep, then sleep
Rule of thumb: spin only when holders are running on other cores and sections are short

cards.title: Trap: spinning on a holder that is not running
cards.body: If the thread holding a spin lock is preempted, or the machine has more runnable threads than cores, waiters spin for their whole time slice while the holder waits to be scheduled. On a single core, spinning cannot succeed until the spinner gives up the CPU. User-space code should almost never use a pure spin lock; use the platform mutex, which falls back to sleeping.

cards.title: Misconception: a fair lock is the fast choice
cards.body: Handing the lock directly to the longest waiter sounds fair, but that waiter is asleep, so every hand-off pays a wake-up while the lock sits idle; meanwhile a running thread that could have taken it at once has to queue. Under heavy contention this forms a lock convoy: throughput collapses to one wake-up per acquisition. Most default mutexes are unfair for this reason; reduce contention rather than demanding fairness.

questions.prompt: A program takes and releases an uncontended mutex 10 million times a second. How many system calls does locking add?

choices.label: About 20 million: one each to lock and to unlock
About 10 million, one per lock-and-unlock pair
Usually none: free locks are taken with an atomic
One per second, when the kernel audits held locks

questions.explanation: With no contention, lock and unlock are atomic operations on a word in user space; the kernel is called only to sleep or to wake a waiter. Two calls per pair would be true of older kernel-object locks, which is why futexes were introduced, and the kernel never audits locks periodically.

questions.prompt: Which situation suits a brief spin before sleeping?

choices.label: A lock held for about 100 ns by threads on other cores
A lock held while a database query runs
A lock on a single-core machine with many threads
A lock held while waiting for a user to click

questions.explanation: A 100 ns hold frees the lock long before a sleep and wake round trip could complete, and the holder is running elsewhere. Holding across a query or a click means milliseconds to seconds of wasted spinning, and on one core the holder cannot run while the waiter spins.

questions.prompt: Under load, a service using a strictly fair (first-come, first-served) lock reaches only a fraction of the throughput of the same code with the default lock. Why?

choices.label: Fair locks use a slower atomic instruction internally
Each hand-off waits for a sleeping thread to wake
Fair locks restrict the program to running on one core
The default lock skips locking whenever load is high

questions.explanation: Handing the lock to the oldest waiter means waking a sleeping thread for every acquisition while running threads queue: a convoy. The atomics are the same, other cores keep running other code, and no correct lock skips locking under load.

questions.prompt: A team replaces a mutex with a hand-written spin lock. On a container limited to 2 CPUs with 16 worker threads, latency gets much worse. Why?

choices.label: Spin locks need a lock-free memory allocator underneath
Spinning uses a lot of memory bandwidth on two cores
Spin locks are invalid inside containers by design
Waiters spin while the holder waits for a CPU to run on

questions.explanation: With 16 runnable threads on 2 CPUs, the holder is often not running, so spinners burn quota without any chance of success. The allocator is irrelevant, bandwidth is a minor effect, and containers place no rule on spin locks.

questions.prompt: A lock is contended 10,000 times a second, and each contended acquisition sleeps and is woken at a cost of about 5 µs of CPU. Roughly how many milliseconds of CPU per second does that cost?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 50 ms per second is 5% of one core spent on waiting alone; at 200,000 contended acquisitions a second it would be a whole core, a sign to shard or shorten the lock.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when thread B tries to take a mutex that thread A holds, until B owns it.

items.label: A unlocks, sees waiters, and asks the kernel to wake one
B’s atomic attempt fails and it marks the lock as having waiters
B wakes, retries the atomic, and takes the lock
B asks the kernel to sleep on the lock’s address

questions.explanation: Fast path fails, sleep on the address, unlock wakes a waiter, the waiter retries; only the contended case touches the kernel.

flashcards.back: An atomic integer in user space; the kernel is called only to sleep or wake when the lock is contended.
Spin for holds shorter than a sleep and wake round trip (microseconds); otherwise sleep.
Every hand-off waits for a sleeping thread to wake, so throughput drops to one wake-up per acquisition.

mechanism.title: The life of a contended mutex
steps: The mutex is a word with three states, for example 0 free, 1 locked, and 2 locked with waiters. Locking tries to change 0 to 1 with compare-and-swap; success means the lock is taken without entering the kernel.
On failure the thread may spin for a short while, re-reading the word without writing so it does not fight over the cache line, and trying again when it reads 0.

If the lock is still held, the thread sets the word to 2 and calls the kernel’s futex wait on its address, asking to sleep only if the value is still 2. That check closes the race with an unlock happening at the same moment.
The kernel hashes the address to a wait queue and puts the thread to sleep. No kernel object exists for an uncontended lock; queues appear only while someone waits.

Unlocking sets the word to 0. If it was 2, the unlocker calls futex wake for one waiter. The woken thread competes again; a running thread may take the lock first, which is unfair but keeps the lock busy.
Priority-inheritance and robust variants add kernel bookkeeping so a waiting high-priority thread boosts the holder, or so a lock held by a thread that died can be recovered.

useWhen: Use the platform mutex by default: it spins briefly and then sleeps.
Use spinning only in code that runs with preemption controlled, such as kernels or pinned threads.
avoidWhen: Avoid pure spin locks in ordinary user-space programs.
Avoid strictly fair locks on hot paths unless starvation has been observed.

numbers.title: When contention starts to show
assumptions: A lock held for 1 µs per operation at 300,000 operations a second (illustrative)
A contended acquisition costs about 5 µs of sleep and wake (illustrative)
steps: Lock utilisation: 300,000 × 1 µs = 0.3 s per second, so it is busy 30% of the time.
About 30% of arrivals find it held; with spinning first, most of those waits end within about a microsecond.
If they all slept instead: 300,000 × 0.3 × 5 µs = 0.45 CPU-seconds per second spent sleeping and waking.
A brief spin turns most of that into about 1 µs of spinning each: 90,000 × 1 µs = 0.09 CPU-seconds.
numbers.result: At 30% utilisation, spinning briefly before sleeping cuts wait overhead from almost half a core to under a tenth of one in this example.

india.title: What the manual says futexes are for
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The futex(7) manual page explains that futex operation occurs entirely in user space for the non-contended case, and the kernel is involved only to arbitrate the contended case. It notes that, as any sane design will strive for non-contention, futexes are optimised for this situation: in its bare form a futex is an aligned integer touched only by atomic instructions, with system calls used solely to wait and to wake.

pitfalls.trap: “Mutexes are slow because they’re system calls.”
pitfalls.say: “Uncontended mutexes are a single atomic; I’d measure contention before replacing one.”

pitfalls.trap: “A spin lock will be faster than the mutex.”
pitfalls.say: “Only if holders are always running and sections are tiny; the mutex already spins briefly.”

takeaways: Free locks are taken with one atomic, no system call.
Spin for holds shorter than a sleep and wake; otherwise sleep.
Spinning on a preempted holder wastes whole time slices.
Strict fairness causes convoys; reduce contention instead.

interactive.title: Spin lock or mutex here?
interactive.prompt: A worker pool of 32 threads runs on a 4-CPU container. Each task takes a lock for about 2 µs to update shared state. Someone proposes a pure spin lock to avoid system calls.

choices.label: Keep the mutex: with 32 threads on 4 CPUs, holders are often descheduled
choices.feedback: Right: spinners would burn CPU while the holder waits to run.

choices.label: Use the spin lock: 2 µs is far below the cost of sleeping
choices.feedback: Short holds favour spinning only if the holder is actually running on another core.

choices.label: Use a fair lock so every thread gets its turn in order
choices.feedback: Fair hand-offs wake a sleeping thread each time and make throughput worse.

interactive.reveal: Oversubscription is the deciding fact: with eight threads per CPU, a spinning waiter usually spins on a holder that is not running. A standard mutex already spins briefly and then sleeps, so it gets the benefit of spinning without the worst case.

seeAlso.why: The mutual exclusion that futexes implement
Context switches are the cost a sleeping waiter pays
Priority inheritance is built into some futex variants

title: Priority Inversion and Real-Time Scheduling
objectives: Explain how a high-priority thread ends up waiting on a low-priority one
Use priority inheritance or ceilings to bound the wait
Know what nice values and real-time policies actually change

cards.title: Priorities and policies
cards.body: Normal threads share the CPU in proportion to weights set by their nice value: lower nice means a larger share, but every runnable thread still makes progress. Real-time policies (first-in-first-out and round-robin with priorities from 1 to 99) are strict: a runnable real-time thread always runs before any normal thread, and a higher real-time priority always runs before a lower one.

cards.title: Worked example: the inversion
cards.body: Three threads on one core, with a lock shared by High and Low.
steps: Low takes the lock and starts a 1 ms update
High wakes, preempts Low, and blocks on the lock Low holds
Medium, which needs no lock, wakes and preempts Low because it outranks Low
Medium computes for 50 ms; Low cannot run to release the lock, so High waits 50 ms or more instead of about 1 ms
With priority inheritance, Low runs at High’s priority while High waits, Medium cannot preempt it, and High waits about 1 ms

cards.title: Two ways to bound the wait
cards.body: Priority inheritance raises a lock holder’s priority to that of the highest thread waiting for the lock, for as long as it holds it. A priority ceiling raises any holder to a fixed priority assigned to the lock, so nothing that could contend with it can preempt it. Both keep the inversion to the length of one critical section; both must be enabled on the lock, since ordinary mutexes do neither by default.

cards.title: Trap: a real-time thread that never yields
cards.body: A thread switched to a real-time policy that loops without blocking will starve every normal thread on its core, including the shell you would use to stop it. Linux keeps a safety margin by default, limiting real-time threads to 95% of each second, but a misbehaving real-time thread still slows everything else to a crawl. Give real-time threads only short, bounded work and block between items.

cards.title: Misconception: lower nice fixes latency
cards.body: Nice values change long-run CPU shares between busy threads, not how quickly a thread is woken. A thread waiting on a lock, a disk or the network gains nothing from a better nice value, and a latency problem caused by a lock held by a low-priority thread is not solved by raising the waiter. Find what the waiting thread is actually waiting for before touching priorities.

questions.prompt: A high-priority control thread misses deadlines. Traces show it blocked on a lock held by a low-priority logger, while a medium-priority analytics thread runs. What is happening?

choices.label: Priority inversion: Medium keeps Low from releasing the lock
Deadlock: High and Low each hold a lock the other needs
Starvation: the scheduler skips High in favour of others
Livelock: High and Low keep yielding to each other

questions.explanation: High waits for Low, and Medium outranks Low, so the lock holder cannot run: a classic inversion. Deadlock needs a cycle of waits, which Medium breaks; High runs when it is runnable but it is blocked, not ignored; and livelock needs threads actively retrying, which none is.

questions.prompt: Which change bounds High’s wait to roughly the length of Low’s critical section?

choices.label: Raising Medium’s priority above High’s for fairness
Giving High a lower nice value than the others
Enabling priority inheritance on the shared mutex
Adding a second core so Medium runs elsewhere

questions.explanation: Inheritance lifts Low to High’s priority while High waits, so Medium cannot preempt it and the lock is released after Low’s section. Raising Medium makes things worse, nice values do not affect real-time priorities or lock waits, and a second core helps only by luck, since Medium and Low can still share one.

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound threads share one core under the normal policy. One runs at nice 0, the other at nice 10. What happens?

choices.label: The nice 0 thread runs and the other waits until it ends
Both get half the core each, since nice only affects I/O
The nice 10 thread runs first until it has finished
Both run; the nice 0 thread gets a much larger share

questions.explanation: Under the normal policy, nice sets a weight, and each nice step changes it by about 1.25 times, so ten steps give the nice 0 thread roughly nine times the share, but both progress. Strict precedence is how real-time policies behave, nice has nothing to do with I/O, and higher nice means lower priority.

questions.prompt: A real-time thread at priority 50 enters an infinite loop on a 1-core machine. What do you expect?

choices.label: Normal threads still get a small slice of each second
The kernel demotes it to normal priority within a second
It runs only when no normal thread wants the CPU
Other threads stop running until it is killed

questions.explanation: Real-time threads outrank all normal ones, but Linux by default reserves 5% of each second for non-real-time work, so normal threads crawl rather than stop. The kernel does not demote it, real-time threads run ahead of normal ones rather than after, and the throttling margin prevents a total freeze.

questions.prompt: Two CPU-bound threads share one core. Their scheduler weights are 1,024 (nice 0) and 335 (nice 5). Roughly what percentage of the core does the nice 0 thread get?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: five nice steps of about 1.25 times each give a ratio of about 3 to 1, so roughly three quarters and one quarter; nice reshapes shares but never stops the weaker thread.

questions.prompt: Order the events of a bounded inversion when the mutex uses priority inheritance.

items.label: Medium wakes but cannot preempt the boosted Low
Low takes the lock
Low releases the lock, drops back to its own priority, and High runs
High blocks on the lock and Low inherits High’s priority

questions.explanation: Boost on block, release, un-boost: High waits only for the rest of Low’s critical section.

flashcards.back: High waits on a lock held by Low, while Medium preempts Low, so High waits on Medium.
A lock holder temporarily runs at the priority of the highest thread waiting for it.
Nice sets proportional shares among normal threads; real-time priorities strictly preempt.

sources.title: Real-Time group scheduling, Linux kernel documentation

mechanism.title: How priorities interact with locks
steps: Each core picks the next thread from its run queue: any runnable real-time thread first, highest priority first, then normal threads by their weighted fair share.
A thread that blocks on a lock leaves the run queue; its priority no longer matters until it is woken. The lock holder keeps its own priority.

If a thread of middle priority becomes runnable, it preempts the low-priority holder, and the high-priority waiter now depends indirectly on the middle thread finishing. The wait is unbounded: as long as middle-priority work exists, the holder cannot run.

With priority inheritance, blocking on the lock records the waiter, and the kernel raises the holder to the waiter’s priority. Chains are followed: if the holder is itself waiting on another lock, that holder is boosted too.
With a priority ceiling, each lock has a fixed priority at least as high as any thread that uses it; a thread holding it runs at that priority, which also prevents some deadlocks.
Real-time scheduling adds throttling: by default real-time threads may use 950 ms of every 1,000 ms, leaving 50 ms for everything else so a runaway thread can still be stopped.

useWhen: Use priority inheritance on locks shared by threads with different real-time priorities.
Use real-time policies only for short, bounded work with hard latency needs, such as audio or control loops.
avoidWhen: Avoid sharing locks between real-time threads and threads that do unbounded work.
Avoid treating nice values as a fix for latency caused by waiting.

rows: Boosts a holder while a higher thread waits
Boosts every holder to the lock’s ceiling
Ceilings must be assigned and kept correct

numbers.title: How long High really waits
assumptions: Low’s critical section takes 1 ms; Medium runs CPU work in 50 ms bursts; High’s deadline is 10 ms (illustrative)
steps: Without inheritance, worst case: High waits for Medium’s burst plus the rest of Low’s section, 50 + 1 = 51 ms.
That misses the 10 ms deadline by 41 ms, and two Medium bursts in a row would double it.
With inheritance: High waits for at most the remainder of Low’s section, about 1 ms.
High then has about 9 ms of its 10 ms budget left for its own work.
numbers.result: Inheritance turns a 51 ms worst case into about 1 ms here; the bound depends only on the critical section, not on unrelated work.

india.title: The real-time safety margin
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Linux kernel’s real-time group scheduling documentation explains that real-time tasks can starve everything else on a CPU, so the kernel limits them by default: the period setting is 1,000,000 microseconds and the runtime setting is 950,000 microseconds, meaning real-time tasks may use at most 0.95 s of every second, leaving 0.05 s for normal tasks. That margin lets an administrator still log in and stop a runaway real-time thread, and setting the runtime to minus one removes the limit entirely, which the documentation treats as a deliberate choice rather than a default.

pitfalls.trap: “Make the slow thread a higher priority.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d first check what it is waiting for; if it’s a lock held by a lower thread, I’d use priority inheritance.”

pitfalls.trap: “Real-time priority will make it fast.”
pitfalls.say: “It makes it preempt others, not run faster; unbounded work at real-time priority starves the machine.”

takeaways: A high-priority waiter can be held up by medium-priority work.
Priority inheritance or ceilings bound the wait to one critical section.
Nice sets shares; real-time priorities strictly preempt.
Real-time threads must do short, bounded work.

interactive.title: How long does High wait?
interactive.prompt: On one core, Low (priority 10) takes a lock for a 2 ms update. High (priority 90) then blocks on that lock. Medium (priority 50) wakes and computes for 40 ms. The mutex uses no special protocol.

choices.label: About 42 ms: Medium runs first, then Low finishes
choices.feedback: Right: Medium outranks Low, so the lock holder cannot run until Medium is done.

choices.label: About 2 ms, since High outranks everyone
choices.feedback: High is blocked, not runnable, so its priority does not help Low.

choices.label: Forever: this is a deadlock
choices.feedback: There is no cycle; once Medium finishes, Low releases the lock.

interactive.reveal: Enable priority inheritance on the mutex and Low runs at priority 90 while High waits, so Medium cannot preempt it and High waits about 2 ms.

seeAlso.why: How the scheduler picks among runnable threads
Lock waiting is where inversions happen
Priority ceilings also help prevent some deadlocks

title: Thread Pools: Sizing, Queues and Rejection
objectives: Size a pool from cores and the share of time tasks spend waiting
Bound the queue and choose what happens when it is full
Avoid deadlocks where tasks wait on the pool they run in

cards.title: Why pools exist
cards.body: Creating a thread costs memory for its stack and a trip through the kernel, and thousands of threads compete for a few cores. A pool keeps a fixed set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue. Three numbers define it: how many workers, how long the queue may grow, and what happens to a task that arrives when both are full.

cards.title: Worked example: sizing from wait time
cards.body: A service on 8 cores (illustrative numbers).
steps: Each task computes for 10 ms and waits 40 ms on a database
A worker keeps a core busy only 10 ÷ 50 = 20% of the time
To keep 8 cores busy: 8 × (1 + 40 ÷ 10) = 40 workers
At full use the pool finishes at most 8 cores ÷ 10 ms = 800 tasks a second; how many workers a given arrival rate needs is a separate question, answered by Little’s Law
More workers than this cannot add CPU; they only queue on the database

cards.title: Trap: one slow dependency takes every worker
cards.body: If one downstream service slows from 20 ms to 2 s, every task that calls it holds a worker a hundred times longer, and soon all workers are waiting on it. Requests that never touch that service now queue behind them too. Give each blocking dependency its own small pool or a concurrency limit (a bulkhead), and set timeouts shorter than the caller’s deadline so a stuck call frees its worker.

cards.title: Misconception: one big pool is simplest
cards.body: If a task running in a pool submits a sub-task to the same pool and waits for it, every worker can end up waiting for sub-tasks that have no free worker to run them: a deadlock. Run sub-tasks on a separate pool, or have the waiting task run them itself, and never block a worker on the pool it belongs to.

cards.title: Watching a pool
cards.body: Four measurements show a pool’s health: active workers, queue length, time tasks spend queued, and rejections. Queue time rising while workers are all busy means the pool or its downstream is saturated; workers idle while the queue grows means tasks are stuck waiting on something. Alert on queue time, which is what callers feel, rather than on thread count.

questions.prompt: A CPU-bound image resizer runs on a 16-core machine and never waits on I/O. About how many pool workers should it start with?

choices.label: About 16, one per core
About 160, so that tasks do not queue
About 4, to leave cores free for the kernel
One per pending request, created on demand

questions.explanation: Tasks that never wait can keep at most one core busy each, so about one worker per core uses the machine fully. More workers add switching and cache misses without more CPU, a quarter of the cores wastes capacity, and one thread per request is the unbounded model a pool exists to avoid.

questions.prompt: Under a traffic spike, a service’s latency climbs from 50 ms to 40 s and memory keeps growing, but it returns no errors. What is the most likely design flaw?

choices.label: The pool has too few workers for normal traffic
Tasks queue without limit instead of being rejected
The garbage collector is tuned for throughput
Workers are pinned to specific cores

questions.explanation: Growing latency and memory with no errors is the signature of an unbounded queue absorbing overload. Too few workers would also show at normal load, collector tuning does not explain 40 s waits with steady growth, and pinning affects cache behaviour, not queueing.

questions.prompt: A report task runs in a 10-worker pool, submits 3 sub-tasks to the same pool and waits for them. With 10 reports in flight, everything stops. Why?
