Detect and declare: triage the alert, and as soon as it looks real, declare an incident and name a lead. Declaring early is cheap; a late declaration loses evidence and hours.
Preserve evidence: export audit and application logs to storage the compromised identities cannot change, snapshot disks, capture memory from running hosts, and record hashes and a timeline in UTC.

Contain: cut the attacker’s access while keeping evidence, for example by isolating hosts at the network layer, disabling credentials and ending sessions. Contain all known footholds at the same moment where possible, so the attacker cannot react by moving to another.

Scope and eradicate: read the logs from the first sign of the attacker, list everything each compromised identity did and could reach, remove persistence, rotate every secret that was readable, and rebuild machines that held root-level compromise.

Recover and notify: restore from known-good sources, watch closely for the attacker’s return, decide with legal advisers whom to tell and by when (the EU GDPR expects the regulator to be told within 72 hours of becoming aware where feasible), then hold a blameless review and fund its actions.

useWhen: Any sign that an attacker or insider accessed systems or data without permission
Leaked credentials, even if nobody is known to have used them yet
avoidWhen: Treating a security incident like an outage and re-imaging first
Closing the incident when the first credential is revoked

rows: Keep the evidence that answers what happened
Rebooting or re-imaging before capturing anything
Stop further access without alerting early
Blocking one foothold while others stay open
Missing users, keys and jobs the attacker created
Return to trusted service and meet duties
Guessing the scope instead of proving it from logs

numbers.title: Why rotation has to be scripted
assumptions: The compromised role could read 120 secrets
Rotating one by hand takes about 15 minutes
A scripted rotation takes about 1 minute per secret
steps: By hand: 120 × 15 = 1,800 minutes
1,800 / 60 = 30 hours of focused work, spread over days in practice
Scripted: 120 × 1 = 120 minutes
numbers.result: In this illustrative case, scripted rotation shrinks the window in which stolen secrets still work from more than a day to about 2 hours.

india.title: NIST and AWS guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 places incident response inside the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, so preparation, detection, response and recovery are treated as ongoing risk management rather than a one-off procedure. NIST SP 800-86 covers collecting and preserving evidence so that it remains trustworthy, including the order in which volatile data such as memory should be captured before it disappears. The AWS Security Incident Response Guide applies the same ideas to cloud accounts: keep audit logs in a separate account, prepare roles responders can assume, and practise isolating resources and rotating credentials before an incident forces you to.

pitfalls.trap: Re-imaging a compromised server straight away
pitfalls.say: Isolate it and capture memory and disk first, then rebuild from a known-good source.

pitfalls.trap: Scoping from the alert time instead of first attacker activity
pitfalls.say: Search the logs back to the first sign of the attacker and scope from there.

pitfalls.trap: Rotating only the leaked credential
pitfalls.say: Rotate every secret the compromised identity could read, and remove what it created.

takeaways: Preserve evidence before changing anything
Contain every known foothold together
Scope from logs and remove persistence
Rotation and notification need preparation in advance

interactive.title: Is the attacker out?
interactive.prompt: A leaked access key was deactivated 10 minutes after the alert. Logs show the key made 40 calls during the 3 hours before that, including creating a role.

choices.label: Not yet: the new role may still give them access
choices.feedback: Right: persistence outlives the key that created it.

choices.label: Yes: a deactivated key cannot be used again
choices.feedback: True of the key, but not of the role it created.

choices.label: Yes, provided the key’s owner changes their password
choices.feedback: Passwords do not affect access keys or roles.

interactive.reveal: Review all 40 calls, delete the role and anything else it made, and rotate what the key could read before you call it contained.

seeAlso.why: Roles, mitigation and blameless reviews from operational incident response
Audit trails supply the evidence that scopes a compromise
Secret rotation must be fast and rehearsed before an incident

title: Securing CI/CD Pipelines
objectives: Treat the pipeline as a privileged system that can reach production
Keep untrusted code away from secrets and write access
Replace stored cloud keys with short-lived, federated credentials

cards.title: The pipeline is a production administrator
cards.body: A delivery pipeline holds deploy credentials, artefact signing keys and write access to registries and repositories. Anyone who can change what the pipeline runs, whether its configuration file, a build script or a test, can act with those powers. That makes the pipeline one of the most valuable targets in an organisation. The OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks list starts with weak flow control (code reaching production without review) and includes poisoned pipeline execution, over-broad pipeline permissions and poor credential hygiene.

cards.title: Poisoned pipeline execution
cards.body: A pull request from an outside contributor can change a test so that it reads environment variables and sends them to an attacker’s server. If the job that runs that test has secrets or a token with write access, they leak the moment the build starts, before anyone reviews the change. The rule is to split by trust: jobs that run unreviewed code get no secrets and read-only tokens, and jobs that hold secrets run only code that has been reviewed and merged into a protected branch.

cards.title: Worked example: a third-party step whose tag moved
cards.body: A build job pulls in a popular third-party step to list the files a pull request changed.
steps: The workflow refers to the step by a version tag, such as v45
A tag is a movable pointer: whoever controls that repository can point it at new code
In March 2025 the tags of tj-actions/changed-files were moved to a commit that printed runner secrets into build logs
Fix: refer to the step by its full commit hash, which cannot be moved, and review each proposed update
Give the job only the token permissions it needs, so a step that turns malicious has little to steal

cards.title: Misconception: secrets are safe because logs mask them
cards.body: Pipeline platforms replace known secret values with asterisks in logs, but masking matches exact strings. Code in the job can print the secret encoded, reversed or split in two, or simply send it over the network, and masking sees nothing. Masking prevents accidents, not attacks. What protects a secret is never giving it to a job that runs code you have not reviewed, and making it short-lived, by federating the job to the cloud for credentials that expire within minutes, so a stolen copy soon stops working.

cards.title: Trap: anyone who can push can deploy
cards.body: If the deploy job runs from any branch, every person with write access, and every stolen developer token, can ship to production. Protect the main branch with required review by someone other than the author, protect the pipeline configuration files with code owners, and gate production deploys on a protected environment that only accepts the main branch and may require an approval.

questions.prompt: A public repository runs its test job on pull requests from forks, and that job has a deploy token in its environment. What is the main risk?

choices.label: The token may be printed in the public build log unless it is masked
A pull request can change a test so it sends the token elsewhere
Fork builds run against an old commit that lacks security fixes
The extra test runs use up the build minutes quota for the month

questions.explanation: Any code in the pull request runs with the token, before review, so it can exfiltrate it. Masking only hides exact strings in logs and does nothing about network calls. Fork builds run the contributor’s new code, not an old commit. Build minutes are a cost issue, not a credential leak.

questions.prompt: A workflow uses a third-party step as some-org/scan@v2, and the job holds a registry write token. Which change best stops a hijacked release of that step from stealing the token?

choices.label: Refer to the step by its full commit hash, and review updates
Refer to the step by its latest tag, so fixes arrive sooner
Turn on log masking for the registry token in that job
Run the step only after the unit tests have passed in the job

questions.explanation: A commit hash names exact code that cannot be swapped later, so a moved tag changes nothing until someone reviews an update. The latest tag pulls in whatever the tag now points at. Masking hides exact strings in logs, not network calls. Running after the tests does not change what the step’s code can do.

questions.prompt: Developers can edit the pipeline file on any branch, and the production deploy job runs from whichever branch triggered it. What fixes this?

choices.label: Ask developers to sign their commits with a personal key
Store the production credentials in a separate secrets vault
Deploy only from the protected main branch after review
Run a static analysis scan on each branch before it deploys

questions.explanation: Tying production to a reviewed, protected branch means one person cannot change the pipeline and deploy on their own. Signed commits prove who wrote a change, not that anyone reviewed it. A vault still hands the credentials to whatever job asks. A scan finds some code flaws but cannot tell a malicious deploy step from a legitimate one.

questions.prompt: A stored key is rotated every 90 days; a federated credential lasts 15 minutes. If either leaks at a random moment, its average remaining life is half its lifetime. About how many times longer does a leaked stored key stay usable?
assumptions: Average remaining life is half the lifetime
questions.workedAnswer: 90 / 2 = 45 days, and 45 × 1,440 = 64,800 minutes on average. 15 / 2 = 7.5 minutes. 64,800 / 7.5 = 8,640 times longer.
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the halving cancels out, so this is just 90 days divided by 15 minutes: 129,600 / 15 = 8,640. Short lifetimes shrink the damage window by orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Design the pipeline for an open-source service that accepts outside contributions and deploys to a cloud account.
constraints: Maintainers want fast feedback on every change

approaches.label: Secret-free test jobs for pull requests; deploy job only on main, in a protected environment, using federation
One job that tests and deploys, with secrets masked in logs
Maintainers deploy by hand from their laptops with an admin key

rationaleOptions.label: Unreviewed code never runs where a credential exists
Production can only be reached through reviewed code on main
Masking secrets in logs is enough to protect them
An admin key on a laptop is safer than one in a pipeline

rationaleConflicts.r3: Code in the job can send a secret over the network, which masking cannot see.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Laptops get lost and phished, and manual deploys skip review and the audit trail.

questions.explanation: Separate jobs by how much you trust the code they run, and give credentials only to the trusted side.

questions.prompt: Order a safe path from pull request to production.

items.label: Build once on main and sign the artefact with provenance
Get approval from a reviewer other than the author
Deploy that artefact from a protected environment using short-lived credentials
Build and test the pull request in a job with no secrets
Merge into the protected main branch

questions.explanation: Untrusted code is tested without secrets, a second person reviews it, and only merged code is built, signed and deployed with credentials that expire soon after.

flashcards.back: Changing code or config the pipeline runs so it acts with the pipeline’s credentials.
A signed identity token exchanged for cloud access that expires within minutes.
Jobs running unreviewed code get no secrets; jobs with secrets run only reviewed code.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-204D: Software Supply Chain Security in DevSecOps CI/CD Pipelines
GitHub Docs: Secure use reference for GitHub Actions

mechanism.title: How to secure a delivery pipeline
steps: Map what the pipeline can reach: list every credential, token and key each job receives and what it can write to, such as registries, repositories, cloud accounts and signing services. That list is the blast radius of a pipeline compromise.

Split jobs by trust: run pull requests from contributors, and especially from forks, in jobs with read-only tokens and no secrets, and keep credentials for jobs that run reviewed code from protected branches.

Use federation instead of stored keys: have jobs exchange a signed identity token for cloud credentials that last minutes, with a trust policy that names the repository, branch and environment allowed to assume each role.

Protect what reaches production: require review by someone other than the author, protect the pipeline configuration files with code owners, deploy only from the main branch, and gate production on a protected environment.

Pin and isolate build steps: reference third-party pipeline steps by an immutable version such as a commit hash, use fresh, short-lived runners so one build cannot tamper with the next, and keep build networks from reaching internal systems they do not need.

Build once and record provenance: build the artefact once on main, sign it with provenance that says which source and pipeline produced it, and have the deploy step verify that signature before releasing.

useWhen: Any repository whose pipeline can deploy, publish or sign
Projects that accept contributions from outside the team
avoidWhen: Giving every job every secret for convenience
Long-lived cloud keys stored as pipeline variables

rows: Triggers that run fork code with base-branch secrets
Long-lived keys leaking and staying valid
Trust policies that accept any branch
Admins allowed to bypass the rules
Version tags that can be moved

numbers.title: What a stored key costs to manage
assumptions: The same cloud key is stored in 30 repositories
Updating it takes about 10 minutes per repository
Policy says rotate every quarter, 4 times a year
steps: One rotation: 30 × 10 = 300 minutes, which is 5 hours
Per year: 4 × 5 = 20 hours of rotation work
Each of the 30 copies is a separate place it can leak from
With federation there are 0 stored copies and nothing to rotate
numbers.result: In this illustrative setup, federation removes about 20 hours a year of rotation work and 30 copies of a key that could leak.

india.title: OWASP and NIST guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks project describes how attackers abuse pipelines, including insufficient flow control, poisoned pipeline execution, inadequate identity and access management, and insufficient credential hygiene. The OWASP CI/CD Security Cheat Sheet turns these into controls such as protected branches, isolated build environments and short-lived credentials. NIST SP 800-204D places these practices within software supply chain security, and the SLSA build levels describe how far a build platform goes towards producing provenance that cannot be forged.

pitfalls.trap: Running fork pull requests in jobs that hold secrets
pitfalls.say: Give those jobs no secrets and read-only tokens; run secret-holding jobs only on reviewed code.

pitfalls.trap: Trusting log masking to protect secrets
pitfalls.say: Assume any code in a job can read its secrets, and keep secrets short-lived.

pitfalls.trap: Letting any branch deploy to production
pitfalls.say: Deploy only from the protected main branch through a protected environment.

takeaways: The pipeline holds production power; protect it like production
Unreviewed code never runs next to secrets
Prefer short-lived federated credentials to stored keys
Only reviewed code on main reaches production

interactive.title: Where does the secret go?
interactive.prompt: A pull request edits a test to run a command that sends all environment variables to an outside server. The test job holds a registry write token, and log masking is on.

choices.label: The token reaches the attacker; masking only edits logs
choices.feedback: Right: the network call never touches the log.

choices.label: Masking blocks it, since the token value is recognised
choices.feedback: Masking rewrites log output only; it does not inspect network traffic.

choices.label: Nothing leaks until a maintainer approves the pull request
choices.feedback: The job ran when the pull request was opened, before review.

interactive.reveal: Give pull request jobs no secrets, so there is nothing for edited code to send.

seeAlso.why: The delivery pipeline this lesson hardens
Dependencies and provenance: the rest of the supply chain
Security tests run inside the same pipeline
Federating CI jobs to the cloud for short-lived credentials, step by step

title: Authorisation Models: RBAC, ABAC and ReBAC
objectives: Choose between role-, attribute- and relationship-based access control for a product
Recognise role explosion and combine models instead
Centralise the decision, enforce it everywhere and keep it fresh

cards.title: Three ways to answer “may this user do this?”
cards.body: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions to roles and puts users in roles: “support agents may view tickets”. Attribute-based access control (ABAC), described in NIST SP 800-162, evaluates rules over attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the context: “staff may view a record if its region matches theirs and they are on shift”. Relationship-based access control (ReBAC) derives permissions from a graph of relationships: “you may edit a document if you are an editor of the folder that contains it”, the model behind many sharing systems.

cards.title: Role explosion
cards.body: RBAC is simple until roles start encoding the resource or the context. If every project needs viewer, editor and admin roles in each region, 40 projects with 3 levels make 120 roles, and 4 regions take that to 480. Nobody can review 480 roles, so people get granted broad ones instead. When role names contain ids, places or times, those parts belong in attributes or relationships, not in more roles.

cards.title: Worked example: may Priya edit document 42?
cards.body: A document app lets people share folders with teams; edit rights inherit from folders to the documents inside.
steps: The service asks the policy decision point: may user Priya perform edit on document 42?
It finds that document 42 sits in folder Finance, which is shared with team Accounts as editor
It finds that Priya is a member of team Accounts, so the relationship grants edit
It checks the attribute rule: documents under legal hold cannot be edited; this one is not
It returns allow, the service performs the edit, and the decision is logged

cards.title: Misconception: you must pick one model
cards.body: Most products mix them. Roles suit coarse job functions such as administrator or billing manager. Relationships suit per-object sharing and inheritance. Attributes suit conditions such as region, data classification, device or time. What matters more than the model is the structure: one policy decision point that answers every question with a default of deny, and enforcement points in every service and endpoint that ask it before acting, as the OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet recommends.

cards.title: Trap: deciding with stale permissions
cards.body: If roles are copied into a token that lasts an hour, a user removed from a role keeps that power until the token expires. Caches of relationships cause the same lag. For sensitive actions, check current permissions at decision time, keep tokens that carry permissions short-lived, and make revocation take effect before new sharing, so removing someone and then sharing a secret document cannot be applied in the wrong order.

questions.prompt: A file app lets users share individual files and folders with people and teams, and access granted on a folder applies to everything inside it. Which model fits best?

choices.label: RBAC, with a viewer and editor role created for every folder
Relationship-based, with sharing and folder links as a graph
Attribute-based, with each file tagged by its owner’s department
Copying the folder’s access list onto every file when shared

questions.explanation: Sharing and folder nesting are relationships, and inheritance is a walk up the graph. A role per folder causes role explosion. Department tags cannot express sharing with an individual person. Copying lists onto every file goes stale whenever a file moves or the folder’s sharing changes.

questions.prompt: Rule: support staff may view a customer’s record only if the customer is in the agent’s region and the agent is on shift. Which model expresses this most directly?

choices.label: RBAC, with one support role for each region and shift pattern
Relationship-based, linking every agent to each customer record
Attribute-based, comparing region and shift at decision time
Access lists on each record, updated when shifts change

questions.explanation: The rule compares attributes of the user, the resource and the context, which is what ABAC evaluates. Roles per region and shift multiply quickly and still cannot see the clock. Linking agents to each customer creates millions of edges that change with every rota. Updating access lists on each shift change is slow and error-prone.

questions.prompt: A user is removed from the finance-admin role but can still export reports for the next 50 minutes. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: Roles are copied into a token that lasts an hour
The database has not yet replicated the role change
The export endpoint does not check roles at all
The browser has cached the export page for an hour

questions.explanation: A permission baked into a token lasts until the token expires, however the role changes. Database replication lag is usually seconds, not 50 minutes. If the endpoint checked no roles, access would never have stopped. A cached page does not let new export requests succeed on the server.

questions.prompt: A product needs viewer, editor and admin access for each of 40 projects in each of 4 regions. How many roles does pure RBAC need?
questions.explanation: Design implication: roles that encode resources and places grow multiplicatively. Keep 3 roles and move project and region into relationships or attributes.

questions.prompt: Twelve services each make authorisation decisions about the same users and resources.
constraints: Auditors ask why access was granted
Some services are written by different teams

approaches.label: One shared policy decision point, called by every service, deny by default
Each service writes its own checks inline in its handlers
Check permissions only at the API gateway, by URL path

rationaleOptions.label: A rule change happens in one place and applies everywhere
Each decision can be logged with the policy that made it
Inline checks stay consistent because the teams share docs
Path rules at the gateway can see which object is requested

rationaleConflicts.r3: Twelve copies of the rules drift apart however good the documents are.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A path shows the object id, not who owns it or how it is shared.

questions.explanation: Decide in one place, enforce in every service, and log each decision.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an authorisation check.

items.label: Load the relevant roles, relationships and attributes
Authenticate the caller and build the subject
Enforce the decision and log it
Identify the action and the resource
Evaluate the policy, denying unless a rule allows

questions.explanation: You cannot decide without knowing who is asking and what for. The decision needs current data, defaults to deny, and is recorded for audit.

flashcards.back: Permissions attach to roles, and users are assigned roles.
Rules evaluate attributes of the user, resource, action and context.
Permissions follow relationships such as owner, member and parent folder.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-162: Guide to Attribute Based Access Control
NIST: Role Based Access Control project

mechanism.title: How to design authorisation
steps: List the questions: write down the real decisions, such as “may this user refund this order?” or “may this team see this folder?”, and the facts each one depends on. The facts tell you which model fits.
Use roles for job functions: keep a small number of roles for broad duties, such as administrator, support agent and billing manager, and review who holds each one regularly.

Use relationships for sharing and ownership: store edges such as user member of team, team editor of folder, and folder parent of document, and derive permissions by following them, so moving a document changes its access automatically.
Use attributes for conditions: express region, data classification, time, device posture or legal hold as rules over attributes, evaluated at decision time.
Centralise the decision: put the rules behind one policy decision point, a shared library or service, so every enforcement point asks the same question the same way and the default answer is deny.

Keep decisions fresh and visible: check current data for sensitive actions, keep permission-carrying tokens short-lived, and log each decision with the inputs and policy version so you can explain it later.

useWhen: Products with sharing, teams, tenants or delegated administration
Systems where auditors ask who can access what and why
avoidWhen: Inventing a role for every resource, place or time window
Copying authorisation rules into every service by hand

rows: Coarse job functions with few roles
Role explosion when roles encode resources or context
Conditions on region, time, classification or device
Rules that are hard to review and to list who has access
Deep graphs that make checks slow without care
Needs a clear owner for the policy

numbers.title: What a relationship check costs on a list page
assumptions: Documents sit up to 6 folders deep
Each relationship lookup takes about 1 ms
A page lists 50 documents, checked one at a time
steps: One worst-case check: 6 lookups at 1 ms each is 6 ms
One page: 50 checks at 6 ms each is about 300 ms
A single query that filters the list by permission does the walk once
That brings the page cost back to a few lookups instead of 300
numbers.result: In this illustrative case, checking a 50-item list one item at a time adds about 300 ms, so relationship systems need batch or list-filtering queries.

india.title: OWASP and NIST guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet recommends enforcing least privilege, denying by default, validating permissions on every request, and preferring attribute- and relationship-based models over plain RBAC when access depends on more than a job title. NIST SP 800-162 defines ABAC, covering subject, object, operation and environment attributes and how policies combine them. NIST’s RBAC project describes the standard role model, including role hierarchies and separation-of-duty constraints that stop one person holding two conflicting roles.

pitfalls.trap: Creating a role for every project and region
pitfalls.say: Keep a few roles and move projects and regions into relationships or attributes.

pitfalls.trap: Baking permissions into long-lived tokens
pitfalls.say: Check current permissions for sensitive actions and keep such tokens short-lived.

pitfalls.trap: Scattering authorisation rules across services
pitfalls.say: Put the rules behind one policy decision point and call it everywhere.

takeaways: Roles for jobs, relationships for sharing, attributes for conditions
Role names with ids or places signal role explosion
Decide centrally, enforce everywhere, deny by default
Stale permissions are a real access bug

interactive.title: What happens to Priya’s access?
interactive.prompt: Priya is an editor of folder Finance. Document 42 is moved from folder Finance into folder Legal, which only the legal team can view.

choices.label: Priya loses edit on document 42 straight away
choices.feedback: Right: access follows the new parent folder.

choices.label: Priya keeps edit, since she had it before the move
choices.feedback: That happens only if access was copied onto the document when it was shared.

choices.label: The legal team loses access to Legal’s other files
choices.feedback: Moving one document does not change the folder’s own sharing.

interactive.reveal: In a relationship model, permissions are derived from current edges, so moving the document changes who can reach it.

seeAlso.why: Every model fails if an endpoint skips the check
Authentication and basic server-side authorisation come first
Tenant boundaries are the outermost authorisation rule

title: Cluster Upgrades: Version Skew, Drains and Disruption Budgets
objectives: Plan a cluster upgrade in the right order, within the supported version skew
Explain how a node drain evicts pods and how disruption budgets slow or block it
Choose between surge upgrades and a new node pool, and estimate how long an upgrade takes

cards.title: Why upgrades never stop
cards.body: Kubernetes ships a minor release roughly three times a year, and each one gets about a year of patch support upstream; managed services publish their own, similar support windows. A cluster left alone falls out of support within about a year and then has to jump several versions under pressure. Teams that upgrade every release, one minor version at a time, keep each step small and practised.

cards.title: Order and skew: control plane first
cards.body: Upgrade the control plane first, then the nodes. The kubelet on a node may be older than the API server, up to three minor versions behind on recent releases, but never newer, so nodes can lag while you roll them. Before starting, check the release notes for APIs removed in the target version: manifests, charts and controllers that still use a removed API version fail to apply after the upgrade, even though the cluster itself looks healthy.

cards.title: Draining one node
cards.body: Every eviction asks the disruption budget first.
steps: Cordon the node so no new pods are scheduled on it
Request an eviction for each pod on the node
The API server checks the pod’s disruption budget
Allowed: the pod gets SIGTERM and its grace period, and its controller recreates it elsewhere
Refused: the drain waits and retries until the budget allows it
When the node is empty, upgrade or replace it

cards.title: Worked example: a 30-node surge upgrade
cards.body: A node pool of 30 nodes is upgraded with a surge of 3: three new nodes are added, three old nodes are drained and removed, and so on. If each batch takes about 10 minutes to boot, drain and delete, the pool needs 30 ÷ 3 = 10 batches, and 10 × 10 = 100 minutes. Raising the surge to 6 roughly halves the time but needs quota for 6 extra nodes and doubles how many pods move at once.

cards.title: Trap: a budget that never lets anything go
cards.body: A service runs 2 replicas with a disruption budget of minAvailable 2, or maxUnavailable 0. Every eviction is refused, so every drain stalls on that node. Managed services wait for a while and then fail the upgrade or force the eviction, depending on the provider. Size budgets so one pod can always go: for example 3 replicas with maxUnavailable 1, spread across zones.

questions.prompt: A cluster runs 1.35 on the control plane and the nodes. You are moving to 1.36. Which order is supported?

choices.label: Upgrade the nodes to 1.36 first, then the control plane
Upgrade the control plane to 1.36, then roll the nodes
Upgrade both at once so that they never differ
Jump the nodes straight to 1.37 while the control plane is upgraded

questions.explanation: Kubelets may lag the API server but must not be newer, so the control plane goes first. Nodes first or nodes at 1.37 would make kubelets newer than the API server, and upgrading everything at once removes the chance to stop if the control plane step goes wrong.

questions.prompt: A drain hangs on one node. The service there has 2 replicas and a disruption budget of minAvailable 2. Why?

choices.label: The node’s kubelet is too old to accept eviction requests
The pods are ignoring SIGTERM, so their grace period never ends
Any eviction would drop below 2 available, so each is refused
Drains only evict pods that have no disruption budget at all

questions.explanation: With minAvailable equal to the replica count, no voluntary eviction is ever allowed, so the drain retries forever. Kubelet version does not affect evictions, a pod ignoring SIGTERM is killed after its grace period, and drains do evict pods with budgets, as long as the budget allows it.

questions.prompt: The cluster upgrade succeeds, but the next deploy fails with “no matches for kind” on an API version. What happened?

choices.label: The deploy used an API version that the new release removed
The new nodes have not pulled the container images yet
The scheduler is still running the previous minor version
The disruption budget blocked the deploy during the upgrade

questions.explanation: Removed API versions are the classic upgrade break: the cluster is fine but old manifests no longer match any kind. Image pulls fail later and differently, the control plane was upgraded as a whole, and disruption budgets limit evictions, not deploys.

questions.prompt: For a critical cluster you want to be able to undo a node upgrade within minutes. Which approach gives that?

choices.label: An in-place upgrade of each existing node, one node at a time
A surge upgrade with a large surge so it finishes sooner
Pausing the cluster autoscaler for the whole surge upgrade
A new node pool on the new version, keeping the old pool

questions.explanation: With a new pool beside the old one, undoing means moving pods back to nodes that still exist. In-place and surge upgrades replace the old nodes as they go, so a rollback is another full upgrade, and pausing the autoscaler changes nothing about reversibility.

questions.prompt: A node pool of 30 nodes is upgraded 3 nodes at a time. Each batch takes about 10 minutes to add, drain and remove. How long does the pool take?
assumptions: No drain is blocked by a disruption budget
questions.explanation: Sanity check: one batch alone is 10 minutes, and one node at a time would be 300; a blocked drain adds its full wait to whichever batch it hits.

questions.prompt: Order a minor-version cluster upgrade.

items.label: Upgrade the control plane
Roll each node pool, draining nodes within their budgets
Check release notes and fix uses of removed APIs
Verify workloads and remove the old nodes
Upgrade cluster add-ons that must match the version

questions.explanation: Fix removed APIs before anything moves, then control plane, add-ons, nodes, and verification.

flashcards.back: Control plane first, then nodes; kubelets may lag the API server but must not be newer.
Cordons the node, then evicts each pod through the eviction API, which checks disruption budgets.

flashcards.front: A budget that blocks every drain?
flashcards.back: minAvailable equal to replicas, or maxUnavailable 0; leave room for one pod to go.

sources.title: Google Cloud: Node pool upgrade strategies

mechanism.title: How a cluster is upgraded without an outage
steps: Prepare first. Read the release notes for the target minor version, list removed and deprecated APIs, and scan manifests, charts and the live cluster for them. Check that add-ons such as the network plugin, DNS, ingress controller and storage drivers support the new version. Upgrade a staging cluster first and run the same checks there, because removed APIs are the most common cause of a successful upgrade followed by failed deploys.

Upgrade the control plane next. On a managed service this is one operation; the provider replaces the API servers and controllers while the API stays reachable. The version skew policy then lets nodes stay behind: a kubelet may be older than the API server, by up to three minor versions on current releases, but never newer. That gap is what allows nodes to be rolled gradually after the control plane is done.

Each node is replaced by draining it. A drain cordons the node so nothing new lands there, then evicts every pod through the eviction API. Each eviction is checked against the pod’s disruption budget, which states how many replicas must stay available or may be unavailable. Allowed evictions terminate the pod with its normal grace period, and its controller recreates it on another node; refused evictions are retried until enough replicas are ready elsewhere.

Surge upgrades add a few new nodes, drain the same number of old ones, and repeat; maxSurge and maxUnavailable trade speed against extra capacity and disruption. A blue-green node pool creates a full pool on the new version, moves workloads by cordoning and draining the old pool, and keeps the old nodes for a soak period, which makes undoing quick at the cost of running two pools for a while.

Disruption budgets must allow progress. A budget that permits zero disruptions blocks every drain; managed services wait for a provider-specific time, then fail the upgrade or force the eviction. Good budgets leave room for one replica to go, and pair with enough replicas spread across zones and readiness probes that only pass when a pod can really serve. Single-replica workloads cannot be both protected and drained, so they need a maintenance window or a second replica.

useWhen: Every cluster, every minor release: small regular upgrades instead of rare forced jumps.
Production services with disruption budgets that leave room for one replica to move.
avoidWhen: Avoid skipping minor versions on the control plane; upgrade one minor at a time.
Avoid budgets of zero allowed disruptions, and in-place upgrades where a fast undo matters.

rows: Move pods back to the old pool
A whole second pool for a while

numbers.title: How long a node pool upgrade takes
assumptions: About 10 minutes per batch to boot, drain and delete
One blocked drain waits 60 minutes before the provider forces it, illustrative
steps: Batches: 30 ÷ 3 = 10.
Normal time: 10 × 10 = 100 minutes.
One blocked drain adds its 60-minute wait to one batch: about 160 minutes in total.
numbers.result: Surge size sets the pace, but a single badly sized disruption budget can add more time than the rest of the upgrade combined.

india.title: Upgrade rules in the Kubernetes docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes version skew policy says the kubelet must not be newer than the API server and may be up to three minor versions older, and that the control plane is upgraded before nodes. The safe-drain task describes cordoning and evicting through the eviction API, which respects disruption budgets. Google Cloud documents surge and blue-green node pool upgrade strategies for managed clusters.

pitfalls.trap: “We will upgrade the cluster when we have to.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d upgrade every minor release, one version at a time, so each step is small and practised.”

pitfalls.trap: “Set the budget to zero disruptions so the service is always safe.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d allow one pod to go and run enough replicas; a zero budget blocks every drain.”

takeaways: Upgrade the control plane first; kubelets may lag but never lead.
Find and fix removed APIs before the upgrade, not after.
Drains evict through disruption budgets; size budgets so one pod can always move.
Surge for speed; a new node pool when a fast undo matters.

interactive.title: The upgrade that stopped at node 7
interactive.prompt: A surge upgrade of a 20-node pool has been stuck on node 7 for 40 minutes. Node 7 runs one pod of a cache with 1 replica and a disruption budget of minAvailable 1.

choices.label: The eviction is refused, because removing the only replica would break minAvailable 1
choices.feedback: Right: with one replica and minAvailable 1, no voluntary eviction is ever allowed.

choices.label: Node 7 is broken and cannot be drained until it is rebooted
choices.feedback: The node is fine; the API server is refusing the eviction.

choices.label: The surge quota ran out, so no new node can be added
choices.feedback: The new nodes already exist; the stall is on emptying the old one.

interactive.reveal: Give the cache a second replica in another zone and set maxUnavailable 1, or schedule a window to drain it deliberately; the provider may otherwise force the eviction after its timeout.

seeAlso.why: Pods, probes and disruption budgets introduced
Spread rules decide where drained pods land
The same safety ideas as a canary, applied to nodes instead of code

title: Stateful Workloads on Kubernetes: Volumes, StatefulSets and Operators
objectives: Explain what a StatefulSet adds: stable names, a volume per pod and ordered rollouts
Predict how zonal block volumes and the volume binding mode constrain where pods run
Decide between running a database with an operator and using a managed database

cards.title: Claims, volumes and classes
cards.body: A pod asks for storage with a persistent volume claim: a size, an access mode and a storage class. The storage class names a provisioner, usually the cloud’s block or file storage driver, which creates a persistent volume and binds it to the claim. The volume outlives the pod, so a restarted or rescheduled pod mounts the same data. The class’s reclaim policy decides whether deleting the claim also deletes the disk (Delete) or keeps it for manual recovery (Retain).

cards.title: What a StatefulSet adds
cards.body: A Deployment’s pods are interchangeable: random names, shared or no storage, replaced in any order. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable ordinal name such as db-0, db-1 and db-2, a stable DNS name through a headless Service, and its own claim from a volume claim template, so db-1 always comes back with db-1’s disk. Rolling updates replace one pod at a time, from the highest ordinal down, waiting for each to be ready before moving on.

cards.title: Misconception: a StatefulSet makes the database highly available
cards.body: A StatefulSet keeps identity and storage attached to each pod; it knows nothing about replication, leader election, failover or backups. If db-0 is the primary and its node dies, the StatefulSet recreates db-0 and reattaches its disk, which can take minutes, but promoting a replica in the meantime is the database’s job, or an operator’s. Three replicas only help if the database itself replicates between them.

cards.title: Where a zonal volume lets a pod run
cards.body: The disk lives in one zone, so the pod must too.
steps: A pod with a claim is created; with delayed binding, no disk exists yet
The scheduler picks a node, taking the pod’s other constraints into account
The provisioner creates the disk in that node’s zone and binds it
Later the pod is rescheduled: only nodes in the disk’s zone qualify
If that zone has no capacity, the pod stays Pending
Recovery in another zone needs a snapshot restore or database replication

cards.title: Trap: binding the disk before the pod is placed
cards.body: With immediate binding, the disk is created as soon as the claim exists, in whichever zone the provisioner picks. The scheduler must then put the pod in that zone, even if the pod’s spread rules or the free capacity point elsewhere, and pods can stay Pending. Storage classes for zonal disks should use the WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode, so the disk is created in the zone of the node the pod was scheduled to.

cards.title: Operators: running a database as code
cards.body: An operator is a controller plus custom resources that encode how to run one piece of software: create a primary and replicas, fail over, take backups, upgrade versions. You declare a cluster resource, and the operator reconciles towards it, much like a Deployment controller does for pods. A good operator makes self-run databases workable, but your team still owns its upgrades, its bugs and every 3 a.m. failover. A managed database moves that work to the provider.

questions.prompt: Why run a three-node database cluster as a StatefulSet rather than a Deployment?

choices.label: Each pod keeps a stable name and its own volume across restarts
A StatefulSet replicates the data between the three pods
A StatefulSet can only be scheduled on nodes with local disks
It promotes a replica to primary when the leader fails

questions.explanation: Stable identity and one volume per pod are what a StatefulSet provides. Replication and promotion are the database’s or an operator’s job, and StatefulSets work with any storage class, network disks included.

questions.prompt: A database pod’s node fails. The pod is recreated but stays Pending, although other zones have plenty of free nodes. Why?

choices.label: The StatefulSet waits for an operator to approve the new pod
Its zonal disk can only attach to nodes in the original zone
The scheduler never reschedules a pod that owns a volume
The new pod must keep the same IP address as the old one

questions.explanation: A block volume lives in one zone, so the pod can only run there, and that zone has no room. No approval is needed, pods with volumes are rescheduled normally within the volume’s zone, and pod IPs are allowed to change.

questions.prompt: A team deletes the claim for a test database, and the cloud disk disappears with it. Which setting caused that?

choices.label: The claim’s access mode was ReadWriteOnce
The volume binding mode was WaitForFirstConsumer
The storage class reclaim policy was Delete
The StatefulSet was set to roll pods in order

questions.explanation: With reclaim policy Delete, removing the claim deletes the volume and its disk; Retain would have kept it. Access mode controls how many nodes can mount it, binding mode controls when it is created, and pod ordering does not touch volumes.

questions.prompt: A small team with no database specialists needs PostgreSQL for one service. What is usually the better choice?

choices.label: A StatefulSet of three pods with the stock PostgreSQL image
A database operator in the cluster, managed by the team
One pod with a volume, and backups when someone remembers
The cloud provider’s managed PostgreSQL service

questions.explanation: A managed service hands failover, patching and backups to the provider, which matters most for a team without specialists. A bare StatefulSet has no failover, an operator still leaves the team owning upgrades and incidents, and ad hoc backups are how data is lost.

questions.prompt: A StatefulSet of 5 pods is updated one pod at a time. Each pod takes about 3 minutes to stop, start and become ready again. How long does the rollout take?
assumptions: Pods are replaced strictly one after another
No pod fails its readiness check
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a Deployment with a surge could replace several pods at once, but a StatefulSet waits for each ordinal in turn, so slow-starting databases make long rollouts.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when a pod with a WaitForFirstConsumer claim is first created.

items.label: The provisioner creates a disk in that node’s zone
The claim exists but has no volume yet
The kubelet attaches and mounts the disk, and the pod starts
The scheduler places the pod on a node
The volume is bound to the claim

questions.explanation: Delayed binding lets scheduling pick the zone first, so the disk is created where the pod will run.

flashcards.back: Stable ordinal names, stable DNS, one volume per pod, ordered one-at-a-time rollouts.
Creates the disk only after the pod is scheduled, in that node’s zone.
Delete removes the disk with the claim; Retain keeps it for manual recovery.

mechanism.title: How state survives on a platform built for replaceable pods
steps: Storage is requested, not configured on nodes. A persistent volume claim asks for a size and access mode from a storage class; the class’s provisioner creates a volume, usually a cloud block disk, and binds it one to one with the claim. ReadWriteOnce volumes attach to one node at a time, which suits databases; shared file storage offers ReadWriteMany at lower performance. Expansion, snapshots and encryption come from the driver and class settings.

StatefulSets add identity. Pods get ordinal names, a headless Service gives each a DNS name such as db-1.db, and a volume claim template creates one claim per ordinal. When db-1 is rescheduled it gets db-1’s claim back. Pods are created in order and, by default, updated in reverse order, one at a time, each waiting to be ready. By default the claims stay when the StatefulSet is scaled down or deleted, which protects data but leaves disks to clean up.

Block volumes are zonal. A pod using one can only run in the volume’s zone, so a zone outage or a full zone keeps it Pending. WaitForFirstConsumer binding creates the volume after scheduling, which keeps spread and capacity decisions with the scheduler. Surviving a zone loss therefore needs replication at the database level across pods in different zones, or restoring a snapshot into another zone, which costs time and recent writes.

The database still has to be operated: replication, leader election, failover, backups, version and schema upgrades, and connection routing to the current primary. Operators package that knowledge as a controller with custom resources, and the mature ones handle failover and backups well. They also add a component to upgrade and debug, and a failure mode where the operator itself is broken during an incident.

Managed database services take on failover, patching, backups and storage scaling, with documented recovery behaviour, in exchange for less control and a higher unit price. For most teams the sensible default is a managed database, with Kubernetes running the stateless tiers; self-running on Kubernetes makes sense when a team has the skills, needs an engine or version the provider lacks, or must run the same stack everywhere.

useWhen: Stateful software that needs stable identity and its own disk, with a mature operator.
Platforms that must run the same database stack on several clouds or on premises.
avoidWhen: Avoid self-running critical databases without the skills to own failover and upgrades.
Avoid assuming a StatefulSet replicates data or survives a zone loss on its own.

rows: Pods wait for the zone; no failover
Operator promotes a replica in another zone
Provider fails over to a standby

numbers.title: Time to recover a primary in a failed zone
assumptions: Primary in zone A on a zonal disk; replicas in B and C
Zone A is down for 2 hours
steps: Without failover: the primary waits for zone A, so writes stop for about 120 minutes.
Operator or managed failover: detect in about 1 minute, promote a replica in about 1 minute, reconnect clients in about 1 minute.
Writes resume after about 3 minutes, losing at most the replication lag if replication was asynchronous.
numbers.result: A StatefulSet alone ties recovery to the zone; replication plus automated failover turns a two-hour outage into minutes.

india.title: Storage and StatefulSets in the docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation describes StatefulSets as giving pods sticky identities and stable storage, updating them in reverse ordinal order by default, and keeping their claims when pods are deleted or scaled down. The storage class page documents reclaim policies and recommends WaitForFirstConsumer for topology-constrained volumes, so the volume is provisioned according to the pod’s scheduling constraints. The operator pattern page explains operators as controllers with custom resources.

pitfalls.trap: “It runs as a StatefulSet, so the database is highly available.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check what replicates the data and who promotes a replica; the StatefulSet only keeps identity and disks.”

pitfalls.trap: “Our database pod can move to any zone if one fails.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check the disk: a zonal volume pins the pod, so we need replication across zones.”

takeaways: Claims request storage; the class decides the provisioner, binding mode and reclaim policy.
StatefulSets give stable names and one disk per pod, not replication.
Zonal disks pin pods to a zone; use WaitForFirstConsumer and replicate across zones.
Default to a managed database unless you can own an operator and its failovers.

interactive.title: Scaling a StatefulSet down and up
interactive.prompt: A StatefulSet of 4 pods, db-0 to db-3, is scaled down to 2 and, a week later, back up to 4. The claims use the default retention settings.

choices.label: db-2 and db-3 come back with their old disks and last week’s data
choices.feedback: Right: by default the claims stay when you scale down, and the same ordinals reattach them.

choices.label: db-2 and db-3 get new, empty disks, because their claims were deleted
choices.feedback: That needs a retention policy that deletes claims on scale-down, which is not the default.

choices.label: The scale-up fails until the old claims are deleted by hand
choices.feedback: The old claims are reused, not in the way.

interactive.reveal: Stale replicas rejoin with week-old data, so the database must resync them; delete or reset the claims on purpose if you want fresh replicas.

seeAlso.why: Pods and controllers, the stateless half of the platform
Scheduling rules that decide which zone a volume ends up in
Backups and restores that still matter when volumes persist

title: Connecting Networks: Peering, Transit Hubs, Private Endpoints and Hybrid Links
objectives: Explain why peering is not transitive and why address ranges must not overlap
Choose between a peering mesh and a transit hub as the number of networks grows
Reach managed services through private endpoints, and pick VPN or a dedicated link to on-premises

cards.title: Peering joins two networks, and only two
cards.body: Peering connects two virtual networks so their private addresses can reach each other over the provider’s backbone, with no gateway in the path. It has two rules that shape every design. Ranges must not overlap, because a route cannot point to the same addresses in two places. And peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A still cannot reach C through B. Each pair that must talk needs its own peering.

cards.title: Worked example: ten networks
cards.body: Ten networks that all need to reach each other need a peering for every pair: 10 × 9 = 90 ordered pairs, halved to 45 peerings, each with route table entries on both sides. Add an eleventh network and that is 10 more. A transit hub, a managed router that networks attach to, needs 10 attachments and one place for route tables, inspection and logging, at the cost of an extra hop and a per-gigabyte processing charge.

cards.title: Private access to a managed service
cards.body: The service appears as an address inside your own network.
steps: The provider’s service, or a partner’s, publishes an endpoint service
You create a private endpoint in your subnet; it gets a private IP
Private DNS maps the service hostname to that private IP
Your app calls the usual hostname and the traffic stays on the provider network
No NAT gateway, internet gateway or public IP is involved
Policies on the endpoint can limit which resources it reaches

cards.title: Private endpoints for managed services
cards.body: Managed services such as object storage, queues and databases have public endpoints by default, so private servers reach them through a NAT gateway and pay its processing charge. A private endpoint puts the service on a private IP in your own network, so traffic never touches the internet path and the service can be locked to accept calls only through that endpoint. Names are the usual catch: private DNS must resolve the service hostname to the endpoint, or clients silently keep using the public path.

cards.title: Reaching on-premises: VPN or a dedicated link
cards.body: A site-to-site VPN runs encrypted tunnels over the internet. It is quick to set up and cheap, but throughput per tunnel is limited to a few gigabits per second at most, and latency varies with the internet path. A dedicated interconnect is a private circuit from your data centre or a colocation site into the provider, with steady latency and 10 or 100 gigabit ports, but it takes weeks to order. Many teams run a VPN as the backup path for the dedicated link.

cards.title: Trap: every team picked 10.0.0.0/16
cards.body: Each team created its network with the console’s default range. Two years later they need to connect, and every network overlaps with every other, so peering and routing are impossible without renumbering or address translation. Plan address space centrally from the start: one non-overlapping block per network, room for growth, and on-premises ranges excluded.

questions.prompt: Network A peers with B, and B peers with C. Can a server in A reach a server in C?

choices.label: Yes, traffic is forwarded through B’s routing table
Only if B runs a NAT gateway for the other two networks
Yes, as long as the three address ranges do not overlap
No; A and C need a peering of their own, or a shared hub

questions.explanation: Peering is not transitive, so A to C needs its own peering or a transit hub. B’s routes do not forward peered traffic, a NAT gateway in B does not route peered traffic, and non-overlapping ranges are necessary but not sufficient.

questions.prompt: Two teams’ networks both use 10.0.0.0/16, and now they must connect. What is the core problem?

choices.label: Peering requires both networks to be in the same region
Routes cannot send the same addresses to two places
The networks need the same security group names first
Peering only works between networks in one account

questions.explanation: Overlapping ranges make routing ambiguous, so peering is refused; renumbering or translation is required. Cross-region and cross-account peering are both widely supported, and security group names have nothing to do with routing.

questions.prompt: Private servers upload terabytes to the provider’s object storage through a NAT gateway, and the NAT bill is large. What fixes it?

choices.label: A private endpoint so storage traffic skips the NAT
A bigger NAT gateway so the traffic costs less per gigabyte
Public IPs on the servers so they can skip the NAT gateway
A VPN tunnel between the network and the storage service

questions.explanation: A private endpoint keeps the traffic on a private path, so it no longer goes through the NAT gateway. NAT pricing is per gigabyte whatever the size, public IPs expose the servers, and a VPN is for connecting networks, not for reaching a provider service.

questions.prompt: A factory must send a steady 8 Gbps to the cloud with predictable latency, for years. Which link fits?

choices.label: A single site-to-site VPN tunnel over the internet
Peering between the factory network and the cloud network
A dedicated interconnect, with a VPN as the backup path
Public endpoints with TLS from the factory over the internet

questions.explanation: Steady high throughput and predictable latency are what a dedicated circuit offers, and a VPN behind it covers circuit failures. One VPN tunnel tops out at a few gigabits with variable latency, peering connects cloud networks rather than sites, and the public internet gives no latency promise.

questions.prompt: Twelve networks must all reach each other. How many peerings does a full mesh need?
assumptions: Every pair needs exactly one peering
No network is reached through another
questions.explanation: Design implication: a transit hub would need 12 attachments instead of 66 peerings, and each new network adds one attachment rather than 12 more peerings.

questions.prompt: A company runs 15 networks across teams, plus a data-centre link, and adds a few networks each quarter.
constraints: Security wants one place to inspect traffic between networks
Network changes must not need edits in every network
A small extra hop is acceptable

approaches.label: Peer every pair of networks directly
Attach every network and the data-centre link to a transit hub
Merge all teams into one large shared network

rationaleOptions.label: New networks need one attachment, not a peering to each other network
A mesh is cheaper at any size because it has no processing charge
Routing, inspection and the on-premises link sit in one place
One shared network removes the need for any access control

rationaleConflicts.r3: Peering avoids the hub’s charge, but 105 peerings and their routes cost far more in operations, and give no central inspection point.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A single network still needs segmentation, and merges every team’s blast radius into one.

questions.explanation: At this size a hub keeps routing and inspection central and makes each new network one attachment; a full mesh would already need 105 peerings.

flashcards.back: Ranges must not overlap, and peering is not transitive.
n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 peerings; a hub needs n attachments.
Private DNS must resolve the service name to the endpoint, or traffic stays on the public path.

sources.title: AWS: What is a transit gateway?
Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Private Link?

mechanism.title: How cloud networks are joined to each other and to the rest of the world
steps: Start with address planning. Every network that may ever connect to another, including on-premises ranges and partner networks, needs a range that overlaps with none of them. A central plan that hands out blocks per account and region, with room to grow, avoids the most expensive networking mistake, which is discovering overlaps when two networks must finally talk.

Peering links two networks directly over the provider backbone. Traffic stays private, there is no extra hop, and peered traffic is billed at internal transfer rates, often free within one zone. Peering is not transitive, so it suits a few networks or a few specific pairs. Each side still controls access with security rules, and route tables on both sides must point the peer’s range at the peering.

A transit hub, offered by each major provider under its own name, is a managed router: networks, VPNs and dedicated links attach to it, and its route tables decide who can reach whom. It scales linearly with the number of networks, gives one place to put inspection firewalls and flow logs, and can separate environments with different route tables. It adds an extra hop and a per-gigabyte processing charge.

Private endpoints bring a managed or partner service into your network as a private IP. Calls to object storage, queues, secrets or a SaaS vendor stay on the provider network, skip the NAT gateway and its charges, and the service can refuse anything that does not arrive through the endpoint. Private DNS zones make the normal hostname resolve to the endpoint, which is the step most often missed.

Hybrid links connect sites. A site-to-site VPN uses IPsec tunnels over the internet, is ready in minutes and suits modest or backup traffic. A dedicated interconnect is a physical circuit at 10 or 100 gigabits per second with stable latency, ordered through the provider or a partner at a colocation site. Routes are exchanged dynamically with BGP, and production designs use two circuits in different locations, or a circuit plus a VPN, so one failure does not cut the site off.

useWhen: Organisations with several accounts, environments or teams that need controlled private connectivity.
Workloads that move a lot of data to managed services or to on-premises systems.
avoidWhen: Avoid full peering meshes beyond a handful of networks.
Avoid default address ranges for any network that may ever connect to another.

rows: No hop; routes on both sides
VPN: limited; circuit: weeks to order

numbers.title: Mesh vs hub as networks grow
assumptions: Every network must reach every other
Counts only; prices vary by provider
steps: Mesh today: 15 × 14 = 210, halved is 105 peerings.
Mesh at 25: 25 × 24 = 600, halved is 300 peerings.
Hub: 15 attachments today and 25 later, one per network.
numbers.result: A mesh grows with the square of the network count while a hub grows linearly, which is why most organisations switch to a hub before about ten networks.

india.title: Peering and private access in provider docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: AWS documents that VPC peering connections do not support transitive peering and cannot connect networks with overlapping ranges, and describes a transit gateway as a regional hub connecting networks and on-premises links. Google Cloud’s Private Service Connect and Azure Private Link both expose services on private IP addresses inside a consumer network, so traffic does not traverse the public internet.

pitfalls.trap: “B is peered with both, so A can reach C through it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d add an A–C peering or a hub; peering is not transitive.”

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll pick address ranges when we need to connect.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d plan non-overlapping ranges now; renumbering later is far more expensive.”

takeaways: Peering is not transitive, and ranges must never overlap; plan addresses centrally.
A mesh needs n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 peerings; a hub needs n attachments.
Private endpoints keep service traffic off NAT and the internet; fix private DNS.
VPN for quick or backup links; dedicated interconnect for steady, high throughput.

interactive.title: The private endpoint nobody used
interactive.prompt: A team creates a private endpoint for the storage service, but the NAT gateway bill does not change. The servers still call storage.example-cloud.com.

choices.label: The hostname still resolves to the public address, so traffic still goes through NAT
choices.feedback: Right: without private DNS for the service name, clients never learn the endpoint’s private IP.

choices.label: Private endpoints only take effect after the servers are rebooted
choices.feedback: Nothing on the servers needs a restart; name resolution decides the path.

choices.label: The storage service blocks endpoints until the bucket is made public
choices.feedback: Endpoints are for private access; making the bucket public is the opposite of the goal.

interactive.reveal: Attach a private DNS zone so the service hostname resolves to the endpoint, then confirm with a lookup from a server and watch NAT traffic fall.

seeAlso.why: The single network, subnets and NAT gateway this lesson connects together
CIDR ranges, which must not overlap between networks
Data transfer and NAT charges that private paths reduce
The IPsec and WireGuard tunnels that site-to-site VPNs and hybrid links are built from
BGP is how routes are exchanged over hybrid links, transit hubs and direct connections

title: Cloud Quotas and Limits: The Capacity You Do Not Own
objectives: Tell adjustable quotas from hard limits, and find the ones a design depends on
Handle API throttling with backoff, jitter and lower concurrency
Plan quota headroom for scaling events, failover regions and IP address space

cards.title: Two kinds of ceiling
cards.body: Every cloud account has ceilings per region: how many vCPUs of each instance family, load balancers, addresses, function concurrency, API calls per second. Most are adjustable quotas, set low by default to protect new accounts and the provider, and raised on request, sometimes within minutes and sometimes after days of review. Some are hard limits fixed by the service’s design, such as a maximum object size or rules per security group, and those must shape the design itself.

cards.title: Throttling is a quota on API calls
cards.body: Control-plane APIs, the ones that create instances, update DNS or read secrets, are rate limited per account, often with a token bucket that allows short bursts. Exceed it and calls fail with a throttling error. A deploy tool firing 300 parallel calls, or every pod reading a secret at start-up, can trip it. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, lower the concurrency, and cache what you read, rather than retrying immediately and making it worse.

cards.title: Finding the limits before an incident does
cards.body: Quota work is part of capacity planning.
steps: List the resources a scale-up or failover would create
Look up the quota for each in every region you might use
Compare the peak or failover need with the quota
Request increases ahead of time, and record them as code where possible
Alert when usage passes about 80% of any quota
Re-check after every architecture change or new region

cards.title: Worked example: pods that eat subnet addresses
cards.body: Some Kubernetes network plugins give every pod an address from the cloud subnet. A /22 subnet holds 1,024 addresses, and the provider reserves a few, here 5, leaving 1,019. If each node uses 1 address for itself and 30 for pods, that is 31 per node, so the subnet fits 1,019 ÷ 31 ≈ 32 nodes. An autoscaler that wants node 33 fails with an address error, even though the vCPU quota has plenty of room.

cards.title: Trap: the failover region with default quotas
cards.body: The disaster recovery plan says to start 200 instances in the second region. That region has never run more than 10, so its quota is still at the default, and the failover stops at the first quota error during the worst hour of the year. Failover regions need the same quotas as production, tested by actually launching at scale in a game day, not by reading the plan.

questions.prompt: Which is usually an adjustable quota rather than a hard limit of the service?

choices.label: The maximum size of one object in object storage
The number of vCPUs an account may run in a region
The maximum length of a function’s single run
The maximum number of rules in one security group

questions.explanation: Regional vCPU quotas exist to protect accounts and the provider, and are raised on request. Object size, maximum run time and rules per group come from how each service is built and are fixed, or adjustable only within narrow bounds.

questions.prompt: A deploy script makes 300 parallel calls to the cloud API and many fail with throttling errors. What is the right fix?

choices.label: Retry each failed call immediately until it succeeds
Run the script from several machines to spread the calls
Back off exponentially with jitter and lower the concurrency
Switch the script to a different region’s API endpoint

questions.explanation: Backoff with jitter spreads retries out, and lower concurrency stays under the rate limit. Immediate retries add load to an exhausted bucket, the limit is per account so more machines do not help, and another region’s endpoint manages different resources.

questions.prompt: During a regional outage, the failover to the second region stops after 10 instances with a quota error. What should have been done?

choices.label: Raise the second region’s quotas to the failover need, and test it
Use larger instances in the failover region to need fewer of them
Keep the failover runbook short so it starts sooner
Request the quota increase as the first step of the failover

questions.explanation: Quotas must already match the failover need, proven by a real test launch. Larger instances still count against the vCPU quota, a shorter runbook does not change the ceiling, and an increase requested mid-outage may take longer than the outage.

questions.prompt: The node autoscaler fails with “insufficient free addresses in subnet” while the vCPU quota is only half used. What is happening?

choices.label: The provider has run out of capacity for that instance type
The cluster has hit its maximum number of nodes
The subnet’s security group rules limit the number of nodes
Pods and nodes have used up the subnet’s address range

questions.explanation: When pods take subnet addresses, the range runs out before compute does. A capacity shortage gives a different error, a node maximum is not about addresses, and security group rules do not consume or limit addresses.

questions.prompt: A /22 subnet has 1,024 addresses, and the provider reserves 5. Each node needs 1 address plus 30 for its pods. How many nodes fit?
assumptions: Every pod gets a subnet address
questions.explanation: Design implication: a /24 would hold only 8 such nodes, so size pod subnets for the largest cluster you expect, or use a plugin mode that gives pods addresses from a separate range.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to make a planned launch-day scale-up safe from quota errors.

items.label: Request increases well before the event
Look up the quota for each in each region
Test by launching at the planned scale
List every resource the scale-up will create
Compare the peak need with each quota

questions.explanation: Inventory, look up, compare, raise early, then prove it with a real launch.

flashcards.back: A quota is a default ceiling you can raise; a hard limit is part of the service design.
Exponential backoff with jitter, lower concurrency, and caching reads.
Raise them to match production ahead of time, and prove it with a launch test.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Azure subscription and service limits, quotas and constraints
AWS: IP addressing for your VPCs and subnets

mechanism.title: How quotas shape capacity planning
steps: The cloud looks unlimited, but each account has ceilings per region and per resource. Quotas cover running vCPUs by instance family, GPUs, addresses, load balancers, managed database instances, function concurrency, storage volumes and more. They start at conservative defaults and are raised through a request, which may be approved automatically or sent for review, especially for scarce resources such as GPUs.

Hard limits are different: they come from how a service is built, such as the largest object or message, the longest function run, or the most rules in one security group, and requests do not move them, or only within narrow bounds. A design that needs more than a hard limit must change, for example by splitting objects, chaining functions or using more groups. Read the limits pages for every service a design depends on before building on it.

Control-plane APIs are rate limited too, per account and often per action, using token buckets that refill at a steady rate and allow bursts. Throttling errors appear during deploys, large autoscaling events and start-up storms, when hundreds of instances or pods call the same API at once. Clients should retry with exponential backoff and jitter, cap their own concurrency and cache results; the provider SDKs do some of this by default, and custom tooling must do it too.

Addresses are a quiet quota. Subnets have fixed sizes, providers reserve a few addresses in each, and some network plugins give every pod a subnet address. Load balancers, endpoints and managed services also take addresses in your subnets. Size subnets for peak node and pod counts with growth, keep spare ranges in the plan, and watch free addresses per subnet as a metric like any other capacity.

Treat quotas as part of capacity planning. For each scaling event and failover plan, list the resources it creates, compare with the quotas in every region involved, raise them in advance, and alert at around 80% of each. Some providers let quota requests be managed through infrastructure as code or organisation templates, so new accounts start with the right ceilings. Prove failover quotas with a launch test, because a quota error in the middle of an incident has no quick fix.

useWhen: Before launches, sales events, new regions and any disaster recovery test.
Accounts where autoscaling or failover may create many resources quickly.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating default quotas as capacity; they are a starting point.
Avoid immediate, unbounded retries against throttled control-plane APIs.

rows: Raise ahead of need, alert at 80%
Size subnets for peak, add ranges

numbers.title: Quota needed for a failover
steps: Failover need: 120 × 8 = 960 vCPUs.
Default quota covers 256 ÷ 8 = 32 instances, about a quarter of the need.
Raise the quota to about 1,200 vCPUs, the need plus 25% headroom, before the plan is relied on.
numbers.result: A failover plan without matching quotas tops out at a fraction of the load it is meant to carry.

india.title: Quotas in provider documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: AWS Service Quotas, Google Cloud’s quotas documentation and Azure’s subscription and service limits page all distinguish adjustable quotas from fixed limits and describe how to view usage and request increases per region. AWS documents that five addresses in each subnet are reserved, which is why a /24 offers 251 usable addresses rather than 256, a detail that matters when pods draw from subnet ranges.

pitfalls.trap: “It’s the cloud, we can scale to whatever we need.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check the quotas in every region the plan uses and raise them before the event.”

pitfalls.trap: “The deploy failed with throttling, so I added retries.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d add exponential backoff with jitter and lower the concurrency, or the retries make it worse.”

takeaways: Quotas are adjustable defaults; hard limits must shape the design.
Throttling needs backoff with jitter and lower concurrency, not instant retries.
Failover regions need production-sized quotas, proven by a launch test.
Subnet addresses are a quota too; size them for peak nodes and pods.

interactive.title: The sale that hit a wall at 40
interactive.prompt: For a flash sale you set the autoscaler maximum to 120 instances of 8 vCPUs. The region’s vCPU quota for that family is 320. Traffic arrives.

choices.label: Scaling stops at 40 instances with quota errors, far below the maximum
choices.feedback: Right: 320 ÷ 8 = 40 instances; the autoscaler maximum cannot exceed the account quota.

choices.label: The autoscaler reaches 120 instances because its own maximum wins
choices.feedback: The autoscaler can only request; the provider refuses launches above the quota.

choices.label: The provider raises the quota automatically to match the autoscaler
choices.feedback: Increases go through a quota request, which may need review; the autoscaler does not raise them.

interactive.reveal: Compare the autoscaler maximum with the quota for each region and family, request the increase days ahead, and alert at 80% of the quota.

seeAlso.why: Autoscaling, whose maximum is bounded by quotas
Subnet sizes that decide how many addresses exist
Zone and region capacity plans that quotas must match

title: Multi-Account Landing Zones and Organisation Guardrails
objectives: Use separate accounts or projects as the strongest boundary for blast radius, access, quotas and billing
Explain how organisation guardrails cap permissions without granting any
Design a landing zone with shared log, security and network accounts and automated account vending

cards.title: The account is the real boundary
cards.body: Every provider has a container that owns resources, permissions, quotas and the bill: an account, a project or a subscription. It is the hardest wall you get, because by default nothing in one can touch another.
