Putting production, staging and development, and often each team, in separate accounts limits what a leaked credential, a bad script or a runaway cost can reach. Inside one shared account the same mistakes only stop at whatever policies you remember to write.

cards.title: Hierarchy and guardrails
cards.body: Accounts sit in a hierarchy: an organisation, then groups such as organisational units, folders or management groups, then accounts. Policies attached high in the tree apply to everything below. Guardrails come in two kinds. Preventive ones deny actions outright, such as creating resources outside approved regions or disabling audit logs. Detective ones only report, such as flagging an unencrypted volume or a public bucket, and feed a ticket or an automatic fix.

cards.title: Misconception: an organisation policy that allows something grants it
cards.body: Organisation-level allow lists set the maximum any principal in the account could ever do; they grant nothing. A role still needs its own policy that allows the action. If the guardrail allows storage actions but the role has no storage permission, the request is denied. And if the role allows everything but the guardrail denies a region, the request is denied too. Access needs both layers to agree.

cards.title: Vending a new account
cards.body: New accounts arrive with the baseline already in place.
steps: A team requests an account through a form or a pull request
Automation creates it under the right organisational unit
Inherited guardrails apply at once from the hierarchy
A baseline is applied: audit logs to the log archive, security tooling, network attachment, budgets
Single sign-on roles are mapped to the team’s groups
The team gets access; nobody holds the account’s root credentials day to day

cards.title: Worked example: the accounts in a small landing zone
cards.body: Eight product teams each get production, staging and development accounts: 8 × 3 = 24. Shared services add three more: a log archive that receives every account’s audit logs and that workload accounts cannot delete from, a security account for tooling and investigations, and a network account that owns the transit hub and the data-centre links. That is 27 accounts, each created by the same automation, so the count is not the hard part; drift between them would be.

cards.title: Trap: one shared account that grew
cards.body: A company starts with one account for everything, and five years later it holds production, experiments and contractor projects. Every role is broad, because narrowing them would break someone, quotas are shared, the bill cannot be split, and a compromised test machine sits next to customer data. Splitting later means migrating live resources. Start with separate accounts per environment, even when it feels early.

questions.prompt: Why put production and development in separate accounts rather than separate subnets of one account?

choices.label: Traffic between separate accounts is faster than traffic between subnets
Separate accounts are cheaper, because each one has its own free tier
A credential or mistake in development cannot reach production
Providers refuse to run production workloads in shared accounts

questions.explanation: The account boundary isolates access, quotas and blast radius by default. Network speed does not depend on accounts, free tiers are not the reason and are often shared across an organisation, and providers do not forbid mixed accounts.

questions.prompt: An organisation guardrail allows all storage actions. A role in the account has no storage permissions. Can the role read a bucket?

choices.label: No, because the guardrail only caps permissions and grants none
Yes, because the guardrail lists storage among its allowed actions
Yes, but only from inside the organisation’s own networks
Only if the bucket is in the same account as the role

questions.explanation: Guardrails set the maximum; the role must also grant the action, so the read is denied. The guardrail grants nothing, network location is a separate condition, and the bucket’s account is not what blocks it here: the role lacks a storage permission.

questions.prompt: Security wants it to be impossible to create resources outside two approved regions in any account. What fits?

choices.label: A weekly report of resources found in other regions
A preventive organisation policy that denies other regions
A naming rule that puts the region in each resource name
A budget alert in each account for spending in other regions

questions.explanation: Only a preventive deny at the organisation level stops the create in every account. A report and a budget alert are detective and act after the fact, and naming rules do not control where resources are created.

questions.prompt: Why send every account’s audit logs to a separate log archive account that workload accounts cannot delete from?

choices.label: Logs are cheaper to store in an account that runs no workloads
Workload accounts cannot write logs to their own storage
Searching logs is faster when they are kept in one account
An attacker in a workload account cannot erase their tracks

questions.explanation: Keeping audit logs out of reach of workload credentials preserves the evidence after a compromise. Storage price does not depend on the account, workload accounts can store logs locally, and central search is a convenience rather than the security reason.

questions.prompt: Eight teams each get production, staging and development accounts, plus three shared accounts for logs, security and networking. How many accounts in total?
assumptions: One account per team per environment
Shared accounts are not per team
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 27 accounts is only manageable because creation and baselines are automated; by hand, each new account is a chance for drift.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of vending a new workload account.

items.label: Apply the baseline: audit logs, security tooling, network, budget
Hand over access to the team
Create the account under the right organisational unit
Map single sign-on roles to the team’s groups
Let inherited guardrails apply

questions.explanation: Placement in the hierarchy brings the guardrails; the baseline and access follow, so the account is safe before anyone uses it.

flashcards.front: Strongest isolation boundary in a cloud?
flashcards.back: The account, project or subscription: separate access, quotas, billing and blast radius.
No. They cap the maximum; a role still needs its own allow.
Log archive, security tooling and network hub.

sources.title: AWS whitepaper: Organizing your AWS environment using multiple accounts
Microsoft Learn: What is an Azure landing zone?

mechanism.title: How a landing zone is put together
steps: A landing zone is the pre-built environment that new workloads land in: an organisation of accounts, the guardrails over them, shared services, identity and networking, all created by code. The goal is that a team can get a new, compliant account in minutes, rather than each team inventing its own setup and the security team auditing a different layout every time.

Accounts are grouped in a hierarchy that mirrors how policy should differ: for example security, infrastructure, production workloads, non-production workloads, sandboxes and a suspended group for accounts being closed. Policies attached to a group are inherited by everything below it, so a rule that applies to all production accounts is written once. Keep the hierarchy shallow and based on policy needs rather than the org chart, which changes more often.

Preventive guardrails cap what is possible: deny regions outside an approved list, deny turning off audit logging, deny leaving the organisation, require encryption, block public access to storage. They do not grant anything, so permissions still come from roles inside the account, and both must allow an action. Detective guardrails evaluate resources continuously and report or fix violations, which suits rules too nuanced to deny outright.

Shared accounts hold what every workload needs. The log archive receives audit and flow logs from every account, with retention locks and no delete access for workload roles. The security account runs threat detection and holds read-only roles into every account for investigations. The network account owns the transit hub, the data-centre links and shared DNS, and workload networks attach to it.

Account vending is the automation that creates an account, places it in the hierarchy, applies the baseline of logging, security tooling, network attachment and budgets, and maps single sign-on groups to roles. Root or owner credentials are locked away with strong MFA and used only for break-glass tasks. Because vending is code, changing the baseline is a reviewed change rolled out to every account, not a manual checklist.

useWhen: Organisations with more than one team or environment, or any regulated data.
Platforms that hand out sandboxes or per-team accounts frequently.
avoidWhen: Avoid one shared account for production and development, however small the company.
Avoid deep hierarchies that copy the org chart; group by policy needs instead.

rows: One account per team and environment
Reports or fixes after the fact

numbers.title: Sizing a landing zone
assumptions: 3 shared accounts: log archive, security, network
Each workload account sends about 2 GB of audit logs a day, illustrative
steps: Workload accounts: 8 × 3 = 24, plus 3 shared, 27 in total.
Log volume into the archive: 24 × 2 = 48 GB a day.
One year retained: 48 × 365 = 17,520 GB, about 17.5 TB, which should go to a cheaper archive storage class after 30 days.
numbers.result: Account count is cheap with automation; the real numbers to plan are log volume, retention and who can delete what.

india.title: Landing zone guidance from providers
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: AWS’s multi-account whitepaper recommends separating workloads into accounts grouped by organisational units, with dedicated log archive and security tooling accounts, and documents that service control policies set maximum permissions without granting any. Google Cloud documents its resource hierarchy of organisation, folders and projects with inherited policies, and Microsoft’s Cloud Adoption Framework describes Azure landing zones built from management groups, policy and platform subscriptions.

pitfalls.trap: “We’re small, one account is fine for now.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d separate production from everything else from day one; splitting a live account later is a migration.”

pitfalls.trap: “The organisation policy allows storage, so the role can read the bucket.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check the role’s own policy; guardrails cap permissions but never grant them.”

takeaways: The account, project or subscription is the strongest isolation boundary.
Guardrails cap permissions and grant none; a role must allow the action too.
Shared log, security and network accounts serve every workload account.
Vend accounts by code so every one starts with the same baseline.

interactive.title: The region that was not allowed
interactive.prompt: A developer with an administrator role in a sandbox account tries to start a VM in a region outside the organisation’s approved list. The organisation has a preventive policy that denies all other regions.

choices.label: The request is denied, because the organisation deny caps even administrators
choices.feedback: Right: the guardrail sets the maximum for every principal in the account.

choices.label: The request succeeds, because the administrator role allows every action
choices.feedback: The role allows it, but the guardrail denies it, and both must allow.

choices.label: The request succeeds, and a detective rule reports it afterwards
choices.feedback: That is how a detective guardrail behaves; this one is preventive.

interactive.reveal: Preventive guardrails are why administrators in member accounts still cannot turn off audit logs or use unapproved regions; only administrators of the organisation itself can change them.

seeAlso.why: Roles that people and pipelines assume inside each account
The transit hub that the network account owns
Quotas, which are counted per account and region
Least privilege inside each account, under the organisation’s guardrails
Secure defaults and hardening baselines that guardrails enforce

title: Policy as Code and Admission Control
objectives: Write platform rules as versioned, tested policy code instead of wiki pages
Enforce the same rules in CI and at admission, so no path around them exists
Roll out a new rule through audit mode, with time-limited exceptions and safe failure settings

cards.title: Rules that a machine can check
cards.body: Platform rules such as “no privileged containers”, “every image from our registry”, “every bucket encrypted” or “resources carry an owner tag” used to live in documents and reviews. Policy as code writes each rule as a small program that takes a resource description, such as a Kubernetes manifest or an infrastructure plan, and returns allow or deny with a message. The rules live in a repository, are reviewed and tested like code, and run the same way everywhere they are enforced.

cards.title: Two checkpoints: the pipeline and the front door
cards.body: In CI, policies check infrastructure plans and manifests before merge, giving fast feedback with the exact line to fix. At admission, the cluster or the cloud checks every create and update request, whoever sends it. CI alone can be bypassed by anyone with direct access; admission alone gives feedback late, at deploy time. Running the same policy code at both points gives early feedback and no way around the rule.

cards.title: How admission control handles a request
cards.body: Every write passes the same checks, whatever tool sent it.
steps: A client sends a create or update request to the API server
Authentication and authorisation check who is asking
Mutating admission may add defaults, such as labels or a sidecar
Validating admission evaluates policies against the final object
A deny returns the policy’s message to the client
Allowed objects are stored and controllers act on them

cards.title: Worked example: rolling out “no latest tags”
cards.body: A new rule rejects images tagged latest. Run in audit mode first, it reports 60 violating workloads out of 400 without blocking anything. Owners are notified with the fix, and teams clear about 15 a week, so after about 4 weeks the count reaches zero and the rule switches to enforce. Two workloads that cannot move yet get exceptions written in the policy repository, each with an owner and an expiry date.

cards.title: Trap: the webhook that blocked every deploy
cards.body: An external admission webhook is set to fail closed, so if it cannot answer, requests are rejected. One day its pods crash. Now no pod can be created anywhere, including the webhook’s own replacement pods, and the cluster cannot heal itself. Exempt system namespaces, run the webhook with several replicas and a short timeout, and choose deliberately per rule whether failing open or failing closed is the smaller risk. Simple rules can use in-process policies that need no webhook at all.

questions.prompt: Policies run in CI, yet a privileged container reached production. How could that happen?

choices.label: Someone applied the manifest straight to the cluster, skipping CI
The CI policy tests were flaky and passed the change by chance
The policy language has no way to express rules about privileged mode
The container image was rebuilt after it passed the CI checks

questions.explanation: CI only sees changes that go through CI, so direct access bypasses it; admission control closes that path. Flaky tests are possible but not the structural gap, privileged mode is one of the simplest rules to express, and rebuilding the image does not change the manifest’s privileged setting.

questions.prompt: A new policy is ready. How should it start in a cluster that already runs hundreds of workloads?

choices.label: Enforce at once, so that new violations stop from the very first day
In audit or warn mode, then enforce once violations are fixed
Only in CI, leaving the running workloads alone for good
Enforce at once, but only in the production namespaces

questions.explanation: Audit mode shows what would break without breaking it, so owners can fix workloads before enforcement. Enforcing at once, in production first of all, blocks deploys of existing workloads, often during an incident; CI only never covers direct changes or existing resources.

questions.prompt: A fail-closed admission webhook crashes, and no pods can be created anywhere. What prevents this next time?

choices.label: Removing the webhook and relying on code review for the rule
Setting a longer timeout on the webhook so calls wait for it
Running it with several replicas and exempting system namespaces
Restarting the API server whenever the webhook becomes unhealthy

questions.explanation: Replicas keep the webhook available and exemptions let the platform heal itself; for simple rules an in-process policy avoids the webhook entirely. Dropping enforcement loses the rule, a longer timeout makes every request slower while it is down, and restarting the API server does not bring the webhook back.

questions.prompt: A legacy workload cannot meet a new rule for three months. How should the exception be handled?

choices.label: Turn the rule off across the cluster until the workload is fixed
Give the team admin rights so it can bypass the policy itself
Tell the team on chat that the rule does not apply to it
A scoped exception in the policy repo, with an owner and expiry

questions.explanation: A scoped, reviewed exception with an owner and an expiry keeps the rule for everyone else and resurfaces when it lapses. Disabling the rule removes it for all, admin rights bypass far more than one rule, and a chat message leaves no record and no expiry.

questions.prompt: Audit mode finds 60 violating workloads. Teams fix about 15 a week, and no new violations appear. How many weeks until the rule can be enforced without breaking anything?
assumptions: Fixes happen at a steady rate
No new violations appear in the meantime
questions.explanation: Sanity check: if new violations kept arriving at the same rate, the count would never fall, so block new ones early with a CI check while the old ones are fixed.

questions.prompt: You need the cluster to reject privileged containers in every namespace except system ones.
constraints: The rule is simple and well known
The cluster must keep working if any add-on is down
Feedback should reach developers before deploy

approaches.label: An external admission webhook running a general policy engine
The built-in, in-process policy check, plus the same rule in CI
A CI check only, with no enforcement in the cluster

rationaleOptions.label: A built-in check needs no extra service, so it cannot be down
Only a webhook can express a rule about privileged mode
The CI copy gives developers the error before they deploy
CI alone is enough when every team uses the pipeline

rationaleConflicts.r3: Privileged mode is covered by the cluster’s built-in pod security checks and simple in-process policies.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Direct applies, break-glass access and other tools skip the pipeline.

questions.explanation: Use the built-in check for a simple, standard rule, so enforcement has no extra moving part, and mirror it in CI for early feedback.

flashcards.front: Why enforce at admission as well as in CI?
flashcards.back: CI only sees changes that use CI; admission checks every write from any client.

flashcards.front: How to roll out a new rule?
flashcards.back: Audit or warn first, fix violations, then enforce; exceptions in code with an owner and expiry.
If it is down, writes are rejected, possibly including its own pods; exempt system namespaces and run replicas.

mechanism.title: How policy as code is enforced end to end
steps: A policy takes structured input, such as a manifest, an admission request or an infrastructure plan, and returns a decision with a reason. Policies are written in a policy language or in the platform’s built-in rule format, stored in a repository, and tested with example inputs that should pass and fail. Because the input is structured, a rule like “no public buckets” checks the actual setting rather than searching text.

Policies run at several points. In the editor and CI, they check plans and manifests before merge. At admission, the Kubernetes API server or the cloud’s policy service evaluates every write request after authentication and authorisation. After the fact, audit scans evaluate resources that already exist, which catches anything created before a rule was introduced. The same policy code at every point keeps the answers consistent.

Kubernetes admission runs mutating policies first, which may set defaults, then validating ones, which allow or deny the final object. Built-in checks such as pod security standards and in-process validating policies run inside the API server, with no network call. External webhooks call a service, which allows any logic but adds latency and a dependency: each needs a timeout, a failure policy and exemptions for the namespaces the platform needs in order to recover.

New rules roll out in stages. Audit or warn mode records or shows violations without blocking, which measures the impact. Owners get the list and the fix. CI enforcement can start early to stop new violations, while existing ones are cleared. Enforcement at admission comes last, once the count is near zero, and the switch is itself a reviewed change that can be reverted.

Exceptions are part of the design. Each one is written in the policy repository, scoped to a specific resource or namespace, with an owner, a reason and an expiry date, and reviewed like any other change. Expired exceptions fail loudly. Tracking violations and exceptions over time shows whether the rules are working, or whether a rule is so often excepted that it needs rethinking.

useWhen: Platforms with many teams where the same rules must hold everywhere.
Regulated environments that must show which rules are enforced and since when.
avoidWhen: Avoid enforcing a new rule before measuring it in audit mode.
Avoid fail-closed webhooks without replicas, timeouts and system exemptions.

rows: Nothing until the next scan runs

numbers.title: Rolling out a rule without breaking deploys
assumptions: About 30 deploys a day across the cluster, illustrative
steps: Violating share: 60 out of 400 is 15% of workloads.
Enforcing on day one: about 15% of 30, so roughly 4 or 5 blocked deploys a day, some during incidents.
Audit first: 60 ÷ 15 = 4 weeks to clear, then enforce with close to zero blocked deploys.
numbers.result: Four weeks of audit mode turns a rule that would block several deploys a day into one that blocks almost none.

india.title: Admission control in the Kubernetes docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation describes admission controllers that run after authentication and authorisation, mutating before validating, and validating admission policies that use expressions evaluated inside the API server as an alternative to webhooks. Its dynamic admission control page documents failure policies, timeouts and namespace selectors for webhooks. Azure Policy documents audit and deny effects for cloud resources, the same audit-then-enforce idea.

pitfalls.trap: “We check policies in CI, so the cluster is compliant.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d enforce the same policies at admission; anyone with direct access skips CI.”

pitfalls.trap: “Ship the rule in enforce mode, it’s obviously right.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d run it in audit mode first to see what it would block, then enforce.”

takeaways: Write platform rules as tested policy code in a repository.
Enforce in CI for feedback and at admission so nothing bypasses the rule.
Audit first, then enforce; exceptions in code with an owner and expiry.
Webhooks need replicas, timeouts and system exemptions, or use built-in policies.

interactive.title: The rule that went straight to enforce
interactive.prompt: A team enables a new “every pod must set memory limits” rule in enforce mode on a Friday. About 20% of existing workloads have no limits. That night an incident requires a hotfix deploy to one of them.

choices.label: The hotfix is rejected at admission until someone adds limits or an exception
choices.feedback: Right: enforcement applies to every new pod, including the urgent ones.

choices.label: The hotfix goes through, because existing workloads are exempt
choices.feedback: Admission checks each new pod; nothing exempts a workload for being old.

choices.label: The running pods are evicted, because they now break the rule
choices.feedback: Admission checks writes; it does not evict pods that are already running.

interactive.reveal: Run new rules in audit mode first, fix the violators, and keep a documented break-glass exception process for incidents.

seeAlso.why: Infrastructure plans that policies check before apply
Admission checks on image signatures in the supply chain
Organisation guardrails, the cloud-level version of the same idea
SAST, DAST and dependency scanning, the other automated checks before deploy

title: Fast, Reliable CI: Caching, Parallelism and Flaky Tests
objectives: Explain why CI speed and trust decide whether people integrate often
Speed up a pipeline with caching, sharding and running only what a change affects
Find, quarantine and fix flaky tests before they teach everyone to click retry

cards.title: Speed and trust are the product
cards.body: Continuous integration only works if people run it on every small change and believe its answer. A pipeline that takes an hour gets batched changes and context switches; one that fails at random gets retried until green, so real failures slip through. Two numbers describe CI health: how long a typical run takes from push to result, and how often a failure is real. Aim for minutes, not hours, and for red to mean broken.

cards.title: Caching: do not redo work that has not changed
cards.body: Most CI time goes on repeating identical work: downloading dependencies, rebuilding unchanged modules and image layers. A cache stores the output under a key built from the inputs, such as a hash of the dependency lock file. Same inputs, same key, so the step is skipped. The key must include every input that matters, or a stale cache produces builds that pass in CI and fail elsewhere. Order image build steps so rarely changing layers come first.

cards.title: Worked example: sharding a slow suite
cards.body: A test suite takes 40 minutes on one runner. Split into 8 shards that run at the same time, each does about 40 ÷ 8 = 5 minutes of tests plus 2 minutes of setup, so the run finishes in about 7 minutes. Total machine time rises from 42 to 8 × 7 = 56 machine-minutes, a cost for a much faster answer. Balance shards by recorded test durations, not test counts, or one slow shard sets the pace.

cards.title: Handling a flaky test
cards.body: A flaky test is a bug to fix, not a reason to retry.
steps: A test fails, then passes on rerun with no code change
CI records it as flaky in a test history
It moves to a quarantine suite that runs but does not block merges
A ticket goes to the owning team with the failure logs
The cause is fixed: timing, ordering, shared state or an external call
The test returns to the blocking suite, or is deleted

cards.title: Trap: automatic retries on every failure
cards.body: Retrying every failed test three times makes the pipeline green again, and hides two problems. Real intermittent bugs, such as race conditions, now pass if they fail only some of the time, and flaky tests pile up because nothing forces a fix. If you retry, record every pass-after-retry as flaky, report it, and cap how long a test may stay in quarantine.

questions.prompt: Developers start batching a week of work into each merge. Which CI problem most likely caused it?

choices.label: Runs take about an hour and often fail for no clear reason
The pipeline runs on each push rather than nightly
Branch protection requires a passing build to merge
Each run posts a full test report as a comment on the pull request

questions.explanation: Slow, untrusted runs make each merge expensive, so people merge less often. Running on every push is what CI should do, requiring green builds is normal protection, and posting a report only changes where results appear.

questions.prompt: A dependency cache is keyed only on the operating system. What goes wrong?

choices.label: The cache misses on each run, so all dependencies download again
A lock-file change can reuse old dependencies from the cache
The cache grows without limit and fills the runner disk
Parallel jobs cannot read the cache at the same time

questions.explanation: The key must include the inputs, such as a hash of the lock file; without it, a new dependency version can be skipped and the build tests the wrong code. A missing key part causes stale hits, not misses, cache storage is bounded by the CI system, and parallel reads are normal.

questions.prompt: A test fails about once in 50 runs on unchanged code. What should the team do first?

choices.label: Delete it, because a test that fails at random has no value
Add three automatic retries so it stops blocking merges
Quarantine it as non-blocking, and ticket its owner to fix it
Raise the timeouts across the suite so that it passes more reliably

questions.explanation: Quarantine stops it blocking merges while keeping it running and visible, and an owner fixes the cause. Deleting it loses coverage that may catch a real race, silent retries hide the flake, and raising timeouts across the suite slows the suite without fixing whatever is non-deterministic.

questions.prompt: A suite is split into 8 shards by test count, but one shard always finishes last by 10 minutes. Why?

choices.label: Test durations vary, so one shard holds most slow tests
Runners are slower when more than four run at the same time
The last shard waits for the others to free the cache
Tests inside each shard run in a different random order on each run

questions.explanation: Equal counts are not equal durations; balance shards by recorded timings. Running several runners does not by itself slow each one, caches are read in parallel, and order within a shard does not change its total time.

questions.prompt: A 48-minute test suite is split into 6 shards balanced by recorded durations, and each shard spends 3 minutes on setup. About how many minutes until every shard has finished?
assumptions: Shards run at the same time on separate runners
Balancing by duration makes each shard about equal
questions.workedAnswer: 8 minutes of tests + 3 minutes of setup = 11 minutes
questions.explanation: Sanity check: machine time rises from 51 to 6 × 11 = 66 runner-minutes, so you pay for a roughly 4.6 times faster answer, and once setup dominates each shard, more shards stop helping.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a pipeline that gives the fastest useful feedback.

items.label: Run unit tests in parallel shards
Restore caches keyed on the inputs
Run slower integration tests against it
Lint and compile
Build the artefact once

questions.explanation: Cheap checks that fail most often run first, so most broken changes fail within minutes; slower tests run against the one artefact that will ship.

flashcards.back: Time from push to result, and how often a failure is real.
A hash of every input that affects the output, such as the lock file.
Record, quarantine as non-blocking, ticket the owner, fix or delete within a time limit.

sources.title: Martin Fowler: Eradicating Non-Determinism in Tests
Docker Docs: Optimize cache usage in builds

mechanism.title: How fast, trustworthy CI is built
steps: A CI run is valuable only if it arrives quickly and tells the truth. Slow feedback pushes people to batch work and switch tasks while they wait, which makes merges larger and failures harder to trace. False failures teach people to retry until green, and once that habit forms, real failures are retried away too. Track the typical and slowest run times, the share of failures that were real, and how often runs are retried.

Caching removes repeated work. Dependency caches are keyed on a hash of the lock file and the platform, so they are reused until the dependencies change. Build caches store compiled outputs by a hash of their inputs, so only changed modules rebuild. Image builds reuse layers when earlier steps are unchanged, so dependency installation goes before copying source code. A wrong key causes stale results, which is worse than a slow build.

Parallelism cuts wall-clock time. Independent stages run at the same time, and large test suites split into shards across runners. Shards should be balanced using recorded durations, and each shard pays the setup cost, so there is a point where more shards add machine time without saving much. Running only the tests affected by a change, using the build’s dependency graph, helps large repositories, with a full run on a schedule as a safety net.

Ordering matters. Fast, likely-to-fail checks such as formatting, linting, compiling and unit tests run first, so most broken changes fail in minutes. The artefact is built once and the slower integration and end-to-end tests run against it, which keeps what was tested identical to what ships. Expensive suites can run after merge or nightly, as long as failures there are owned and fixed quickly.

Flaky tests are bugs in tests or code. Common causes are timing assumptions, order dependence, shared state between tests, and calls to real external services. CI should record which tests pass only on retry, move them to a non-blocking quarantine with an owner, and limit how long they stay there. Fixing the cause, by controlling time, isolating state or replacing external calls with fakes, is what restores trust.

useWhen: Teams that merge many small changes a day and need answers in minutes.
Large suites where caching and sharding turn hours into minutes.
avoidWhen: Avoid blanket automatic retries that hide flaky tests and real races.
Avoid cache keys that leave out inputs, which produce stale builds.

rows: Stale results from a bad key
Missed tests if the graph is wrong

numbers.title: A pipeline before and after
assumptions: Dependency install takes 4 minutes, 30 s with a warm cache
A 40-minute serial test suite, 8 shards with 2 minutes of setup each
About 5 minutes of lint, compile and build, illustrative
steps: Before: 4 + 40 + 5 = 49 minutes per run.
Tests in shards: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 minutes, plus 2 minutes setup, so about 7 minutes.
After: about 0.5 + 7 + 5 = 12.5 minutes, roughly four times faster.
numbers.result: Caching and sharding cut an illustrative 49-minute run to about 13 minutes, which is the difference between waiting and batching.

india.title: Non-determinism in tests
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Martin Fowler’s article on eradicating non-determinism in tests describes how flaky tests destroy trust in a suite, recommends quarantining them so they do not block the build, and warns that quarantined tests must be fixed quickly. His continuous integration article argues that a fast build, around ten minutes, is part of what makes integrating often practical, and Docker’s documentation explains ordering build steps so cached layers are reused.

pitfalls.trap: “The build is red again, just rerun it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check whether that test is flaky, quarantine it with an owner, and fix the cause.”

pitfalls.trap: “CI takes an hour, so I’ll merge once at the end of the week.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d cache dependencies and shard the tests so each small change gets an answer in minutes.”

takeaways: CI must be fast and trustworthy, or people batch work and ignore red.
Cache by a hash of the inputs; a wrong key gives stale builds.
Shard by recorded durations and run cheap checks first.
Quarantine flaky tests with an owner and a time limit; fix the cause.

interactive.title: Retries for everything
interactive.prompt: To stop random failures, a team configures every test to retry up to 3 times. Months later a race condition is introduced that makes one test fail about 30% of the time.

choices.label: The race reaches production, because a retry usually passes
choices.feedback: Right: with three retries, a 30% failure passes almost every time, so the bug ships.

choices.label: The test fails every run, so the race is caught at once
choices.feedback: A 30% failure is intermittent; retries turn most of those failures into passes.

choices.label: CI marks the change as flaky and blocks the merge for review
choices.feedback: Only if it records passes-after-retry; plain retries just report green.

interactive.reveal: Record every pass-after-retry as flaky, report it, and treat a newly flaky test after a change as a likely real bug.

seeAlso.why: The pipeline stages and build-once rule this lesson speeds up
Image layers and why their order decides cache reuse
Progressive delivery that relies on trustworthy test results
The unit, integration and contract tests a service’s CI pipeline runs
The front-end test mix whose speed and flakiness CI has to manage
Security scans that run in the same pipeline and add to its duration

title: Immutable Infrastructure and Machine Images
objectives: Explain why replacing servers beats patching them in place
Choose what to bake into an image and what to configure at boot
Run an image pipeline that builds, tests, promotes and retires images

cards.title: Replace, do not repair
cards.body: In immutable infrastructure a server is never changed after it starts. To patch, upgrade or reconfigure, you build a new image, launch new servers from it and remove the old ones. Every server from the same image is identical, so what was tested is what runs, and rollback is launching the previous image. The opposite is a long-lived server patched by hand over years, a snowflake that nobody can rebuild exactly.

cards.title: Misconception: immutable means nothing ever varies
cards.body: An immutable image still runs in different places with different settings. What is fixed is the software: the operating system, packages, agents and usually the application. What varies is injected at boot: the environment name, endpoints, feature settings and secrets, fetched from a parameter store or secrets manager using the instance’s identity. Bake the slow, stable parts; inject the small, changing parts.

cards.title: An image pipeline
cards.body: Images are built and promoted like any other artefact.
steps: A schedule or a change triggers an image build from code
The build starts from the latest patched base and installs packages and agents
Scans and tests run against an instance booted from the image
The image gets a version and an ID, and is shared to staging
After staging soaks, the same image ID is promoted to production
Old images are retired after a set age so nothing launches unpatched

cards.title: Worked example: baked vs configured at boot
cards.body: An instance that installs its packages at boot takes 7 minutes to serve traffic; one from a baked image takes 1 minute. During a spike the autoscaler adds 40 instances. Configured at boot, each spends 6 more minutes not serving, so the fleet loses 40 × 6 = 240 instance-minutes of capacity exactly when it is needed. Boot-time installs also depend on package mirrors being up during the incident that caused the spike.

cards.title: Trap: one quick fix over SSH
cards.body: During an incident an engineer logs in to one server and edits a config file. It works, and the change is never written back to code. Weeks later the autoscaler replaces that server, and the bug returns on a server that looks identical to the others. Treat interactive access as read-only in normal operation, turn every fix into a code change and a new image, and alert on manual sessions so drift is noticed.

questions.prompt: A critical OS patch is released. What does an immutable approach do?

choices.label: Runs the package manager on each live server overnight
Patches one server by hand and copies its disk to the rest
Builds a new image with the patch and replaces the servers
Waits for the next major release to include the patch

questions.explanation: Immutable servers are replaced, not modified: a new image is built, tested and rolled out. In-place patching makes servers diverge when some updates fail, copying a hand-patched disk spreads an untested snowflake, and waiting leaves a known hole open.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in the image rather than being fetched at boot?

choices.label: The database password for this environment
The monitoring and log-shipping agents it runs
The name of the environment the server runs in
The endpoint of this region’s message queue

questions.explanation: Agents are slow to install and the same everywhere, so they are baked. Secrets, environment names and regional endpoints differ by deployment and should be injected at boot, and baking a secret into an image leaks it to everyone who can launch it.

questions.prompt: A bug fixed by hand on one server returns weeks later. What most likely happened?

choices.label: The server was replaced from an image that lacked the fix
The fix was rolled back by a scheduled overnight package update
The load balancer started routing to an older version
The config file on disk was corrupted by a reboot

questions.explanation: A manual fix lives only on that disk, so the next replacement from the image brings the bug back. Package updates and reboots do not usually revert a config edit, and the load balancer routes to whatever servers exist rather than to versions.

questions.prompt: Why retire images after a set age, such as 30 days?

choices.label: Old images cost more to store the longer they are kept
Providers delete custom images after a month
Launch templates can only refer to recent images
So nothing launches with months of missing patches

questions.explanation: An old image may still be launched by an autoscaler or a forgotten template, bringing back every patch since it was built. Storage cost does not grow with age, providers keep custom images until you delete them, and templates can refer to any image you keep.

questions.prompt: Instances configured at boot take 7 minutes to serve; baked ones take 1. The autoscaler adds 40 instances during a spike. How many instance-minutes of serving capacity does configuring at boot lose?
assumptions: All 40 launch at the same time
Both kinds serve equally once ready
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 240 instance-minutes is the work of 40 instances for 6 minutes, lost during the spike itself, which is why scale-out paths should use baked images.

questions.prompt: Order the life of a machine image.

items.label: Scan and test an instance booted from it
Promote the same image ID to production
Build from the latest patched base
Retire it once it passes its age limit
Version it and promote it to staging

questions.explanation: Build, test, promote by ID through environments, and retire on a schedule so stale images cannot launch.

flashcards.back: Never changed after launch; to change it, build a new image and replace it.
Bake slow, stable parts (OS, packages, agents, app); inject config and secrets at boot.
So nothing launches with months of missing patches.

sources.title: AWS: What is EC2 Image Builder?
Google Cloud: Image management best practices

mechanism.title: How immutable infrastructure works in practice
steps: Mutable infrastructure keeps servers for years and changes them in place with scripts, configuration management or hand edits. Over time servers drift: a failed update here, a manual fix there, until no two are the same and no one can rebuild one exactly. Immutable infrastructure stops changing running servers and replaces them instead, the same idea as container images applied to whole machines.

Images are built by code from a base image the provider or your security team maintains. A build tool boots a temporary instance, installs packages, agents and often the application, hardens the operating system, and snapshots the result. Builds run on a schedule, such as weekly, to pick up patches, and on demand when a package or the application changes. Every image gets a version and an immutable ID.

What to bake is a trade-off. Baking everything gives the fastest, most predictable boot and no dependency on package mirrors during scale-out, but every change needs a new image. Configuring at boot is flexible but slow and fragile. The usual split is to bake the operating system, packages, agents and the application, and to inject environment-specific settings and secrets at boot from a parameter store or secrets manager, using the instance’s identity.

Images are tested and promoted like any artefact. Scans check for known vulnerabilities and configuration benchmarks, and smoke tests boot an instance and check that services start and health checks pass. The same image ID moves from staging to production, and fleets move to it by rolling replacement, usually through an instance group or autoscaling group refresh with health checks, so a bad image stops after the first batch.

Drift still has to be prevented. Interactive logins should be rare, logged and read-only by default, with every fix turned into code and a new image. Old images are deprecated and deleted after an age limit so autoscalers and templates cannot launch stale software. With this in place, recovering any server, or a whole fleet in a new region, is a launch from a known image rather than an archaeology project.

useWhen: Fleets behind autoscaling, where new instances must be identical and fast to start.
Regulated environments that must show exactly what software runs where.
avoidWhen: Avoid baking secrets or environment-specific settings into images.
Avoid manual fixes on running servers that are never written back to code.

numbers.title: Keeping a fleet patched by replacement
assumptions: 200 instances; a new image every week
steps: Time per refresh: 10 × 6 = 60 minutes.
Weekly images keep every instance at most about 7 days behind on patches, plus the hour of the refresh.
numbers.result: Replacement is routine when each refresh takes about an hour, so the patch gap is set by how often you build images, not by how long patching takes.

india.title: Immutable servers in published guidance
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Martin Fowler’s ImmutableServer article describes servers that are never modified after deployment and are replaced to change them, as a cure for configuration drift. HashiCorp Packer documents building identical machine images for several platforms from one template, and AWS EC2 Image Builder and Google Cloud’s image management guidance describe automated pipelines with testing, versioning, sharing and deprecation of images.

pitfalls.trap: “I’ll just SSH in and fix it on the box.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d put the fix in the image code and roll it out, or the next replacement brings the bug back.”

pitfalls.trap: “Bake everything, including the database password.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d bake the software and fetch secrets at boot with the instance’s identity.”

takeaways: Replace servers to change them; never patch running ones in place.
Bake the OS, packages, agents and app; inject config and secrets at boot.
Build images on a schedule, test them, promote by ID and retire old ones.
Every manual fix becomes code and a new image, or it will be lost.

interactive.title: The forgotten launch template
interactive.prompt: Your pipeline builds a patched image every week. A rarely used batch job’s launch template still points to an image from 14 months ago. Tonight the batch job scales from 0 to 50 instances.

choices.label: 50 instances start with 14 months of missing patches
choices.feedback: Right: nothing forced the template forward, so the old image is launched as is.

choices.label: The provider substitutes the newest image from the same family
choices.feedback: A template that names an image ID launches exactly that image.

choices.label: The launch fails, because images older than a year cannot start
choices.feedback: Old images still launch until someone deprecates or deletes them.

interactive.reveal: Retire images after an age limit, point templates at a family or parameter that tracks the latest promoted image, and alert on launches from stale images.

seeAlso.why: Container images, the same build-once idea for processes
Infrastructure as code that defines the fleets images run in
Rolling replacement and rollback strategies for a new image
Signed, scanned images are the supply-chain side of building infrastructure once

title: Toil, Runbooks and Automation
objectives: Recognise toil and measure how much of a team’s time it takes
Decide which manual tasks to automate first, using frequency and payback
Move a task from runbook to script to self-service to automatic, safely

cards.title: What toil is
cards.body: Google’s SRE book defines toil as operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, without enduring value, and that grows as the service grows. Restarting a stuck job by hand every week, resizing disks on request or copying config between environments are toil. Designing a fix, writing a postmortem or attending a planning meeting are not toil, even if they feel like chores. The test is whether a machine could do it and whether it comes back.

cards.title: Misconception: all operations work is toil
cards.body: Responding to a novel incident needs judgement and teaches the team something, so it is not toil; responding to the same alert for the fiftieth time with the same steps is. Overhead such as meetings and reviews is not toil either. Measuring toil means logging repeatable, automatable tasks and their time. Google’s SRE teams aim to keep toil below 50% of each engineer’s time, so at least half goes into engineering that removes future toil.

cards.title: From runbook to automation
cards.body: Each step removes a human from part of the loop.
steps: A task is done by hand from memory
A runbook writes down the steps and the checks
A script runs the steps, started by a person
Self-service lets the requesting team run it with guardrails
Automation runs it on a trigger, with limits and logging
The underlying cause is fixed so the task is not needed

cards.title: Worked example: is it worth automating?
cards.body: A manual task takes 15 minutes and happens 40 times a month: 15 × 40 = 600 minutes, or 10 hours a month. Automating it takes an estimated 30 hours, so it pays back in 30 ÷ 10 = 3 months, and keeps paying as the service grows. A task done twice a year for 10 minutes would never pay back 30 hours; a good runbook is enough for that one.

cards.title: Trap: automation that hides the problem
cards.body: A service leaks memory, so someone automates a restart whenever memory is high. Pages stop, and the leak grows unnoticed until restarts happen every few minutes and a release makes it worse. Automatic fixes need limits, such as a maximum number of actions an hour, a log of every action and an alert when they run more often than expected. Automate the response, but keep fixing the cause.

questions.prompt: Which of these is toil?

choices.label: Writing the postmortem for a new kind of outage
Rotating the same credentials by hand every month
Designing a migration plan for the main customer database
Reviewing a teammate’s change to an alert rule

questions.explanation: Manual, repetitive, automatable work that returns every month is toil. A postmortem for a new outage produces lasting learning, migration design is engineering, and reviewing changes is valuable overhead rather than toil.

questions.prompt: Which task should a team automate first?

choices.label: A 2-hour task done once a year, during the annual security audit
A 5-minute task done twice a quarter by one person
A 1-hour task done once, during a planned migration
A 20-minute task done 30 times a month, growing with users

questions.explanation: At about 10 hours a month and growing, the frequent task pays back fastest. The yearly task totals 2 hours a year, the twice-a-quarter one under an hour, and a one-off task has nothing to repeat, so a runbook is enough for each.

questions.prompt: What makes a runbook useful at 3 a.m.?

choices.label: A history of how the system was designed and why
Exact steps with checks, linked from the alert itself
A complete list of the metrics and dashboards the service exposes
The names of the engineers who built the service

questions.explanation: Responders need concrete steps, how to verify each one, and to find the runbook from the page. Design history belongs in architecture docs, a full metric list is too much to scan, and names help only if those people are awake and still on the team.

questions.prompt: An auto-remediation restarts a service whenever memory is high. What safeguard matters most?

choices.label: A cap on restarts per hour, with an alert when it is hit
Running it only during working hours
Restarting all instances together so the fix takes less time
Hiding the restarts from dashboards to reduce noise

questions.explanation: A rate limit stops runaway loops, and alerting when it triggers often makes the hidden cause visible. Working-hours-only defeats the purpose, restarting everything at once causes an outage, and hiding actions removes the evidence of a growing problem.

questions.prompt: A 15-minute manual task happens 40 times a month. Automating it takes about 30 hours. After how many months does the automation pay for itself?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: if the service doubles, so does the task count, and the payback halves, which is why toil that grows with the service is the first to automate.

questions.prompt: Order the usual path from manual task to no task.

items.label: Scripted and started by a person
Done by hand from memory
Root cause fixed, so the task disappears
Written down as a runbook with checks
Run automatically on a trigger, with limits

questions.explanation: Each step removes human effort; writing it down first makes the script correct, and fixing the cause is the final goal.

flashcards.back: Manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work with no enduring value that grows with the service.
Below 50% of each engineer’s time.
Build time ÷ hours saved per month.

sources.title: Google SRE book: The Evolution of Automation at Google

mechanism.title: How teams measure and remove toil
steps: Toil is the operational work that scales with the service rather than with the team’s ideas: tasks that are manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical and leave nothing lasting behind. A little is unavoidable, but too much crowds out engineering, makes on-call miserable and causes mistakes, because people doing the same steps by hand eventually skip one. Google’s SRE teams set a goal of keeping toil below 50% of each engineer’s time.

Measuring comes first. Teams log interrupts, tickets and on-call tasks for a few weeks, tagging each as toil or not, with its duration and frequency. The totals show where time goes and which few tasks make up most of it. Trends matter more than a single number: toil that grows with traffic or customers will take the whole team eventually unless removed.

Prioritise by payback and risk. Time saved per month is the task duration times its frequency; payback is the build time divided by that. Tasks that are frequent, growing, error-prone or done under pressure at night go first. Rare tasks may only need a clear runbook. Include upkeep: a script nobody maintains becomes the next source of incidents.

Automation is a ladder. A runbook captures the steps and checks, which also documents what a script must do. A script turns the runbook into one command. Self-service lets the team that needs the task run it, with guardrails, instead of filing a ticket. Full automation triggers on events, with rate limits, logging and an alert when it acts more than expected. The top rung is removing the need altogether by fixing the cause.

Automation changes failure modes. Automatic actions can amplify a mistake across a whole fleet in seconds, so they need limits on scope and rate, a dry-run mode, and a clear way to stop them. They also hide symptoms, so their activity must be visible. Reviewing automation actions alongside pages keeps the team aware of what the system is doing on its behalf.

useWhen: Teams whose time goes to repeated tickets, manual deploys or the same pages each week.
Services that are growing, where manual work grows with them.
avoidWhen: Avoid automating a rare task where a runbook would do.
Avoid auto-remediation without rate limits, logging and an alert on repeated use.

numbers.title: Finding the toil worth removing
assumptions: A team of 6 logs its work for a month
Each person works about 160 hours, illustrative
steps: Team hours: 6 × 160 = 960 hours.
Toil share: 400 ÷ 960 ≈ 42%, under the 50% cap but close to it.
If the top three tasks are 250 of those hours, automating them alone brings toil to about 150 ÷ 960 ≈ 16%.
numbers.result: A month of logging shows that a few repeated tasks make up most of the toil, so automating three of them frees about a quarter of the team’s time.

india.title: Toil in Google’s SRE books
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Google’s SRE book defines toil as work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly as a service grows. It describes an advertised goal of keeping toil below 50% of each SRE’s time. The SRE workbook gives practical steps to measure, prioritise and eliminate toil, and its automation chapter describes moving from manual work to fully automatic systems.

pitfalls.trap: “Ops work is all toil, so let’s automate everything.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d log the repeated tasks, then automate the frequent ones with the best payback.”

pitfalls.trap: “Pages stopped since we auto-restart it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d cap the restarts, alert when they rise, and fix the leak behind them.”

takeaways: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that grows with the service.
Measure it, and keep it below about half of the team’s time.
Automate by payback: build time ÷ hours saved per month.
Climb from runbook to script to self-service to automation, with limits.

interactive.title: The helpful restart
interactive.prompt: An automation restarts any instance whose memory passes 90%, with no limit and no alert. It runs about twice a day at first. A new release doubles the leak rate.

choices.label: Restarts become frequent and capacity drops, unnoticed until users see errors
choices.feedback: Right: restarts hide the leak, so the first visible signal is user impact.

choices.label: The automation pages on-call once restarts become frequent
choices.feedback: It was built with no alert, so nothing tells anyone it is busy.

choices.label: Memory stops leaking, because restarts reclaim it each time
choices.feedback: Restarts free the memory but leave the leak in the code, so it grows back.

interactive.reveal: Give remediations a rate limit, alert when it is reached, and keep a ticket open for the cause.

seeAlso.why: Incidents and postmortems that reveal repeated manual work
Alert reviews that find pages worth automating
Infrastructure as code, which removes many manual changes

title: Alerting and Healthy On-Call
objectives: Write alerts on user-facing symptoms that a person must act on now
Route each signal to a page, a ticket or a dashboard by urgency
Keep on-call load sustainable with alert reviews, rotations and handoffs

cards.title: Every page should need a human, now
cards.body: A page interrupts sleep and focus, so it must be urgent, actionable and about something users feel. Alert on symptoms such as errors, latency and failed jobs, measured against the SLO, rather than on causes such as high CPU on one host, which may or may not matter. Causes belong on dashboards to help diagnose a symptom once it pages. If the right response to an alert is to wait and see, it should not page.

cards.title: Page, ticket or dashboard
cards.body: Urgency decides where a signal goes. A page is for user impact now or within the hour. A ticket is for problems that need a person within days, such as a disk that will fill in two weeks or a certificate that expires next month. A dashboard or log is for information that helps diagnose but needs no action. Many noisy setups page on what should be tickets, and train people to ignore pages.

cards.title: Reviewing an alert
cards.body: Each page earns its place or is changed.
steps: A page fires and on-call responds
The response is logged: real impact, action taken, or no action
A weekly review looks at every page from the rotation
Pages with no action are removed, retuned or downgraded to tickets
Repeated causes get a fix or automation
Alert count and pages per shift are tracked over time

cards.title: Worked example: sizing a rotation
cards.body: Google’s SRE book caps on-call at 25% of an engineer’s time. A rotation that always has a primary and a secondary, in week-long shifts, has 2 people on call at any moment. To keep each person at 25%, you need 2 ÷ 0.25 = 8 engineers, so each one is on call one week in four. A team of 4 can cover the same rota only at 50% each, which leaves little time to fix what pages them.

cards.title: Trap: adding an alert after every incident
cards.body: After each incident someone adds an alert for its exact cause. A year later there are hundreds, most for causes that never recur, many firing together for one problem. Prefer one symptom alert that would have caught the incident, group related alerts into one notification, and delete alerts that have not led to action in months. The SRE book suggests no more than about two incidents per 12-hour shift, so there is time to handle each one properly.

questions.prompt: Which alert is best suited to paging someone at 3 a.m.?

choices.label: CPU on one web server has been above 90% for 10 minutes
A database replica is two seconds behind its primary
Checkout errors are burning the monthly budget fast
Disk use on the log volume reached 75% today

questions.explanation: Checkout errors are a user-facing symptom tied to the SLO, so someone must act. High CPU on one host may cause no user impact, two seconds of replica lag is often within normal bounds, and a disk at 75% is a ticket for working hours.

questions.prompt: A TLS certificate expires in 21 days and renewal is manual. How should this be signalled?

choices.label: A page now, so nobody can forget about it
A ticket to the owning team, paging only if it is days away
A dashboard panel showing the days left until the certificate expires
No signal, since renewal will happen before it expires

questions.explanation: Three weeks out it needs a person within days, which is a ticket, with a page as a last-resort backstop. A page now interrupts someone for something that can wait, a dashboard needs someone to look, and assuming renewal will happen is how certificates expire.

questions.prompt: A review shows most pages last month needed no action. What should change?

choices.label: Retune, downgrade to tickets or delete those alerts
Add a second on-call person to share the extra pages
Raise the paging threshold on all of the alerts by 20%
Mute the alerting system outside business hours

questions.explanation: Each non-actionable page should be fixed individually, which is what the review is for. A second person shares the noise rather than removing it, a blanket threshold change also delays real alerts, and muting at night stops all pages, including real ones.

questions.prompt: A database failure triggers 120 alerts in two minutes, all paging the same engineer. What helps most?

choices.label: Raising the paging rate limit so none of them are dropped
Paging a different engineer for each group of alerts
Turning those alerts off until the database is stable
Grouping related alerts so the incident sends one page

questions.explanation: Grouping and dependency-aware suppression turn one cause into one page with the details attached. More pages, or more engineers paged, add noise to the same incident, and turning alerts off removes the signal you need to see it recover.

questions.prompt: A rotation always has a primary and a secondary on call, in week-long shifts. With on-call capped at 25% of each person’s time, how many engineers does the rotation need?
assumptions: Both roles count as on-call time
questions.explanation: Sanity check: with 8, each person is on call one week in four, which matches the 25% cap; forgetting the secondary gives 4, which doubles everyone’s load.

questions.prompt: A batch export that users read each morning sometimes fails overnight; a rerun takes 20 minutes.
constraints: Users read the export from 8 a.m.
Failures happen about twice a month
The team wants fewer night pages

approaches.label: Page on-call the moment any export run fails
Retry it automatically, and page only if it is still failing close to its deadline
Open a ticket for the morning and let users wait

rationaleOptions.label: An automatic retry fixes many transient failures with no human
Paging at once is needed because every failure is urgent
Paging near the deadline still protects the 8 a.m. readers
A ticket is enough because users can wait for the export

rationaleConflicts.r3: A failure at 1 a.m. with a 20-minute rerun is not urgent until the deadline is close.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Users rely on it at 8 a.m., so a morning ticket means they start the day without it.

questions.explanation: Page on the user-facing deadline, not on the first failure: automate the retry and wake someone only when the symptom is about to reach users.

flashcards.back: Urgent, actionable, user-facing symptoms, usually tied to the SLO.
Page for impact now; ticket for things that need a person within days.
At most about 25% of time on call and about two incidents per 12-hour shift.

sources.title: Google SRE book: Monitoring Distributed Systems
Google SRE workbook: Alerting on SLOs

mechanism.title: How alerting and on-call stay sustainable
steps: Good alerting starts from what users experience. Symptom alerts fire when a user-facing signal, such as error rate, latency, freshness or throughput, threatens the SLO. Cause-based signals, such as CPU, memory, queue depth or replica lag, are kept for diagnosis on dashboards, because the same cause can be harmless one day and critical the next. Alerts on the SLO with burn-rate windows give pages that are both early and rare.

Each signal gets a destination by urgency. Pages are for impact now or imminent. Tickets go to a queue that the team works through in normal hours, for slow trends and upcoming expiries. Dashboards and logs hold everything else. The same condition can have both: a ticket when a disk will be full in two weeks, and a page if it will be full in two hours.

Alerts decay unless they are reviewed. Each page is logged with what was done; a regular review removes or changes pages that needed no action, merges duplicates, and turns repeated manual fixes into automation. Grouping and inhibition send one notification per incident rather than one per failing component. Every alert has an owner and a linked runbook that says what to check first.

On-call load is a capacity question. Google’s SRE book suggests no more than 25% of an engineer’s time on call, and no more than about two incidents per 12-hour shift, so each one can be handled, followed up and written up. With a primary and a secondary, that means about 8 people for a single-site rotation of week-long shifts, or two sites splitting the day so nobody is paged at night.

People need support as well as tools. Clear escalation paths, a secondary who can take over, handoff notes at the end of each shift, compensation or time off after a hard night, and blameless postmortems keep on-call humane. Tracking pages per shift, night-time pages and time to acknowledge shows whether load is going up, and is the evidence for fixing noisy alerts or adding people.

useWhen: Services with an SLO and a rotation that should be paged only for real user impact.
Teams whose on-call has become noisy and needs a review process.
avoidWhen: Avoid paging on causes such as CPU or memory that may not affect users.
Avoid adding a new page for the exact cause of every past incident.

rows: User impact now or within the hour

numbers.title: Cutting pages after a review
assumptions: A rotation gets 30 pages a week
The review finds 18 needed no action
Week-long shifts with one primary, illustrative
steps: Actionable pages: 30 − 18 = 12 a week.
Per day: 12 ÷ 7 ≈ 1.7 pages, against roughly 4.3 before.
Fixing the 18 removes 60% of interruptions without losing a real signal.
numbers.result: One review that removes non-actionable pages cuts an illustrative rotation’s load by more than half and brings it under two pages a day.

india.title: On-call guidance from Google’s SRE books
india.label: Publicly reported
india.body: Google’s SRE book recommends alerting on symptoms rather than causes and keeping pages actionable. Its Being On-Call chapter describes keeping on-call to at most 25% of SRE time, a maximum of about two incidents per 12-hour shift, and a minimum of eight engineers for a single-site rotation with a primary and secondary on week-long shifts. The SRE workbook adds practical guidance on reducing pager load.

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s page on CPU over 90% so we catch problems early.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d page on the user-facing symptom and keep CPU on the dashboard for diagnosis.”

pitfalls.trap: “We had an outage, so let’s add an alert for that exact cause.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check whether a symptom alert would have caught it, and only add one if not.”

takeaways: Page only for urgent, actionable, user-facing symptoms.
Route by urgency: page now, ticket within days, dashboard for context.
Review every page; remove, retune or downgrade the ones with no action.
Cap on-call near 25% of time and about two incidents per shift.

interactive.title: The alert for everything
interactive.prompt: A service has 400 alerts, most added after past incidents. On-call gets about 50 pages a week, and engineers have started to acknowledge pages without looking.

choices.label: A real outage is acknowledged and missed among the noise
choices.feedback: Right: alert fatigue makes every page look like the usual noise, including the real one.

choices.label: Coverage is complete, so the next outage is caught at once
choices.feedback: More alerts do not help if nobody reads them; coverage on paper is not attention.

choices.label: The paging system starts dropping pages above its rate limit
choices.feedback: Paging tools handle this volume; the failure is human attention, not the system.

interactive.reveal: Cut pages to actionable symptoms, review them weekly, and track pages per shift so the noise cannot creep back.

seeAlso.why: SLOs and burn rates that symptom alerts are built on
Incident response that starts when a page fires
Turning repeated alert fixes into automation and runbooks
Real user monitoring supplies the user-facing signals worth alerting on

title: Dates, Time Zones and Daylight Saving in Business Logic
objectives: Store past instants in UTC and keep the IANA zone for anything tied to a person’s or a place’s calendar
Schedule future local events from a local time plus zone, not a precomputed UTC instant
Handle daylight-saving gaps and overlaps, and compute “today” in the zone that defines it

cards.title: Instants, local times and zones
cards.body: An instant is one point on the timeline, such as when a payment was captured; store it in UTC, for example in PostgreSQL’s timestamptz, which normalises to UTC. A local date and time like “09:00 on 3 March” is not an instant until you add a zone. A zone is an IANA identifier such as Asia/Kolkata or America/New_York, not an offset like +05:30: offsets change with daylight saving and with law, while the identifier carries the rules. India uses +05:30 all year; New York switches between −05:00 and −04:00.

cards.title: Worked example: a 9 a.m. reminder across a clock change
cards.body: A user in New York sets a daily 09:00 reminder in January, and the service stores it as 14:00 UTC. That works until 8 March 2026, when New York moves to UTC−4: 14:00 UTC is now 10:00 local, an hour late, every day until November. Store the rule instead, 09:00 with zone America/New_York, and compute each run’s UTC instant from it: 14:00 UTC in winter, 13:00 UTC in summer.

cards.title: Scheduling the next run of a local-time job
cards.body: The stored rule stays in local time; only the next run becomes a UTC instant.
steps: Stored: 09:00 every day, zone America/New_York
Take the next local date: 9 March 2026
Ask the time-zone database for that date’s offset: UTC−4 after the 8 March change
09:00 local becomes 13:00 UTC; enqueue the job for that instant
After it runs, repeat from the next local date, never by adding 24 hours

cards.title: Gaps and overlaps
cards.body: On a spring-forward day, US clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00, so 02:30 does not exist. On the autumn day, clocks go back from 02:00 to 01:00, so 01:30 happens twice. Libraries resolve both with a policy: for a gap, usually move forward; for an overlap, pick the earlier or later offset. Choose on purpose: a nightly job at 02:30 should still run once on the gap day, and one at 01:30 should run once, not twice, on the overlap day. Those days are also 23 and 25 hours long, so “add one day” and “add 24 hours” give different answers.

cards.title: Trap: “today” in the server’s zone
cards.body: A daily spending limit resets at midnight. If the code takes the date from the server clock in UTC, an Indian user’s day starts at 05:30 IST, so a purchase at 03:00 IST on 5 March counts towards 4 March. Compute business dates in the zone that defines them, whether the user’s, the merchant’s or the one a contract names, and store that zone with the record. Run servers in UTC and never let a result depend on the host’s zone setting.

questions.prompt: A payment was captured. What should the database store for when it happened?

choices.label: The local time in the user’s zone, no zone kept
The UTC instant, in a zone-aware timestamp type
The server’s local time, without any zone
Only the calendar date, as YYYY-MM-DD

questions.explanation: a: without the zone, nobody can tell later which instant it was, or order it against other events. b: correct, a past event is a fixed instant, and UTC in a zone-aware type compares and sorts correctly everywhere. c: the server’s zone can change with a migration, and the value carries no record of it. d: a date alone loses the order of events and the time needed for disputes.

questions.prompt: A user in New York picks their time zone in settings. What should the service save?

choices.label: −05:00, the offset on the day they signed up
EST, the abbreviation shown in the app
America/New_York, the IANA zone name
The hours between their zone and the server’s

questions.explanation: a: New York is −04:00 for most of the year, so a fixed offset is wrong for months at a time. b: abbreviations are ambiguous (CST is used for US Central, China and Cuba) and carry no daylight-saving rules. c: correct, the identifier carries the rules, past and future, through the time-zone database. d: it ties the user’s data to wherever the server happens to run.

questions.prompt: A 09:00 weekly meeting for a London team was saved in January as 09:00 UTC. What happens after UK clocks go forward on 29 March 2026?

choices.label: It starts at 10:00 local, an hour late
It starts at 08:00 local, an hour early
It stays at 09:00, as UTC adjusts itself
It is skipped on the day of the change

questions.explanation: a: correct, in summer London is UTC+1, so 09:00 UTC is 10:00 local. b: that would need London to move behind UTC, which it never does. c: UTC never changes; that is why a fixed UTC instant drifts against local time. d: an instant set in UTC always exists; only local times can be skipped.

questions.prompt: A job runs at 02:30 New York time every night. What happens on 8 March 2026, when clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00?

choices.label: The time does not exist; a policy must move it
It runs twice, once at each 02:30
It runs at 02:30 UTC that night instead
Nothing: every local time exists every day

questions.explanation: a: correct, 02:00 to 02:59 is skipped that night, so the library or your code must choose, usually 03:00. b: repeated times happen on the autumn change, not the spring one. c: nothing converts a local schedule to UTC on its own. d: on spring-forward days an hour of local time is missing.

questions.prompt: An app on UTC servers resets each user’s daily limit at server midnight. When does the limit reset for users in India?

choices.label: At 00:00 IST
At 05:30 IST
At 18:30 IST
At 23:30 IST

questions.explanation: a: that would need the reset computed in Asia/Kolkata, not in UTC. b: correct, India is UTC+05:30, so midnight UTC is 05:30 IST. c: that subtracts the offset instead of adding it; 18:30 IST is 13:00 UTC. d: no offset between UTC and IST gives this.

questions.prompt: Order how a service computes the next run of “09:00 daily, America/New_York”.

items.label: Convert 09:00 on that date to a UTC instant
Pick the next local calendar date
Enqueue the job at that instant
Read the stored local time and zone
Look up that date’s UTC offset in the time-zone database

questions.explanation: The rule stays local; the offset is looked up for the specific date, so the conversion is right on both sides of a clock change.

questions.prompt: New York’s clocks go back from 02:00 to 01:00 on 1 November 2026. How many hours long is that local day, midnight to midnight?
assumptions: Local midnight to the next local midnight
One hour of local time repeats
questions.workedAnswer: 24 hours of clock time + the repeated hour from 01:00 to 02:00 = 25 hours
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the spring-forward day is 23 hours, so a job that adds 24 hours to its last run drifts an hour at each change.

flashcards.back: An instant is one point on the timeline, stored in UTC; a local time needs a zone to become one.

flashcards.front: Store an offset or a zone?
flashcards.back: The IANA zone, such as Asia/Kolkata; offsets change with daylight saving and with law.
Store 09:00 plus the zone and compute each UTC instant when it is needed.

sources.title: RFC 3339: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

mechanism.title: How a service handles time from request to schedule
steps: At the API edge, timestamps arrive as RFC 3339 strings with an offset, such as 2026-03-05T09:00:00+05:30, and become instants. A string with no offset is either rejected or read in a zone the API documents, never silently in the server’s. Responses send instants in UTC or with an explicit offset.

Instants are stored in UTC in a zone-aware type, and servers run with UTC as their zone, so nothing depends on where a container happens to start. Durations, such as a token valid for 3,600 seconds or a timeout, are arithmetic on instants and need no zone.

Anything defined by a person’s or a place’s calendar is stored as a local date or time plus an IANA zone: a recurring reminder, a shop’s opening hours, a billing period that ends at local midnight, a flight’s departure.
